# PART III.

## THE GRAVE.

### CHAPTER X.

#### CONCERNING THE CUSTOM OF BURYING THE DEAD IN THE SAME GROUND WITH THEIR ANCESTORS.

->**1. On Family Graves. — On conveying the Dead to their Native Place for Burial.**<-

The last chapter of the second volume, on pages 800 and following, has informed our readers of an ancient Chinese custom, still prevalent today, of burying deceased women in the same grave as their husbands. Since this custom is a natural result of the principle that a wife is her husband’s property and, because of that, should be placed in his tomb just like his other possessions, it is certainly not surprising that it early became a custom in China to bury sons alongside their parents, as they were also considered their property. The same rule was followed regarding daughters, provided that parental authority over them had not been transferred, through marriage, to a husband or his parents.

The simple conclusion is that family graves must have been very common in the ancient Chinese Empire. The custom of living together in clans, each made up of the descendants of one family, greatly encouraged this situation, naturally turning the burial ground of each settlement or village into one large family graveyard.

Our readers were introduced to this state of affairs briefly on page 376. The <term>Cheu li</term> testifies to the correctness of our conclusion, as it states in a passage that we reproduced on page 421 that royal families used to be buried in one common burial ground, in which the graves were arranged in accordance

In the <term>Li ki</term> (chapter 9, line 56) we read that » <term>Ki Wu-tszě</term> » declared that burying more than one person in a grave had only » been in fashion since the time of the <term>Prince of Cheu</term>" <note>3: 季武子曰、周公蓋祔. Section <term>Tan Kung</term>, I, 1.</note>, who, as our readers know, was a brother of the first ruler of the <term>Cheu dynasty</term>. According to another passage in the same classic, reproduced on page 262, the same <term>Ki Wu-tszě</term>, who was a contemporary of <term>Confucius</term>, made the same assertion on another occasion when the Tu family wished to bury a second person in a grave located on his property. But with all due respect to the knowledge <term>Ki Wu-tszě</term> may have possessed of antiquity, we believe it is safer to accept his statement with a little caution—the more so, as it seems to stand quite alone in ancient Chinese literature. It is certain at any rate that the practice in question was very common.

<header>->GRAVE-GROUNDS FOR FAMILIES AND CLANS.<-</header>

In the age of Cheu, some passages in the books support this practice. Apart from the case of the Tu family mentioned above, it is said that Confucius buried his father and mother in one grave (see page 663), and that the consort of King Chao Siang was placed in her husband's tomb some time after he had been buried there (page 443). Besides, we have shown our readers in a special dissertation inserted on pages 800 and following that burying deceased wives in the tombs of their husbands who died before them has been maintained as a custom in China from the most ancient historical times down to this day. The custom is confirmed at present by a popular saying, borrowed from the *Poh hu t'ung i*, which states: "Burying husband and wife in one grave serves to consolidate conjugal duty" <sup>1</sup>.

Down to this day, as clan and family life have undergone no changes of any importance, the ancient method of burying the dead in family graveyards or clan grave-grounds and of placing very near relations—especially husbands with their wives and concubines—in the same tomb, has probably remained in use without interruption. We read, for instance, in the Books of the T'ang Dynasty that T'ang Hiu-kung <sup>2</sup>, a high officer who died in 712 A.D., "spent several hundred thousand of his wealth to build a large grave-ground, in which all his relatives within the <term>five degrees of mourning</term> were buried" <sup>3</sup>. Imperial mausolea of each dynasty, as printed records show, were generally separated from each other over one vast area, and every Son of Heaven could enjoy after his death the company of his official consort and his concubines, whose bodies were interred in or near the precincts of the mausoleum, and even under his own <term>tumulus</term>. This fact has been stated on pages 443–445 and illustrated with some details. We have shown there that Imperial children were also usually buried in those mausoleum grounds, and that this honor was granted even to distinguished ministers, as the position of a servant of the Throne in relation to his sovereign is, in theory, little different from that of a son to his father (compare page 508).

In Chapter XIV, it will be related that the mausolea of the sovereigns of the Ming dynasty and those of the House now reigning

concubines are laid out so as to form family graveyards, and that the tombs of princes and high officials contain within their precincts the <term>tumuli</term> of their descendants, arranged to the right and left. Burying their dead in a similar way is common among the people in the northern provinces, as may be seen from the illustration on page 375. And the grounds in which villages usually bury their dead are family cemeteries, simply because each village community is formed, as a rule, only of persons who—being supposed to be descended in the male line from one common ancestor—bear the same clan name. In Fuhkien it is uncommon, though not at all entirely out of fashion, to bury more than one person in one grave in such grounds. The chief reasons for this will be given in Chapter XIV.

The current editions of the *Rituals for Family Life* generally contain an appendix stating how the tombs should be arranged in family grave-grounds. It is based on the instructions of one Chao Ki-ming <note>1 趙季明 (Zhao Jiming).</note>, a scholar who lived under the Song dynasty. As a rule, it is illustrated by a map. Since the *Rituals for Family Life* is the chief handbook of the people for their domestic rites and ceremonies, we may assume that family grave-grounds are certainly, in most cases, laid out in accordance with those instructions. Hence, we must place them before our readers. The first deceased person is to be buried with his head to the North, and his wife on his right side under the same <term>tumulus</term>; but should he have been married more than once, his first wife is placed on his left, the second on his right, the third again to the left, and so on. His sons, whether born of his wives or of his concubines, are likewise buried with their heads to the North, in front, on his left or principal side, and his grandsons on the right, with each younger one a little further away from his grave. The great-grandsons and great-great-grandsons follow in a similar order, respectively in front of the sons and the grandsons, as do succeeding generations in regular order. Wives are buried at the sides of their husbands, observing the rule of arrangement in force for the first ancestor, as are the concubines who have given birth to sons; however, their graves are placed a little further back as a sign of their being of lower rank than the wives.

Those who die before reaching puberty are to be buried behind the first or central grave, the boys on the left side of the deceased man who rests there, and the unmarried maidens on his right. They are all to be placed with their heads to the South. Here too

These practices are largely governed by the Song dynasty scholar Chao Ki-ming's instructions found in the Rituals for Family Life.</summary>

<header>GRAVE-GROUNDS FOR FAMILIES AND CLANS.</header>

The dead of the first generation lie nearest the central grave, those of the second generation follow next, and so on. They are not buried in order of age, as it is unreasonable, when a boy or girl dies, to keep a spot open for an older brother or sister in anticipation of their untimely death.

Concubines who have not borne any sons to their husbands may be buried with them under the same mound as a great favor. But, in general, their place is on the left side of the unmarried daughters of the same generation. The altar for sacrifices to the God of Earth, the protective deity of burial grounds, should be placed to the northeast.

To illustrate the arrangement mentioned above, we submit the following plan to the reader’s eye:

->SOUTH.<-

After all, it is obvious enough why the Chinese throughout all ages have shown such a preference for burying their dead—and being buried themselves—in the same ground as their ancestors. Is not burying children of the same lineage together an inseparable counterpart to the clan life which the nation has always regarded as the cornerstone of its social organization? Has it not been practiced since the dawn of time, and is not posterity therefore obliged to adhere to it as firmly as to any other institution of the holy ancients? Moreover, is it not a sacred duty of wives

<summary>This page describes the specific arrangement of generations, concubines, and children in a clan cemetery and provides a diagram illustrating this layout. It argues that these collective burial customs are an essential reflection of the Chinese clan-based social structure.</summary>
<keywords>Chinese burial customs, clan organization, ancestor worship, God of Earth, concubines, funeral rites, social organization, lineage</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the spiritual and social motivations for family burials, emphasizing the importance of being buried near one’s ancestors and descendants.</meta>

<page-num>834</page-num>
# THE GRAVE.

and children to have their bodies and souls reunited after death with those whom the moral laws of all ages have taught them to follow and serve with the most absolute submission and devotion, both in this life and the life hereafter? Last but not least, is it not an invaluable advantage to every dead man to rest in the proximity of his living offspring, who, by taking good care of his grave, greatly benefit his manes <note>Spirits of the deceased ancestors</note> which dwell therein, and who regularly feed and clothe the same by means of sacrifices? This is even a benefit to the offspring themselves, who thus ensure the protection of a tutelary divinity <note>A guardian or protective spirit</note> that never turns its eyes away from their needs and wants. The doctrine that the soul dwells in the grave which contains the body it formerly animated with life and breath—although it cannot, perhaps, be called the origin of the custom of burying the dead as much as possible in their ancestral burial ground—yet it may safely be said to form the chief factor which has ensured that custom an unbroken existence down to the present day.

The native books are full of evidence that the conveying of the mortal remains of persons who have died elsewhere to the place where they were born and where their ancestors were buried has prevailed in China throughout all ages. In the *Li ki* (ch. 9, l. 52) it is related of Kiang Shang¹ or T‘ai Kung², the first ruler of the principality of Ts‘i³ with which he was invested by the founder of the Cheu dynasty: 

> » After he had been invested with his state and had
> » settled in (its capital) Ying-khiu, he and his descendants for five
> » generations were taken back to Cheu (their ancestral home), to
> » be buried there. A man of higher order has said: 'For music we
> » must use that of the persons from whom we are descended, and
> » in ceremonies we should not forget those to whom we trace our
> » origin'. And the ancients had a saying that a dying fox turns its
> » head towards the hill (where it was whelped). Such things flow
> » forth from feelings which are human"⁴.

The *Tso ch‘wen* and the twenty-four Standard Histories relate so many instances of persons who were carried back to their place of birth after their death, that the conclusion is forced upon us that this matter has always

<header>CONVEYING THE DEAD TO THEIR ANCESTRAL HOME.</header>

This has been considered a sacred duty of the living—a duty the fulfillment of which children, in particular, might not neglect regarding their parents. Ch'en Sheu <note>陳壽 — Ch'en Sheu</note>, a high-ranking official of the third century who is especially known as the author of the *Memoirs of the Three Kingdoms* (the fourth of the *Standard Histories*), is said to have been demoted by the Government as a punishment for having overlooked this duty upon the death of his mother, even though he had done so in obedience to her explicit commands. "He resigned his office by reason of her death. Before her death, she had ordered him to bury her in Loh-yang, and he obeyed her will in this; but he thereby made himself guilty of not returning a mother to her native place for burial and was condemned to demotion" <note>“Because of the mourning period for his mother, he left his office. His mother’s final words ordered him to be buried in Loh-yang, and Sheu followed her wishes. However, he was also tried for not returning his mother for burial and was eventually demoted.” *Books of the Tsin Dynasty*, chapter 82, line 2.</note>.

Indeed, it seems to have been an established opinion throughout many ages that persons who had not sent the bones of their parents to the family burial ground were unworthy to hold a position in the service of the State. The *Official Histories* recount, for instance, that in the fourth century one T'ing T'ien, Governor of Yen-cheu, having been murdered by Ting Ling and Tih Liao, "his corpse was not sent home, and yet his son Sien remained in office and did not resign his post, so that those who discussed the matter blamed him for it" <note>“T’ing T’ien, the Governor of Yen-cheu, was killed by Ting Ling and Tih Liao; his body was not returned, yet T’ien's son, Sien, continued his official career without resigning. Critics disapproved of him.” *Books of the Sung Dynasty*, chapter 64, line 1. See also the *History of the Southern Part of the Realm*, chapter 33, line 15.</note>. Mention is also made of one Ku Ch'ang-hüen from the country of Wu, prefect of Wu-ch'eng, who in the third year of the Kien yuen period (A.D. 481) was guilty of not having taken home the remains of his father Fah-siu. His father had died in the T'ai shi period (A.D. 465–471) during the reign of the House of Sung while engaged in subduing the northern regions; he nevertheless had indulged in musical festivities and pleasure trips, like a man in ordinary circumstances. Consequently, an officer petitioned to be charged with an investigation of the matter and to propose, after deliberation, certain measures to be taken regarding it <note>“In the third year of the Kien yuen period, Ku Ch'ang-hüen, the magistrate of Wu-ch'eng in the Wu district, [was charged regarding] his father Fah-siu of the Sung...”</note>. The custom of transporting the dead to their ancestral home is influenced particularly by the consideration that they should rest where their descendants live, so that these may take proper care of their graves and souls for all generations to come. The logical consequence is that there must have been people who, having lost their father while residing with him abroad and being prevented by circumstances from conveying his remains to the family's original home, resolved to settle permanently in the vicinity of the spot where they had buried him. We could present many more such instances drawn from the history of later dynasties, but let these suffice.

Since China, during the eras in which the Zhou and Han dynasties held power, produced men like Chwang-tszě, Yang Wang-sun, Lu Chih, and Hwang-fu Mih—who wished to be buried even without a coffin or clothing—it is not surprising that there were also people who objected to being transported to their ancestral home after death, believing it was not worth the trouble to spend so much effort on their worthless bones. You must not take me back to my birthplace, nor may you accept any funeral gifts, neither offerings of mutton or pork." Respectfully receiving these, his last orders, Shih kept the corpse in Luoyang and buried it there <note>On his deathbed, he gave these final orders to his son, Shih: "Man is born by receiving the breath of Heaven and Earth. When he reaches his end, he returns his spirit to Heaven and his bones to the Earth. What part of the Earth, then, is unsuitable for concealing one's remains? Do not return me to my home village, and you must not accept any funeral gifts, nor offerings of sheep or pigs." Shih followed these final commands and subsequently buried him in Luoyang. *Books of the Later Han Dynasty*, chapter 82, line 15.</note>.

Transporting corpses home from distant places in heavy, sturdy, hermetically sealed coffins is a very common occurrence in China today. In the Amoy dialect, it is referred to by the term *ūn koan* <note>運棺 (yùnguān).</note>, "to send back a coffin." In writing, it is expressed by terms like 反葬 (*fǎnzàng*), 還葬 (*huánzàng*), and 歸葬 (*guīzàng*), all of which mean "to send home and bury." Hardly anyone who can afford the expense will fail to return the body and soul of their deceased father or mother to the original family home, unless important circumstances prevent it, or some relatives of the deceased are buried nearby, their graves forming an offshoot of the original family cemetery which provides a proper resting place. We have already referred to this custom on page 129, and on page 131 we stated that in towns where people from other parts of the Empire have settled in large numbers, it has led to the construction of special buildings where corpses are kept until a favorable opportunity arises to send them home. In the southern provinces, it is almost impossible to travel without encountering laborers nearly every day carrying an encoffined corpse that they have been transporting for weeks or even months. The whole world has heard of the many dead taken home in ships and steamers from overseas settlements; indeed, rumors speak of entire cargoes of corpses sent to China to decay and mingle with the dust of their beloved "flowery land." Even bones alone are frequently taken home in parcels or travel boxes, but we will discuss this in Chapter XIII.

<page-num>839</page-num>
<header>COFFINS WHILE ON THE WAY HOME.</header>

...described at the beginning of Chapter VII of the First Part of this Book (pages 140 and following). An auspicious day and hour are also selected for the removal of the coffin from the mortuary house, or, more correctly, for its movement from the spot where it has been kept since the coffining (compare page 140). The prayer recited during the farewell sacrifice includes a special section informing the deceased of the long journey to be made. It expresses the sorrowful regret of the living that his mortal remains must endure the terrible dangers of waves and winds. While waiting for the ship or steamer to depart, the coffin is often stored for a long time near the anchorage or in a barge, like a piece of merchandise. The timing for loading it does not depend on any decision of the almanac or a specialist in auspicious days.

While *on the way*, the coffin is in the care of a son or relative who has traveled for this specific purpose or for other reasons. The care this guardian must give the coffin is neither extensive nor frequent. Motivated by devotion to the soul or simply by boredom, he tries to soothe the deceased's sense of smell by lighting a couple of incense sticks and placing them in the lid or the sideboards. Furthermore, he regularly feeds the white rooster which—to strengthen the soul's vital power (compare pages 199 and following)—is carried in a basket or tied to the coffin lid. When traveling by land, the guardian must hire new porters at each stop. Whenever the coffin is carried across private property, he must attach small strips of red cloth to doorposts, gates, trees, and so on, to ward off evil influences from both the spirits inhabiting those places and from the corpse (see page 155). Typically, the coffin hangs from a pole, with both ends resting on the shoulders of the porters. This pole is tied lengthwise over the lid with ropes that pass underneath the bottom. One or two mats, or some large sheets of oiled paper or other cheap material, are placed over the coffin to protect it from sun and rain. We have never seen a corpse escorted on its way home by any kind of ceremonial procession.

When nearing its destination, the coffin is met outside the town or village, or at the landing place, as the case may be, by the closest relatives. They are dressed in the mourning clothes required for their specific degree of relationship. The primary mourners kneel and offer their funeral wails, after which the bearers

If the grave is ready and the day happens to be auspicious for the burial of the body, the procession meets one or more bands of musicians ordered by the family, as well as various people and groups carrying the tools for a complete burial procession, including a number of "auxiliary pavilions" sent by friends (see page 167). There is also a pavilion containing a temporary tablet for the spirits of the dead (*hûn péh*, see p. 70); but if such a tablet has been brought along with the body from abroad, an empty pavilion is sent out to fetch it. In many cases, they also place the rooster inside it, or else on top of it. Without wasting time, everything is arranged and a regular funeral procession is formed, which conveys the body straight to the tomb, where it is buried with the customary ceremonies.

But, as our readers know from page 103, every burial which takes place eight or more days after death requires the selection of an auspicious day and hour. Consequently, when a body arrives from a long distance, it is generally necessary to postpone the burial. It is then met by the mourners only and, without much ceremony, taken to a <term>*síp ts'ù*</term>, or to some spot assigned for keeping encoffined bodies such as those mentioned on pages 127 and following; from there, it is later transferred to the grave with the required pomp. In many cases as well, when it is expected that the burial will be possible soon after the arrival, the coffin is placed somewhere in an open field or under a huge boulder in the mountains to await burial. Custom strictly forbids a body from being taken into the dwelling¹. It is indeed self-evident that people who object to persons dressed in mourning, or even messengers announcing a death, entering their houses for fear they may introduce death (see pages 641 and following), would, *all the more so*, refuse entrance to death itself in the form of a human body. Only things of a fortunate nature may enter a house, and they must be invited in as often as possible; but things of an unfortunate nature may only leave it.

Here we have, however, to do with a superstition in defense of—

As the ancient Chinese did not object to having dead bodies taken into their houses, it certainly appears to be a strange contradiction that—as stated on page 641—it was a rule among them that nobody wearing mourning garments or a dress indicating mourning might enter the gate of a Ruler, and that nothing resembling funereal implements should be brought there. Our readers were informed on page 642 that the first part of this decree is still in force at present, as people in the three-year mourning period are not allowed to enter the Imperial Palace, nor any government building or fortress. Its second part is also maintained to this day, for no dead body may be taken into any walled city whatever without a special permit from the Board of Rites or, in the case of Peking, from the Emperor. The "*Imperial Regulations for the Board of Rites*" <note>欽定禮部則例 (Qinding Libu Zeli).</note> contain the following decree:

> case the family has presented a petition to this effect—is entitled
> to give them a letter to the local authorities, ordering them to
> allow the deceased to be carried into the city for the
> preparations for burial. But should an encoffined corpse be sent
> to the Metropolis, it is not permitted to bring it within the
> city walls, except in the case of high officers of the first or

A complete funeral train—the longest and most splendid the family can afford—escorts it. A large number of citizens, all real or claimed relatives by blood or friendship, send "auxiliary pavilions" or follow behind, eager to be seen by the public and to attract to themselves a part of the admiration bestowed on the illustrious dead. Magistrates, seated in state palanquins, emerge from their Yamens, each with an entourage of lictors and soldiers, and accompany the procession until it leaves the city through another gate. Other authorities and many admiring citizens honor the deceased at the roadside by offering incense when the coffin passes, and by bowing and prostrating themselves behind a table decorated with sacrificial food. Is it surprising that, in most cases, the family considers it necessary to leave the body outside the walls for a few days beforehand in order to give everyone time to prepare for its glorious entry?

Supposedly for the glorification of the deceased, but in reality for the exaltation of the family, the latter send out printed notices to relatives, friends, and acquaintances, informing them of the "happy event" of which they are so proud. These documents closely resemble the death announcements described on pages 111 *and following* and represented by Plate VII; they are printed with the same type, folded in the same way, and the names of the sons, grandsons, brothers, etc., are displayed at the end in a similar manner. The content is also mostly the same. Instead of the character 訃 (announcement of death), they bear on the outside the word 告, "announcement." The unfilial sons... have personally seen the remains gathered and clothed, and have carried them back to the ancestral home; and now they intend to bring them within the walls of the city in accordance with the Regulations, and to prepare his funeral. You are hereby carefully informed of this.

We have carefully selected the fourth day of the twelfth month to receive your cards¹"².

Sending the deceased back to their native soil is generally understood by the people in China to be a matter for the government’s care, in so far as soldiers are concerned who have died in distant garrisons or in the dependencies of the Empire. It is doubtful, however, whether the government really considers itself bound to do anything in this respect or to make it the responsibility of the mandarinate to assist in the discharge of such a duty. But, since an example was set in ancient times by one of the most renowned occupants of the throne, it may not be unreasonable to suppose that many emperors have subsequently sent home the remains of their soldiers; every era in China, including the one in which the current dynasty reigns, has produced monarchs who were most

The care which the great founder of the Han dynasty ordered to be paid to the remains of his soldiers so many centuries ago far exceeded that which is shown by the officials of the present day to the warriors who are recruited in other parts of the Empire only to end their lives in the garrisons in Formosa and the Pescadores. The only thing the authorities do for these corpses is to send them across the Formosa Channel to Amoy, the nearest seaport on the continent, and to keep them there for some time at the disposal of their families, in case they should claim them and carry them home. The airtight coffins are stored in a poorly built clay shed, which as recently as 1890 stood a few paces beyond the large, massive granite gate known locally as the <term>Tìn-lâm koan</term>³, "Barrier Dominating the South." A custodian, paid by the authorities, lives nearby. Each coffin is inscribed with the name and birthplace of the deceased man inside. The building is commonly called <term>hâi chiùⁿ</term>⁴: "the shed for human bones." In former years, the coffins were kept within the grounds of the <term>Hái-sín sī</term>⁵, or "Convent of the Sea-clams," a small Buddhist monastery located on the shore of the outer harbor; the monks there acted as custodians for an annual payment. ->INTERMENT OF EVOKED SOULS.<-

### 2. On burying the Souls of the Dead without their Bodies.

In the previous pages, it has been shown that the root of the custom—so generally observed by the Chinese in all ages—of carrying the dead back to their native soil, is nothing other than a recognized necessity of taking the soul there. The people have always been perfectly certain that the soul does not separate from the body after death. When considered carefully, it is the soul that has always been the chief object of this custom; the corpse is merely regarded as the means by which the soul is to be lured back to the ancestral home.

With this fact before us, we understand why the Chinese since ancient times have tried to bring back to their homes the souls of those dead whose bodies had been lost, or could not be taken home from foreign lands because of the great distance or for some other reason. They called upon the soul to return home, prepared a grave for it, and buried it there—probably, in most cases, by using a soul tablet or the clothes of the deceased. We find such curious burials mentioned in books as "interments with the summoning of the soul" or "burials of summoned souls" <note>Summoning the soul burial (招魂葬).</note>. We will try to shed light upon their antiquity and the part they have played in religious life by providing some extracts from native literature that refer to them.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The coffins and remains of traveling soldiers and civilians were transported and stored in a coffin depository established within the Haitao Temple (Temple of the Sea-mound). The Maritime Sub-prefect of Xiamen (Amoy) sent word to the sub-prefectures and districts of the deceased's original homes, summoning their relatives to identify and claim them. A one-year limit was set; if this limit passed, they were buried in Xiamen. Ship owners who transported them twice a year—in the first and fifth months—were exempt from carrying military grain. Regarding expenses, the one sub-prefecture and four districts of Taiwan each donated ten taels of silver annually. In the 37th year [of the Qianlong period, 1772], the donation was increased to fifteen taels each, totaling seventy-five taels. This was kept in the Taiwan district treasury; twenty-four taels were given to the temple monks for incense, lamps, and sacrifices for the "abandoned souls," and the remainder was used for burial expenses. In the 37th year, the monks' stipend was increased by six taels.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Later, because the donated funds were not collected regularly, the remains piled up excessively. From the first year of Jiaqing [1796] onward, the Maritime Sub-prefects of Xiamen—Qiu Zengshou, Ye Shaofen, Xian Cheng, and Mai Xiang—successively donated money to buy land for burial. In the first year of Daoguang [1821], the Provincial Treasurer Sun Erzhun established a detailed plan: starting from that year, the Provincial Treasurer, the Taiwan Circuit Intendant, the Prefect, and the three sub-prefectures and four districts would each donate fifteen taels, totaling one hundred and fifty taels. <note>Chapter II, lines 56 and 57.</note>

The Standard Annals of the Han dynasty afford evidence that the custom prevailed in the Imperial family as early as the first century of our era, the emperor Kwang Wu having observed it with regard to his sister, whose grave had been destroyed—like those of so many other members of his family—during the serious uprisings which marked the first years of his reign. When her husband Teng Chʻen $^1$ died (A. D. 49), "the Emperor ordained that her soul, which was established in a tablet at Sin-yé, should be called back, ushered in, and placed with Teng Chʻen in the same grave at Poh-mang" $^2$.

Such things were by no means practiced by the Court alone, as it is stated of Li Ku $^3$, a military commander in the second century who died in prison on the charge of high treason: "His son Sieh, after his death, performed the funeral rites, the burial, and everything connected with it. He immediately selected auspicious days, had a coffin made, prepared a burial dress of silk, and fixed a piece of white glossy satin underneath the collar of it. Upon this, as upon an ancestral tablet, were written the titles and names of the deceased and the year and month of his birth; and having thereupon called upon the soul, he placed that dress in a coffin and placed it in a tomb" $^4$.

In another work we read: "According to the *Description of Yü-chang* (the present province of Kiangsi), the grave of Hü Tszĕ-tsiang is located at a distance of four miles from the local capital. In former times, this Tszĕ-tsiang came here from afar because an awful rebellion was harassing the Middle Kingdom; he crossed the Yangtze, joined the troops of Liu Yiu, died, and was buried inside the Chʻang gate. This occurred under the Han...

During the period when the above episode reportedly occurred, many people seriously objected to the practice of burying souls in empty graves. It is likely that deep reflection on the matter led the more thoughtful people to the conviction that a disembodied human soul—which must stay with the body it once inhabited for its own preservation—cannot help but feel highly uncomfortable in a grave where that natural support is completely missing. They believed such a grave could not possibly promote the soul's happiness. Furthermore, these unusual burials were disapproved of because no mention of them is made in the writings of the *Cheu* dynasty or earlier times; this lack of precedent was enough to label them as heterodox inventions. The opposition to this became so strong that "the Emperor forbade them in the first year of the *T'ai hing* period (A.D. 318)." <note>² 太興元年初禁招魂葬. *Books of the Tsin Dynasty*, chapter 6, line 8.</note> This prohibition, which shows that such burials were then practiced on an extensive scale, was apparently the direct result of the following event regarding *Yueh* <note>³ 越.</note>, prince of *Tung-hai* <note>⁴ 東海王.</note>, a military...

the attention of wise and philosophical men. And no wonder, for nothing is so intimately connected with the doctrines of <term>hiao</term> (filial piety) as burials and funeral observances. Many Chinese embraced the views of Fu Shun, maintaining that a disembodied soul, when the body cannot be recovered, ought to be lodged in a tablet and not in a tomb. Others, however, also after mature deliberation, held that since burying the dead ranks among the highest duties prescribed by <term>hiao</term>, no one can dispense with it—even though the corpse is not at hand—unless there is uncertainty regarding the death of the person in question. Some of those who have viewed the matter from this perspective emphasize the advantage that, by burying the soul, a fixed date is obtained from which the different stages in the period of mourning may be calculated, as well as the various sacrifices and observances which custom requires to be celebrated at fixed times after the burial.

Since Chinese moralists were far from unanimous regarding the propriety of the custom now under notice, it continued to be practiced in the following centuries. In the year 693, two consorts of the Emperor Jui Tsung<note><sup>1</sup> 睿宗.</note> of the T'ang dynasty, bearing the family names Liu<note><sup>2</sup> 劉</note> and Teu<note><sup>3</sup> 竇</note> respectively, were put to death by order of the Empress-dowager Wu<note><sup>4</sup> 武</note>, who had usurped the throne; and "when Jui Tsung resumed the government (in A.D. 710), he summoned their souls and buried them to the south of the walls of the capital,"<note><sup>5</sup> 睿宗卽位招魂葬於都城之南. *Old Books of the T'ang Dynasty*, chapter 51, lines 16 and 17.</note> it being unknown what had become of their corpses. Later ages also provide instances of such burials. The *History of the Ming Dynasty* relates that, during the conquest of the capital city <term>Nanjing</term> by the rebellious King of <term>Yen</term> <note>2. The King of Yan (later the Yongle Emperor).</note> in A.D. 1402, the conqueror ordered the capture of the wife and two daughters of the minister <term>Hwang Kwan</term> <note>3. Huang Guan.</note>. He wished to hold them as hostages to control this faithful supporter of the dynasty, who was then leading troops against him. However, these heroic women, along with more than ten members of their family, acted before he could reach them by drowning themselves from a bridge. Before news of their death reached him, <term>Hwang Kwan</term> said: “My wife possesses such resolve and self-sacrificing devotion that she will certainly have already lost her life,” and he summoned her soul and buried it on the banks of the <term>Yangtze River</term> <note>4. “My wife has such principles that she must be dead; I will summon her soul and bury it by the river.” *History of the Ming Dynasty*, chapter 143, page 5.</note>. The Code of Laws of the dynasty currently on the throne explicitly mandates that the violation of a grave in which a summoned soul is interred shall be punished just as severely as the violation of a grave containing a corpse (see page 868). This shows that the Government recognizes such burials as a virtuous custom, deserving the protection of law and justice. Considering that these practices have been widely prevalent for at least eighteen centuries, we can hardly doubt that they still occur today.

# CHAPTER XI.

## THE CARE BESTOWED BY THE PEOPLE AND THE AUTHORITIES UPON THE DEAD OF OTHERS.

### 1. Public Charity towards the Dead.

The customs and concepts relating to the grave, which have been described in this work, have no doubt fully convinced our readers that in the Middle Kingdom, graves are viewed in quite another light than among ourselves. On the other side of the globe, they are not a means to rid oneself of useless mortal remains in a way considered the most decent; nor are they merely rendered sacred to the memory of the dead. In China, the grave is sacred, but in quite a different sense. It is sacred especially as a home for the soul, which is not only indispensable for its happiness, but also for its existence; for no disembodied spirit can long escape destruction unless the body coexists with it to serve as a natural support. Both the body and the soul require a grave for their preservation. Hence the grave, being the primary shelter of the soul, virtually becomes the principal altar dedicated to it and to its worship.

Such ideas still prevail in China, and have prevailed there since ancient times. Consequently, the people have always regarded it as a dire calamity to be buried in an incomplete manner, and the greatest possible disaster not to be buried at all. It has been stated in our chapter on Coffins and Grave vaults (pp. 280 *onward*) that to be committed to the earth without a coffin was anciently regarded as a curse; how much more terrible then must it have been to be deprived of a grave, with the disembodied soul being thus wretchedly exposed to all the harshness of the weather, to the scorching summer sun, the merciless rains, snows, frost, and ice which the various seasons bring!

The concept that souls are doomed to a pitiful condition if their bodies are badly buried is brought out in sharp lines in the following legend, found in a work of the fourth century. In the opinion of the nation, it is no legend, but an historical

Because these seeds were larger in the South, Yuen took a full cartload with him when his army returned, for the purpose of sowing them. Although the people at that time considered them to be remarkable and precious southern products, and every man of wealth and influence coveted them, nobody reported the matter to the Throne, as Yuen was then in full enjoyment of imperial favor. But when he died, someone slandered him in a report to the Emperor, stating that what he had brought home in that cart was nothing less than brilliant pearls and veined precious stones. The Emperor's wrath was incensed to such a degree that Yuen's wife and children, bewildered with fear, did not venture to transport his corpse to the old family sepulcher. They selected a plot of ground of a few acres to the west of the city, purchased it, and contented themselves with burying him there in a slovenly manner. Not a single visitor or old friend ventured to come and offer condolences." <note>3. ...the Standard Histories of those times recount that Liang Sung ¹, maternal grandfather of Emperor Hwo ² and paternal grandfather of the magnate Liang Shang mentioned on page 411, died in prison in A.D. 83. Indeed, it was the rule in the early centuries of our era to refuse a decent burial to people who died in jail. It is recorded that Emperor Hiao Wen ⁴ of the Wei dynasty issued an edict in A.D. 473, stating that "from then on, criminals detained in the capital and elsewhere in the empire who died in prison before their sentences were pronounced should be buried by the authorities in a coffin and with burial clothes, unless they had close relatives (to provide for them in this way). Their remains were no longer to be left exposed in the open air" ⁵. Even as late as the Ming dynasty, people who died in captivity were treated no differently, as the following episode proves: "When Mr. Li Tung-kang of Kao-mi (in Shantung province) was Governor of Kansuh, he happened to notice a heap of bleached bones in a corner of the jailer’s house walls in the provincial capital. He was informed that these were the remains of convicts from many years ago. Moved by compassion, he said: 'But these dead men have already paid for their crimes; why, then, are their bones exposed to the air?' He established a public cemetery outside the city and buried them there" ⁶.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of burial practices by explaining the religious and social motivations behind them, moving from the specific case of the Governor of Kansuh's public cemetery to the broader Chinese belief in the spiritual rewards for interring the dead.</meta>

<page-num>860</page-num>
<header>THE GRAVE.</header>

The miserable condition to which the Chinese believe souls are doomed when their bodies are not properly buried is one of the main reasons they provide a decent burial for their parents and relatives. This is considered one of the very first duties imposed upon mankind by their social laws. Furthermore, it fully explains the fact that burying an unburied or poorly buried corpse of any individual, even one to whom a person is not related, is considered by the nation as the greatest service that can be rendered to a soul. Consequently, it is viewed as a charitable deed of such merit that it is certain to bring blessings upon the person who performs it. Indeed, the good and evil that happen to a man in this world are generally attributed to spirits who reward or punish him. As we saw on page 283, even in the oldest of the Standard Histories, the burial of the most depraved tyrant who ever lived is presented as an act of merit deserving the special reward of the high Heavens. Books from later ages also contain various tales concerning rewards given by souls to those who had shown their bodies the greatest care that can be paid to a dead man. We will quote a few of these tales to give readers an idea of their general message. The simple fact that they are recorded in writing makes them historical events in the eyes of the Chinese; it would never occur to even the greatest skeptics to doubt their truth.

He then took three gold mirrors from the box at the head of the coffin, gave them to Tsung, and suddenly disappeared. It would be easy to gather dozens of such tales from Chinese books. They are accepted by the people as historical truths and are handed down by oral tradition with endless variations, exerting a broad influence on the behavior followed regarding neglected human remains. Hopes of reward and, no less, fear of the wrath of the souls involved if they are heartlessly left in their miserable condition, give rise from time to time to charitable societies for the distribution of coffins and the repair of the graves of the poor. Such coffin societies are, as a rule, long-standing organizations; but most grave-repairing societies only exist for a short time, being dissolved when the restoration of a certain number of graves has been completed, or when a pre-determined sum of money has been spent on that work of charity.

Because each family and each clan considers it their appointed duty to help their poor members obtain what is necessary for burying the dead, very few people have to apply to public charity for coffins. Consequently, the organizations that distribute them are not very numerous. They are especially found in towns and cities, as clan ties are weaker there than in the countryside. In 1886, there were only three in Amoy.

Coffin-distributing societies are organized very simply. Some wealthy men provide a fixed amount, creating a fund maintained by annual or monthly contributions. The expenses required for the charity are paid out of this fund. A salaried cashier, who also acts as the bookkeeper, is appointed to manage the daily business. When a poor person applies to a member of the society for a coffin, a messenger is sent with them, if necessary, to inquire whether the family's circumstances are truly

...as to require assistance. After this, a ticket marked with the seal of the society is given to the applicant. This entitles them to receive a coffin at a coffin shop whose owner has contracted with the society for the delivery of a specific number. If the society has a reputation for being well-managed, its funds are constantly supplemented by voluntary donations from charitable men, who are anxious to gain merit for themselves by helping the dead. Moreover, many men and women contribute to fulfill vows made to the gods for the purpose of obtaining a cure from sickness or rescue from danger, either for themselves or for members of their family.

Some societies operate in this way for several years, dissolving only when no more money comes in and the funds are exhausted. Many have only a short existence, being founded by men who desire only to distribute a limited number of coffins. The formation of such a temporary society is announced to the public by posters put up in the streets, and especially by long wooden signboards in front of the houses where the poor in need of coffins must apply. These state in large characters that "The firm N.N. will distribute such-and-such a number of coffins," or bear some other inscription of a similar nature. When the last coffin has been given away, the boards are taken down, and from then on, the poor must look for help elsewhere. Occasionally, a well-to-do person distributes coffins in a similar manner entirely at his own expense, chiefly with the object of gaining popularity; indeed, reputation, respectability, and prestige—or, as the Amoy people say, <term>t'é biēn</term> <note>體面 (tǐmiàn): social face or prestige</note>—is eagerly sought by whoever has enough money to aspire to it. In 1886, and for many years previously, a rich merchant named Yeh Teh-shui <note>葉得水 (Yè Déshuǐ)</note> stood foremost in Amoy among this class of philanthropists. He also served his fellow citizens well by providing free medicines to the poor.

As a rule, such charitable institutions and individuals add to their charity by supplying a small sum of money with each coffin they give away—people say, half a dollar on average—to help the family pay for the funeral expenses. In many cases, they also give a certain quantity of lime to be mixed with the clay that is placed around the coffin during the burial (compare page 213).

<page-num>865</page-num>
# GRAVE REPAIRING SOCIETIES.

Some societies even go so far as to have Buddhist masses celebrated every few years in a temple in the town or its neighborhood. The goal is to comfort the souls of the dead whom they have helped, and thus deliver them from the torments of hell.

We now come to the temporary organizations that seek to save the souls of the many deceased poor from suffering by repairing their graves. Because the graves of the needy are covered only by very low <term>tumuli</term> (burial mounds), families often soon lose track of them. They disappear without leaving a trace and are then destroyed by others who wish to bury their own dead on the same spot. Preventing this is the purpose of these organizations.

Each grave-repairing society is represented by a few men who make up a management committee. They spend their money primarily on vast burial grounds on the outskirts of cities and towns—barren hills or plains unsuitable for farming. These areas are crowded with the graves of the poor who were unable to bury their dead in more favorable locations. The repair work is usually contracted out in lots. The contractors begin work only on days designated by the almanac as suitable for digging in the ground; if they do otherwise, they believe their workmen will suffer accidents and illnesses sent by the angry spirits of the soil <note>compare page 105</note>, who never patiently tolerate any reckless disturbance of their rest.

In the island of Amoy, repairs are rarely made with any material better than broken jars, pots, or fragments of tiles. The numerous holes formed in the graves due to shallow burial and the decaying wood of the coffins are filled by the workmen with this kind of rubbish. A layer of earth is spread over it, and then the entire surface of the graves is plastered with a mixture of lime and clay, finished with a thin coating of lime alone. After such a supposed restoration, great care is required when walking over the graves, lest one’s feet sink down with every step and ruin the repairs. However, in a country where the prevailing belief is that paper treasures and furniture enrich the dead, and that paper houses are perfectly fit to shelter them, a rotting coffin covered with a fragile layer of potsherds and plaster is hardly considered insufficient to house their souls. It is unnecessary to say that, within a short time, these repaired graves show as many openings as before, created by the hooves of stray cattle or runaway horses.

<summary>This page describes societies in Amoy that repair the neglected graves of the poor to prevent them from being destroyed or built over. It details the inexpensive materials used for these repairs and the spiritual beliefs—such as consulting almanacs to appease soil spirits—that govern the work.</summary>

->THE GRAVE.<-

Nevertheless, no new repairs are made until a new corporation undertakes another general restoration.

Once the work is finished, the burial ground looks like a vast field of snow, with irregular waves that dazzle the eyes when bathed in sunlight. Often, the corporation completes its commendable work with a Buddhist mass, paid for at its own expense and celebrated in a temple near the graves. They expect the souls of all those dead to be miraculously comforted by the priests and carried up to the regions of higher bliss accessible through Buddha’s Church.

Repairing other people’s graves is never undertaken without the authorization of the local magistrates. Otherwise, employers and workmen would undoubtedly become the victims of corrupt officials and unscrupulous people who, eagerly welcoming an unasked-for opportunity to extort money, would enforce the law against the malicious violation of others' graves—unless such a denunciation were bought off with a bribe. Not even the highest form of charity known in China is safe from such evil practices! But there is another reason why the corporations always inform the authorities of the virtuous work they wish to perform. They want to draw attention to it and thereby open the way for some official reward. The Collective Statutes of the reigning House state that, "when public-spirited men have buried a great number of the bodies of the poor, or have covered and interred large quantities of withered bones, the authorities shall investigate the act and then reward it with marks of distinction in the form of inscribed boards to be hung over their doors" <note>1 如 有 好 義 之 人 收 葬 貧 屍、及 掩 埋 枯 骨 數 多 者、有 司 勘 實 給 扁 旌 奬. *Wu hioh lu*, chapter 2, l. 16.</note>. As stated previously on page 791, even an honorary gate can be granted if the amount spent reaches a thousand <term>taels</term> or more.

<page-num>867</page-num>
# OFFICIAL RESCRIPTS FOR FUNERALS AND BURIALS.

...upon their own deceased relations and the neglected dead of others almost necessarily presupposes that the Government of the Empire can never have been behindhand in its concern for the proper burial of its subjects. The Government could not, indeed, follow any other course of action without the risk of contradicting its own motto, adopted perhaps at the foundation of the State: namely, that the whole nation is one single family and the rulers are an essential part of it. Moreover, should the Government neglect this matter, it would commit a great inconsistency, since active attention to burials forms a natural part of the Religion of the Dead, which is intimately bound up with *hiao* <note>filial piety or devotion</note>; indeed, it would thus fail to fully enforce the great national virtue which, as our readers know, has always held a primary place in its concerns as the foundation of its policy toward society.

Over many centuries until the present day, the care given by the Chinese Government to the bodies of its subjects has had many and varied aspects. Our readers are already familiar with one of them: namely, the rules established by successive dynasties for the disposal of the dead of each social class—that is to say, Emperors, members of the Imperial family, nobles and mandarins of all grades, the gentry, and the common people. These rules form part of each dynasty’s code of ritual institutions and official decrees for the practice of the State Religion. A few details on this subject have been given already in the first volume of this work (pages 235 and following).

Besides these official attempts to ensure that everyone in the Empire receives treatment after death in accordance with their rank, dignity, or social standing, every dynasty has likely made strict laws against the violation of corpses and the desecration of graves. Unfortunately, only those currently in force, as set out in the Code of Laws, are accessible. Because only a small portion of them has ever been translated into any European language, we shall provide all these articles in the following pages.

#### First Fundamental Article.

凡發掘他人墳塚見棺槨者杖一百流三千里。已開棺槨見屍者絞監候。發而未至棺槨者杖一百徒三年。招魂而葬亦是。為從減一等。

> "Anyone who, while digging in the earth, finds a corpse that has no owner and does not immediately cover it with earth, shall receive eighty blows with the <term>long stick</term>.
>
> "If any person smokes foxes out of a grave that belongs to others, and thereby sets fire to the coffin or the vault, he shall be punished with eighty blows with the <term>long stick</term> and be banished for two years. If the corpse is burned, he shall receive a hundred blows and be banished for three years. If the corpse is that of a superior or senior member of his family for whom he must mourn in any of the <term>five degrees</term>, each of these punishments shall be increased one degree for each higher degree of mourning; but if an inferior or junior relative of his is buried in the grave, the punishment shall be in proportion to the mourning which the perpetrator must observe for him—that is to say, it will be the same as is inflicted in the case of a corpse belonging to another family, but with the reduction of one degree for each higher degree of mourning.
>
> "If a son or grandson smokes a fox out of the grave of one of his parents or paternal grandparents, or if a male or female slave does such a thing in the grave of his or her master, or a hired workman in that of his employer, the culprit shall receive one hundred blows with the <term>long stick</term>. Should the coffin or the vault have suffered from the fire, the punishment shall be one hundred such blows and three years' <term>banishment</term>; and if the corpse is burned, <term>strangulation</term> shall be inflicted, with the culprit being previously kept in jail until the sentence has been confirmed by the higher authorities.

### Sixth Fundamental Article.

若地界內有死人、里長地鄰不申報官司檢驗而輒移他處及埋藏者杖八十。以致失屍者首杖一百、殘毀及棄屍水中者首杖六十徒一年。棄而不失及髦髮若傷者各減一等、杖一百。

> » When a person is found dead within the boundaries of a place, the village headman and the people living in the neighborhood shall be punished with eighty blows with the <term>long stick</term> if they neglect to inform the magistrates of the fact so that they may hold an inquest, or if they arbitrarily move the corpse to another spot or bury it. If the corpse is lost as a result, the chief culprits among them shall receive one hundred blows; and should it be mutilated (by others) or thrown into the water, they shall then receive sixty blows and be <term>banished</term> for one year. Should it be cast away but not lost, or if only the hair is damaged, a punishment one degree less severe—that is to say, one hundred blows with the <term>long stick</term>—shall be inflicted upon them.
> » If, in such a case, people have stolen the clothes from the corpse, they may be tried for ordinary theft and the punishment fixed according to the value of the items taken; however, they do not need to be branded <note>See notes 1 and 2 at the foot of page 869.</note>.

The fundamental articles above have been completed, partly modified, and made stricter by various supplementary articles enacted at different periods. Some earlier editions of the Code contain a few such articles that are sought for in vain in later editions. We provide them as found in an edition published in 1882, the latest reprint available to us.

### First Supplementary Article.
->(Dating from 1870)<-

發掘常人墳塚開棺見屍為首者擬斬立决。為從、無論次數、俱擬絞監候。

其發塚見棺鋸縫鑿孔抽取衣飾、尚未顯露屍身、為首者擬絞立决。為從俱擬絞監候。

其發塚見棺鋸縫鑿孔為從幫同鑿棺鋸棺三次及三次以上者入於情實、一二次者入於緩决。在外瞭望六次者入於情實、一次至五次者入於緩决。

> » If an ordinary person's grave has been dug up, the coffin opened, and the corpse exposed, the ringleaders will be sentenced to immediate beheading, and their execution will not be postponed for confirmation of the sentence by higher authorities. >
> » Anyone who has opened a grave and exposed the coffin, then sawed a seam or made a hole in it and removed clothes and ornaments—even without exposing the corpse—will, if they acted as the ringleader, be sentenced to immediate strangulation and executed without waiting for confirmation of the sentence by higher authorities. All accomplices will likewise be sentenced to death by strangulation and held in prison until their sentence has been confirmed by higher authorities.

If they have been guilty of this only once or twice, they shall be ranked among those whose execution must be delayed. Those who were present as spectators without being actively engaged in the crime shall, if they have been present on six occasions, be ranked among the criminals whose cases are fully verified. If they have been present between one and five times, they shall be classed among those whose execution is to be delayed until the Imperial confirmation of their sentence has been granted.

» If the grave of an ordinary person has been dug up so that the coffin or vault has become visible, the ringleaders shall be exiled for life to a province not far away <note>1</note>. However, if they are fifty years old or older, they shall be exiled for life to an adjacent province. The accomplices shall receive one hundred blows with the long staff and be banished for three years (Compare the first fundamental article).

### Second Supplementary Article.
->(Dating from 1821)<-

盜未殯未埋屍柩鋸縫鑿孔爲首一二次者杖一百徒三年。三次者總徒四年、四次五次者發邊遠充軍、六次及六次以上者發極邊烟瘴充軍。

爲從一二次者杖九十徒二年半。三次者杖一百徒三年。四次五次者總徒四年。六次七次者發邊遠充軍。八次及八次以上者發極邊烟瘴充軍。

> » If a person has once or twice stolen a coffin containing a corpse that was not yet temporarily or permanently buried, and has then sawn a seam or made a hole in it, he shall, if he acted as the chief culprit, be punished with one hundred blows with the heavy bamboo <note>This refers to the "long stick" mentioned in the original text.</note> and three years of banishment. Should he commit such a crime three times, he shall be banished for four years. If he does so four or five times, he shall be banished for life to a distant province; and if he has committed the offense six or more times, he shall be banished forever to the remotest province where a malaria-infested climate prevails (Kwangtung).
>
> » Regarding the accomplices: if they have joined in the crime once or twice, they shall be liable to ninety blows with the heavy bamboo and banishment for two years and a half. If they have done so three times, they shall receive one hundred blows and be banished for three years; and if four or five times, the banishment shall last for four years. Should they join in such a crime six or seven times, they shall be sent into lifelong banishment to a distant province; and if they have done so eight or more times, they shall be sent into lifelong banishment to the remotest province where a malaria-infested climate prevails.

### Third Supplementary Article.
->(Dating from 1806)<-

凡奴婢雇工人發掘家長墳塚、已行未見棺者爲首擬絞監候。爲從發近邊充軍。

見棺槨者爲首絞立決。爲從絞監候。

> » Whenever slaves or hired laborers excavate the grave of their master: if the act has been carried out but the coffin has not yet been reached, the chief culprit shall be sentenced to strangulation, with the execution to be delayed until after the next judicial revision. The accomplices shall be sent into military exile at the nearby borders.
> 
> » If the inner or outer coffin is exposed, the chief culprit shall be sentenced to immediate strangulation. The accomplices shall be sentenced to strangulation, with the execution to be delayed until after the next judicial revision.

開棺槨見屍者為首斬立決梟示。為從斬監候。

> » Any slave, whether male or female, who has opened the grave of their master, or any hired laborer who has opened the grave of their employer—if the work has begun but the coffin is not yet visible—shall, if they acted as the chief culprit, be strangled after being held in prison for the confirmation of the sentence by the higher authorities. Accomplices shall be sentenced to lifelong banishment in a nearby province.
>
> » If the coffin or vault has become visible in such a case, the chief culprits shall be strangled, and their execution shall not be delayed until the sentence is confirmed. Their accomplices shall also be executed in the same manner, after being held in prison for the confirmation of their sentence by the higher authorities.
>
> » If the coffin or vault has been opened and the corpse has become visible, the chief culprits shall be decapitated without waiting for a review of their sentence, and their heads shall be displayed on stakes as a warning to the public. The accomplices shall also be subject to decapitation but shall be kept in prison to await confirmation of their sentence by the higher authorities.
>
> » Finally, if the corpse has been mutilated, discarded, struck, or tossed about, both the chief culprits and the accomplices shall be beheaded; their execution shall not be delayed for the confirmation of their sentence, and their heads shall be displayed as a warning to the public.
> 
> » If, in the cases mentioned above, the chief culprits and accomplices include elders of the deceased person’s family, or their superior or inferior relatives, or members of other families, each person must be sentenced individually as a chief culprit or accomplice. This sentence will be based on the degree of mourning they were required to observe for the deceased, or according to the circumstance of their having no relation to them.

### Fourth Supplementary Article.

貪人吉壤將遠年之墳盜發者、子孫告發、審有確據、將盜發之人以開棺見尸律擬絞監候。

如非其子孫、又非實有確據之前人古塚、但因有土墩見人埋葬輒稱伊遠祖墳墓、勾引匪類夥告夥証、陷害無辜、審明、將為首者照誣告人死罪未決律杖一百流三千里。為從各照誣告為從律科斷。

若實係本人遠祖之墳被人發掘盜葬、因將所盜葬之棺發掘拋棄者、照祖父母父母被殺子孫不告官司而擅殺行兇人律杖六十。

若盜葬者並無發掘等情、止在切近墳旁盜葬、而本家輒行發掘者、應照地界內有死人不報官司而輒移他處律科斷。如有毀棄屍骸、照地界內有死人而移尸毀棄律科斷。

若非係墳地、止在田地場園內盜葬、而地主發掘開棺見屍、仍照律擬絞。其不開棺見尸者各照本律減一等治罪。

如兩造本係親屬、其所侵損之墳塚棺槨屍骸與本身皆有服制者各照律內服制科斷。

> » If someone, desiring another’s burial ground because it is believed to bring good luck to one's descendants, has fraudulently dug up an ancient grave, and the descendants of that deceased person file a complaint against them with the magistrates, who, upon investigating the case, find undeniable proof of the crime, the perpetrator shall be sentenced to death by strangulation. This is in accordance with the basic law against opening coffins and exposing the corpses within. They shall be imprisoned until their sentence has been confirmed by the higher authorities <note>This refers to the "絞監候" or strangulation after a period of imprisonment</note> (See the first basic article).
>
> » However, if the deceased person has no descendants, or if there is no undeniable proof that the old grave truly belongs to someone from the past, and it appears that people—upon seeing a burial conducted in a place where there was a mound of earth—have claimed without justification that it was a grave of their distant ancestors, and they then incite groups of criminals to file joint complaints and provide false evidence to frame innocent people; if this is proven, the leader shall be sentenced to 100 strokes of the cane and banishment to a distance of 3,000 *li*, according to the law for making a false accusation of a capital crime that has not yet been decided. Accomplices shall be sentenced according to the law for accomplices in false accusations.
>
> » If a person's ancestral grave is actually dug up and used by another for a secret burial, and the descendant digs up and discards the intruder's coffin instead of reporting it to the authorities, they shall be sentenced to sixty strokes of the cane. This follows the law for cases where descendants kill a murderer without notifying the government.
>
> » If the intruder did not dig up the existing grave but merely performed a secret burial close to it, and the family of the original grave digs it up, they shall be sentenced according to the law for moving a corpse found on one's property without reporting it to the authorities. If the corpse is destroyed or discarded, the punishment shall follow the law for moving and destroying a corpse found on one's property.
>
> » If the site is not a designated cemetery but merely a field or garden where a secret burial took place, and the landowner digs up the grave and opens the coffin so the corpse is visible, they shall still be sentenced to death by strangulation. If the coffin is not opened and the corpse is not visible, the punishment shall be reduced by one degree from the standard penalty.
>
> » If both parties are relatives, and the damage to the grave, coffin, or corpse involves those to whom the perpetrator owes mourning duties, the sentencing shall be determined according to the degrees of kinship specified in the law <note>"服制" refers to the system of mourning degrees which dictates legal status and punishment among relatives</note>.

### Fifth Supplementary Article.

民人、除無故空焚已葬屍棺者仍照例治罪
外、其因爭墳阻葬開棺易罐埋藏占葬者亦照

其侵犯他人墳塚者照發掘他人墳塚律治

如果審係地師教誘、將教誘之地師均照詐
教誘人犯法律分別治罪。若地方官隱諱寬縱、
不實力查究、照例參處。

> » If—apart from cases where people, without valid reasons, take a buried coffin out of a grave and burn it, which is a crime that must be punished in accordance with the supplementary articles—it should occur that obstacles are placed in the way of a burial because the ground is in dispute, and yet such a burial is arrogantly performed in those grounds after the parties have opened a coffin buried there, placed the remains in an urn and interred them, they shall also be punished according to the (first and second) fundamental articles which contain provisions against opening coffins, making corpses visible, and mutilating them.

### Seventh Supplementary Article.

->凡愚民惑於風水擅稱洗筋檢筋名色、將已葬父母及五服以內尊長骸骨發掘檢視占驗吉凶者均照服制以毀棄坐罪。帮同洗檢之人俱以為從論、地保扶同隱匿、照知人謀害他人不卽阻首律杖一百。<-

> » If among the ignorant people who are led astray by *feng shui* theories, anyone—pretending without valid reasons that they ought to wash and examine the remains—should exhume the bones of their buried father or mother, or of a superior and senior member of their family for whom they must observe mourning in one of the <term>five degrees</term>, and examine the bones to predict good or evil fortune, they shall be sentenced as if they had mutilated the corpse or thrown it away. This sentence shall be in accordance with (the relationship existing between them and the deceased according to) the <term>regulations on mourning</term> (See the third fundamental article). Those who have assisted them in washing and examining the bones shall all be treated as accomplices. The headman of the ward and his assistants, if they have concealed the matter, shall be punished with one hundred blows of the long stick, as required by the law against those who, knowing that someone intends to do harm to another, do not immediately take measures to prevent the conspirator.

> » If the remains are transferred to another grave for valid reasons and with observance of the proper ceremony, the case is, according to the (second) fundamental article, not punishable.

### Eighth Supplementary Article.
->(Enacted in this form in 1810)<-

If, in a case of intentional murder committed during a brawl, the murderers suggest mutilating or mangling the corpse, or throwing it into the water, those who follow these instructions to help carry and discard the body—regardless of whether they personally inflicted any injuries at the scene—shall all be punished as accomplices under the law against discarding a corpse. They shall receive one hundred blows with the heavy rod and be sentenced to three years of penal servitude. If they bury the corpse to destroy evidence, those who followed orders to help with the burial—if it is determined they were present at the scene, assisted in the assault, and caused injuries that would legally warrant a full sentence of blows—shall also receive one hundred blows with the heavy rod and three years of penal servitude. Those who were present but did not personally inflict any injuries, and only followed orders to help bury the body, shall be punished according to the law for village heads or neighbors who discard a corpse: sixty blows with the heavy rod and one year of penal servitude.

[If other persons involved in the case suggest mutilating, discarding, or burying the corpse to destroy evidence, they shall still be punished as principals under the law for discarding a corpse: one hundred blows with the heavy rod and perpetual banishment to a distance of three thousand *li*].

In cases where the corpse is not actually lost, the punishment shall be reduced by one degree in each instance. If someone is hired to carry or bury a corpse and is truly unaware of the criminal circumstances, they shall be punished according to the law for finding a deceased person within one's property and moving or hiding the body without reporting it to the authorities: eighty blows with the heavy rod.

Regarding cases of theft or robbery: if a fight occurs on a boat in a lake or river resulting in death, and the corpse falls into the water and is swept away and cannot be recovered; or if a person is suddenly attacked in a dangerous mountain pass or valley and the corpse falls into a mountain stream—where there was clearly no intent to discard or destroy the body—the case shall still be decided according to the fundamental law for killing in a fight. The law regarding the discarding of a corpse should not be applied in these circumstances.

If a person kills a criminal caught at night in the act of adultery or robbery inside their home, or kills a resisting bandit in an open field or on the road—acts for which the killer would normally not be prosecuted—but then proceeds to destroy, discard, bury, or throw the corpse into a pit or well, they shall be punished according to the law for having a deceased person on one's property and secretly burying the body without reporting to the authorities: eighty blows with the heavy rod. If this results in the loss of the corpse, they shall be punished according to the law for moving a corpse from one's property to another location, thereby causing the loss of the body: one hundred blows with the heavy rod.

If, after killing someone, the perpetrator acts out of lingering hatred and proceeds to violently mutilate, discard in water or fire, or skin and damage the corpse, they shall be sentenced according to the fundamental law for destroying and discarding a corpse.

Any other persons who assisted in the capture or participated in the fight and are guilty of discarding, destroying, moving, or burying the corpse shall be dealt with separately according to these specific regulations.

> » If in a case of intentional murder committed during a brawl the murderers suggest the mutilation or mangling of the corpse, or the casting of it into the water, those who allow the corpse to be carried off and thrown away shall all be punished, as accomplices, under the (third) fundamental article which provides against the throwing away of corpses; and, without it being taken into consideration whether they have or have not inflicted any wounds on the spot, they shall receive one hundred blows with the heavy rod and be banished for three years.

<summary>The Eighth Supplementary Article outlines the punishments for mutilating or hiding a corpse after a killing, distinguishing between active participants in a murder and those who merely help dispose of the body. It also provides leniency for cases where a body is lost accidentally during a fight or when a justified killing is followed by an improper burial.</summary>

And if an attack has been made in a house, under the cover of darkness, resulting in manslaughter due to fornication or robbery, or if thieves or robbers have murderously attacked anyone in an open field or on the public highway, then the following applies to those who cannot be brought to trial for the primary crime but who permitted the mutilation of the corpse, its being cast away, buried, or taken to an abyss or well and thrown into it. ### Ninth Supplementary Article.

凡盜葬之人、除侵犯他人墳塜發掘開棺見
屍者仍各按照律例治罪外、如因盜葬後被地
主發掘棄毀、無論所葬係尊長及卑幼屍柩、俱
照強占官民山塲律杖一百流三千里。
  如於有主墳地及切近墳旁盜葬、尚無侵犯、
致被地主發掘等情者照強占山塲滿流律量減
一等、杖一百徒三年。

Whoever illegally buries a person—excepting those who violate another’s grave by digging it up and opening the coffin to expose the corpse, who shall still be punished according to those specific laws—if the illegal burial results in the landowner digging up and destroying the remains, regardless of whether the buried person was an elder or a junior relative, the offender shall be punished according to the law for the forcible occupation of public or private land with one hundred blows of the heavy rod and banishment to a distance of three thousand miles.

If someone illegally buries a body in a private graveyard or very near an existing grave, but has not yet committed a violation of an existing tomb, and this leads to the landowner digging up the remains, the punishment shall be reduced by one degree from the law for the illegal occupation of mountain land: one hundred blows of the heavy rod and three years of penal servitude.

**凡子孫發掘祖父母父母墳塚、均不分首從。已行未見棺槨者皆絞立決。見棺槨者皆斬立決、開棺見屍並毀棄尸骸者皆凌遲處死。**

> "If people claim a deceased person is a drought-demon who causes drought, and they dig up his grave and mutilate the corpse, the ringleaders shall be punished under the first fundamental article regarding the excavation of graves, the opening of coffins, and the exposure of the corpse. They shall be sentenced to strangulation but kept in prison to await the confirmation of their sentence by the higher authorities. If it is clearly proven during the judicial investigation that the culprits cannot be suspected of using the accusation against the dead as a pretext, their sentence shall be categorized during the provincial autumn review among those to be delayed for Imperial confirmation in Peking. However, if it is proved that they acted out of a grudge or an outburst of hatred, the case shall be categorized during the autumn review as 'properly verified' and will not be sent to the capital for delay.
> 
> "As for the accomplices who assisted in digging up the grave and mutilating the corpse, they shall be sent into lifelong exile in a nearby province; if they are over fifty years of age, they shall be sent to an adjacent province. Those who merely followed along or accompanied the culprits without taking part in the act shall receive one hundred blows with the heavy staff and be banished for three years."

### Twelfth Supplementary Article.
->(Enacted in this shape in 1814)<-

子孫盜祖父母父母未殯未埋屍柩、不分首從、開棺見尸者皆斬立決。如未開棺槨、事屬已行確有顯跡者皆絞立決。

> » Sons or grandsons who steal a coffin containing the corpse of their parent or grandparent that has not yet been buried, whether temporarily or permanently, shall be beheaded immediately—whether they are ringleaders or accomplices—without the execution being delayed for confirmation by higher authorities, if they have opened the coffin and exposed the corpse. Should they not have opened the coffin or the vault, but clear evidence exists that the crime was attempted, they shall all be strangled immediately, without the execution being delayed for confirmation of their sentence.
> 
> » If, in the cases mentioned above, there are senior or junior relatives of the deceased, or members of other families, among the ringleaders and accomplices, each person must be sentenced individually as a ringleader or accomplice according to the mourning grade they must observe for the deceased, or according to the fact that they are not related.

### Thirteenth Supplementary Article.
->(Enacted in this shape in 1814)<-
