» Junior members of a family who have stolen a coffin containing the body of a senior relative who has not yet been buried (whether temporarily or permanently) shall, if they are required to mourn for the deceased, be sentenced as follows—provided they have not opened the coffin or the vault: if they acted as the ringleaders, they shall be banished for life to a remote province 4,000 miles away if they are junior relatives of the second degree of mourning; they shall be sentenced to lifelong transportation to a distant province if they are relatives in the three lower degrees of mourning. If they acted as accomplices, those of the second degree of mourning shall be sent into lifelong banishment to a distant province; those of the three lower degrees of mourning shall be sent to a nearby province.

» However, if they have opened the coffin and exposed the body, ringleaders who are junior relatives of the deceased and must mourn for him in the second degree shall be permanently banished for life to a remote province with a malarious climate, such as Yunnan, Guizhou <note>Kweicheu</note>, Guangxi <note>Kwangsi</note>, or Guangdong <note>Kwangtung</note>. If they are relatives in the three lower degrees of mourning, they shall be sent into lifelong banishment to a remote province 4,000 miles away. Among the accomplices, those who are junior mourners of the second degree shall be banished for life to a remote province 4,000 miles away, while those in the third, fourth, or fifth degrees shall be sent to a distant province.

» If, in the cases mentioned above, senior relatives of the deceased or members of other families are among the ringleaders and accomplices, each person must be sentenced individually as a ringleader or accomplice according to the mourning grade they must observe for the deceased, or according to the fact that they are not related to him.

## Fifteenth Supplementary Article.
->(Dating from 1810)<-

有服尊長盜卑幼未殯未埋屍柩、開棺見屍者總痲尊長為首依發卑幼墳塚開棺見屍杖一百徒三年律減一等。未開棺槨者再減一等。如係小功以上尊長為首、各依律以次遞減。為從之尊長亦各按服制減為首之罪一等。

如有卑幼或外人為首為從、分別服制凡人各以首從論。

> Senior members of a family who have stolen a coffin containing the corpse of a junior relation that has not yet been buried (either temporarily or permanently) shall, if they are required to mourn for the deceased, be sentenced as follows if they opened the coffin and made the corpse visible: if they are senior relations who must mourn in the fifth degree and have acted as the primary offenders, they shall be subject to the second fundamental article. This article stipulates one hundred blows with the long stick and three years of banishment for those who dig up the grave of a junior relation, open the coffin, and make the corpse visible; however, their punishment shall be reduced by one degree. If they did not open the coffin or the vault, their punishment shall be reduced by one additional degree. Furthermore, if they are senior relations in the fourth or a higher degree of mourning, their punishment as primary offenders shall be reduced proportionally, in accordance with the same fundamental article. If they acted as accomplices, each of them shall be punished one degree less severely than the primary offender.

> If junior relatives or outsiders acted as the primary offenders or accomplices, the degree of mourning shall be distinguished, and they shall be judged as primary offenders or accomplices according to the laws for ordinary people.

## Seventeenth Supplementary Article.
->(Dating from 1821)<-

平治他人墳墓為田園、未見棺槨、止一塚者仍照律杖一百。如平治多塚、每三塚加一等、罪止杖一百徒三年。

卑幼於尊長有犯、緦麻功服各加凡人一等、期親又加一等。若子孫平治祖墳並奴僕雇工平治家長墳、一塚者杖一百徒三年。每一塚加一等、仍照加不至死之例、加至實發雲貴兩廣極邊烟瘴充軍為止。

其因平治而盜賣墳地、得財者均按律計贓准竊盜論加一等。贓輕者各加平治罪一等。知情謀買者悉與犯人同罪、不知者不坐。

如因平治而强佔或盜賣、計畝數多按例應擬徒流充軍。

以至因平治而見棺見屍並棄毀屍骸、按例應擬軍遣斬絞凌遲者仍照各本例從其重者論。

其子孫因貧賣地、留墳祭掃並未平治又非盜賣者不在此例。

> Anyone who has leveled a grave mound belonging to others to create a field or garden shall—if they have not exposed the coffin or the vault and have leveled only one grave—be punished with one hundred blows with the heavy stick in accordance with the law. If they have leveled multiple graves, the penalty shall be increased by one degree for every three additional graves, up to a maximum of one hundred blows and three years of penal servitude.
> 
> If junior relatives commit this offense against their seniors, the penalties for those in the *sima* <note>relatives for whom one mourns for three months</note> and *gongfu* <note>relatives for whom one mourns for five or nine months</note> degrees of mourning shall be one degree higher than for unrelated people; for *jiqin* relatives <note>relatives for whom one mourns for one year</note>, the penalty is increased by another degree. If descendants level their ancestors’ graves, or if servants or hired laborers level their master’s family graves: for one grave, the penalty is one hundred blows and three years of penal servitude. For every additional grave, the penalty increases by one degree. Following the regulations for penalties that do not reach the death penalty, the sentence may be increased until it reaches military exile in the most remote, malaria-infested borders of Yunnan, Guizhou, Guangdong, or Guangxi.
> 
> If, during the process of leveling, the grave land is illegally sold for profit, the offenders shall be judged according to the law for theft, with the penalty increased by one degree based on the value of the profit. If the profit is small, the penalty for leveling the grave shall be increased by one degree. Those who buy the land while knowing the circumstances shall receive the same punishment as the offender; those who were unaware shall not be prosecuted.
> 
> If the leveling leads to forcible occupation or illegal sale, and the acreage is large, the offender shall be sentenced to penal servitude, exile, or military service according to the regulations.
> 
> Furthermore, if the leveling results in the coffin or corpse being exposed, or the remains being discarded or destroyed, the offender shall be judged according to the respective regulations for military exile, deportation, beheading, strangulation, or "death by a thousand cuts" <note>lingchi</note>, with the most severe applicable penalty being imposed.
> 
> This law does not apply to descendants who, due to poverty, sell their land but keep the graves for ritual worship and have neither leveled the graves nor illegally sold the actual grave sites.

"Should junior or lower-ranking members of a family violate the grave of a superior or senior relative in the manner described above, their punishment—if the perpetrators are mourners in the three lowest degrees—shall be one degree more severe than if they had violated the grave of a person not belonging to their family; the penalty shall be increased by another degree if they are mourners in the second degree. "If people who have leveled another person's grave fraudulently sell the ground, they shall—if they have received money—be sentenced for ordinary theft according to the amount received, in accordance with the fundamental law concerning such offenses¹, but with the addition of one degree of punishment. If only a small sum has been obtained by the sale, each culprit shall be punished one degree more severely than if he had merely leveled the grave. And if those who have bought the ground were aware of the circumstances of the case, they shall be punished in the same way as the offenders; however, they shall not be punished if they bought it unwittingly.

"And if people who have leveled another's grave seize the ground by abuse of power and then fraudulently sell it or keep possession of it, a sentence of temporary or lifelong banishment shall be pronounced on them, in accordance with the supplementary articles, in proportion to the size of the ground in question.

"Should the coffin or the corpse become visible during the leveling of the ground, or the remains be thrown away or mutilated—so that the supplementary articles requiring lifelong banishment, decapitation, strangulation, or slow death by slicing become applicable—then in each of these cases, the most severe punishment required by the relevant supplementary article shall be applied.

### Eighteenth Supplementary Article.
->(Dating from 1821)<-

奴僕雇工人盜家長未殯未埋屍柩、未開棺槨、事屬已行確有顯跡者照發塚已行未見棺例為首絞監候、為從發近邊充軍。

> "If slaves or hired laborers steal a coffin containing the body of their master or employer before it has been buried (whether in a temporary or permanent grave), they shall—if the coffin was not opened but there is clear evidence that they had begun to do so—fall under the third supplementary article regarding the opening of a master’s or employer’s grave without exposing the coffin. Specifically, the principal offenders shall be strangled after being held in prison for the confirmation of their sentence by higher authorities, and the accomplices shall be sent into life-long exile in a nearby province."

> "If they have opened the coffin and exposed the body, they shall fall under the third supplementary article regarding the digging up of a master’s or employer’s grave so that the coffin or vault is exposed. In this case, the principal offenders shall be strangled immediately, and the accomplices shall also be strangled after being held in jail for the confirmation of their sentence by higher authorities."

> "And if they have mutilated, discarded, struck, or thrown the body about, they shall fall under the same supplementary article; both the principal offenders and accomplices shall be beheaded immediately, without their sentences being reviewed by higher authorities."

## Nineteenth Supplementary Article.
### (Dating from 1821)

發掘墳塚並盜未殯未埋屍柩、無論已開棺未開棺及鋸縫鑿孔等項、人犯各按其所犯本條之罪、分別首從、倂計科斷。

如一人叠竊有首有從、則視其爲首次數與爲從次數罪名相比、從其重者論。若爲首各次倂計罪輕、准其將爲首次數歸入爲從次數內倂計科罪、不得以爲從次數作爲爲首次數倂計。亦不得以盜未殯未埋屍柩及鋸縫鑿孔之案歸入發塚見棺及開棺見屍案內倂計次數治罪。

> When graves have been dug up, or coffins containing corpses not yet buried (whether stored temporarily or permanently) have been stolen—regardless of whether the coffins in those graves have been opened, or whether seams have been sawn or holes made in those stolen coffins, or other similar matters have occurred—then for every offender, the punishment shall be determined after comparing the various punishments they are liable for in each of those crimes, according to their role as either a principal offender or an accomplice.

> If a person has stolen a corpse multiple times as either a principal offender or an accomplice, then the punishments they are subject to for all cases in which they acted in either of these capacities must be compared, and the most severe punishment shall be inflicted upon them. If the punishment for the cases in which they acted as the principal offender, calculated by comparison, turns out to be less severe, it is permitted to include such cases among those in which they acted as an accomplice and to determine the punishment by the same comparative method; however, the cases in which they acted as an accomplice shall never be counted as cases where they acted as the principal offender for the purpose of calculation. Furthermore, it is not permitted to group cases in which they have stolen a coffin containing a corpse not yet buried (temporarily or permanently), or in which they have sawn a seam or drilled a hole in such a coffin, with cases in which they have opened a grave and exposed the coffin, or opened such a coffin and exposed the corpse, for the purpose of determining a combined sentence.

### Twentieth Supplementary Article.
### (Dating from 1821)

受雇看守墳墓並無主僕名分之人、如有發塚及盜未殯未埋屍柩並鋸縫鑿孔與未開棺槨者、或自行盜發、或聽從外人盜發、除死罪無可復加外、犯該軍流以下等罪悉照凡人首從各本律例上加一等問擬。

> If a paid keeper or custodian of a grave digs it up, regardless of whether he opens the coffin or the vault; or if a person who is legally a servant in name and duty steals a coffin containing his master’s body (whether it was temporarily or permanently unburied), and saws a seam or makes a hole in it; the culprit—whether he opened the grave himself, committed the theft, or allowed others to do so—shall be sentenced under current laws as an ordinary person would be for the same crime, acting as either a principal or an accomplice. However, the punishment shall be increased by one degree if the crime would normally result in life-long exile or a lighter penalty; if the penalty is already death, it cannot be increased further.

### Twenty-first Supplementary Article.
### (Enacted in this shape in 1870)

凡發掘貝勒貝子公夫人等墳塚、開棺槨見屍者為首斬立決、梟示、為從皆絞立決。見棺者為首絞立決。為從皆絞監候。未至棺者為首絞監候、為從發邊遠充軍。

如有發掘歷代帝王陵寢及會典內有從祀名位之先賢名臣、並前代分藩親王或遞相承襲分藩親王墳墓者俱照此例治罪。

若發掘前代分封郡王及追封藩王墳墓者、除犯至死罪仍照發掘常人墳塚定擬外、餘各於發掘常人墳塚本罪上加一等治罪。

以上所掘金銀交與該督撫、飭令地方官修葺墳塚。其王帶珠寶等物仍置塚內。

Whoever digs up the tombs of <term>Beile</term>, <term>Beizi</term>, Dukes, or their wives, and opens the coffin to the point of exposing the body, shall be sentenced as follows: the principal offender to immediate decapitation and public exposure of the head, and all accomplices to immediate strangulation. If the coffin is reached but not opened, the principal offender shall be sentenced to immediate strangulation, and the accomplices to strangulation after the autumn assizes <note>imprisonment pending execution</note>. If the excavation has not yet reached the coffin, the principal offender shall be sentenced to strangulation after the autumn assizes, and the accomplices to life-long exile in remote border regions for military service.

If anyone digs up the mausoleums of past emperors, the graves of ancient sages or famous officials listed in the Collected Statutes for sacrificial honors, or the tombs of former feudal princes and their successors, they shall be punished according to these same regulations.

If someone digs up the graves of former secondary princes (<term>Junwang</term>) or posthumously titled princes, the punishment—unless the crime already carries the death penalty according to the laws for digging up an ordinary person's grave—shall be determined by increasing the standard penalty by one degree.

Any gold or silver recovered from the aforementioned excavations shall be delivered to the Governor-General or Governor, who shall order local officials to use the funds to repair the tombs. Items such as royal belts and jewelry shall be returned to the interior of the tomb.

» Whoever digs up the grave of an Imperial prince of the third or fourth rank (<term>Beile</term> or <term>Beizi</term>), or the grave of a prince's consort, or anyone of a similar rank, and has opened the coffin or vault so that the corpse is visible, shall—if he acted as the chief culprit—be beheaded with the sword. This execution shall not be delayed until the sentence is confirmed; his head shall be displayed in public as a warning to the people. All accomplices shall be strangled immediately, without waiting for the confirmation of the sentence. Should the coffin have been only made visible, the chief culprits shall be strangled without delay for confirmation, and the accomplices shall be strangled after being kept in custody until such confirmation arrives. If they have not dug deep enough to reach the coffin, the chief culprits shall be strangled after being kept in jail until their sentence has been confirmed by the higher authorities, and the accomplices shall be sent into lifelong exile in a distant province.

» This article shall also apply to those who have dug up the mausoleum of an emperor or ruler of a former dynasty, or the grave of an ancient sage or renowned statesman whose memorial tablet is worshipped at the official state sacrifices in obedience to the Collective Statutes. It also applies to the grave of a regional Imperial prince, any other prince closely related to the Imperial family of the past dynasty, or anyone who inherited such a rank by birth.

» Those who have dug up the grave of a second-generation Imperial prince of the past dynasty who was granted a fief, or anyone who was posthumously granted the dignity of a regional Imperial prince, shall be punished one degree more severely than those who have dug up the grave of an ordinary person. The exception is when they already incur the death penalty, in which case they shall be sentenced as if they had dug up the grave of an ordinary person.

» The gold and silver which might have been exhumed in any of the above cases shall be delivered to the provincial Governor-General or Governor, who shall order the local magistrates to repair the violated grave. The pearls, precious items, and other things which the royal occupant of the grave wore on his body shall be placed back into the tomb.

## Twenty-second Supplementary Article.
->(Dating from 1825)<-

夫毀棄妻屍者比依尊長毀棄期親卑幼死屍律於凡人杖流上遞減四等、杖七十徒一年半。不失屍及毀而但髡髮若傷者再減一等、杖六十徒一年。

> » If a husband mutilates or discards the corpse of his wife, the (third) fundamental article—which contains provisions against senior relatives who mutilate or discard the corpse of a junior family member for whom they must mourn in the second degree—shall be applicable to him. He shall therefore be condemned to a punishment four degrees more severe than the beating and exile that would be inflicted if he had committed the same crime against an unrelated person: specifically, seventy blows with the long stick and banishment for one and a half years. If the corpse is not lost, or if the mutilation only involves cutting the hair or causing an injury, his punishment shall be reduced by one degree, resulting in sixty blows with the long stick and banishment for one year.

## Twenty-third Supplementary Article.
->(Dating from 1852)<-

凡發掘墳塚及鋸縫鑿孔偷竊之案、但經得財俱核計所得之贓、照竊盜贓科斷。如計贓輕於本罪者仍依本例定擬、若計贓重於本罪者即從重治罪。

> » Whenever theft occurs in connection with digging up a grave, sawing a seam in a coffin, or boring a hole in it, the value of the stolen goods shall be precisely calculated only if property has been taken, in order to sentence the offender according to the value of the theft <note>1</note>. If the punishment required for such an amount of theft is lighter than what the offender would suffer for the primary crime (the violation of the grave or coffin), the standard laws for grave violation shall be applied. However, if the punishment for the theft is heavier than that for the violation of the grave, then the more severe punishment shall be inflicted.

<page-num>901</page-num>

### LAWS FOR THE PROTECTION OF CORPSES AND GRAVES.

It would certainly be difficult to find clearer evidence of the great emphasis Chinese rulers place on the sacredness of the dead and their graves than the collection of laws mentioned above, which provide so specifically against their desecration in every possible way. It is likely true to say that no other people on earth possesses a legal code on this subject of such length and severity. This further suggests that the "Religion of the Human Corpse" is nowhere as highly developed as it is in China. 

Still, readers should not assume that these laws include everything the current dynasty has enacted on the subject. An article, the text of which was given on page 133, forbids people from leaving the dead unburied for more than a year; others, which will be included in the last chapter of this volume, forbid throwing them into the water or burning them <note>See chapter 17 of the Code, § Funeral and Burial.</note>. The Code even protects the corpses of executed criminals, prescribing that:

> "Anyone who mutilates a corpse after an execution shall be punished with fifty blows with the short bamboo stick" <note>“Anyone who further mutilates or destroys a corpse after execution: fifty blows.” Chapter 37, § Improper Sentencing.</note>. 

Elsewhere we read: 

> "Anyone who mutilates or damages inscribed stone tablets or stone animals in someone else's burial ground shall be punished with eighty blows with the long stick" <note>“If anyone destroys steles or stone animals within a person's grave site: eighty blows.” Chapter 9, § Abandoning or Destroying Property and Crops.</note>. 

> "And any person who, within the boundaries of an imperial mausoleum, has caused a fire by accident shall—if the fire did not spread—receive eighty blows with the long stick and be banished for two years. But if the fire spreads over the forest covering the mountains or damages the trees growing in the burial ground, he shall be punished with one hundred blows and lifelong banishment to a country two thousand miles away" <note>“If a fire is accidentally started within the boundary of a mountain tomb: even if it does not spread, eighty blows and two years of penal servitude; if it spreads to the mountain forests or the trees within the boundary: one hundred blows and exile to two thousand miles.” Chapter 34, § Accidental Fire.</note>.

However, this article is by no means the only one through which the Government protects the trees that, since ancient times, devoted descendants have considered it a sacred duty to plant upon the graves of...

# 大 清 律 例 卷 二 十 三
## 刑 律。 賊 盜 上
### 盜 園 陵 樹 木

## CHAPTER XXIII OF THE LAWS OF THE GREAT QING DYNASTY.
### CRIMINAL LAWS. — REBELLION, ROBBERY AND THEFT, I.
### STEALING TREES FROM MAUSOLEUMS.

### **Fundamental Article.**

凡盜園陵內樹木者皆、不分首從、杖一百徒三年。若盜他人墳塋內樹木者首杖八十、從減一等。

若計贓重於徒杖本罪者各加盜罪一等。

> » Those who steal trees that grow in a mausoleum shall all be punished with one hundred blows with the heavy staff and banishment for three years, regardless of whether they acted as the leaders or as accomplices. And if trees growing within another person’s burial ground are stolen, the leaders shall receive eighty blows with the heavy staff and the accomplices shall be punished one degree less severely.

> » If the punishment for the theft of items of the same value as the stolen trees is more severe than the banishment or the blows prescribed by this article, the punishment for the theft of that amount of loot shall be imposed <note>Compare note 1 at the foot of page 869.</note>, increased by one degree.

» In general, there are boundaries both in front of and behind the high grounds (where the Imperial mausoleums are located) that no one is allowed to cross. If anyone within the **red posts** cuts down trees with the intent to steal, removes earth or stones, builds a kiln to fire pottery or bricks, or sets fire to the hills, they shall be punished as though they had violated the law regarding the theft of sacred objects used in Great Sacrifices, which is beheading, subject to a final imperial decision. Accomplices shall be sent to nearby frontiers for military servitude.

» If such acts occur outside the **red posts** but within the boundaries of the **official mountains**, a distinction is made for certain activities. Gathering firewood, branches, and leaves remains permitted as before. Similarly, the public is not prohibited from digging holes less than ten feet deep to repair houses or graves, taking loose stones from the mountain less than ten feet long, or cutting down trees they have planted themselves. However, those who steal official trees, quarry stone, dig moats, build kilns, or set fire to the hills between the **red posts** and the **white posts** shall be punished one degree less than the penalty for the area within the red posts. The leaders shall be sentenced to military servitude on the nearby frontiers, and accomplices shall receive one hundred blows with the heavy staff and three years of penal servitude.

» If these crimes occur outside the **white posts** but within the **green posts**, the leaders shall receive one hundred blows with the heavy staff and three years of penal servitude; accomplices shall be punished one degree less, receiving ninety blows and two and a half years of penal servitude. If the crime occurs outside the **green posts** but remains within the boundaries of the **official mountains**, the leaders shall receive ninety blows and two and a half years of penal servitude; accomplices shall be punished one degree less, receiving eighty blows and two years of penal servitude.

» If the value of the stolen goods warrants a punishment more severe than the prescribed penal servitude, the penalty shall be increased by one degree in each case.

» Where the boundaries of the **official mountains** extend beyond twenty *li*, the limit shall be set at twenty *li*. If the boundaries are within twenty *li*, the limit shall be where the **official mountain** ends.

» If military officers or soldiers take bribes and intentionally allow these crimes, they shall receive the same punishment as the offender if the crime warrants military or penal servitude. If the bribe is large, they shall be punished more severely for perverting the law based on the amount received. If the offender’s crime warrants beheading, the officers and soldiers shall be sentenced to death by strangulation.

» In cases where no bribe was taken but information was secretly shared, allowing the offender to escape, those involved shall also receive the same punishment as the prisoner if the crime warrants military or penal servitude. If the crime warrants beheading, the punishment for the officers and soldiers shall be reduced to military servitude in the most remote, malaria-infested regions.

» Those who are merely negligent in their guarding duties shall be punished as follows: soldiers shall receive one hundred blows with the heavy staff, and officers shall be turned over to the Ministry for disciplinary action.

» If people with an intent to steal cut down trees belonging to the Government outside the red posts, but still within the limits of the grounds reserved for the Government, or if they open the mountains there to collect stones, dig in the earth to make a canal, erect a kiln for burning pottery or bricks, or set the hills on fire, they shall be punished one degree less severely than if they had done the same thing within the red posts, provided the crime is committed outside the red posts and within the white posts. If the markers are placed beyond twenty miles, the boundaries shall nevertheless be deemed to terminate at twenty; and if they are placed within twenty miles, the boundaries shall be considered to terminate at the points to which the government grounds extend.

If officials or soldiers (settled in the mausoleum grounds as guardians) have knowingly tolerated an offense such as the above in exchange for a bribe, they shall—if the actual culprits are to be punished with life-long or temporary banishment—be imprisoned with them and receive the same punishment. If the stolen (or damaged) items represent a considerable value, their value shall be calculated, and the heavier of the two punishments required by the violated laws shall be imposed on them. Should the perpetrators deserve decapitation, however, those officials and soldiers shall be sentenced to strangulation.

And if they have not received any bribes, but have secretly informed the offenders so that the latter could escape, they shall—if the offenders are to be punished with life-long or temporary banishment—be imprisoned with them and receive the same punishment. But if the offenders are sentenced to decapitation, such officials and soldiers shall be punished one degree less severely and be banished for life to the most distant province with a malarious climate.

Those who have merely been negligent in maintaining the regulations regarding the guarding of the ground shall, if they are soldiers, be punished with one hundred blows with the long stick; and if they are officials, they shall be delivered over to the Board to which they belong to be brought to trial.

### Second Supplementary Article.
#### (Dating from 1801)

Villains who knowingly and privately purchase trees from burial grounds that were stolen and sold by the descendants of the deceased shall have their punishment reduced by one degree compared to the punishment for the descendants who committed the theft and sale.

If the trees were stolen and sold by others, the private buyers—regardless of whether the trees have already been cut—shall, for a first offense, be punished with one hundred blows with the long stick and one month in the cangue (<term>jia-hao</term>). For a second offense, they shall receive one hundred blows and three months in the cangue. For a third offense, according to the law for third-time theft, they shall receive one hundred blows and be banished for life to a distance of three thousand <term>li</term>. Accomplices shall have their punishment reduced by one degree. If the trees have not yet been cut, the punishments shall each be further reduced by one degree. Those who were unaware that the items were stolen shall not be punished.

Those who privately purchase houses, monuments, bricks, tiles, or timber from burial grounds shall all have their punishment reduced by one degree compared to the crime of stealing and selling such items.

Trees and other such property shall be either confiscated by the government or returned to the owner, respectively.

<meta>This page continues the legal codes regarding the protection of burial grounds, specifically focusing on the penalties for those who illegally purchase trees or structures from these sites and the laws regarding the theft of timber from graves.</meta>

<header>THE GRAVE.</header>

If a wicked individual has knowingly bought trees growing in a burial ground, and if it was the sons or grandsons of the deceased who fraudulently sold them to him, he shall receive a punishment one degree less severe than the punishment imposed on the sellers for that sale.

If other individuals have fraudulently sold the trees, the number of trees shall not be counted, nor will it matter whether they have already been cut down or not. Instead, if the buyer has committed the act for the first time, he shall be punished with one hundred blows with the long stick and exposure in the <term>cangue</term> for one month. If he has committed the crime twice, he shall receive the same number of blows and be exposed in the cangue for three months; if three times, he shall fall under the provisions of the supplementary article against those who commit theft for the third time, and be subject to one hundred blows with the long stick, followed by lifelong exile to a region three thousand miles away. His accomplices shall be punished one degree less severely, and their punishment shall be reduced by one further degree if the trees have not yet been cut down; if they have acted unknowingly, they shall go unpunished.

Anyone who has bought buildings, stone tablets, stones, bricks, tiles, or wooden structures belonging to a burial ground shall be punished one degree less severely than the individual who fraudulently sold those things to him.

The trees and other articles shall, in the first case, be confiscated, and, in the second case, be returned to the legal owners.

### **Third Supplementary Article.**
->(Enacted in this form in 1814)<-

盜砍他人墳樹、初犯杖一百枷號一個月、再犯杖一百枷號三個月。計贓重於滿杖者照本律加竊盜罪一等。犯案至三次者即照竊盜三犯本例計贓分別擬以軍流絞候。

其糾黨成羣、旬日之間叠次竊砍至六次以上、而統計樹數又在三十株以上、情同積匪者、無論從前曾否犯案、即照積匪猾賊例擬軍。如連日竊砍在六次以下三次以上、樹數在三十株以下十株以上者、照積匪例量減擬徒。仍各按竊盜本例刺字。

Stealing and cutting trees from another person’s grave: for a first offense, the penalty is one hundred blows with the long stick and one month in the <term>cangue</term>. For a second offense, the penalty is one hundred blows and three months in the cangue. If the value of the stolen goods results in a penalty heavier than the maximum number of blows, the punishment shall be increased by one degree beyond the standard laws for theft. For those who commit the crime three times, they shall be judged according to the specific laws for three-time thieves, with the punishment—ranging from military exile to execution by strangulation—determined by the value of the stolen goods.

Those who form gangs and repeatedly steal and cut trees six or more times within ten days—if the total number of trees is thirty or more and they act like habitual criminals—shall be sentenced to military exile according to the laws for habitual criminals, regardless of whether they have prior offenses. If they have stolen and cut trees between three and six times over several days, and the number of trees is between ten and thirty, they shall be sentenced to penal servitude according to the laws for habitual criminals, with a slight reduction in severity. In all cases, they shall be branded as thieves according to the standard laws.

### Sixth Supplementary Article.
->(Enacted in 1830)<-

If <term>Bannermen</term> or commoners steal <term>ginseng</term> weighing fifty taels or more from within the "red posts," the leader shall be beheaded according to the law for stealing items used in Great Sacrifices to the gods and the Emperor, and a request for a final decision shall be submitted to the throne. Accomplices shall be sent to <term>Xinjiang</term> to serve as slaves for the soldiers. If the amount is twenty taels or more, the leader shall be sent to <term>Xinjiang</term> to serve as a slave for the soldiers, and the accomplices shall receive one hundred blows with the long stick and be banished for three thousand miles. If the amount is ten taels or more, the leader shall be sent to the malarial regions of Yunnan, Guizhou, Guangdong, or Guangxi to serve in the army, and the accomplices shall receive one hundred blows and be banished for two thousand miles. If the amount is less than ten taels, the leader shall be sent to the nearby frontiers to serve in the army, and the accomplices shall receive one hundred blows and three years of penal servitude.

For those who steal <term>ginseng</term> weighing fifty taels or more outside the "red posts" but inside the "white posts," the leader shall be sentenced to strangulation (awaiting confirmation), and the accomplices shall be sent to the nearby frontiers to serve in the army. If the amount is twenty taels or more, the leader shall be sent to the malarial regions of Yunnan, Guizhou, Guangdong, or Guangxi to serve in the army, and the accomplices shall receive one hundred blows and be banished for three thousand miles. If the amount is ten taels or more, the leader shall be sent to the nearby frontiers to serve in the army. If the amount is less than ten taels, the leader shall receive one hundred blows and be banished for three thousand miles, while the accomplices shall receive one hundred blows and three years of penal servitude.

For those who steal outside the "white posts" but inside the "blue posts," they shall be punished according to the laws regarding the theft of ginseng from mountain fields.

If the <term>ginseng</term> was not actually obtained, the punishment for each case shall be reduced by one degree from the established penalties.

Those who knowingly sell the stolen <term>ginseng</term> shall have their punishment reduced by one degree from the penalty for the theft itself; those who were unaware shall not be prosecuted.

Offenders who obtained the <term>ginseng</term>, both leaders and accomplices, shall be branded with the three characters "Thief of Official Ginseng." Those who did not obtain the <term>ginseng</term> and those who sold it shall be exempt from branding. The confiscated items shall be taken by the government. If <term>Bannermen</term> commit these offenses, they shall be removed from the banner rolls and handled in the same manner as commoners.

*Burial of Unclaimed Human Remains by the Authorities. Official Assistance Provided to the Poor in Burying Their Dead.*

If it is admitted that the <term>Cheu li</term> is a work actually dating from the <term>Cheu</term> dynasty, we may infer from it that already in ancient times the Government of China was not indifferent to its subjects being properly buried, and even went so far as to take upon itself the duty of burying human remains neglected by others. Indeed, this book contains certain decrees concerning the burial places of the people and the official control to be exercised over them—decrees which we have reproduced on page 830. Moreover, we read there:

> ”The Officer whose duty it is to guard against carrion insects is responsible for removing decaying human remains. Whenever a Great Sacrifice takes place in (the suburbs of) the capital, he shall order that unclean matter be cleared away in the villages of the district, and that those who have been punished with physical mutilation, people in penal labor, or those wearing mourning clothes are not to be admitted into the suburbs. He shall act in the same way when there is a large assembly of troops or a formal reception for important visitors. When a body is found on the road, he shall order it to be buried and signs to be set up, inscribed with the day and month; the clothes and personal effects found on the body he shall hang up at the residence of the local officer, to be kept there for the relatives. He is also responsible for enforcing the regulations that are in effect in the capital for the treatment of human remains in a state of decomposition.” 1

1 蜡氏掌除髑。凡國之大祭祀令州里除不蠲、禁刑者任人及凶服者以及郊野。大師大賓客亦如之。若有死於道路者則令埋而置楬焉、書其

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the burial of unclaimed human remains by the authorities, moving from the legal codes to the historical and philosophical foundations found in the <term>Cheu li</term> and legends surrounding <term>King Wen</term>.</meta>

<page-num>915</page-num>
<header>CARE FOR UNBURIED CORPSES IN ANCIENT CHINA.</header>

Since the <term>Cheu li</term> is a plan for a constitution that almost everyone has always believed was a product of the era of <term>Wen</term>, the founder of the <term>Cheu</term> dynasty, and since this glorious ruler from the golden days of old has constantly been presented to the nation as a model for all emperors and princes, it naturally follows that the care which the government bestowed upon the mortal remains of the people during his family's reign—as recorded in the <term>Cheu li</term>—has been greatly admired in later times. During the <term>Han</term> dynasty, traditions were common which portrayed <term>Wen</term> as having shown exemplary benevolence toward human remains on various occasions. In a work titled <term>Sin shu</term><sup>1</sup> or "The New Book," attributed to <term>Kia I</term><sup>2</sup>, who lived in the second century B.C., we read:

> ”King <term>Wen</term>, taking a nap during the day, dreamed that a man climbed the walls of the city and exclaimed: ‘I am the dry bones from the northeastern corner. Bury me without delay, with the ceremony appropriate for a king!’ ‘It shall be done,’ <term>Wen</term> answered. Upon waking from his sleep, he ordered his officials to go to the spot and look around there, and they actually found the bones. At that point, the king told them to bury them immediately, as if they were the remains of a ruler. ‘They are not owned by anyone,’ the officials said, ‘so we request that they be buried with the ceremony appropriate for a Great Officer of the fifth rank.’ But the king replied: ‘In my dream, I pledged my word; how can I possibly take it back?’ When the gentry and the common people heard what had happened, they said: ‘Our king does not abandon dry bones he only saw in a dream; how much less will he abandon the living!’ Because of this, his subjects fully entrusted themselves to their sovereign” <sup>3</sup>.

Another work from the Han dynasty, titled *Sin shu*¹ or "A New Series," which was written in the first century B.C. by <term>Liu Hiang</term> (whom our readers encountered on page 433), relates:

> "When King <term>Wen</term> of the <term>Cheu</term> family built a terrace imbued with spiritual influence, they found some human bones while digging the pond. When the officials informed the king of this, he told them to bury them again. They objected, saying the bones were without an owner. But <term>Wen</term> said: 'He who possesses the world is the owner of the world, and he who possesses the whole realm is the owner of it. Therefore, I myself am unquestionably the owner of these bones, so why then do you need to look for their owner elsewhere?' Following this, he ordered them to clothe the bones, place them in a coffin, and re-bury them. When the nation was informed of what he had done, everyone unanimously exclaimed: 'What an excellent man our King <term>Wen</term> is! The blessings he bestows extend even to dry bones; how much more, then, shall they extend to living men!'" ²

It is also recorded that, when the Emperor <term>Chih</term>² occupied the throne in 146 A.D., his consort gave orders for similar acts of charity, publishing a decree to this effect: "In times of old, King <term>Wen</term> buried dry bones, and the people entrusted themselves to his virtuous guidance. Now I commission delegates to act according to this precedent."³

Like master, like man. Several mandarins of their own free will have imitated the example of their imperial masters, motivated, no doubt, also by the hope that blessings of every kind would be bestowed upon them by the poor, abandoned souls who benefited from their charity. Regarding <term>Ts‘ao Pao</term>⁴, a high military commander at the end of the first century of our era, we read: "In more than a hundred places there were stored coffins that had not been committed to the grave. <term>Pao</term> visited these places in person to inquire into the reasons, and the officials told him they were mostly the remains of persons who had died since the <term>Kien wu</term> period (25–57 A.D.) and could not be buried because they had no descendants at all. This moved <term>Pao</term> to such pity that he purchased a plot of vacant ground and buried all those neglected corpses there, setting out sacrificial items to offer to them."⁵ Of <term>Ch‘en Ch‘ung</term>⁶,

->THE GRAVE.<-

...in the first century of our era, the Governor of Kwang-han¹ in the present province of Szĕ-ch'wen, we read:

> "Previously, whenever it was cloudy or rainy, wailings resounded to the south of the city walls of Loh-hien—wailings so loud that they could be heard in the magistrate's mansion. This had been going on for several decades. When the wailings reached Ch'ung’s ears, he pondered the cause and ordered some of his subordinates to go and find out what it was. They reported, upon their return, that during the unrest when the dynasty was in decline, many people had died in that vicinity; because their bones had not been buried, they were still lying on the spot. At this, Ch'ung was moved to compassion. He sighed with emotion and immediately ordered the district magistrates to collect those bones and bury them. From that time on, the wailings ceased."²

This passage is of particular interest because it introduces us to a noteworthy concept which has, through all ages, been the driving force behind the government's conduct regarding unburied human bones. It teaches us that those souls wailed and lamented mainly when the weather was rainy. This is very natural, as unsheltered human souls feel uncomfortable when the weather is bad, just like unsheltered living men. Naturally, this belief has given rise to another: namely, that such souls try by every means in their power to protect themselves from such misery by preventing the rain from falling, or by influencing other invisible powers to scatter the clouds on their behalf. In other words: if people leave the dead unburied, drought follows.

This is a superstition of very long standing. It is already mentioned in a work titled *Kwan-tszĕ*³, "*The Philosopher Kwan*", which is believed to contain the writings of the statesman Kwan Chung (referred to on page 660), who lived in the seventh century...

# DROUGHTS ARE CAUSED BY UNBURIED HUMAN BONES.

...century before our era. "If during the spring season, dry bones and decaying human remains are not cleared away" — so we read in this book — "and withered trees are not cut down and removed, then the summer drought will be extreme"¹. In the *Li ki* (ch. 20, l. 43) this decree appears: "During the first month of spring, dry bones must be covered, and decayed human remains must be buried"².

Since droughts are more feared in China than any other disaster—because they often lead to poor harvests, scarcity, and famine—we should not be surprised to find many instances in the records of authorities burying dry bones to stop this terrible scourge and bring down the rains. The Standard History of the Han dynasty mentions a certain "Zhou Chang <note>Cheu Ch'ang</note>, whose courtesy name was Bozhi <note>Poh-ch'i</note>, a man who possessed a very humane and compassionate character. When he was Governor of Henan <note>Honan</note>, a drought prevailed in the summer of the second year of the Yongchu <note>Yung ch'u</note> period (108 AD). After prayers had been offered in vain for a long time, Chang had the bones of over ten thousand strangers—who had died outside the city walls of Luoyang <note>Loh-yang</note>—collected and buried. Immediately afterward, the rains fell in quantities perfectly suited to the needs of the season, so that the crops were very abundant that year"³. In another work, we read: "In the fourth month of the fifth year of the Taihe <note>T'ai hwo</note> period (481 AD), the emperor (Xiaowen <note>Hiao Wen</note>) issued a decree that read as follows: 'The seasonal rains do not fall, so the tender sprouts of spring wilt. Wherever human bones lie, the authorities must issue orders to have them buried, and none may be left uncovered, so that the spirits may notice these acts and the catastrophe may be averted <note>deprecated</note>'"⁴.

# OFFICIAL CARE FOR UNBURIED HUMAN REMAINS.

"...because of a prevailing drought”<note>“In the third year of the Khien fu period, because of a drought in the third month, exposed skeletons were buried.” The same work, chapter 9, line 7.</note>. During the Ming dynasty, emperors continued to follow the same course of action during times of famine.

For example, regarding Shi Tsung<note>Shi Tsung.</note>, we read: “In the thirty-second year of the Kia tsing period (1553 AD), in the ninth month, he asked Yen Sung: ‘What are we to do, seeing that so many of our subjects are in need of food?’ The reply was: ‘From all directions, starving people are pouring into the capital in search of food, so that in a very short time the price of rice has risen considerably. I humbly propose that several tens of thousands of stones of rice be sold from the government granaries at a fair price.’ The emperor gave his consent and added: ‘We suspect that some of our people must have died on the roads and that their remains, exposed as they are to the burning heat, ought to be given shelter somehow.’ Agreeing with a proposal that Sung made to him for this purpose, he ordered that the censors of the five quarters should investigate whether this was the case within the streets of the capital and bury any such remains. He further ordered that the same should be done outside the capital by the provincial governors and all officials invested with administrative power”<note>The Chinese text reads: 嘉靖三十二年九月上問嚴嵩、民多無食、何以。嵩曰、四方飢民來京求食、一時米價騰貴、請以太倉米數萬石平價發糶。上允之、復曰、我思必有斃諸途者、暴露骸骨宜有所處。嵩請、勅在京行五城御史、在外撫按各督有司查視掩埋. It still makes it incumbent upon the staff of mandarins to provide, within certain limits, for the burial of individuals whose relatives are too poor to fulfill their obligations in this respect. An official decree, included among the Collected Statutes, reads as follows:

> » When anywhere in the provinces dry bones owned by nobody are exposed to the harshness
> » of the weather, the local authorities shall establish a burial ground for free use and
> » take such measures as shall lead to the collection of the remains and their being
> » buried therein; and they shall inform the Board of Rites of these proceedings” ¹.

That the mandarins are, moreover, bound by an official decree to encourage the people to undertake such charitable works has been stated on page 866.

It is no doubt because such duties are imposed upon the mandarinate that, for many years, an institution has existed in Amoy under its control and patronage to provide the poor with free coffins. It is administered in a similar way to the private coffin-distributing societies, of which we have said a few words on pages 863 and following. The local authorities entrust the primary management to one or two so-called *táng-sū* ² or “managers of the business,” who are generally literary graduates. These managers must present an account of the income and expenditure to the authorities every year. The income is derived chiefly from the rent of houses owned by the institution, and further from interest on a small capital invested in a mortgage. A coffin shop, run by a carpenter who has contracted with the managers for the delivery of coffins, is connected with the institution. It is to this so-called “gratuitous storehouse of the authorities for the distribution of coffins” ³ that the poor, who cannot afford to buy receptacles for their dead, must apply.

<header>THE GRAVE.</header>

there is no reason to suppose that Amoy is unique in this respect. There is even less doubt that the authorities in various parts of the Empire, especially in the vicinity of towns and cities, maintain public cemeteries where the poor are permitted to bury their dead without paying for the grave. In these places, neglected remains are buried by the officials themselves in devout imitation of previous rulers and in obedience to the decrees of the current ruling dynasty. As for Amoy, the Memoirs <note>Chapter 2, lines 55 and 56.</note> list no fewer than six graveyards that were laid out between 1797 and 1822 by local magistrates for the Formosan soldiers whose bodies were kept in the Convent of the Seaclams and never claimed by their relatives <note>Compare page 846.</note>, as well as one graveyard for the victims of the 1820 epidemic which, as stated above, led to the creation of the official institution for distributing coffins. Moreover, the Memoirs provide the names of thirty places where public burial grounds for the poor had been established by the authorities in even earlier times; however, no specific details about them are recorded in that work, as its authors did not find any stone memorial inscriptions there. A description of such cemeteries will be provided in Chapter XV.

### *Official Care of the Graves of Emperors and Famous Men of Former Dynasties.*

Providing the remains of every individual, even those of the humblest origin, with a suitable resting place in the earth has been recognized in China throughout the ages as an important duty of the Government. This duty has naturally led to the obligation of providing official care for the graves of rulers of former dynasties, as well as those of their princes and ministers. Since the care of neglected graves and bones is primarily motivated by the hope that the abandoned spirits, benefited by such care, will become favorable to people and cease their vengeful resentment, it naturally follows that such care is given first to the graves and remains of persons who once held the highest power in the State. By virtue of that former power, they now occupy the highest positions in the spirit world and are, consequently, either the most dangerous enemies of man or his most powerful friends and protectors, depending on the circumstances. Such illustrious dead may become especially—

Records in the histories of subsequent dynasties show instances of emperors taking the fate of former occupants of the throne to heart by restoring their mausoleums and enacting decrees to prevent their violation. But we cannot provide translations of all these passages, as their endless repetition would only weary the reader. Let us simply note that, aside from cases that may have escaped our attention, such measures are stated to have been taken in AD 606 by Yang <note>1: 煬.</note>, the second monarch of the House of Sui <note>2: Books of the Sui Dynasty, ch. 3, l. 8.</note>; in the year 630 by T'ai Tsung <note>3: 太宗.</note>, the second emperor of the T'ang dynasty, who also ordained that official sacrifices should be offered in spring and autumn to all the sovereigns, statesmen, and worthies whose tombs had been repaired <note>4: Old Books of the T'ang Dynasty, ch. 3, l. 2; and the New Books, ch. 2, l. 8.</note>; and by Hüen Tsung <note>5: 玄宗.</note> of the same house, who issued an edict for that purpose in 745 <note>6: *Jih chi luh*, ch. 15.</note>. 

But no monarch of any dynasty ever extended his care over as many graves as T'ai Tsu <note>7: 太祖.</note>, the founder of the Sung dynasty. In the very same year that he ascended the throne (AD 960), he decreed that imperial mausoleums or the tombs of historical figures of the past that had been left to the mercy of wood gatherers and the harshness of wind and rain should be placed by the authorities under the protection of families specifically appointed for that purpose, and repaired if damaged. Three years later, this provisional decree was followed by another, specifying what was to be done. It stipulated that the graves of Yao and Shun <note>8: Concerning the alleged graves of these worthies, see page 418.</note> and four other mythical rulers whom Chinese historians place at the beginning of their chronology, the sepulchers of Yü, T'ang, Wen, and Wu <note>9: See page 666.</note>, the mausoleums of the founder of the Early Han dynasty and the founder of the Later Han dynasty, and those of the first two emperors of the House of T'ang, should henceforth be guarded by five families each, and a bullock should be sacrificed there every year in spring and autumn. ## CHAPTER XII.

### FUNG-SHUI.

#### 1. Introductory Notice.

We have several times had to refer in this work to a custom of the Chinese of placing graves in a situation that they believe will bring the occupants happiness and comfort, while at the same time securing the prosperity of themselves, both in this world and in the world to come. In connection with this, we have mentioned certain theories popularly called Fung-shui$^1$ or Wind and Water. We will now consider this custom in detail and try to answer the question: What is Fung-shui?

The answer is suggested by the word itself. Fung 風 means the wind, and shui 水 means the water from the clouds which the wind distributes over the world; thus, the two words combined indicate the climate. In China, climate is regulated, in the first instance, by the winds, which bring dry or rainy weather depending on whether they blow from the North in winter, or from the South or Southwest in summer. Fung-shui, consequently, denotes the atmospheric influences which hold absolute power over the fate of man, as none of the principal requirements of life can be produced without favorable weather and rains. In a figurative sense, however, Fung-shui means a *quasi-scientific system, supposed to teach men where and how to build graves, temples, and dwellings, in order that the dead, the gods, and the living may be located there exclusively, or as far as possible, under the auspicious influences of Nature.*

This system is by no means a creation of modern times. It originated in ancient ages from the then-prevailing beliefs—easily traceable in books—that the inhabitants of this world all live under the absolute power of the influences of heaven and earth, and that everyone wishing to ensure their own happiness

<note>1 風水.</note>

<summary>This chapter introduces Fung-shui (Feng Shui), explaining its literal meaning as "wind and water" and its significance as a system for aligning human structures with natural and atmospheric influences. It traces the origins of the practice to ancient Chinese beliefs regarding the power of heaven and earth over human fate.</summary>

must live in perfect harmony with those influences. If—so the reasoning went—human acts disagree with the almighty <term>Tao</term><note>1 道.</note> or "Path," the unalterable Course of Nature, conflicts will follow in which man, being the weaker party, must inevitably yield and become the sufferer. This reverential awe of the mysterious influences of Nature is the fundamental principle of an ancient religious system usually called <term>Taoism</term> by foreigners. Popular opinion in China, as well as the experts on <term>Fung-shui</term> theories, are unanimous in considering Fung-shui to be almost as ancient as China itself.

It follows from the above that building graves, houses, villages, and towns in accordance with Fung-shui theories is looked upon by the nation as an absolute necessity—as indispensable because it is impossible to withdraw oneself from the power of the forces of Nature. It is no wonder, then, that Fung-shui holds the nation in its grip and reigns supreme throughout the Empire, across its whole length and breadth. It derives prestige and sanctity from its antiquity, which gave birth to the principal dogmas and concepts upon which it is based. Because its leading ideas are the same as those of Chinese philosophy in general, it commands the sympathy of everyone as a system that embraces whatever combined human wisdom and insight have suggested as practically useful over many ages. It is considered in China to be the greatest benefactor of mankind, though in reality, as we shall see soon, it is one of their greatest scourges.

The <term>hiao</term>, the pious reverence which every Chinese person gives to their deceased parents and nearest relations, naturally compels them to place their graves in a location where they may find themselves under the same beneficial influences of Nature that they would desire to concentrate upon their own home. In this way, they not only ensure their ancestors' rest and comfort but also make them well-disposed toward themselves, arousing in them feelings of gratitude that must necessarily bear fruit in the form of various blessings showered upon their descendants. Besides, the heavens are Nature's great source of life, for it is they who distribute warmth, light, and rain; life and vigor are naturally given to those souls that dwell in graves placed under the full influence of the heavens. Then, they are enabled to act vigorously as protectors of their descendants and to distribute liberally among them

the vitality that they themselves borrow from the heavens, thus promoting the birth of sons, which is the most coveted of all blessings in China. This conviction is confirmed by the fact that it is not only the living who profit from this, but also the souls themselves; a numerous offspring of sons ensures for the dead sacrifices and worship for many generations to come and, moreover, high rank in the spirit world, where those surrounded by a large clan will be the bearers of power and influence, just as in this world.

Thus, as Dr. Edkins has wisely remarked <note>1 The Chinese Recorder and Missionary Journal, vol. IV, p. 275.</note>, "filial piety which, in obedience to the lessons of ancient and modern mentors of the nation, takes good care of the graves of parents and grandparents, receives a material reward; on the other hand, the lack of it invites a retribution involving poverty, sickness, loss of descendants, and social degradation." Through <term>Fung-shui</term>, graves are turned into mighty instruments of blessing or punishment, the spirits of the ancestors dwelling within them being the divinities of the nation, with whose protection and goodwill all social happiness is intimately bound up. But souls do not only dwell in graves. They also reside in tablets exposed for worship on domestic altars, and in temples specifically built to shelter them. There, too, for the exact same reasons, they ought to be made to live under the favorable influences of Nature. Consequently, <term>Fung-shui</term> is firmly entwined with house-building and the construction of ancestral temples. It plays an important part even in the erection of altars and sanctuaries dedicated to gods and saints of whatever kind or description.

As an essential part of the Chinese religion in its broadest sense, <term>Fung-shui</term> demands a place among the subjects to be treated in this work. In the present volume we must, however, confine ourselves to noting the part it plays in grave-building, and reserve for another volume most of what we have to say on its influence in other branches of the religious system.

Since Nature has never been studied in China in a scientific manner, <term>Fung-shui</term> is not based on any sound ideas acquired by an experimental and critical survey of the heavens and the earth. Starting with the hazy notion that Nature is a living organism, the breath of which pervades everything and produces the varied conditions of heaven and earth, and with some dogmatic formulas to be found in ancient works and trusted as verdicts of the most profound human wisdom, <term>Fung-shui</term> is a mere chaos

...of childish absurdities and refined mysticism, held together by fallacious reasoning into a system which is, in reality, a ridiculous caricature of science. But it is highly instructive from an ethnographic point of view. The errors into which the human mind may fall when, unguided by practical observation, it searches for a logical knowledge of Nature, are more clearly demonstrated by this than by any other phenomenon in the life and history of nations. It fully reveals the dense cloud of ignorance that hangs over the entire Chinese people; it exposes the low condition of their mental culture and the fact that natural philosophy in that part of the globe is a massive pile of learning without a single trace of true knowledge in it.

Since it encompasses the entire scope of Chinese natural philosophy, we do not have space here to present the <term>Fung-shui</term> system to our readers in detail. Such a work would require many years of painstaking study and yet yield only meager results; in fact, the webs of absurd, childish speculation built up by the system are hardly worthy of serious study. All we can provide here is a very brief outline—a rough sketch—drawn primarily from information we received in Amoy from professional experts and supported by evidence gathered from native literature.

Furthermore, to thoroughly understand what <term>Fung-shui</term> is, it is quite unnecessary to examine and untangle the jumble of absurdities that make up its details. A basic knowledge of the main principles upon which it is founded will suffice, if those principles are understood in the way the people and the practitioners of the art understand and apply them. <term>Fung-shui</term> is, in fact, a practical art. Its theories, as explained in books, are seldom noticed even by the most distinguished experts among the initiated. Being a pseudo-science, it is practiced as a pseudo-science—that is to say, as charlatanism. Every member of the educated class considers himself an expert in it simply because he has studied the Classics and understands the leading principles of national philosophy. The people even consider themselves morally obligated to possess some expertise in <term>Fung-shui</term> matters, and the common proverb says: "No son of man should be ignorant of matters relating to grounds and mountains, nor of the medical art" <note>1 As a son, one must not be ignorant of geomancy (mountains) or medicine.</note>. It is no wonder, then, that even the least educated among the people show an astounding amount of knowledge about Fung-shui. Women and children may be heard chattering and talking about it with great authority; and when there is a dispute about imaginary injuries done to the Fung-shui of a grave or a house, old matrons are generally the loudest in expressing a firm opinion.

Since every Chinese person is more or less initiated into the secrets of the system, a practical interaction with the people is sufficient for a foreigner to gain a reasonably clear idea of what it is and the role it plays in the various branches of religious life. Our explanation will be found to deviate very little from that which was given twenty-two years ago by Dr. Eitel in a treatise entitled: *Feng-shui, or the Rudiments of Natural Science in China*. Minor differences that our readers may observe between the conclusions of this distinguished Sinologist and our own are to be attributed chiefly to the fact that his investigations were made in Canton or Hong Kong, and ours in the southeastern part of the province of Fuhkien.

### 2. Fung-shui as regulated by High Grounds and Watercourses.

In China, the people are not bound, either by law or custom, to bury the dead in cemeteries. Everyone has full liberty to bury his dead wherever he chooses, provided he owns the ground or holds it by some title acquired from the legal owner. The question of whether a spot is suitable for a burial ground is decided by Fung-shui theories.

Fung-shui, or *Hong-súi* according to the local pronunciation in Amoy and the surrounding districts, is known by several other names. The principal among these is <term>Khan-yü</term><note>1. 堪輿 (Kanyü: a term for geomancy).</note>, pronounced *Kham-ú* in the Amoy language and used especially in a literary style. *Khan* means the canopy of heaven, and *yü* a cart or chariot, or, metaphorically, the earth which contains and bears the human

race; the term <term>Khan-yü</term> may accordingly be translated as: "the system which occupies itself with heaven and earth." A third name is <term>Ti li</term> (Am. *Tê lí*)¹, "the natural influences that pervade the earth." The experts or professors of the art, who make a living from searching out favorable spots for burying the dead and building houses and temples, are called <term>sien sheng</term>² (Am. *sien sing*) or <term>shi</term>³ (Am. *su*), with the prefix <term>Fung-shui</term>, <term>Khan-yü</term> or <term>Ti li</term>. <term>Sien sheng</term> signifies "an earlier born man," and may be rendered as "an elder, a master, or a professor"; <term>shi</term> means "a leader or a master"; and both words are terms of respect denoting men of learning, including teachers, soothsayers, quack-doctors, etc. Foreigners are in the habit of calling the <term>Fung-shui</term> experts <term>geomancers</term>, which is correct, provided the earth is also considered as a depository of influences continuously poured down upon it by the celestial sphere. Besides the six terms above, the professors are often styled <term>Yin Yang sien sheng</term>⁴ (Am. *Im ióng sien sing*) or <term>Yin Yang shi</term>⁵ (Am. *Im ióng su*), "Masters of the Yin and Yang," which two supreme powers of the Universe are respectively identified with Earth and Heaven, as our readers know.

The word <term>Fung-shui</term> indicates that the first thing to be attended to in selecting a spot for a grave, house, temple, village or town, is wind or air, <term>fung</term>. Noxious winds must as far as possible be prevented from striking a tomb or building at the back or side. Hence, a mountain slope flanked by two ridges forking out from it, and affording a rather wide view in front, is deemed to be good ground for burying and building, especially if those ridges form a double fence, both visible from the grave or building. Their utility is not in the least reduced by distance. Even when they are so far off that they are hardly discernible, professors take them into account as elements of the highest importance, for theoretically they screen off the winds, and, in <term>Fung-shui</term> matters, theory and speculation are everything.

Pernicious and life-destroying influences of the winds or the air are denoted in the special <term>Fung-shui</term> nomenclature by the term <term>fung shah</term>⁶ (Am. *hong soah*), "noxious effects of the winds." There exist various means to ward them off. Suppose it is feared they will burst forth from some break in the mountains, it is then

The experts or professors of this art, who earn a living by searching for favorable spots to bury the dead and build houses and temples, are called <term>sien sheng</term> <note>Amoy dialect: sien sing</note> or <term>shi</term> <note>Amoy dialect: su</note>, with the prefix <term>Fung-shui</term>, <term>Khan-yü</term>, or <term>Ti li</term>. <term>Sien sheng</term> means "an earlier born man" and can be translated as "an elder, a master, or a professor"; <term>shi</term> means "a leader or a master." Both words are respectful terms for men of learning, including teachers, diviners, folk doctors, and others. Foreigners typically call <term>Fung-shui</term> experts <term>geomancers</term>, which is correct, provided the earth is also viewed as a storehouse of influences constantly poured down upon it by the celestial sphere. In addition to the six terms mentioned above, these professors are often called <term>Yin Yang sien sheng</term> <note>Amoy dialect: Im ióng sien sing</note> or <term>Yin Yang shi</term> <note>Amoy dialect: Im ióng su</note>, or "Masters of the Yin and Yang." As our readers know, these two supreme powers of the Universe are associated with Earth and Heaven respectively.

The word <term>Fung-shui</term> indicates that the first priority in selecting a location for a grave, house, temple, village, or town is wind or air (<term>fung</term>). Harmful winds must, as much as possible, be prevented from hitting a tomb or building from the back or the side. For this reason, a mountain slope flanked...

It is considered necessary to build the grave in such a way that this opening cannot be seen from the spot where the corpse lies, or so that it is hidden from view by some mountain boulder, house, or other object. In many cases, the dangerous gap is artificially made invisible by means of stones piled up at a correct distance from the grave, in accordance with the instructions given by Fung-shui professors. These so-called <term>Fung-shui t'ah</term> <note>風水塔</note> or "Fung-shui pagodas" are very numerous in the mountainous provinces of the South. As a rule, they are so far from the spot they are supposed to protect that, in reality, they do not screen it from the wind at all; this proves that Fung-shui wisdom in evading dangers is on a level with that of the ostrich.

Since gaps or breaks in the mountains are harmless to a grave if they are invisible from the place where the corpse lies, it follows that the danger may be avoided by burying the corpse deep enough. However, this method is not very often used because, in most cases, it would cause the dead to lose sight of the protecting ridges and brows of the mountains, thus destroying their beneficial effects. For, as Fung-shui combines its own logic with wisdom, it cannot help but conclude that, just as unseen dangers are no dangers, unseen protection is no protection.

As a matter of course, a grave surrounded by mountains without any gaps or deficiencies is hardly obtainable. Nor is it easy to find a spot from which the person buried there can "see" a surrounding range of hills. These difficulties are cleverly overcome by building a well-finished artificial ridge around the back and the sides of the tomb. This is a low embankment of earth (see Plate XXIV), which also serves to prevent rainwater flowing down from the surrounding high ground from washing away the <term>tumulus</term> <note>burial mound</note>. Our readers know that Chinese coffins are usually high, bulky, and, among the wealthy, considerably broader at the head than at the foot (see pages 319 and following). When such a coffin is buried in the proper way—specifically, with the head up against the slope and in a shallow pit so the dead do not lose sight of the brow of the mountains—the <term>tumulus</term> thrown up over it naturally takes an elliptical shape, the broad side of which, like that of the coffin, lies highest. This mound, in turn, determines the shape of the embankment. Because the latter surrounds the three larger sides, its form necessarily becomes that of a horseshoe, or, even more often, of

Many of these embankments are built of masonry, or of puddled clay mixed with lime and plastered over with white mortar, forming low walls one or two feet in height. A few are made of solid granite. Several graves have a double fence, one of solid masonry or granite and then a much broader one of earth, the latter always being on the outside of the first (see Plate XXV). Both are called in Amoy *bōng moa* <note>墓垞 or 墓廡</note>, which may be translated as "the piazza or side gallery of the grave," the term being an allusion to the verandas on the right and left of mansions and temples.

A *bōng moa* never extends along the front. For, according to theory, there is no necessity at all to ward off any *fung shah* from that side, as graves and buildings of every kind, though they may in fact face any point of the compass, are supposed to be turned toward the mild and blessed south—the cradle of warmth, light, life, and productive summer rains. Furthermore, there are strict reasons forbidding the presence of objects that obstruct the view in front of graves, which we shall review on pages 945 and following.

As far as we know, no attempt is ever made to attract the good influences of the winds toward graves, houses, or temples. Perhaps no means to achieve this have been invented, as they are totally unnecessary because of the prevailing notion that good and beneficial influences naturally reach their full potential wherever counteracting or neutralizing evil influences are sufficiently warded off.

The Chinese attempts to control the winds which strike the graves of the dead, the temples of the gods, and the homes of living men are by no means simply intended to protect those beings from the harshness of the climate and its immediate consequences, such as sickness and ailments of all kinds. The scope of the Fung-shui system extends much farther. Since the climate is ruled by the winds, the winds become the cause of all things, good or evil, which Nature showers down upon this earth. Therefore, the grand art of controlling their influences is the art of regulating the fortunes and happiness of mankind. Winds blowing from the North and Northeast, as they generally do in...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the influences of the winds and rains in Chinese culture, specifically how they relate to the principles of Feng-shui and agricultural prosperity.</meta>

<page-num>943</page-num>
<header>INFLUENCES OF THE WINDS AND RAINS.</header>

China, from October until February or March, freeze the northern provinces, and in the South, they scarcely send down a single drop of rain, thus destroying the plant kingdom and halting agricultural pursuits. The southern or south-western winds which prevail during the other half of the year, on the contrary, produce warmth and growth, blessing the empire with copious rains and abundant crops. But, should these monsoons deviate from their regular course, or become disturbed, calamities are sure to follow. Dry winds in summer result in poor crops and scarcity, dooming the people to starvation. When typhoons rage, whole provinces in the South are flooded by rains, which cause the streams and rivers to overflow and destroy the crops in countless fields. No wonder, therefore, that the Chinese people are deeply conscious of their dependence on the winds, and feel the greatest reverence and sympathy for a system which promises everyone protection against their harmful influences, ever holding up before their eyes the unquestionable motto:

-> "When the winds (*fung*) blow in harmony and the rains (*shui*) fall regularly, the kingdom shall flourish and the people will live in peace and comfort" ¹. <-

This principle is found in a very old book, namely the *Historical Records*, in the following words: "If the Way (*Tao*) of the Universe is such that cold and heat do not come in their proper season, diseases will spread; and if it is such that winds and rains do not come at the proper time, there will be famine" ².

Since winds primarily control the influences of nature upon the earth, Feng-shui practitioners are perfectly correct in considering them the first and principal element of their system. They do not, however, go so far as to attribute constant beneficial influences to certain points of the compass and harmful influences to others. Even the cold and harsh blasts from the North may be beneficial, and the mildest southern breezes extremely dangerous, depending on whether they have been in contact with certain celestial or terrestrial influences. Every geomancer holds his own private views on this subject, which it is scarcely possible, and certainly quite useless, to endeavor to untangle.

Nor do geomancers devote less of their attention to the chief results of the favorable operation of the winds—namely, rains and water—indicated by the second syllable of the word *Fung-shui*. Water

<meta>This page continues the explanation of Feng-shui principles, transitioning from the influence of winds to the vital importance of water (shui) and its spiritual agencies (shui shen) in determining the prosperity of the living and the peace of the dead.</meta>

<page-num>944</page-num>
<header>THE GRAVE.</header>

As water is an element indispensable to life, and especially necessary for an agricultural people like the Chinese, neither living men in their dwellings, nor disembodied souls in their graves and temples, nor divinities in their sanctuaries, can ever be at ease or enjoy prosperity unless its blessed influences are concentrated upon those spots. These influences are called <term>shui shen</term>¹ (Amoy dialect: *tsúi sîn*): "aquatic spiritual agencies."

Rivers and rivulets, brooks and gullies, lakes, tanks, ponds, and seas, being the carriers of the waters showered down from the heavens, are all carriers of these <term>shui shen</term>. Even when perfectly dry, they are still regarded as such, as Feng-shui philosophy relies on its own theories. The sources of the watercourses which cross inhabited glens and valleys, and the mountains and mountain ranges in which they take their rise, are specifically held to control human destiny because they send down the precious fluid on which agriculture depends. Their position is carefully considered whenever a site for a grave, house, or temple has to be selected.

Neither a wet nor a dry watercourse is allowed to run straight toward a grave, a human dwelling, or a sanctuary. Otherwise, this building would become an obstacle in the way of the descending aquatic influences—even a rude declaration by the living that they do not desire to have anything to do with these influences. Without a doubt, the insulted element would avenge itself by accumulating evil on the spot, or, in any case, by flowing away to the right and left without benefiting the place in the least. A good Feng-shui may be obtained when the water flows down from the right or left, either in front of the spot in question or at the back of it, and then, passing along the front, finds its outlet in a lateral direction. It is all-important, however, that the water, in flowing away, should be invisible from the place where the corpse lies, or from the tabernacle in which the soul or the god is seated, as, otherwise, the soul or god would be able to see the beneficial aquatic influences flowing away and thus derive no advantage from them.

As no water may flow down straight in front, it follows that it is always dangerous if the prospect in front is screened by a mountain slope which may send down water in that direction. Besides, such a slope may obstruct the free natural course of the aquatic influences coming down from the opposite side and consequently, in the case of a grave, obstruct the free expansion

<header>OBJECTS OBSTRUCTING THE PROSPECT IN FRONT.</header>
