Hence, it is an established principle of geomancy that "Feng-shui which is too cramped"—*hong-súi khah pik* <note>Feng-shui that is narrow and cramped.</note>, as the Amoy Chinese say—is bad Feng-shui. This does not mean that mountains in front are always harmful. They may even have a beneficial influence if they are located at a sufficient distance or meet certain conditions; and it is the professors who decide this through their wise calculations.

Bad effects may also be felt by a grave if walls, houses, or boulders obstruct the view in front. For this reason, the walls surrounding the gardens and grounds of European houses in some of the Treaty Ports often have a section of open-worked masonry, or a few small holes, made there at the request of the owner of a grave behind it, for the purpose of preserving both his prosperity and his descendants from destruction. For the same reason, in the province of Fuhkien, trees or shrubs are hardly ever allowed to grow in front of a grave. Everything that happens to take root there is ruthlessly destroyed, and geomancers, with the remarkable sharpness and wit that distinguish them, are constantly pointing out herbs and shrubs that are harmful. However, trees growing at the back or the sides of a grave are generally considered beneficial, as they have the same effect as a *bōng moa*. Yet, since grounds deemed suitable for burial are usually crowded with graves, such trees are rare, because they might exert bad influences upon the graves of others. Consequently, grave sites in the mountainous South are generally dreary wastes, sparsely covered with grass and weeds and appearing poorly suited to serve the dead as a pleasant resting place—especially in summer, when they are scorched by the tropical heat. But such considerations do not seem to occur to the Chinese when the question is asked: where shall we bury our dead?

This fact is also attributed to the doctrine that Feng-shui must not be cramped in front of a grave; namely, that stone images of men and animals have seldom, if ever, been erected there in recent times. We have already called attention to this point on page 822. It proves that objects nowadays considered harmful to a grave were not regarded as such in former times, and it illustrates the powerful hold Feng-shui has upon the nation, since the highest classes have now given up...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Feng Shui principles regarding the surroundings of a grave, transitioning from physical obstructions to the artificial control of environmental influences like wind and water.</meta>

...in obedience to a time-honored privilege which, being granted by the Sons of Heaven <note>The Emperors of China</note>, brought the greatest honor and distinction to the memory of their dead.

Just as the wind-driven <note>Originally "æolian"</note> influences can be controlled, so too can those of the water element be artificially managed. Should no natural watercourse run past a grave, house, or temple, this deficiency is often corrected by building a tank in front of it to catch the water that flows down from all sides when it rains; this tank becomes a reservoir for aquatic influences, from which they spread beneficially over the immediate surroundings. In large mansions, palaces, and temples, the tank is located in the center of the courtyard, which in ancient times was painted partially or entirely red; therefore, these tanks are generally called *tan ch'i* <note>丹墀 - Vermilion Courtyards</note>. As a rule, they are curved on one side; the opposite straight side runs parallel to the front of the grave or building, while the curved side faces away from it. Great temples and palaces have the largest and deepest tanks, which are generally paved at the bottom and lined on all sides with square blocks of granite, marble, or dolomite. Those in front of graves are small, rarely deeper than one or two feet, and made of plastered masonry or earth mixed with lime (compare Pl. XXIV and XXV); in a few cases they are square, and sometimes circular.

The Feng Shui doctrines prescribe that the greatest attention should be given to the opening through which the water leaves such a tank; for, as our readers will easily understand, it completely controls the influences of the *shui shen* <note>Water spirits or aquatic energy</note> accumulated in the tank. It must be neither too small nor too large; in other words, the water must not flow away either too slowly or too quickly. The location of the opening is also calculated with the utmost precision and must, in any case, be invisible from the spot where the corpse lies or, in the case of a temple, from the shrine occupied by the ancestral tablets or the images of the gods. It makes no difference if such tanks are dry. They do not lose their effectiveness because of this, any more than brooks or gullies do. Those in front of graves are often made without any intention of being filled with water, which keeps the grave drier and less exposed to the attacks of termites.

As stated on pages 436 and 437, they are mentioned in Chinese literature in connection with the mausoleums of Hoh Lü and his daughter, who lived in the fifth century before Christ, and also in certain accounts of the burial of Shi Hwang and the imperial mausoleums of the Han dynasty. We may note here, by the way, that the curious custom mentioned on page 101—of coffining the dead at flood tide or while several pails of sea water, taken at high tide, are standing in the same room—likewise belongs to those practices intended to concentrate aquatic influences in the graves. Nobody doubts that this water, drawn at *high tide*, will *fully* work upon the corpse while it is being encoffined, and its influences are thus, so to speak, enclosed in the coffin and afterwards deposited in the tomb.

Undoubtedly, it is with the same object of imbuing corpses with aquatic influences that the Chinese of Amoy place them under a cover embroidered with clouds and dragons while they are being conveyed to their last resting place; dragons have been the emblems of fertilizing rains in China since very ancient times (see page 181). We may, furthermore, again refer to our statement made on page 213, that it is considered a very auspicious omen when rain falls while a grave pit is being filled up: indeed, Nature itself then showers down its most beneficial influences, which cannot help but yield precious fruits of happiness to the offspring of the deceased man.

The topography of the ground is also important in another respect. Landscape features are carriers and storehouses for the influences of the heavens, and as such, they can work most beneficially upon the fate of man.

Our readers already know what these influences are, namely the so-called *t'ien khi*¹ or "Celestial Breath," the energy of the Yang or highest power of the universe, specifically identified (compare page 22) with Heaven, as it encompasses light and warmth. It shares supreme rule in nature with the "Terrestrial Breath" *ti khi*², or the energy of the Yin principle, which represents darkness and cold and is identified with Earth (page 22). Through the cooperation of these two principles, life is created; in other words, as Yang and Yin alternately rule in nature and blend their influences, they cause constant growth and decay, life and death, and the annual cycle of creation and destruction. Indeed, the *Li ki* (ch. 38, l. 11) explicitly states:

> "Everything that exists is created after Heaven and Earth
> have joined together"³, and (ch. 20, l. 37) "when in the first
> month of the spring season the Celestial Breath descends and
> the Terrestrial Breath ascends, Heaven and Earth unite har-
> moniously and the plant kingdom is revealed and set in
> motion"⁴. The *Yih king* also declares that: "When Heaven and
> Earth exert their influences, all things are transformed and given
> life"⁵.

<header>CELESTIAL AND TERRESTRIAL BREATH.</header>

who lived in the twelfth century, formally subscribed to these ancient doctrines, declaring that "the Two Breaths, by uniting and exciting each other, produce and reproduce everything."¹

As a matter of course, in every part of the ground, in every chain of mountains, in every bluff or rock, Nature has laid down a certain quantity of **Yin** or **Terrestrial Breath**. But, according to the above doctrines, it cannot exert any life-producing influences unless it is at the same time imbued with some **Yang** or **Celestial Breath**. Geomancers alone are capable of deciding whether this latter is represented in an adequate proportion, and whether the ground has any value for building purposes and grave making. They derive their conclusions from the outlines and forms of the surroundings. Starting from the fact that the celestial sphere has, since ancient times, been divided into four quarters, namely the **Azure Dragon**, the **Red Bird**, the **White Tiger**, and the **Black Tortoise**, identified respectively with the East, the South, the West, and the North (compare page 317), their wise predecessors have taught, over a long series of ages, that no part of the soil can be fully impregnated with the beneficial influences of Heaven unless those four quarters operate upon it together; that is to say, unless it is surrounded by mountains, bluffs, boulders, or buildings which can be identified with those symbolic animals. Graves and buildings being, in theory, facing South, they must have a Tiger on the right or theoretical western side, a Dragon on the left, a Tortoise at the back, and a Bird in front. All-important is the presence of a Tiger and a Dragon. For these animals represent all that is expressed by the word **Fung-shui**, namely both wind and water influences—Confucius being reputed to have said that "the winds follow the tiger,"² and the Dragon having, since time immemorial, played the part of chief spirit of water and rain in Chinese cosmological mythology.

So, for instance, Amoy is unanimously declared by all the wise men of the town to be indebted for its prosperity to two knolls flanking the inner harbor, and commonly called *Hó-t'aó soan*³ or "Tiger-head Hill" and *Lîng-t'aó soan*⁴ or "Dragon-head Hill."

The costs of these improvements were paid by several wealthy citizens anxious to promote their own prosperity and that of their fellow townsmen. It then gathers its beneficial influences in three large reservoirs or lakes dug on the west side, and finally flows past the entire front of the inner Palace, where it bears the name of The Golden Water (compare page 635). Its course, therefore, perfectly aligns with the principles which are applied to grave brooks and grave tanks (compare page 944).

In thus making use of the configurations which render the relative position and extent of the influences of the four Celestial Animals favorable or unfavorable, there is room for countless combinations. Every mountain, rock, bluff, house, or tower may form a good Animal, and at one spot serve for a Tiger and at the same time as a Dragon, Bird, or Tortoise for another spot, the fancy and creative ingenuity of geomancers being allowed free scope in all cases. Sadly, however, the value of such predictions is generally somewhat diminished by the variety of opinions prevailing among geomancers, each of whom is filled with professional jealousy and holds the rather arrogant conviction that his own wisdom is always necessary to correct the opinions pronounced by his colleagues.

Dragons and Tigers are by no means equally important in the Feng-shui system. Professors are accustomed to say: "Any spot is auspicious that has a Dragon and no Tiger; but a spot is not necessarily inauspicious if it has only a Tiger and no Dragon" <note>3. 有龍無虎亦爲吉、有虎無龍未是凶 (Having a Dragon and no Tiger is also auspicious; having a Tiger and no Dragon is not necessarily unlucky).</note>. This preeminence of the Dragon is due in the first place to its heading the list of the four Celestial Animals and to its being the emblem of spring (see p. 317), which is the first of the seasons, and further, to its identification with Water, the all-important element without which all Feng-shui is null and void. Practically, Feng-shui professors are accustomed to speak of a Dragon when referring in reality to a Dragon and Tiger; in short, the word Dragon encompasses the high grounds in general, and the water-streams which have their sources within them or wind their way through them. Such combinations are generally indicated by special fancy names, mostly derived from objects they resemble. These names, too, are believed to exercise a mighty influence upon the destiny of those who live under the Feng-shui of such configurations; all of them are calculated to call up in the mind ideas associated with either felicity or misfortune.

The doctrine that the configuration of the ground is a sure index to the presence of celestial influence is better understood when we bear in mind that objects—such as soul tablets and images—which call to mind spirits or so-called *shen*, are generally believed by the Chinese to be inhabited by such spirits. Consequently, they are made for the dead and the gods so that the latter may radiate their beneficial influences from them over mankind. Since such *shen* are composed of *Yang* (compare page 110) or Celestial Breath, the Chinese have every reason to believe that the *shen* of the four Animals or quarters of the sphere will settle in objects such as hills, mountains, or other configurations which, by their shape and situation, call them to mind.

The active operation produced in the earth by the proper intermixing of the Celestial and Terrestrial Breath is denoted by the term *shan ling*<note>1. 山靈 (Shan ling).</note>, "effective operation of high grounds"; we might call it the living and active spirit of a configuration. Each configuration is a collection of mere lifeless forms when the two Breaths confined within it are latent and inactive. Its Feng-shui in such cases is, as geomancers express it, dead.

Like a current of vital power, the *shan ling* flows in every direction through favorable sites, especially through the ledges and edges of hills which geomancers cleverly identify with the limbs of Dragons, Tigers, Tortoises, and Birds. Thanks to the wisdom and experience of these men, it is possible to learn which limbs are thoroughly imbued with *shan ling* and are, accordingly, the most preferable for making graves or building houses. Sloping ledges are generally considered to be favorable spots in this respect; indeed, even a child can understand that *shan ling* with a descending motion must develop great vigor and energy, particularly at the end of its downward course. # THE ACTIVE SPIRIT OF CONFIGURATIONS.

Wherever in its downward course it meets with some elevation sufficient to absorb and collect it, or to impede its course and prevent it from flowing away, such sites are called <term>ling meh</term>¹ or "(shan-) ling pulses," where the spirit lives and throbs just as the vital power does in the pulses of a man. Geomancers identify the ledges in question by the term <term>ling tsih</term>²: "backbones of the (shan-) ling."

A body filled with vitality is generally a breathing body. Geomancers, inverting this principle, teach that ground formations possess no <term>shan ling</term> unless they contain what is called <term>ling khi</term>³, "(shan-) ling breath." Again, it is the configuration which indicates the presence of the latter. It is found exclusively in undulating ground; hollow, flat, or straight-lined formations do not breathe and are therefore of little or no use for burial or building purposes. In preparing graves, attention should also be paid to the fact that hard, rocky soil is breathless; compact, reddish loam, on the contrary, is full of breath and life. Consequently, it prevents the rapid decay of the coffin and the corpse, making the bones hard, white, and suitable for binding the soul to the grave for a long time. Besides, termites and other voracious insects do not inhabit such loamy soil, a fact which geomancers attribute to the influence of the breath. This breath can be active or latent, accumulated or expanded, powerful or weak, floating on the surface or hidden underneath, pure or mixed with other substances, and the shrewdness of the experts must detect all these qualities. Due to various circumstances, which they alone know how to trace, the breath may also partly or entirely vanish, which is proof that the operation of the <term>shan ling</term> has been stopped and the <term>Feng-shui</term> of the spot is dying or dead.

Even though a configuration may be such as to leave no doubt about the presence of an abundant quantity of <term>Yang</term> and <term>Yin</term>, it is not yet certain that these two Breaths produce <term>shan ling</term> and would thus work together beneficially for the grave. They may be inert and exercise no influence upon each other; however, this state of inactivity cannot last long. In the end, they must awake from their torpor, as happens in spring when they fill the Universe with vital energy and revitalize the plant kingdom. Not infrequently at burials, geomancers deem it necessary to arouse the two Breaths from their lethargy so that the family may immediately begin to benefit from the grave. To this end, they proceed in the way—

Since ancient times, the four heavenly quadrants or Animals have each been subdivided into seven constellations, called <term>siu</term><note>1 宿.</note>. These twenty-eight groups, about which we shall have more to say on pages 971 and following, are irregularly distributed over the sphere as it is visible in China. As hills and mountain ranges are the embodiment of the influences of the Four Animals, their various parts are considered to each stand under the influence of a *siu*. In this manner, geomancy is cleverly combined with astrology, and the field of speculation is greatly expanded. Because the *siu* are important elements in astrological science, they contribute much to making Fung-shui a dark art so mysterious that it can only be practiced successfully by the experts who earn a living from it.

In their theories, geomancers also give a place to other groups of stars which they believe correspond with certain parts of the Earth and determine its fate. It is, in fact, constantly on their lips as a core principle of their system that "the stars of the Heavens above and the configurations of this Earth below correspond with each other"<note>2 The stars of the heavens and the configurations of the earth correspond with each other (天星地形上下相應).</note>. This doctrine directly arises from the great fundamental principle of both ancient and modern astrology, namely, that every human affair has a star or asterism controlling it. Practically, however, the combination of astrology with geomancy plays a very minor role; so we do not need to delve into its complexities.

Hills and mountains are also very powerful in their influence upon the destiny of man if their outlines are such as to allow the imagination to see in them lucky or unlucky omens. For instance, if a hill has a large boulder on its peak that weighs heavily upon it, the fortunes of the people nearby may be crushed, and poverty and misfortune may always prevail among them. If people, however, believe they recognize in its outlines some animal portending good luck or misfortune, those who dwell under the influence of its Fung-shui will enjoy that luck or suffer

Some books on geomancy provide long lists of objects that have disastrous or beneficial effects when identified in the outlines of hills and mountains.

### *The Five Elements.*

It may be supposed that in a system which claims to command the influences of Nature, an important place is also allotted to the elements from which Nature is built and which play a major role in its organization: namely, water, fire, wood, metal, and earth. No configuration is perfect unless these five elements work together harmoniously.

In the *Shu king*, the five elements are the first topic in a treatise titled "The Great Plan" <gloss>1</gloss>, a curious scheme of government intended as a guide to sovereigns in the discharge of their duties toward themselves and their subjects. This fact proves that even at the dawn of history, the conviction prevailed that the happiness of the nation, and even the lives of the people, depend entirely on those elements, and that mankind cannot exist without their beneficial influence. Being produced, like everything else in the universe, by the *Yang* and *Yin*, they are the natural agents of this dual Breath, acting favorably or unfavorably upon the living and the dead. Is it not evident, for instance, that wherever fire or heat, which is an emanation from the *Yang*, predominates, disaster will follow unless it is properly counterbalanced by another element, such as water, which is produced by *Yin*, the opposite breath? Is it not evident also that if the element of earth is overruled

Now, regarding any specific location, it is vital to determine whether the elements represented by the landscape's features form a harmonious union. It would, for instance, be highly damaging if hills or boulders representing both fire and wood were close to graves or houses, as this would surely make those houses susceptible to frequent fires. Human settlements often suffer from murderous raids by robbers and rebels if they are located at the foot of a large hill representing metal, or if the graves of the dead are situated near such a spot. And so on. On the other hand, there are many beneficial combinations of elements. Fire and water, for example, when combined harmoniously and in the right proportions, promote fertility. This can make the fields productive and lead the residents of a house, or the descendants of a buried person, to have many children.

They can also cut off the point of a dangerous rock and thus convert fire into wood, metal, or any element they choose, or redirect a brook in a favorable direction to quench the fire of such a rock. Or, if a flat elevation disturbs the harmony of the landscape, they simply have to place a convex or pointed pile of stones on top, as high and broad as they see fit. With the object of thus correcting the Fung-shui of cities, towns, and valleys, towers or pagodas have been erected in large numbers throughout the Empire at the cost of much money and labor. In this way, man’s foresight and energy may rule the influences of the Universe; thus he can direct his own destiny and fortunes, and those of his offspring, into any channel he pleases.

<header>THE GEOMANTIC COMPASS.</header>

It has been customary among the Chinese to consider the five planets as embodiments of the influences of the five elements and to denote them by the names of these latter: Venus they call the Star of Metal <note>1 金星 (Metal Star)</note>, Jupiter that of Wood <note>2 木星 (Wood Star)</note>, Mercury that of Water <note>3 水星 (Water Star)</note>, Mars the Star of Fire <note>4 火星 (Fire Star)</note>, and Saturn the Star of Earth <note>5 土星 (Earth Star)</note>. Thus every part of the terrestrial surface, when identified with one or more elements on account of its shape, is under the influence of the corresponding planets, and also under that of the constellations through which those planets move.

### *The Geomancer's Compass.*

To solve the problems relating to the construction of dwellings for the living, graves for the dead, and temples for the ancestors and the gods, geomancers have invented a remarkable instrument in which the principal matters and factors that play a part in their art are combined for handy use. It is a circular piece of wood, rounded down at the bottom like a tea-saucer; the upper surface has, in the center, a round excavation containing a small magnetic needle, seldom longer than one inch, which moves freely upon a pivot and is kept in its place by a glass cover fixed in the rim of the excavation. A straight line at the bottom of this "needle-house" gives the direction from North to South. The surface of the instrument, which is generally painted yellow and varnished, is inscribed with several concentric circles containing the various geomantic factors. Small compasses have a smaller number of circles, while larger ones have a greater number, and these latter enable the geomancers to take more precise bearings. The average diameter is about two decimeters, but we have seen several of both a larger and a smaller size. In many cases, the reverse side is lacquered black and bears a short table giving the contents of the circles, as well as the name of the manufacturer of the instrument.

Such compasses are called <term>lo king</term> <note>6 羅經 (Luojing / Geomantic Compass)</note>, or, in the Amoy dialect, *ló king*. This term, which signifies "reticular tissue," is probably an allusion to the circular lines on the surface, which, being intersected by other lines radiating from the center, remind one of a net. The concentric circles are called <term>ts'eng</term> <note>7 層 (Layers or stories)</note>.

<header>THE GRAVE.</header>

...geomantic compasses and the relative position of the circles, we give in Plate XXVI an unreduced picture of one of average size. The center in which the needle revolves is understood to represent the T'ai Kih<sup>1</sup> or "Great Ultimate Principle" which, according to ancient philosophy, is the progenitor of the so-called Liang I<sup>2</sup> or "Two Regulating Powers," namely the superior Breaths, Yang and Yin, which, as our readers know, create the phenomena of Nature by their cooperation. The first or inmost circle contains eight characters, which indicate Heaven and Earth or the two principal agents of the Universe, and six chief powers and elements which work in the latter; all these powers are produced by the Two Regulators, which, mutually extinguishing and giving way to each other, keep at work a ceaseless process of revolution which produces the phenomena of existence. They are:

Khien 乾, Heaven, the sky, the celestial sphere.
Tui 兌, watery exhalations, vapors, clouds, etc.
Li 離, fire, heat, the sun, light, lightning.
Chen 震, thunder.
Sun 巽, wind, and wood.
Khan 坎, water, rivers, lakes, seas, etc.
Ken 艮, mountains.
Khwun 坤, Earth, terrestrial matter.

This system of cosmogony and natural philosophy, represented by the compass, has been handed down from time immemorial. It is the basis of a system of divination laid down in the *Yih King* or Canon of Metamorphoses, and invented and expanded, according to tradition, by the royal founders of the Cheu dynasty. We read in the said Classic (chapter 14, lines 16 and 17):

> "Hence there is in the system of the metamorphoses of Nature the Great Ultimate Principle, and this produces the two Regulating Powers. These Powers produce the four Forms, which again produce the eight Trigrams. These Trigrams determine good and evil, and good and evil cause the great business of human life"<sup>3</sup>.

<header>THE EIGHT TRIGRAMS.</header>

To understand this passage entirely, it is necessary to know that, in the *Yih king*, the principle Yang is represented by an unbroken line <image-desc>a single horizontal line</image-desc>, and Yin by a line broken in two <image-desc>two short horizontal line segments separated by a small gap</image-desc>, and that from these lines are derived four diagrams representing the four Forms, namely:

<image-desc>Two horizontal solid lines stacked vertically</image-desc> called the Major Yang 太陽, representing the sun and heat.
<image-desc>Two horizontal broken lines stacked vertically</image-desc> called the Major Yin 太陰, representing the moon and cold.
<image-desc>A horizontal broken line above a horizontal solid line</image-desc> the Minor Yang 少陽, or Yang *under* the Yin, corresponding to the stars, daylight, etc.
<image-desc>A horizontal solid line above a horizontal broken line</image-desc> the Minor Yin 少陰, or Yin *kept under* by the Yang, corresponding to the planets, night, etc.

Placing each of these lineal figures under an unbroken and a broken line, the eight trigrams are obtained, of which the above extract speaks. They are called *kwa*¹ by the *Yih king* and represent the eight previously mentioned powers and elements, showing the relative quantities of Yang and Yin breath present in each of these:

<image-desc>Horizontal arrangement of eight trigrams. 1. Khien: three solid lines. 2. Tui: broken line over two solid lines. 3. Li: broken line between two solid lines. 4. Chen: two broken lines over one solid line. 5. Sun: two solid lines over one broken line. 6. Khan: solid line between two broken lines. 7. Ken: one solid line over two broken lines. 8. Khwun: three broken lines.</image-desc>
->Khien&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Tui&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Li&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Chen&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Sun&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Khan&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Ken&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Khwun<-

The principal *kwa* are Khien and Khwun, or Heaven and Earth, entirely composed of Yang lines and Yin lines, and therefore styled "unalloyed Yang"² and "unalloyed Yin"³.

Thus the geomantic compasses teach us that a prominent place is given in the Fung-shui doctrines to the *Yih king*, the same ancient book which the sages and learned men of all ages have held in high veneration as a clue to the mysteries of Nature and as an unfathomable lake of metaphysical wisdom explaining all the phenomena of the Universe. On many compasses, the lineal figures representing the *kwa* are inscribed around the needle, instead of the characters that denote them. Being combined by the *Yih king* with the seasons and the eight cardinal points, the *kwa* allow a wide play to the imaginative ingenuity of geomancers. "All things endowed with life," that Classic says (chapter 17, line 7), "have their origin in Chen, as Chen corresponds to the East. They exist in harmonious existence in Sun, because Sun corresponds with the East and the South. Li is brightness and renders all things

> » visible to one another; and it is the *kwa* which represents

> » dowed with life receive food. Tui corresponds to the middle of

Little insight is required to understand this extract in detail. The East is reasonably represented as the quarter in which the life of everything is rooted, the great progenitor of life being born there every day. It is identified also quite correctly with the *kwa* Chen, which represents thunder (see page 960); indeed, the vernal season, identified with the East because it is, so to speak, the morning of the year, is particularly characterized in China by heavy thunderstorms caused by the return of the southern monsoon. The *Li ki* (chapter 21, line 11) says:

> » In the month of mid-spring,
> » when day and night are of equal length, thunder raises its voice
> » and lightning begins to flash" <note>2</note>.

For just as plausible reasons, the South, where the God of Light daily reaches the zenith of his glorious course, is identified with brightness; the North, which he never visits, is identified with death. Tui, declared to correspond to the middle of autumn or the evening of the year, naturally belongs to the West or the evening of the day, this corroborating the identification of the East with the middle of the spring and naturally implying an identification of the South with midsummer, and of due North with mid-winter. Finally, in Ken, the *kwa* of the Northeast, everything which has life is stated to terminate and to originate, the North being identified with death, and the East with life.

Not only do the eight *kwa* <note>trigrams</note> correspond to the eight points of the compass and the seasons of the year, but they also symbolize the virtues and properties attributed to those points and seasons. Wu 戊 and Ki 己 do not designate specific points on the compass, but rather the center, which corresponds to the element of earth. The *Li ki* says (ch. 23, lines 14 and 15): "The center is earth, and its days are Wu and Ki" ¹.

The method described above of representing twenty points of the compass using characters derived from the denary <note>ten-fold</note> and the duodenary <note>twelve-fold</note> cycles is very old, as Liu Ngan uses it when enumerating the twenty directions in which the tail of the Great Bear points during its apparent yearly revolution around the pole ². It is also used in the *Historical Records*, in the twenty-fifth chapter, which is dedicated to natural science for divination purposes; that text refers to the cycles as "the Ten Mothers" ³ and "the Twelve Children" ⁴.

<page-num>967</page-num>
<header>THE TWENTY-FOUR SEASONS.</header>

drawn from those cycles, arranged in an order the leading idea of which we cannot grasp. Some characters appear in it two or three times. The fourth circle gives the characters of the <term>denary cycle</term> <note>ten-fold cycle</note> in alternate succession, in twelve combinations of five; between every two combinations a blank is left, two characters being skipped over. With this circle the tenth corresponds, but the inscriptions on it are shifted slightly to the right.

The fifth circle gives the five elements twelve times, in varied permutations. It combines the influences of the elements or planets with the points of the compass inscribed on the third and fourth circles.

The sixth and the eighth circles are identical with the third. They do not, however, like the latter, indicate the center of each of the twenty-four points of the compass, but their extreme limits, thus ensuring accuracy in taking bearings. For some occult reason, each character in these circles is combined, through the next cycle, with the characters 丁, 辛, or 丙, 庚, borrowed from the <term>denary cycle</term>.

The eighth circle contains, moreover, the twenty-four subdivisions of the year, and is therefore a calendar indicating the season during which a house, temple, or tomb, for which a favorable locality is assigned by the compass, ought to be built. According to the national philosophy, these seasons are produced by **Yang** and **Yin**, the two "breaths" which, through the course of every year, blend together in constantly varying proportions, **Yang** having the upper hand in the hottest weather, and **Yin** in the coldest. Hence they are logically called <term>tsieh khi</term>¹, "breaths of the divisions (of the year)", or simply <term>khi</term>², "breaths".

They are arranged on the circle in such a way that mid-spring corresponds to due East, midsummer to due South, mid-autumn to due West, and mid-winter to due North; this being, as stated on page 962, in perfect accordance with the speculative philosophy of the ancients. Also in the writings of the philosopher Kwan I-wu, who lived in the seventh century BCE (see page 660), it is stated that 

> "the seasons belonging respectively to the East, South, West, and North are the spring, the summer, the autumn, and the winter" ³.

冬至 Winter Solstice.
小寒 Little Cold.
大寒 Severe Cold.

The division of the year into the above seasons dates from early times. A calendar of the Hia dynasty, still existing under the title of *Hia siao ching* <note>Xia Xiao Zheng.</note>, mentions the Resurrection of hibernating Insects under the name "Emergence of hibernating Insects" <note>Qi zhe.</note>, and also the Winter solstice. In the writings of Kwan I-wu <note>Guanzi, chapter 3, section 8.</note> the names Pure Brightness, Great Heat, and Slight Heat are used to denote certain periods of the year. The *Kwoh yü* <note>Guoyu.</note> or "Discussions about the States"—a narrative of events in several feudal kingdoms during the Cheu dynasty, said to have been composed by the author of the *Tso ch'wen*—mentions the name "Limit of Heat" as having been used by one Fan Wu-yü <note>Fan Wuyu.</note>, who lived in the sixth century before our era <note>Chapter 17, which is the first part of the "Narratives of Chu."</note>. The section of the *Li ki* known as the Monthly Precepts

All the above facts merely serve to prove that many of the twenty-four names of the seasons were popular before the Han dynasty, but they do not give us any certainty that they formed a series like the one in present use at that time. We have slight evidence that this series really was used during the reign of the House of Zhou <note>Cheu.</note> in the fact that it is given in its entirety by the *Books of the Zhou dynasty obtained from the tomb in Ji* <note>Kih; see p. 416.</note>, in the section entitled: "Explanation of the Doctrines about the Seasons" ⁵. But it is far from certain whether this work is the product of the time indicated in the title, and it may probably contain spurious references to matters of a later date. It indicates the seasons by the same word <term>khi</term> <note>Qi.</note> by which they are known today. Liu An <note>Liu Ngan.</note>, summarizing the principal phenomena proper to the successive periods of fifteen days, which he calls <term>tsieh</term> <note>Jie.</note>, gives these twenty-four seasons in nearly the same sequence in which they are placed nowadays ⁶. They are enumerated also in the section on chronology contained in the *History of the Early Han Dynasty* ⁷, and have probably had an official status in China ever since, down to this day.

line divides the compass into twelve points, indicating these by the characters of the duodenary cycle, each repeated four times (compare this with the third circle). The next circle, the twelfth, is more important. It is divided into sixty portions of unequal sizes, inscribed with the names of the five elements in varied sequence, so that each element recurs twelve times. This useful circle enables the geomancer to judge by which element or planet any spot whatsoever is influenced, and whether the adjoining places are dominated by elements which might work either productively or destructively upon it. Suppose, for instance, a certain spot indicated by the compass as representing water is shown by this instrument to have the element earth at its side; its useful effects may be greatly reduced, or even rendered null and void, because earth neutralizes water (see page 957). Should, however, metal lie close by, the aquatic effects will be greatly invigorated, since metal produces water. Thus, clever geomancers are competent to continually discover favorable and unfavorable conjunctions of all kinds and descriptions, without torturing their brains over the question of whether a leading idea underlies the arrangement of the elements on this circle, or whether these latter are merely distributed arbitrarily upon it.

The same circle is also very useful in another respect. Enabling geomancers, as it does, to discover in the surroundings of a place the elements by which they are influenced, it reveals to them at the same time certain of the idiosyncrasies of those surroundings—namely, those which the books on philosophy, and the venerable *Shu king* <note>Shujing</note> in particular, attribute to the elements themselves. This Classic contains the following profoundly wise remarks:
> "Water may be described as moistening and descending, fire as blazing and ascending, wood as being crooked or straight, metal as flexible and changeable, while the virtue of earth is seen in sowing and reaping. That which moistens and descends produces a salt taste, that which is crooked or straight produces sourness, that which is flexible and changeable an acrid taste, and sowing and reaping produces sweetness." ¹

The use of the magnetic needle for geomantic observations suggests that the Chinese are perfectly aware that an oblong piece of iron, freely suspended, naturally points north and south. There is, however, not the slightest indication that they possess any knowledge of the variation of the compass, or that they are able to make a distinction between the magnetic North and the exact North.

The chief use of the geomantic compass is to find the line in which, according to the almanac, a grave ought to be made, or a house or temple built. Indeed, as has been stated on page 106, in this most useful of all books, it is decided every year which two points of the compass form the lucky line for that year, and which point is absolutely inauspicious. This circumstance not only leads to the postponement of many burials—since it is not always possible to find a grave that answers all geomantic requirements in the lucky line of the year—but it regularly compels the owners of houses and temples to postpone repairs or rebuilding until a year in which the line where their properties are situated is declared to be lucky. For this reason alone, many buildings are allowed to fall into ruin for years, and it is not uncommon to see whole streets simultaneously demolished and

---

It is a well-known fact that the Hindus, Parsis, and Arabs also possess a similar system of dividing the heavens into twenty-eight parts. The Hindu divisions are styled <term>nakshâtra</term> ("stars or asterisms"); the Arab divisions are called <term>manâzil al-kamar</term> ("lunar mansions" or "stations of the moon"). This latter term bears a marked resemblance to the Chinese names <term>siu</term> and <term>shé</term>, according to the explanation by Szě-ma Kwang mentioned above. Detailed dissertations on the coincidence between the Hindu and Arab systems have been written by Sir William Jones in the *Asiatic Researches* for 1790, and by Colebrooke in the *Asiatic Researches* for 1807, vol. IX (see also his *Essays*, vol. II, page 321). However, the identity of the Chinese system with the Hindu and Arab systems was first demonstrated and established by M. J. B. Biot, assisted by his son, the translator of the <term>Cheu li</term> (see page 19), in a series of articles published in the *Journal des Savants* for 1840. The conclusions reached by this eminent scholar were that this system of celestial division was invented by the Chinese and borrowed from them by the Hindus and Arabs for purely astrological purposes. To this day, no significant considerations have overturned these views; although they have been vigorously challenged by Weber, Max Müller, and other renowned authorities, it seems that most investigators of oriental astronomy silently agree with them.

<header>REVERENTIAL AWE FOR THE GEOMANTIC COMPASS.</header>

Chinese books make no mention of the inventor of the compass. Without a doubt, such combinations as we find on compasses today were used for geomantic purposes at an early date; the most important of them were, indeed, simple representations of the pre-Christian doctrines regarding the eight <term>kwa</term> and their relation to the seasons and the points of the compass. It is very probable that, before the invention of better writing materials, those combinations were written on small boards which, through improvements over time, have become the well-finished compasses of today.

Considering that the <term>geomancer's compass</term> includes all the principles of Chinese physical science, and that the characters and cycles inscribed on it are supposed to exert much of the same influence as the powers they represent, we cannot wonder that the people regard it with reverential awe. Geomancy professors themselves are fully aware that, by manipulating it, they concentrate the benefits of those powers onto any spot they select for a grave or a building—namely, to summarize, the powers of the two great Breaths of the Universe and the elements and agencies represented by the <term>kwa</term>; those of the four, eight, twelve, and twenty-four points of the compass; the elements or planets; the seasons and days of the year; the 360 degrees of the globe; the twenty-eight stellar divisions, and so on. All of this makes the compass an invaluable collection of supernatural wisdom to every Chinese person and one of the most useful instruments ever devised by the human brain. It derives an air of sanctity from its antiquity; the characters inscribed on it, their arrangement in cycles, and the specific positions of the circles relative to each other date back—as we have shown according to tradition—to the holy founders of the <term>Cheu dynasty</term>, or even to the age of the mythical <term>Fuh Hi</term>. To the uninitiated, who may know the names of all the terms and cycles but understand almost nothing of the many bewildering combinations that can be calculated for any specific spot, the compass becomes a powerful magic box in the hands of the professors. It contains an inexhaustible source of predictions that promise wealth and happiness to everyone and are sold at a high price, thus providing a steady source of income for the professors.

Even the most learned among the people—even the skeptics who do not have much faith in the system—generally receive the prophecies of those experts with the same superstitious dread with which they

So far, only the main principles of the <term>Feng-shui</term> system have been reviewed. No useful purpose is served by trying to dive deeper into its inconsistencies and the mechanical interplay of empty abstractions; however, we must still mention a few of the many other matters that play a more or less important role in the practical application of its doctrines and theories. When making a grave, the experts attach great importance to the characters forming the horoscope of the person who is to be buried there. It was already stated on page 103 how the twelve Branches are combined with the ten-part cycle of <term>kan</term> into a cycle of sixty binomial terms. These are used to count the years, months, days, and hours in a continuous rotation, providing every individual with a horoscope of seven or eight characters that indicate the year, month, day, and hour of their birth. Since these characters are firmly believed to determine a person's fate forever, no burial place can meet <term>geomantic</term> requirements if the cyclical characters for the occupant's birth year align on the compass with the lower end of the line that the almanac has decreed as auspicious for the current year—which is, of course, where the coffin is to be placed. 

Suppose, for example, this line runs from south to north, so that the long axis of the grave falls within the segment defined on the compass by the limits of the point 子 (the North), as indicated on circles VI and VIII. If the deceased was born in a year represented by a binomial term containing the character 子, his horoscope is considered to clash with the positive influences flowing from south to north, neutralizing their benefits. No blessings could ever be expected from a grave placed in this direction. Therefore, the axis of the grave must be shifted slightly to the right or left without leaving the northern quadrant. If it is feared that the beneficial influences of the auspicious line will be lost by doing this, the burial must be postponed. The month, day, and hour of the deceased's birth may cause similar clashes, though they are less dangerous since those dates form the less important parts of the horoscope. In fact, certain combinations may be found that neutralize such dangers. But if these cannot be found, the family is forced to delay the burial until the almanac designates another direction as particularly auspicious.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Feng-shui principles, transitioning from the orientation of individual graves to the geomantic impact of straight lines and the symbolic shapes of entire towns and villages.</meta>

<page-num>977</page-num>
<header>DANGEROUS SHAPES OF TOWNS AND VILLAGES.</header>

Another important geomantic law is that no road, no row of trees, nor any watercourse may run in a straight line toward a tomb. Geomancers say that straight lines are like dangerous darts which, by striking the core of a grave, may inflict a deadly wound. They also lead the way for harmful influences, which the specific <term>Feng-shui</term> terminology denotes by the word <term>sha</term> (compare page 940); furthermore, as has been stated on page 953, they indicate that the surrounding landscape is devoid of breath and vitality. Indeed, it is not uncommon to hear people who claim some knowledge of <term>Feng-shui</term> matters declare that a grave provides no benefit to the descendants of the person buried there because it is, as they say, "violated by the <term>sha</term> of a path or a road"¹; in other words, because a path has been accidentally formed in front or at the side by the footsteps of passersby. It is because of this superstition that the avenue to the mausoleum of the Ming dynasty's founder near Nanking, and the road leading to the tombs north of Beijing where his successors are buried, follow a curve in the section lined with stone statues of men and animals.

Regarding towns, cities, and villages, their own shape is considered a very significant factor—one that has as much to do with their destiny as the contours and arrangements of the surrounding environment. Geomancy experts in <term>Ts'üen-cheu-fu</term> are quite serious when they relate that, in ancient times, this city—the shape of which strongly resembles a carp—frequently fell victim to the raids of the people from the neighboring town of <term>Yung-ch'un</term>², because that town is shaped like a fishing net. Fortunately, about a thousand years ago, the ancestors of the current population neutralized this evil by building two pagodas in the center of the town. These pagodas still tower over it today, preventing the imaginary fishing net of their hostile neighbors from being hauled over their heads. Many towns in China have met with misfortune because of their ominous shapes. For example, it is recorded in the <term>Khi leh p'ien</term>³, a small work written in the twelfth century by <term>Chwang Ki-yü</term>⁴, that "the people of Chu avoid speaking of the head of a black tortoise, claiming that when the capital of that depart-"

A natural result of the primary geomantic principle—that favorable influences concentrated on a grave produce blessings that the descendants benefit from—is the doctrine, already introduced on page 57, that objects of good omen, when placed in a tomb, will cause the blessings they represent or symbolize to be shared by the descendants of the deceased. It is therefore an established funeral custom to place various items at the bottom of coffins and graves that represent a numerous progeny and an abundance of food and wealth. These include iron nails, hemp, peas, wheat, millet, <term>paddy</term> (unhusked rice), and coins (see pages 189 and 209); indeed, even good wishes are placed inside with the same goal. Similarly, the clothes and body ornaments of the dead are believed to work favorably on the fate of their offspring if they symbolize blessings, and for this reason they generally do so, as shown in our chapter on Grave Clothes. This same doctrine explains why the people are so inclined to dress their dead in "longevity garments" and the robes of a <term>mandarin</term> (official), as long life and official status are the things most desired by the Chinese. Furthermore, this doctrine accounts for the belief, mentioned on page 65, that five suits of grave clothes, or any odd number of them, may have a disastrous effect on the primary family members of the deceased who is sent to his final resting place prepared in such an unusual way.

Along the same lines as these curious results of geomantic beliefs is the ancient custom, mentioned on pages 813 and 819 and the following, of decorating the graves of emperors with stone images of unicorns. Since these animals foretell the birth of excellent sovereigns (see page 824), their images may—through the graves upon which they stand—work beneficially for the fortunes of the nation. Moreover, they may prevent the imperial lineage from ending, thus securing the dynasty’s eternal possession of the Throne.

Since symbols are placed in and on tombs to bring about the realities they represent to the mind, it is very natural

# SYMBOLIC INSCRIPTIONS AND FIGURES ON GRAVES.

Many tombs bear inscriptions expressing happiness, such as the characters <term>福</term> ("happiness and prosperity"), <term>祿</term> ("an official position with a large income"), and <term>壽</term> ("a long life") (see Plate XXVII). These are the same blessings which, as our readers know, are sown inside the graves by means of the clothes in which the deceased are dressed. Often also, animals symbolizing these same good things—such as bats, stags, and cranes (compare pages 53 and 55–57), and even unicorns—are carved on slabs of granite forming part of the tomb. Many graves also bear the <term>eight kwa</term> <note>The eight trigrams (Bagua) of the I Ching.</note>, evidently so that the influences of Nature, which they represent, may be concentrated upon the spot; in Plate XXVII, they are placed in a circle above the tombstone. Probably for a similar reason, over two thousand years ago, the sepulcher of the mighty ruler of <term>Ts'in</term> <note>The First Emperor of the Qin Dynasty.</note> was, as <term>Szĕ-ma Ts'ien</term> <note>Sima Qian, the grand historian.</note> tells us (see page 400), adorned with stars and constellations and with the configurations of the earth. We read also that the grave of <term>Li Szĕ-chao</term> <note>Li Sizhao (李嗣昭).</note>, a certain prince of imperial blood,

> "when broken open by robbers in the year <term>ki-szĕ</term> of the <term>Ching t'ung</term> period (A.D. 1449), was found to contain a burial chamber of chiseled stone and, moreover, representations of the sun, the moon, the stars, and the <term>Great Bear</term>" <note>In the *jisi* year of the Zhengtong period, robbers broke into Sizhao's tomb. Inside, they found a burial chamber carved of stone, featuring representations of the sun, moon, stars, and the Big Dipper. From the *Ku kin t'u shu tsih ch'ing* (Gujin Tushu Jicheng), section Kunyu, chapter 134.</note>.

For the same purpose of attracting the beneficial influence of the Universe to the grave, coffins were, during the <term>Han dynasty</term> and in subsequent ages, painted with a sun, a moon, constellations, and with the four <term>Celestial Animals</term>; and the board representing the seven stars of the <term>Great Bear</term> <note>The Big Dipper.</note>, with which coffins have been furnished for many centuries, is probably used for the same reason (see pages 316 and following).

The <term>Fung-shui</term> doctrines being a mere web of speculative dreams and idle abstractions—the product of a credulous faith in absurd whims—we are not surprised to find that, in deciding whether a spot will be a lucky burial place, much value is set on omens of all kinds. So, for instance, as we have stated on page 213, if rain happens to fall while a coffin is being placed in the grave, this is deemed a proof that the <term>Fung-shui</term> of that grave will work beneficially, Nature herself showing in this way that the influences of an element which holds a place of the highest signi-

### 3. The History of Feng-shui.

Our explanation of the Feng-shui system has shown that its leading principles originate in remote antiquity. Its first seeds, indeed, grew out of the worship of the dead, which even in the distant past was the actual religion of the Chinese. Deceased ancestors were then their primary patron divinities, who influenced the fate and fortunes of their descendants in every way. Everyone appeased them systematically, and from this worship, a tendency gradually arose to place the dead in subterranean dwellings that would provide rest, comfort, and happiness to their spirits <note>The original text uses the term "manes" to refer to the spirits of the deceased.</note>. And the answer to the question of which grounds are best suited for burial places was naturally sought in the shapes and features of the surroundings.

<header>FUNG-SHUI IN ANCIENT CHINA.</header>

That the elementary principles of the Feng-shui system were already applied in practice during the Zhou dynasty cannot reasonably be doubted, since we find that already in the fifth century before our era, grave sites were improved by human hands by means of artificial brooks and tanks. Instances of this are given in the excerpts describing the mausoleums of King Hoh Lü and his daughter, translations of which have been inserted on pages 396 and 419 of this work.

Another significant step that the ancients took in the direction of Feng-shui was to connect the qualities of a grave with the influences supposed to be exerted upon it by the celestial canopy and its cardinal points. This custom, too, can be traced back to the time of Hoh Lü. On page 396, our readers will have noted that the tomb of this ruler was called the Tiger’s Hill, because a white tiger settled on the summit on the third day after it was finished. Doubtless, this statement is an allusion to the White Tiger of the sphere, the western quadrant, whose influences were supposed to have begun operating upon the royal remains soon after their entombment.

This view is supported by the author of the *Records of the Country of Wu* (see page 296), who says that, "according to the *Annals of Wu and Yue* <note>However, we have not been able to find this statement in any of the copies of this work that we possess.</note>, three days after the burial of the king, the essence of the element metal assumed the shape of a white tiger and crouched down on the top of the grave" <note>吳越春秋云、葬經三日金精化為白虎、蹲其上. *Ku kin t‘u shu tsih ch‘ing*, sect. 坤輿, ch. 140.</note>. Now, in the pre-Christian era, metal was identified by Chinese philosophers with the West. Kwan-tszĕ wrote: "The breath of the East is wind, and wind creates wood. The breath of the South is Yang, which creates fire. The Center is earth. The breath of the West is Yin, which gives birth to metal; and that of the North is cold, by which water is produced" <note>東方其氣曰風、風生木。南方其氣曰陽、陽生火。中央曰土。西方其氣曰陰、陰生金。北方其氣曰寒、寒生水. *Kwan-tszĕ*, chapter 14, § 40.</note>. Liu Ngan also stated that "the East belongs to wood, the South to fire, the West to metal, and the North to water" <note>東方木也、南方火也、西方金也、北方水也. *Hung lieh kiai*, ch. 3, l. 3.</note>. These theories are easily explained—

The vegetable kingdom—that is, wood—revives in spring, the season identified with the East; fire naturally belongs to the South or the region of heat, and water, its opposite element, to the opposite cardinal point; metal, therefore, had to be assigned to the West, as no other place was left for it.

Distinct traces of attempts to place the dead in their graves under the proper influences of Nature are also to be found in the *Li ki*. This Classic states (chapter 12, line 34): "To bury the dead in the north and with their heads turned to the north was a custom generally observed during the first three dynasties" <note>葬於北方北首三代之達禮也. Sect. 檀弓, II, 1.</note>. In another section it says (chapter 30, line 20): "Thus the dead are placed with their heads to the north, but the living turn their faces to the south; all this is done in imitation of primeval usage" <note>故死者北首、生者南鄉、皆從其初. Sect. 禮運, I.</note>. According to the *Historical Records*, the last sovereign of the Yin dynasty was buried in the north of his capital (see page 283); and the *Tso ch'wen* likewise proves that we are not dealing here with a mere theoretical practice: it mentions, for instance, that the ruler Chwang was buried twice in the northern suburbs (page 841).

From these and other passages, the Chinese generally draw the conclusion that the houses of the living, as well as the graves of the dead, used to face the south in those ancient times. This peculiar method of building has been touched upon already on page 16. As stated on page 942, it is still maintained at the present day, though, in by far the most cases, only theoretically. Of course it is not probable that this rule anciently extended to buildings of minor importance and to the dwellings of the common people. Perhaps it was then chiefly in force for the palaces of rulers and the mansions of grandees who assisted them in the administration of the realm, as it is noted in one of the appendices of the *Yih king* (chapter 17, line 7): "The trigram Li represents light and renders all things visible to each other; it is also the trigram of the South. Sage rulers face the south when they give audience to all under the sky, and they turn themselves to that region of light in administering government" <note>離也者明也、萬物皆相見、南方之卦也。聖人南面而聽天下、嚮明而治. Sect. 說卦傳.</note>. This rescript has always been observed to the letter by the emperors of succeeding dynasties,

Hence the Imperial Palace, and all the principal buildings within its walls which serve for audiences or other government business, face due south; and this is also the case with the capital city, in the center of which the Palace stands, its walls and gates exactly facing the four cardinal points.

From the fact that the ancient Chinese considered the South to be the primary source of the blessings of the Universe—their country being regularly visited every year by the deadening influences of the rigorous North—and that they applied the influences of the South to the position and construction of princely residences with the object of accumulating blessings upon the rulers and their subjects, we must conclude that they had made considerable progress in the direction of <term>Fung-shui</term>. We shall find this inference confirmed, if we may place any trust in the *Annals of the States of Wu and Yueh*; but this work is filled with too many anecdotes and romantic tales to be worthy of unreserved credit, and, moreover, it was not composed before the first century of the Christian era. # THE BRANCHES COMBINED WITH THE TWELVE ANIMALS.

This long extract requires explanation. The twelvefold cycle of Branches, indicating the twelve points of the compass and used to denote the years, months, days, and hours, is combined for divination purposes with the Twelve Animals mentioned on page 44, in the following way:

Accordingly, the *Annals of Wu and Yueh* lead us to believe that this combination of the Branches and Animals was in use in the sixth century before Christ, as the book mentions the Dragon in connection with *Ch'en*, and the Serpent in connection with the branch *Szě* (that is, the Southeast; see page 965). However, as stated above, the work was written in the first century of our era, and the whole episode may owe its existence to the imagination of the author. Yet, at any rate, it is reasonable to conclude that the Branches and Animals were commonly combined for geomantic and necromantic purposes when its author lived. This is confirmed by the fact that in a contemporary work, entitled *Lun heng*¹ or "Discussions and Criticisms," the following odd passage occurs: "The

That the combination of the Branches with the Animals was popular at the beginning of the Christian era is also proved by the *Shwoh wen*, the famous dictionary which dates from the first century, for it says that "the character *Szě* represents the shape of a serpent" <note>¹ The character *巳* (szě) is the pictograph of a serpent.</note>. Native books show that since the Han dynasty, the Twelve Animals have played an important part in Chinese life as factors in fortune-telling and divination, as they were believed to exercise an influence—according to the attributes ascribed to each—over the years, days, and hours denoted by the Branches to which they respectively belong. But this subject, which was mentioned on page 44, must not occupy any further space here.

The cycle of Animals is generally called "the Twelve Animals" <note>² Twelve Animals (十二禽).</note> and the combination of the two cycles is called "the Dozens which belong to each other" <note>³ The Twelve Corresponding Animals (十二相屬).</note>. The origin of the cycle of Animals is shrouded in mystery and is a puzzle for Chinese authors, as no trace of it is found in the Classics. Some have attributed its use in China to the influence of interactions with other nations, because it is popular among the Mongols, Koreans, Japanese, Siamese, and other Asiatic peoples. Schlegel has tried to demonstrate on astronomical grounds that it must be of purely Chinese origin <note>⁴ *Uranographie Chinoise*, pp. 565 ff.</note>.

Hoh Lü's attempt to establish his supremacy over the surrounding kingdoms by building his city in such a way that the influences of the heavens and the earth were represented by it, and consequently acted upon it, provides proof that our statement on page 936 is correct: the rise of *Fung-shui* coincides with that of *Taoism*. This is the philosophical and religious system which taught people that because man lives under the absolute rule of Nature, he best ensures his happiness by adapting and conforming himself to the influences of the Universe. The ancients even went so far as to let the heavens themselves decide the location of the graves and dwellings they intended to build. For this purpose, they used the stalks of a certain plant called *shi* <note>² The milfoil or yarrow plant (*蓍*).</note>, which they believed were filled with an extraordinary supply of vital force or so-called *shen*. This force was composed of *Yang* substance (compare page 110), and the stalks were therefore considered more capable than anything else of revealing the will and intentions of the heavens, which are the great embodiment of the *Yang*. Those stalks were manipulated in a way that produced the linear figures or *kwa*, and these figures were subsequently interpreted with the help of sentences found in the *Yih king* and other similar books.

In its section on the funeral ceremonies for ordinary officers and their nearest relatives, the *I li* contains a very clear account of how this peculiar method of consulting Nature took place when a grave had to be made. It reads literally as follows:

> » Consultation of the divining stalks about a home for the deceased.
> » The Officer for the Grave Mounds having measured out a spot for

<header>SEEKING BURIAL PLACES BY MEANS OF DIVINATION.</header>

This excerpt teaches us that the first indications about favorable burial sites used to be obtained by consulting tortoise shells. Tortoises, like the divining plant, being considered entirely pervaded with *shen* substance, their shells were scorched with hot instruments for the purpose of deducing predictions from the lines and spots thus made visible. The details of this curious divining method we shall give in our Second Book. The *Cheu li* says: "On the death of the sovereign, the Sub-Intendant of Religious Worship finds out by means of a tortoise shell the place where the sepulchre is to be made, and he repeats this when they begin to dig the pit" ¹. Those readers who understand written Chinese will see that, in this passage, the place assigned by a tortoise shell as fit for a grave is denoted by the same character which the *I li* uses in the above extract to express the same thing—namely 兆—which Chinese etymologists say is a hieroglyphic representation of the lines and marks found on a tortoise shell. So, also, in the description of the functions of the Officer for the Grave Mounds (see page 421), the *Cheu li* denotes burial sites by the term 兆 域, which means: "places (域) appointed by the lines and spots on a tortoise shell." In many other works of antiquity, reference to what they generally style *puh tsang* 卜 葬, "drawing prognostics about burial places from tortoise shells," is made often enough to justify the conclusion that this practice was then most common.

This ancient method of allowing the heavens themselves to assign graves through the medium of tortoises and *shi* stalks has been adopted by subsequent dynasties and incorporated into their ceremonial institutions. The *Khai yuen* Ritual contains decrees on this subject which, in the main, are the same as those of the *I li*; but they declare that a tortoise shell may be consulted only for officers of the five highest ranks, specifically at the same time as the stalks are being used. Moreover, they state that this double augury—

That the dynasty which enacted those decrees also practiced them at the death of emperors can be seen from the description of the ritual that was established for the burial of Tai Tsung in A.D. 780 <note>1. Compare the "Record of the Ceremonies for the Yuen Mausoleum" 元陵儀注, inserted in the *T'ung tien* of Tu Yiu, and reproduced in the *Ku kin t'u shu tsih ch'ing*, section 禮儀, chapter 56.</note>. Chapter 92, line 7.</note> do not, however, make any reference to the ancient method of selecting graves.

The devotees of geomancy themselves are fully convinced that their art has been practiced since the earliest times recorded in literature. If asked for proof to support this belief, they unanimously point to a certain passage occurring in one of the Appendices of the *Yih king* (chapter 13, line 12), which says:

> By looking up to contemplate the heavenly bodies, and by looking down to examine the natural influences of the earth, man may acquire a knowledge of the causes of darkness and light. <note>3. 仰以觀於天文、俯以察於地理、是故知幽明之故. Section 繫辭傳, I.</note>

Yet this passage in itself is valueless for determining the antiquity of the system, even apart from the fact that the Appendix containing it shows internal evidence of having been written after the time of Confucius, though native scholars claim that it is a product of the sage's own pen. Nor is the fact that the <term>kwa</term>, cycles, constellations, etc., which play a prominent part in the system, have been used for chronological, astrological, and horoscopic purposes since very early times any argument for the antiquity of Fung-shui, despite the established opinion of its experts and professors.

The early traces of geomantic superstition take on sharper outlines during the Ts'in and Han dynasties. It has already been remarked that grave brooks and grave tanks were then essential features of royal tombs (page 947); that Shi Hwang’s mausoleum was decorated with stars, constellations, and the configurations of the Earth; and that coffins were typically painted with heavenly luminaries and figures of the four Celestial Animals (page 979), all of which practices...

# EARLY WORKS ON FUNG-SHUI.

had clearly no other purpose than that of concentrating the influences of the Universe around the deceased. In addition, much other data that marks the progress achieved by Feng Shui during the Han dynasty is provided by the books. They teach us that as early as the second century before our era, China possessed a class of experts in geomancy. The *Historical Records* <gloss>1</gloss> mention such a category of persons under the name of *Khan-yü kia* <gloss>2</gloss>, "the Khan-yü Class" (compare page 940), among various types of diviners whom the emperor *Hiao Wu* <gloss>3</gloss>, who reigned from the year 140 to 86 B.C., one day consulted upon the question of whether a certain date was suitable for performing a marriage, and from whom he received entirely different answers. The books show furthermore that, during the Han dynasty, there existed a Feng Shui literature. The "Memoir on Skillful Writings" <gloss>4</gloss> in the Official History of that epoch mentions, under the heading: *Authors on the Five Elements* <gloss>5</gloss>, thirty-one titles of works on divination, one of which, entitled: *The Golden Khan-yü Thesaurus, in fourteen Chapters* <gloss>6</gloss>, leaves no room for doubt that it was devoted to geomancy. The same Memoir also summarizes six works of *Authors on the Rules concerning Forms, who treated on a wide scale the configurations in the nine subdivisions of the Empire and derived from them the shape of cities and dwellings; they also treated the dimensions and numbers in the skeletal system of man and the six domestic animals, and of the forms and capacity of vessels and implements, thus determining for everything the respective sound and breath, the value or lack of value, and the auspicious or inauspicious operation* <gloss>7</gloss>. Among these six works, one was probably more specifically devoted to geomancy than the others, being entitled: *On the Configurations of Grounds for Mansions and Houses, in twenty Chapters* <gloss>8</gloss>.

<page-num>996</page-num>
<header>THE GRAVE.</header>

That treatises on geomancy and divination were numerous during the Early Han dynasty is demonstrated by the following passage relating to Wang King <note>¹ Wang King (王景).</note>, a high official of great renown for his learning and accomplishments in hydraulics. "From the very first it had been his conviction that, although the six Classics all contain references to divination by means of tortoise-shells and stalks, so that every undertaking or action was decided by the divining plant and the tortoise, yet all the books still in existence contained erroneous and confused statements on this subject, and the notions about the auspicious or inauspicious character of auguries contradicted each other. Therefore, he compared and organized the existing treatises of every author on the art of making calculations, as well as the notions about the matters that were prohibited and to be avoided during grave-making and house-building, the elements of geomancy, horoscopy, etc.; and he compiled everything, as far as it was of any practical use, into a work entitled: *The Fifty Original Groundstones*" <note>² 初景以爲六經所載皆有卜筮、作事舉止質於蓍龜、而衆書錯糅、吉凶相反。乃參紀衆家數術文書、冢宅禁忌、堪輿、日相之屬、適於事用者集爲大衍玄基云. *Books of the Later Han Dynasty*, chapter 106, line 8.</note>.

Under, or perhaps shortly after the Han dynasty, there existed a work called: *The Canon of Dwellings* <note>³ *The Canon of Dwellings* (宅經).</note>, which is generally considered to be the oldest surviving example of Fung-shui as it is still practiced today. Its origin was attributed to Hwang Ti <note>⁴ Hwang Ti (黃帝).</note>, "the Yellow Emperor," a mythical sovereign of the 27th century before our era, forever famous as the father of civilization and the art of government. We can scarcely suppose this attribution to have been a pointless attempt to give the book a holy aura of antiquity. We think it must be taken simply as an indication that the doctrines laid down in the book were based upon the pure, unmixed orthodox conceptions about the Universe and its influence upon the fate of man which had been in fashion since the dawn of civilization. A small treatise under the same name still exists; but it is far from certain whether it is not a production of more recent date <note>⁵ A reprint of it is inserted in the *Ku kin t'u shu tsih ch'ing* (古今圖書集成), section 藝術 (Arts), chapter 651.</note>.

--- Page 191 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Han dynasty's influence on geomantic literature, specifically describing the contents and impact of "The Canon of Dwellings" and the "Canon of Burials."</meta>

<page-num>997</page-num>
<header>FUNG-SHUI DURING THE REIGN OF THE HAN DYNASTY.</header>

It greatly extends geomantic speculation by distinguishing between buildings in which either the Yang or the Yin has the upper hand, and it contains directions for planning both categories in such a way that they ensure a maximum of glory and honor, wealth, prosperity, and official dignities for the inhabitants and their unborn offspring for many generations. It also elaborates extensively on the layout of graves and gives many useful hints regarding the restoration and rebuilding of the dwellings of the living and the dead. It is said that the so-called *Canon of Burials*¹ also dates from the Han dynasty; its authorship is attributed to a certain Master Blue Raven², whose real name, if it was ever known, has been forgotten. Only a few poor fragments have escaped the destructive hand of time and are reprinted in the *Ku kin t'u shu tsih ch'ing*³; they may be consulted with profit by those who can afford to waste more time and labor on a study of the development and growth of Fung-shui vagaries than we can.

The development of Fung-shui and its literature during the Han dynasty naturally coincided with the revival of ancient studies which marked that era. Under imperial auspices, every written relic that had escaped the incendiary whims of Shi Hwang was eagerly collected, studied, and explained; the Classics were cast in their present form; and during the revival of a general interest in literature, philosophers emerged who indulged in wild speculations on Nature and its Tao (or unalterable course)—speculations for which they found ample material in the Classics. Thus, a literature was created that abounded in cosmogonic vagaries, astrology, and alchemy, constantly providing material for new speculation of the same kind. Being guided only by the traditional notions borrowed from the ancients, it was gradually consolidated into the Fung-shui system in force today—a system destined, it seems, to crush China under its weight during the existence of its stagnant culture. Since the fundamental ideas and practices of the system can be traced back to very ancient times, and their development is intimately linked with the expansion of early speculations on Nature, the history of Fung-shui becomes the history of Chinese philosophy in general.

The role that Feng-shui superstition played in grave-building during the Han dynasty is explained by the following two episodes, said to have occurred respectively in the first and the second century of our era. » When Yuen Ngan’s father died, his
» mother ordered him to look for a place to bury him. On the
» road, he met three scholars who asked him where he
» was going. He informed them of his purpose, and they
» pointed out a certain spot to him, saying: “Bury him there;
» that place will surely produce for several generations of your family the
» highest office in the state.” At that same moment, they vanished.
» Ngan was interested in the prediction, and he immediately buried
» his father on the spot those men had discovered through divination. Sub-
» sequently, his descendants were showered with fame and glory for
» several generations ¹.

> » When Wu Hiung was a lad, his family was so poor that, on
> » the death of his mother, he looked at a plot of ground
> » in which nobody had made graves, and there he selected a place
> » to bury her. He performed the burial with such haste,
> » without inquiring whether the hour or day was favorable,
> » that the medical and spiritual mediums unanimously prophesied
> » that it would lead to the extermination of his clan. But Hiung took
> » no notice of their talk, and three generations of his family—
> » namely himself, his son Yin, and his grandson Kung—became Comman-
> » ders of the Palace Guard and distinguished themselves as famous
> » writers on legislation ² .

From these episodes, we learn that, in those times, <term>geomancy</term> focused its efforts especially on the discovery of graves that would ensure the promotion of the occupants' descendants to high state offices.
