Kwan Loh’s fame, great as it is, is almost entirely eclipsed by the halo surrounding the name of Kwoh Poh <note>2. Guo Pu (郭璞).</note>. This man, who lived from 276–324 A.D., was a scholar of high attainments, and his name is inseparably connected with several works of antiquity which he annotated and commented upon. Not only is he ranked among the highest authorities on antiquarian subjects, but all the proficients, professors, and adepts of <term>Feng-shui</term> look up to him as the great patriarch of their art, and even as their patron divinity. He was at the same time a first-rate soothsayer; the art of fortune-telling is, as our readers know, intimately connected with <term>geomancy</term> and practiced with the aid of much the same factors and cycles. His biography in the *Standard History* of the dynasty under which he lived recounts that » there lodged in Ho-tung (his native place) a gentleman of the same surname as his own, who was very clever in drawing prognostics from tortoise shells and divining stalks; he followed that person, learned from him the secrets of the art, and having received from him a ‘Book on the Contents of the Blue Bag’ in nine chapters, he thoroughly understood the arts relating to the Five Elements, Astrology, and Divination, knowing how to expel calamities, how to avert disasters, and how to bring complete succor in hopeless cases. Even King Fang and Kwan Loh could not surpass him. *Books of the Tsin Dynasty, chapter 72, l. 1.*</note>.

# THE FAMOUS GEOMANCER KWOH POH.

"...burial in the weaker spot, and thus he became Director of the Court of Imperial Entertainment and died at the age of sixty-four; but his children and grandchildren had a glorious career" <note>1. Originally, [Zhang] Yu's great-grandfather Cheng was about to bury his father, and Guo Pu divined the burial ground. He said, "If you bury him in a certain place, he will live to be over a hundred years old and reach the rank of the Three Excellencies, but his descendants will not flourish. In another place, his age will be reduced by half and his rank will only be that of a high official, but for generations his descendants will be noble and prominent." Cheng then chose the inferior spot; he became a Minister of Imperial Entertainments, died at sixty-four, and his descendants flourished accordingly. *History of the Southern Part of the Realm*, ch. 31, l. 2.</note>.

It might be expected that a man of Kwoh Poh's skill would have first of all selected a grave for himself so perfect as to raise his offspring to the highest earthly glory. It is stated that "he never failed to cut off and bury his nails and hair whenever he found an auspicious spot; as a result, graves of Kwoh Poh are to be found everywhere" <note>2. Whenever he encountered an auspicious site, he would cut his nails and hair and bury them there; thus, graves of Guo Pu are found everywhere. *Tan yuen tsung luh*, quoted in the *Ku kin t'u shu tsih ch'ing*, section on Earth, ch. 140.</note>; and yet his biographer only mentions one of his sons who was called to an official position—namely, that of prefect of Lin-ho <note>3. Lin-ho.</note> in the present province of Kwangsi. It does not, however, appear that this simple fact has ever, to this day, shaken the national belief in the efficacy of <term>Fung-shui</term>.

The biographer of Kwoh Poh relates that "his disciple Chao Tsai stole the *Book of the Blue Bag*, and that it fell victim to the flames before he could begin to study it" <note>4. Pu's disciple Zhao Zai once stole the *Book of the Blue Bag*, but before he could read it, it was consumed by fire. *Books of the Tsin Dynasty*, ch. 72, l. 1.</note>. Therefore, it must not be confused with the work attributed to Kwoh Poh which is currently known under the title of "Canon of the Blue Bag and the Corners of the Seas, revealed by the mysterious Virgins of the nine Celestial Spheres" <note>5. *Jiu tian xuan nü qing nang hai jue jing*. These Virgins have been mentioned already on page 105.</note>. This title refers to a treatise on the heavens, which are indeed a sort of blue bag containing everything, and dealing, moreover, with the earth, which is surrounded at the four cardinal points by oceans. In short, it is a book on natural philosophy based on revelations given in the ancient past by certain mystic beings regarding the evolution of the Universe.

...from chaos or primary nothingness. Starting from the origin of the Cosmos, it elaborates on the numerical proportions supposed to lie at the basis of the laws of Nature and to be expressed by the characters and cycles with which our readers are now acquainted. It places these formulas in concentric circles and combines these circles together in various ways, as is still done by geomancers today. It explains at great length the <term>kwa</term>, the influences which the twenty-eight stellar mansions exert on this earth, and all the other factors which we have reviewed, connecting the influences of the five Elements or planets with the outward forms of hills and mountains in the manner we set forth on page 956.

Kwoh Poh is also the reputed author of a treatise which, under the title of *The Book on Burial* <note>1. *Zang Shu* (葬書).</note>, ranks among the products of Fung-shui literature as a standard work. There are, however, good reasons for doubting whether it is really from his hand. No work by that name is mentioned in his biography in the *Books of the Tsin Dynasty*, although it gives the titles of three other works he wrote, and of half a dozen books he commented upon and annotated. Nor does the *Catalogue of Classical and Other Works* contained in the *Books of the Sui Dynasty* <note>2. Chapters 32–35.</note> mention a *Book on Burial*; nor is it certain that the treatise appearing in the *Catalogue* in the *Two Official Histories of the House of T’ang* <note>3. The *Old Books of Tang*, chapter 47, line 16, and the *New Books of Tang*, chapter 59, line 28.</note> under the title of "Book on Burial and Canon on the Pulses of the Earth, in one Chapter" <note>4. *Book on Burial and Canon of the Earth's Pulses, in one Chapter* (葬書地脈經一卷).</note> is from Kwoh Poh's hand, as no author's name is appended to it. For the first time, the work in question appears in the *Catalogue of Books* in the *History of the Sung Dynasty* under the explicit title: "Kwoh Poh's Book on Burial, in one Chapter" <note>5. *Kwoh Poh's Book on Burial, in one Chapter* (郭璞葬書一卷). Chapter 206, line 22.</note>. Probably this is the same treatise which is reprinted in the *Ku kin t'u shu tsih ch'ing* under the title of "Kwoh Poh's Canon of Burial, based on Antiquity" <note>6. *Kwoh Poh's Ancient Version of the Burial Canon* (郭璞古本葬經). Section on Arts (藝術), chapter 665.</note>.

Without doubt we may consider the age in which Kwoh Poh lived as the golden era of Fung-shui, as the epoch in which the ascendancy of its power reached its zenith and its eccentricities struck

### FUNG-SHUI SINCE THE TSIN DYNASTY.

...ineradicable roots in all classes of society, involving them once and for all in its intricate net of error and delusion. In fact, the *Books of the Tsin Dynasty* refer to Feng-shui matters far more often than the Annals of earlier times, and certainly just as often as those of subsequent dynasties. The belief that even emperors and princes could be produced by the selection of proper graves then grew strong. We read, for instance, of the military official Yang Hu <note>1. 羊祜.</note>, who lived in the second half of the third century:

> » The site of his grandfather’s tomb was declared by a man who
> » was skilled in observing the properties of graves to possess a
> » breath which could produce emperors and kings, but the occu-
> » pant would remain without offspring if it were hacked into. Hu there-
> » fore hacked into it, whereupon the other, on perceiving what he
> » had done, said it would now still produce a Minister of State
> » with a broken arm. Finally Hu fell from his horse and broke his
> » arm; and he became a minister, but fathered no sons" <note>2. 有善相墓者言、祜祖墓所有帝王氣、若鑿之則無後。祜遂鑿之、相者見曰、猶出折臂三公。而祜竟墮馬折臂、位至公、而無子。 *Books of the Tsin Dynasty*, ch. 34, l. 12.</note>.

From nothing does it appear that, since those times, the belief in the efficacy of Feng-shui has ever been seriously shaken in China. It has held undisputed sway over the nation down to the present day. Nevertheless, there have existed some minds which, though not disbelieving in the system, were far from placing absolute confidence in everything that the practitioners and experts presented to the public as genuine geomancy. Yen Chi-t'ui, for instance, wrote in the sixth century:

> » The art of utilizing the two Breaths of Nature
> » having originated with Heaven and Earth themselves, confidence
> » must be placed in the indications of that art with respect to good
> » luck and ill, prosperity and woe. But a long time has elapsed since the
> » ancients lived. Therefore, the writings on that art, transmitted from
> » one generation to another, are altogether the product of unsettled
> » popular notions and contain gossip of a common and superficial
> » kind; little therein is trustworthy, and much is pure nonsense.
> » Yet, by opposing the art in question, by deviating from it,
> » or by refusing to utilize it, calamity might finally be incurred.
> » Unfortunate results cannot always be avoided by attending to it...

In general, the arts of Yin and Yang coexist with Heaven and Earth; their signs of good and bad fortune, as well as their principles of virtue and punishment, cannot be ignored. However, since the time of the sages is now remote, the technical books passed down through generations all come from common sources; their language is crude and shallow, they provide little evidence, and they contain many falsehoods. For example, the practice of "fan-chi" is unusable and eventually leads to harm. Even following taboos regarding "returning" or "temporary lodging" does not prevent a tragic end; being restricted by many taboos is of no benefit. *Domestic Instructions*, § 19.</note>.

In the seventh century, the emperor T'ai Tsung <note>2. 太宗.</note> of the T'ang dynasty appointed a commission of more than ten scholars. Under the presidency of Lü Ts'ai <note>3. 呂才.</note>, a famous man of letters, they were ordered to sift through the existing literature on divination and geomancy and to gather from it everything that was orthodox and of real practical value. The result of their labors was a work in one hundred chapters, which was published by the emperor’s order. They passed a sweeping judgment on the literature then existing on these subjects, flatly condemning any selection of auspicious graves and lucky times for burial that was not sanctioned by ancient precedents. A full account of how these scholars performed their task is given in the two Standard Histories of the T'ang dynasty <note>4. *Old Books of T'ang*, ch. 79, lines 12 and following; *New Books of T'ang*, ch. 107, lines 4 and following.</note>.

This imperial effort to check the boundless expansion of unauthentic geomantic theory and superstition was entirely without effect, and the literature on the subject has continued to grow from age to age. The catalogue of literature in the *Books of the Sui Dynasty* gives only about a dozen titles of works and treatises; the catalogue in the *Books of the T'ang Dynasty* contains a much larger number <note>5. *Old Books of T'ang*, ch. 47, and *New Books of T'ang*, ch. 59.</note>, and in that of the *History of the House of Sung* we count over a hundred <note>6. Chapter 206.</note>. Needless to say, under every dynasty the books contain numerous names of renowned geomancers and various stories illustrating their skills and marvelous attainments.

These authors and experts generally based their theories upon the so-called <term>hing shi</term> <note>7. 形勢.</note>, the "influence or power of forms and outlines"—that is to say, the influence and power of the Elements

# THE TWO SCHOOLS OF GEOMANCY.

In the latter half of the ninth century, the most prominent figure in this School of Forms was Yang Yun-sung ¹, a native of Teu-cheu ², which is a part of the department of Yuh-lin ³ in Kwangsi. He is frequently mentioned by his other name Shuh-meu ⁴ and is commonly known as "the Master who saved mankind from poverty" ⁵, probably because of his great achievements in finding grave sites that never failed to make the descendants of the occupants wealthy and fortunate. Under the reign of Hi Tsung ⁶ (874—888), he held the office of Imperial Geomancer and was even honored with the high rank of Director of the Court of Imperial Entertainment ⁷. The later period of his life he spent as a geomancer in Kiangsi province, in the department of Kan-cheu ⁸, which was at that time called Khien-cheu ⁹. Because of both his widespread fame and the works he wrote, he has always been regarded as the great patriarch of the School of Forms, which has since been known as the "Kan-cheu Method" ¹⁰. He laid particular stress upon the shape of mountains and the direction of watercourses; or, in other words, upon the influences of the Dragon (compare page 951), an imaginary animal that plays a part in his system under various names and aspects. Consequently, the titles of three of his writings are: "Canon on the Means to Set Dragons in Motion" ¹¹, "Book of Thirty-Six Dragons" ¹², and "Canon for the Approximation of Dragons" ¹³. His treatise titled "Method of the Twelve Lines" ¹⁴ still holds the rank of a standard work for tracing out favorable spots in connection with the contours and configurations of high ground and mountains.

Yang Yun-sung had many disciples, most of whom wrote geomantic works and treatises. The leading figure among them was Tseng Wen-ch'wen ¹⁵, who composed a "Treatise on the Art of Searching for Dragons" ¹⁶, "Questions and Answers about the Two Breaths of Nature" ¹⁷, and other works <note>18. The above information is gathered from the *Ku kin t'u shu tsih ch'ing*, section 藝術 (Arts), chapter 679.</note>.

<page-num>1008</page-num>

# THE GRAVE.

Under the influence of the metaphysical speculations by which, during the Sung dynasty, a well-known school—of which Chu Hi was the principal leader—sought to explain the principles of creation and reproduction on a broader scale than ever before, and to expound the influence that the heavens are thought to exercise over earthly affairs, a second school of geomancy arose. This school particularly emphasized the <term>kwa</term>, the Branches, and <term>kan</term> (the Constellations), etc., assigning minor importance to the physical features of the earth. It is generally called the "Method of Man" (that is, Fuhkien)¹, its first chief representative being Wang Kih², also named Chao-khing³ or Khung-chang⁴. He was a native of Kan-cheu who spent the later part of his life in northern Fuhkien, namely in Sung-yuen⁵, now called Sung-khi⁶. His "Canon of the Core or Centre"⁷ and his "Disquisitions on the Queries and Answers"⁸ were published by his pupil Yeh Shuh-liang⁹. The Fuhkien School is frequently called the "Houses-and-Dwellings Method"¹⁰. It is more committed to the use of the compass than the Kan-cheu School; the latter uses that instrument only as a secondary aid—namely, to gauge the influences of the surrounding countryside after its shapes and contours have been judged to be favorable.

These two schools have shared dominance in the <term>Feng-shui</term> system down to the present day. As far as we know, no other significant school has arisen alongside them. It is hardly possible to define the present status and relative position of each, along with their influence in the various parts of the Empire. Professors of geomancy unanimously assert that a distinct line of demarcation still exists between the two schools, but that they are fused together to the extent that no good expert in either ever neglects to practice the methods of the other school as well as his own. In the mountainous southern provinces, the School of Forms obviously predominates. Even in Fuhkien, no geomancers are so highly esteemed as those who claim to practice their vocation in strict accordance with the Kiangsi method, and in every town of that province, there are houses with signboards to attract patrons.

# THE PRESENT FUNG-SHUI LITERATURE.

Many such accomplished experts are accustomed to introduce and recommend themselves to the public by means of placards posted in squares and at street corners.

The <term>Fung-shui</term> literature is currently as rich as ever. Popular expositions of the theory and its practical application are on sale in every bookshop, mostly quite voluminous and illustrated with woodcuts. In general, such products are subdivided into three main sections. The first deals with the "Rules concerning the Dragon" <note>1. 龍法 (Dragon Law)</note>—that is to say (see page 951), the situation and configurations of mountains and the direction of watercourses. This section often commences with a dissertation on the doctrine, set forth by eminent expositors of the system, that the whole Empire has a Dragon which rules the fortunes of all its inhabitants; namely, the immeasurable <term>Kwun-lun</term> <note>2. 崑崙</note>, a range of mountains in the northwest between Tartary and Tibet, the "progenitor of all the mountains of the world" <note>3. 天下諸山之祖</note> and the "center of the Earth" <note>4. 地之中</note>, in which the great rivers—which carry the beneficial influences of the Dragon to the south and southeast—originate. Often this section also contains dissertations, illustrated with maps, on the <term>Fung-shui</term> of every province as a whole, such as the "Authors on the Rules concerning Forms" had already written two thousand years ago (see page 995); furthermore, it generally gives astronomical maps elucidating the relations between certain parts of the canopy of heaven and their counterparts on earth (compare page 954).

The second section elaborates on the five Elements or Planets, and the art of discovering their presence or influence in the forms of hills, mountains, and terrestrial objects. The third section is practically the most important, being devoted to a technical application of the doctrines expounded in the first and second sections; that is to say, it gives directions as to how a <term>hüeh</term> <note>5. 穴 (a site or cavern)</note>—that is, a favorable site for a grave or building amidst good and bad surroundings of every sort and description—is to be found at any given place. Generally, it is profusely illustrated and gives examples of graves of great renown for their good <term>Fung-shui</term>; besides, it contains systematic enumerations of things that are detrimental or dangerous, and wise rules

In many books, this section is subdivided into two parts, titled "Rules concerning Gravel or Sand (that is, the ground)" <note>1. 砂法 (Rules for Sand/Gravel)</note>, and "Rules concerning Water" <note>2. 水法 (Rules for Water)</note>, respectively teaching how to utilize every part of the configurations of mountains, hills, lakes, or watercourses for all sorts of purposes.

It now remains for us to provide some information about the <term>Fung-shui</term> professors and the way they work among the people, which will give our readers some idea of the extent of influence geomancy exerts over social life in China.

### 4. The Professors of Fung-shui. The Influence of Fung-shui on Practical Life.

As stated on pages 938 and following, every member of the educated class who has gained a smattering of knowledge of the classical works and philosophical principles by learning to read and write is, to some extent, a geomancer in China; indeed, even men and women with no literary education at all claim to know much, if not everything, about <term>Fung-shui</term>. However, the true professor of this art, who earns his living by it, is distinguished from these amateurs by many characteristics.

He adopts all the mannerisms of the literati and the gentry, dressing in a long gown as they do and wearing a pair of large spectacles, even if he is not short-sighted. He inspires admiration and respect in his patrons by rarely opening his mouth, except to utter a few wise words or a classic phrase borrowed from books. Others, on the contrary, build and maintain their reputation through talkativeness, overawing everyone by speaking a mystifying, learned jargon and making apocalyptic pronouncements that the ordinary Chinese person understands next to nothing about. Many professors are very dignified in their habits, maintaining a grave and haughty expression and strutting about like peacocks among the common birds around them. There is an air of classic decorum in all their movements; it is no wonder, therefore, that the masses regard geomancers as fountains of wisdom and marvels of learning, capable of fathoming all the mysteries of heaven and earth.

Yet, to tell the truth, scarcely any of them have acquired their skill

through profound and serious studies of the books written by the nation's sages and philosophers. A geomancer has, as a rule, learned to read and write at school; but, for the rest, he has picked up almost all his wisdom by strolling about in the open country for a few years at the heels of some professor who had adopted him as his disciple, catching from his lips a large supply of empty phrases about dragons, tigers, branches, and other mysteries of the compass. Although he has the name and outward appearance of a literary man, he is, like Chinese scholars in general, quite ignorant of his national history and literature; nor does he possess the slightest knowledge of the history and literature of the art in which he calls himself an expert. At best, he may have consulted one or two poorly printed handbooks; but he seldom looks into these products a second time, finding it easier to rely upon his own inventiveness and eloquence, which both he and others are quite inclined to regard as wisdom and innate genius. But his ignorance casts no shadow upon his reputation. For, after all, he knows more about the art than the bulk of the people; moreover, he is extremely smart in bewildering his employers by bullying them, whenever he thinks fit, with a flood of technical expressions and hazy utterances about tigers and dragons, branches and <term>kwa</term>, elements, and spiritual influences of all sorts and descriptions.

Clever <term>Fung-shui</term> professors are accustomed to resort to other devices in order to keep up the reputation of their calling and that of their own persons. The names of the ancient sages and sovereigns, revered by the whole nation as the holiest and most perfect of creatures the Universe ever produced, are constantly on their lips, especially those of the reputed inventors of the <term>kwa</term> and the authors of the *Yih king*, namely King Wen and the Prince of Cheu, his son (see p. 691); frequently also they appeal to the illustrious Chu Hi, the father of modern philosophy and an ardent votary of good, orthodox <term>Fung-shui</term>. Thus they ably contrive to get themselves associated by the people with great and famous names in history. They further enhance the general admiration of their wisdom by concluding each flow of words from their lips with this refrain: "Yet many other arguments could I adduce, were they not too numerous to be summed up."

The people are perfectly aware that geomancers are not only useful, but also dangerous. Indeed, these men can supply them with graves and dwellings which establish the prosperity of whole families;

<header>THE GRAVE.</header>

But they also have the power to plunge families into woe and misery by ruining the graves and houses that have good Fung-shui through their cunning tricks. The professors themselves take great care to maintain this dual reputation by constantly spreading stories and anecdotes that illustrate their two-fold power. Through these, the people are constantly reminded how advisable it is to cultivate their friendship and to gain their goodwill in all circumstances of life. They often tell a story that, once upon a time, there lived a family who became very rich and prosperous due to the influence of a grave site found for them by a geomancer of great renown. Upon discovering this priceless spot, he realized it would cost him his eyesight if anyone were buried there; yet he did not hesitate to assign it to that family, on the condition that they would house, clothe, and feed him for the rest of his life, and give him a decent burial after his death. So he lived with them, quite blind but happy and free from worldly cares, leading an enviable life of leisure and idleness. One fine day, it happened that a kid belonging to the family fell into an open latrine and was suffocated. The Chinese are a thrifty people, and even the wealthy classes are reluctant to throw useful things away. Therefore, because none of them wanted to eat the kid, the family decided to cook it for the professor, who, being blind and unaware of the circumstances, would certainly enjoy the savory food. This was done; but, unfortunately, a talkative woman in the family told him in secret how shamefully the others had taken advantage of his helpless condition. Our readers can guess the end of the story: the professor mercilessly destroyed the good Fung-shui of the grave by giving bad advice about it, and thus he brought the family back to the same extreme poverty from which he had rescued them. We are not told, however, whether he recovered from his blindness after he had taken his revenge.

In spite of such professional tales and numerous accounts of graves that have made their owners prosperous for many generations—accounts which, whether illustrated by woodcut figures or not, are included in many handbooks—and despite the fact that many a geomancer is so sharp and clever that he can tell at a glance from the moss or weathered spots on a gravestone whether the Fung-shui of the grave is good or bad—yet there are many people bold enough to refuse to trust everything they say implicitly. Such skeptics are perhaps more numerous now than they were in the past. To none

### THE PROFESSORS OF GEOMANCY.

Among them, does it ever occur to anyone to doubt the perfection of the principles of the system? These form the chief cornerstone of natural philosophy as explained by the holiest and wisest men. But the simple fact that many—who, in the hopes of buying a grave site that will make them rich and prosperous, pour half their wealth into the laps of the professors and yet become poor, while others, not wealthy enough to employ a professor, rise to wealth and distinction—acts as a great check upon the credulity of the public. Among the educated classes, it is an open secret that the predictions of geomancers are all guesswork, and that all they have to offer is a little experience collected in the course of their practice. It is no wonder then that, in Amoy, people often make fun of their geomancers and deride them in the following quatrain:

->*Tē-lí sien-sing koàn soat hong,*<-

A <term>Fung-shui</term> professor would be a nobody among his colleagues if he did not have a store of wise sophistry with which to counteract popular prejudice. We geomancers, he argues, can in reality thoroughly understand, through profound study, the secrets of the *<term>Ti li</term>* or natural influences pervading the earth (see page 940), and thus we can discover means to direct human happiness into any desired channel. But these influences are in every respect dominated by those of the heavens—namely, the *<term>Tien li</term>* <note>The laws or principles of Heaven (天理).</note>—the earth being swayed by the supreme celestial powers surrounding it. services, and, secondly, the factor which, through the hand of heaven, bestows such a destiny upon him—namely, a virtuous character, manifesting itself through meritorious deeds. Is it not set forth as a golden principle by all the authors of <term>geomancy</term>: "Nobody should neglect to cultivate secret virtues, as the accumulation of virtuous deeds is the only firm foundation for all searching for felicitous grounds"?¹ Should a man without virtue acquire the most propitious graves for his dead and the best possible dwellings for himself, their <term>Fung-shui</term> can profit him nothing, as it is doomed to impotence and inactivity because of the refusal of the <term>T'ien li</term> to cooperate in making him happy. From this, we see that <term>Fung-shui</term> is not a *creator* of happiness, but merely the indispensable medium through which a happy fate, held in store by the heavens, is delivered to its destination.

Of course, it seldom occurs to anyone to investigate his own merits and inner qualifications before squandering his possessions in search of spots for building or grave making. What man in this world ever entertains the least doubt of his own excellence? Who would presume to anticipate the decrees of the high heavens regarding his destiny, even by a humble investigation of his own faults and unworthiness? Not until the effectiveness of a grave or dwelling has been watched for some time can it be decided whether the virtues required to make it yield profit are present or absent in the persons concerned. These theories, the logic of which no Chinese person ever contradicts, have the advantage of absolving the professor of all blame if the places selected by him bring no blessings. He can, moreover, use them to explain the fact that children—who, for want of money to pay a professor, have buried their parents in a site decried as valueless from a geomantic point of view, or even in a bad spot from which others, by the advice of clever experts, have removed their dead—sometimes rise to wealth and distinction. In such a case, it is the <term>T'ien li</term> who, moved by the virtues of the persons in question—virtues of which they themselves were probably unconscious—have compelled the <term>Ti li</term> to work in their favor with all their energy. Even the doctrine of the transmigration of souls is brought to bear here, as events such as the above are often declared to be rewards for deeds performed in some previous incarnation. But most generally they are ascribed to long-forgotten merits of some an-

...ancestor, as it is a settled doctrine that good acts are often rewarded in the offspring of the individual who performed them, just as his crimes and sins must be atoned for by them.

From the above, our readers will perceive that the <term>Fung-shui</term> doctrines, when handled with skill and eloquence, can explain all the phenomena of human life and fate. Thanks to the wise and useful theory of the supremacy exerted by the <term>T'ien li</term> over the <term>Ti li</term>, no clever professor can ever be cornered. When asked why he did not bury his own relatives in the excellent graves he boasts of having found for others, he is humble enough to confess that they would be of no use to him, since his virtues are so few and insignificant, his natural fate consequently so bad, and his chance of prosperity in this world so small; nor have his ancestors stored up enough merit to enable him to reap the profits of his geomantic knowledge himself. This shows that <term>geomancers</term> can also put on an air of humility when it suits them. Again, when asked how it is that previous generations have not used up all the good grounds—given that they produced so many thousands of perfect and virtuous men—the answer is:

> "The <term>T'ien li</term> do not reward the virtuous any less today than they did in the past. Just as in olden times, they imbue various parts of the earth with beneficial influences on their behalf, thus continuously creating new favorable sites for building and burial purposes. It often happens that entire valleys, completely lacking good geomantic influence, are converted into inexhaustible sources of <term>Fung-shui</term> by the <term>T'ien li</term> when a change in the curves of a stream is caused by a rain shower, or by a small landslide, or the fall of a rock through the action of wind and rain. How, then, could there ever be a concern about the supply of burial sites being exhausted?"

— Near every village and every town, there are in fact numerous unknown spots—the favorite dreams of the inhabitants—which promise an income of ten thousand gold coins, and promotion to the very highest literary degree as well, to whoever buries his father or mother there. But no professor, even if he were the reincarnation of <term>Kwan Loh</term> or <term>Kwoh Poh</term>, can detect those grounds unless set to work by such men of virtue as are chosen by the <term>T'ien li</term> to enjoy such great happiness. Is it any wonder, then, that every person with common sense, upon the death of their parents, applies to the best professor their money can afford, in the hope that they may be among the number of the chosen?

Emperor Tai Tsung of the Tang dynasty commanded Lü Tsai to write a discourse to deeply refute it, yet he ultimately could not stop it. Those acting as sons or grandsons are confused by theories of misfortune and blessing; they invite burial masters to seek auspicious land, dissect the earth's veins, deliberate on orientations, and Diviningly select years, months, days, and hours. The poor cannot choose land, while the rich choose with too much detail; consequently, the remains of ancestors are left exposed in the open fields. a day, unless the family is too poor to pay the professor high wages. Naturally, the family must pay all the expenses resulting from such excursions. They must also provide palanquins and bearers for the professor and themselves, as walking is considered lowly work, unsuitable for people of distinction who have the means to avoid physical exhaustion.

While learned discussions are held regarding the landscape's contours, and hands are constantly moved up and down and in every direction of the compass, the party stays under the shade of paper or silk umbrellas. Around most towns, hardly a tree or shrub provides shelter against the scorching sun, as all vegetation has been thoroughly destroyed over time under the direction of <term>geomancers</term>. Now and then the professor brings his compass from a linen bag hanging from his shoulder. Lying at full length or creeping on the ground, he takes the bearings by placing a so-called *hun-kim soàⁿ* <sup>1</sup>, or "thread for subtle measurement," over his instrument. This is a red cord with a copper coin dangling from each end to keep it stretched. He pronounces his judgment regarding every chosen spot in technical jargon; and although his decisions may sometimes be questioned by those who accompany him, they are generally received with respectful awe and superstitious dread.

Finally, after the professor has received many generous payments for his efforts, a spot is discovered where favorable geomantic influences are highly concentrated, and which consequently promises to fulfill the family's greatest hopes. Many days are then spent bargaining with the owner of the land through an agent or broker. Eventually, however, this man is persuaded to accept a small deposit of earnest money. In exchange, he allows the family to test the properties of the soil and binds himself not to sell it to anyone else until they have decided against the purchase. Without delay, a small quantity of pig bones is bought from the butcher and buried on the spot in a small wooden box or earthen jar. After about a year, the family digs them up and examines them. If they come out hard, dry, and white, the soil is approved, as this shows it has enough preservative power to keep the skeletal remains of the dead in good condition for a very long time to come.

->THE FUNG-SHUI PROFESSORS.<-

and, consequently, to attach his ancestral spirits permanently to the spot. A shorter experiment is to bury some duck’s eggs and later examine them to see whether they dry up or rot away. Pieces of charcoal are also used because, being moisture-absorbing, they soon reveal whether the spot is dry enough to serve for burial purposes.

In Amoy, these proceedings are called *ìm khoàn*$^1$, “hiding experiments,” or *t'àm khoàn*$^2$, “sounding experiments.” If the soil is found to be poor, it is decided in some cases to improve it by digging away the earth around the place where the coffin must lie and filling the void with soil of a better quality.

It is by no means rare for a family, after having conducted these experiments, to consult a second professor in order to verify the decisions of the first. In nine cases out of ten, this new “marvel” of wisdom—with a stream of clever critical remarks—contradicts everything his colleague has done. For, although <term>Fung-shui</term> professors are dignified in their demeanor, they are subject to the influences of professional jealousy just like the rest of mankind and are by no means a mutual-admiration society. The family’s new advisor does not take long to discover, for instance, that there is a dangerous bed of stones or solid rock under the soil, through which it will be impossible for the <term>Terrestrial Breath</term> to break its way and reach the corpse. Some diggers are set to work immediately, and no sooner do they find a couple of stones than . . . . everything has to be done over again from the beginning. The deposit is lost; the expenses for the numerous excursions into the mountains were made in vain; and neither the payments made to the professor nor the advances he obtained can be recovered. Even the money the family spent to win over the dangerous man with dinner parties now becomes a total loss; indeed, they had still generously entertained him many times for fear he should ruin their entire future destiny by providing them with a grave that was completely worthless from a geomantic perspective.

Now the new “marvel” in turn subjects the family to more expense. He borrows money from them whenever an opportunity presents itself, demands payment for every minor task he performs, and is most likely to scheme with the owner of each plot of ground he declares to meet the family's needs; for why should he refuse his “honest” share of the purchase money which he enables this man to squeeze out of the family? While waiting to acquire an auspicious grave, the deceased parent remains unburied, either in the house or somewhere in a shed or temple. Although, as our readers know (see pages 132 and following), public opinion denounces long postponements of burial as the height of being unfilial, and both law and government threaten it with severe punishment, these three powerful factors combined remain powerless in the matter. Regularly every year, thousands of the dead are deprived of a timely burial because of the requirements of <term>Fung-shui</term>. To a certain point, this phenomenon may be explained by the fact that postponing burial was a legal custom in ancient China, based on the ideas of a resurrection prevailing at that time <note>See our special chapter on this subject on pages 263 and following.</note>, so that the Chinese cannot help but regard it as perfectly defensible on the grounds of tradition and fashion. It may also be explained by the fact that the ancients used to keep the dead for some time in their dwellings before conveying them to their last resting place, and that this custom has been passed down to future generations by such a venerable book as the *I li* and authorized by many dynasties as a legal rite of the state religion (see pages 363 and following).

Cases of long burial postponements have undoubtedly been numerous in China ever since <term>Fung-shui</term> has held influence there. Many have been caused by the recognized necessity of selecting auspicious dates for burials, a custom which, as our readers know, is most closely connected with <term>Fung-shui</term> doctrines. We read, for instance, about Ho Siün <note>賀循.</note>, a statesman who lived in the third and the beginning of the fourth century, that:

> "when he was
> "finally appointed as the governor of Wu-khang (a part of
> "modern Chehkiang), it was very common among the people to bury
> "their dead at great expense; there were also those who,
> "harboring a superstitious dread of years and months in which
> "certain things ought not to be done, stored up their dead instead
> "of burying them in the earth. These practices were forbidden by
> "Ho Siün once and for all" <note>最後為武康令、俗多厚葬、及有拘忌廻避歲月、停喪不葬者。循皆禁焉. *Books of the Tsin Dynasty*, chapter 68, line 15.</note>.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the legal and social consequences of delaying burials, specifically focusing on dynastic laws that excluded subjects who failed to bury their parents from holding public office.</meta>

<page-num>1021</page-num>
<header>POSTPONEMENT OF THE BURIAL OF PARENTS.</header>
<sig>66</sig>

To put a check on the evil in question, several dynasties have formally excluded from state service those subjects who postponed the burial of their parents. It is stated that "under the Wei dynasty and the House of Tsïn, the only reason for excluding a man from an official post was the fact of the corpse of his grandfather or father being kept uncoffined or unburied" <sup>1</sup>. This rule also prevailed during the T‘ang dynasty, for we read in the biography of Yen-chen-khïng <sup>2</sup>, who lived in the eighth century: When he held a high post in the region of Ho-tung, "there was living there one Ching Yen-tsu, who after his mother’s death had left her corpse unburied for twenty-nine years within the walls of a Buddhist monastery. Chen-khïng reported the case to the Throne, with the result that the man and his brothers were not registered among the officials for thirty years, and the whole empire was alarmed and moved" <sup>3</sup>. Still later, in 952, during the short-lived Cheu dynasty, the emperor Ts‘ai Tsu <sup>4</sup> issued a decree stating that "henceforth, in every case of a paternal grandparent or parent not having been buried after their death, the elders of the family over which they presided during their life shall not be entitled to seek official rank, nor will the officers already descended from that family be granted any promotion or transfer to another post; but these decrees did not apply to junior or lower-ranking relations, nor to the members of the family still lower in status" <sup>5</sup>.

Szĕ-ma Kwang, the famous statesman and ethical philosopher whom our readers have already encountered elsewhere in this work (page 238), stands foremost among those who, during the Sung dynasty, turned their sharp pen against <term>Fung-shui</term>, be-

...because it deprived so many of the dead of a decent and timely burial. In A.D. 1084 he wrote:

"The people nowadays do not bury the dead more luxuriously than they did in ancient times, but the importance attached to the prohibitions created by the Yin-and-Yang system has become much greater! The treatises on burial now in circulation investigate the influences of the forms of mountains and water-courses, rocks and fields; they examine the <term>Branches</term> and <term>kan</term> <note>Heavenly Stems</note> which indicate the years, months, days, and hours, considering the low or high rank of the offspring in the social scale, their wealth and poverty, late or early death, and intelligence or stupidity to be entirely bound up with those factors. Consequently, burials cannot be performed unless in such-and-such grounds and at such-and-such times.

The whole nation is bewildered by these theories and places belief in them; as a result, it frequently occurs that those who lose their parents postpone their burial for a considerable time. If asked the reasons why they do so, they say: 'The year and month are not yet propitious,' or: 'We have not yet found a felicitous plot of ground,' or: 'Some of our family reside far from here in the service of the State and have not yet found an opportunity to come home,' or: 'We are so poor that we are not yet able to procure the requirements for the burial.'

These are the causes of there being people who do not perform one single burial during their whole lives—indeed, during many generations in succession—in consequence of which encoffined corpses are abandoned and lost sight of, so that it becomes unknown where they are. Oh! How is it possible that such things do not make a man sigh and lament from the bottom of his heart!" <note>1. Modern people do not bury their dead more lavishly than the ancients, but they are far more constrained by Yin-and-Yang prohibitions. Current burial manuals analyze the topography of mountains, rivers, and fields, and calculate the stems and branches of years, months, days, and hours. They believe that the status, wealth, lifespan, and intelligence of descendants are all tied to these, so that a burial cannot take place except at a specific time and place. The whole world is misled and believes this; thus, those who lose their parents often delay burial for a long time. When asked why, they say the timing is unfavorable, or they have no auspicious land, or they are serving as officials far away and cannot return, or they are too poor to afford the burial. This results in burials being delayed for lifetimes or generations, until the coffins are abandoned and lost, their locations forgotten. Alas, does this not cause profound grief and pity?</note>

With a view to the life to come, a man sets great value upon having posterity, so that they may properly bury his remains. But if his offspring act in the way described above, a man is worse off than

<header>THE GRAVE.</header>

In another piece from his hand, Szĕ-ma Kwang laments the same subject in a somewhat different tone. "The people, placing trust in the gossip of burial experts, are accustomed to seeking good influences from the forms and contours of mountains and watercourses even after they have selected auspicious years, months, days, and hours for the burial. They believe the wealth and social position of their sons and grandsons, their mental abilities, and the length of their lives depend on these factors in every respect. But there is so much diversity of opinion among those experts, and they confuse matters with their quarrelsome discussions to such an extent, that no decision can be reached regarding a date for the burial. Consequently, some people do not bury any of their dead during their whole lives—even for several generations. It also happens that descendants do not bury their dead because a decline in their fortunes causes them to forget or lose sight of the place where they have left the remains. Supposing for a moment that burials could actually make a person happy and prosperous, would it even then be tolerable for sons and grandsons to cruelly leave the decaying remains of their nearest relations exposed to the open sky, with the goal of reaping profit for themselves? Such acts are the greatest sins against the rites and the worst violations of human duty that can be."

> "The sorrowful resentment a grieving filial son carries in his heart is profound, and his grief extends far. Hence he fears that, if he does not bury the remains deep enough, others will dig them up, and that, if he places them too deep in the ground, they will become wet and mold away quickly. Consequently, he certainly searches for a place where the earth is thick and the water is deep beneath the ground, and there he buries the corpse; in this respect, he must certainly select a proper place" <note>1</note>.

...family. To this day there has been no other cause. I have often been troubled by the way geomancers establish false theories to delude the masses and cause trouble for families in mourning; it is especially severe. Recently, while serving as a Censor, I submitted a memorial requesting a ban on burial books throughout the Empire, but at that time the officials in power did not take it to heart. Now I write this discourse, in the hope that future descendants will bury their dead at the proper time. If you want to know that burial items need not be lavish, look at my ancestors; if you want to know that burial books are not to be trusted, look at my family. *Ku kin t’u shu tsih ch'ing*, sect. 禮儀, *ch. 97*.

<header>POSTPONEMENT OF BURIAL PUNISHED BY GOVERNMENT.</header>

When Szĕ-ma Kwang thus applied his wisdom to improving the customs of the nation at a time when his authority and influence had reached their height, the ruling Son of Heaven was endeavoring to stop the postponement of burials through stricter measures. In the fifth year of the Yuan-feng period (1082), he decreed that those who did not bury their deceased relations without delay should be banished for two years, and that those who kept such men in official employment should be punished ¹. About the same time, as the histories of that era recount, one Wang Tszĕ-shao ², a high-ranking official in Hunan, "was denounced by the censor Chang Shang-ying for not having buried his parents, and he was dismissed from his office because of it" ³. A few years later, "Liu Ping—who, while in charge of the government of Ch'en-cheu, had along with his younger brother Hwan been raised to the dignity of Minister in immediate attendance on the Throne—was stripped of this rank as punishment for not having buried his deceased parents and dismissed from his position as prefect" ⁴.

The Ming dynasty likewise decreed that punishments should be inflicted upon those who were guilty of such detestable acts. "In the fifth year of the Hung-wu period (1372 AD), it was decreed by the emperor that, whereas there were

Their methods are also quite different, and their arguments are so numerous and confused that a decision can never be reached. This results in some people remaining unburied for their entire lives, or even for several generations. In some cases, as the descendants' fortunes decline, they lose or forget the location, and the remains are abandoned and left unburied. Even if burial practices truly could bring good or bad fortune, how could a son endure letting his parents' remains rot and be exposed just to seek his own profit? Nothing is a greater violation of the rites or a more serious injury to morality than this.

However, the heart of a filial son considers potential troubles far into the future. He fears that if the grave is shallow, it will be dug up by others; but if it is deep, moisture will cause the body to rot quickly. Therefore, he must seek a place where the soil is thick and the water table is deep to bury them; for this reason, one must choose a site carefully. <gloss>Ku kin t'u shu tsih ch'ing, section on Rites, chapters 92 and 63.</gloss>

# GRAVES DO NOT PROFIT ALL THE CHILDREN.

and that of their children will be entirely bound up with the graves of their parents-in-law.

The theory that a grave can rarely bestow blessings on all sons equally is one of the greatest inventions of the geomantic sages. It protects their system from some of the most dangerous attacks from skeptics, as it immediately silences all those who might ask: "Showers of blessings descend upon my brother’s house because, as the experts say, the position of our father’s grave is extremely auspicious; why then am I, though also his son, overwhelmed by poverty and misfortune?" Such remarks are also easily disarmed by the following argument: "That one brother is poor and the other is rich is simply a consequence of the latter neglecting to give the former a fair share of the profits the grave produces for him. To share those profits with his brother is his moral duty; but instead of fulfilling his duty, he keeps everything for himself, even at the risk of ruining his own fortunes. In doing so, he is foolishly amassing a store of demerit that will eventually provoke the indignation of the *T'ien li*. They will inevitably punish him by withdrawing their protection from the grave, and so cause its *Feng-shui* to flow away, which will leave him poorer than he ever was before."

The doctrine that a grave may yield great profits to one member of a family without benefiting the others is by no means a modern invention. We already read in the histories of Emperor Wu <gloss>1</gloss> of the Liang dynasty:

> When Lady Ting, the emperor’s first-rank concubine, died, the heir-apparent (her son) delegated some men to find a favorable place to bury her. When they were about to clear the plants and shrubs from that spot, an individual who had a plot of ground for sale tried to sell it through the eunuch Yu San-fu, promising him one million if he managed to get three million for it. San-fu secretly approached the emperor, telling him that the ground the heir-apparent had secured could not ensure imperial prosperity to the same degree as the plot he had now found. The emperor, who was in the final years of his life and entertained various superstitious fears, ordered him to purchase it.

<header>GRAVES MADE DURING LIFE.</header>

From what has been presented in the preceding pages, it is clear enough that the possession of sons and money is not an absolute blessing, for the consequences may be fatal to a Chinese person after their death. Indeed, if each son is anxious to secure his own specific fortune through his father’s grave, and enough money has been left to them to provide what they believe to be a perfect <term>Fung-shui</term>, discord arises. Because of this, the burial of the old man is postponed for months and years, to the detriment of his <term>manes</term>. No wonder, therefore, that many a well-to-do father, if blessed with numerous sons, endeavors to avoid this disaster by having his grave made during his lifetime, while observing all the rules of <term>geomantic science</term>.

This custom may be considered on par with that of obtaining, during life, one’s own grave clothes and coffin. It saves many a poor soul from the gloomy fate of wandering about in the other world as a homeless <term>pariah</term>, an outcast without a shelter where they can retire from the evils and nuisances of the spirit world. Moreover, it is considered very grand in this present life to possess one’s own grave, especially if it has been built by the care of the sons under the guise of filial devotion.

A grave made during the life of the person who is to occupy it is called in Amoy a *<term>siū hík</term>* ^2, "longevity region". This term owes its origin to the same idea as "longevity garments" and "longevity boards" or "longevity wood," which are terms respectively denoting grave clothes and coffins made before death (see pages 61 and 323).

To prepare one’s own grave during life is a custom of very ancient date. The emperor <term>Shi Hwang</term> started the works for his mausoleum shortly after his accession to the throne (see page 399), and the same course of action was followed by the sovereigns of the <term>Han dynasty</term> (page 423), for which reason their sepulchers are often referred to in the annals of their reign as "longevity mausolea" ^3.

<header>THE GRAVE.</header>

That the custom was also popular among the official class at that time is proved by the histories of that era, which relate that the grandee Heu Lan, "having on the death of his mother in the second year of the Kien ning period (169 A.D.) returned home and there built a large sepulchre, the Circuit Judge, Chang Kien, impeached him in a memorial addressed to the Throne for having prepared for himself a longevity sepulchre with a stone vault, a gate with two entrances, and high side buildings one hundred feet tall" <note>1</note>. And of the minister Chao Khi <note>2</note> we read: "In the sixth year of the Kien ngan period (201 A.D.) he died, having previously built a longevity tomb for himself" <note>3</note>. Instances of this same custom are also regularly recorded after the Han dynasty. For instance, at a time corresponding to about the year 480 A.D., a high official named "Ch'en T'ien-fuh ordered his family to build a longevity tomb for him" <note>4</note>.

Geomancers never have such a grand opportunity to show off their ability and cleverness as when a *<term>siū hík</term>* is being made. There is then plenty of time for the family to consult any number of them and to admire that display of profound learning with which each of them can undo what the other has planned and executed. Of course, in the end, the one chosen is the person who demonstrates more scholarship than all the others by speaking ambiguous nonsense, while also showing a great deal of respect for the views expressed by the male and female members of the family, who indeed feel sure they know all about the art. After an experiment with pig's bones produces good results, the grave is finished under the guidance of that "wisest of the wise," the mound is built, and an inscribed gravestone is erected in front of it. If the *<term>mater-familias</term>* <note>the mother of the family</note> is still alive, a tomb is generally built for her at the same time on the right-hand side; the left side belongs to her husband, as it is considered the place of honor in both life and death.

<page-num>1033</page-num>
<header>GRAVES MADE DURING LIFE.</header>

When the grave is ready, it is necessary to prevent it from emitting the influences of premature death onto its future occupant. To this end, a piece of red paper is pasted over his name, which is carved into the gravestone. This sheet does not need to be replaced with a new one after time and rain have destroyed it; according to geomancers, the influences of the grave will have blended harmoniously with those of the universe by that time and, so to speak, become one with it, thereby losing their dangerous character. Now the old man feels perfectly at ease and greatly enjoys the happy prospect of being buried promptly after his death. The sons also cheerfully look forward to the future and the wealth and fortune it is sure to bring them.

Still, in many cases, everything goes wrong. Unrelenting, insidious death may strike the old man in a year when the alignment in which his grave is made is not auspicious, thus forcing a long delay of the burial; or—and this is much worse—the expert under whose auspices and directions the grave was made may have died in the meantime or moved to another part of the country. His colleague, whom the family entrusts with the burial, will then tell them that the *Fung-shui* is not worth a brass farthing. Struck with consternation, the men vent their sorrowful resentment in heated discussions, and the women through loud shouting and outbursts of wrath. But as this does not remedy the situation, the coffin is kept at home and another burial site is sought. The *<term>siū hīk</term>*, which was so dearly paid for, is sold to others, or used to bury a slave, an unmarried daughter, or a person without offspring who might wish to profit from their ancestor's earthly resting place.

Of course, not every *<term>siū hīk</term>* turns out to be such an unlucky business; otherwise, people would have stopped making them long ago.

Because *Fung-shui* often prevents people from burying their parents with suitable promptness, it becomes a great nuisance, especially for those who cannot afford to buy coffins good and sturdy enough to be kept in the house without emitting a nauseating smell. On the island of Amoy, such families—as well as those who, wishing to avoid being accused of being unfilial, do not want to postpone burials, but also do not want to give up their chances of profiting from the grave through the medium of *Fung-shui*—often resort to a provisional interment. They call this *<term>t'ao tái</term>* <note>1. 偷埋 (Stealthy burial)</note> or *<term>t'ao tsōng</term>* <note>2. 偷葬 (Stealthy interment)</note>, » a stealthy or

"clandestine burial". Under the escort of a simple funeral procession, they take the coffin into the mountains or into the open country, place it somewhere on the ground, and cover it with earth without having the properties of the spot examined by a Fung-shui expert. They do not erect a gravestone, thereby indicating that the coffin is not in a permanent grave, but is to be removed later to a resting place under favorable geomantic influences. Now it may happen that, before the new grave is found, the family begins to prosper. Such unexpected happiness can, of course, only be attributed to the good Fung-shui of the provisional grave. They are secretly pleased because they have won the great prize in the lottery of life by pure accident or through the unforeseen merits of themselves or their ancestors. Now they are certain not to move the corpse, nor do they turn the spot into a tomb worthy of the dead man, for fear that the Fung-shui, sensitive as it is, might be shattered by a mistaken blow with a hoe or be permanently ruined by a single brick applied in the wrong place. Thus, the dead man is forced to live like a pauper in a miserable dwelling, unworthy of his rank and status. But this causes no guilt, for the blessings he gives to his family are strong proof that he feels perfectly happy and comfortable where he is.

Although the poorer classes cannot, of course, afford great expenses for their dead, they rarely neglect consulting a Fung-shui expert when they have to bury their father or mother. This man does not take long to find a suitable site when he knows there is not much money to be made from his clients; he has quite a stock of second-rate plots in store for them, which he constantly increases when in search of good burial places for the wealthy. The poor know very well that they can hope to buy very little Fung-shui for the small sums they are able to pay. Therefore, they are modest in their demands, merely seeking graves that are protected from the worst aeolian influences <note>Influences related to the wind, which are central to Fung-shui</note> and located on a slope that is not unfavorably positioned; they employ an expert specifically to ensure the coffin is placed in the grave in the favorable alignment of the current year.

As hinted above, the Fung-shui of even the best grave or dwelling is considered to be a fragile combination of imaginary influences fitting into and acting upon each other like the different parts of a machine, where the slightest defect may bring the whole thing to a standstill. It is a great benefit to the experts that such ideas prevail. Indeed, Fung-shui being of such a delicate nature,

<page-num>1035</page-num>
<header>FUNG-SHUI CAN BE WOUNDED AND KILLED.</header>

No one, however economical or greedy they may be, is brave enough to do without the guidance of an expert; and this ensures them a constant source of income. Besides, since Fung-shui is so easily disturbed, experts always have a ready excuse at hand if their prophecies are not realized: the Fung-shui, they say, was perfect at the start, but it has been "wounded" by some accident or by the malicious act of a bad neighbor.

Such wounds may be inflicted by a mere trifle. A stone carelessly thrown away, or set up somewhere in the neighborhood by a person wishing to improve the Fung-shui of one of their own graves; the erection of a stone boundary mark; the building of a hut or shed at some distance from the grave or on a visible mountain ridge; in short, anything may prove fatal. But nothing is so dangerous for a grave as the construction of another grave on the neighboring land. In general, it is the expert who discovers the approaching danger. He does not delay for a moment to open the eyes of the family to the sorrowful fact that the new grave will block the influences of a watercourse, or that—being built higher up, right in the "pulse" through which the beneficial influences of the tail or leg of the <term>Tiger</term> or <term>Dragon</term> previously used to flow—it "cuts off their effective operation": <term>chan ling</term> <note>斬靈</note>. At the same time, he convinces the family that only prompt and severe measures can heal the wound, and that if these are not immediately taken, the benevolent Animal will bleed to death and the Fung-shui will be forever destroyed.

Therefore, everyone sets to work immediately. Negotiations are opened with the owners of the "murderous" grave, but without any good result, as they zealously stick to their legal right of keeping a spot obtained at the cost of much study and money. Geomantic measures satisfactory to both parties are hardly possible, for what is good for one grave is generally harmful to the other, and the learned combinations of factors to which both must correspond almost inevitably clash. Hard cash may perhaps lead to a better result. But the suffering party usually retreats from the high demands of the other, who is certain to demand an excessive sum, especially if any of them are graduates or rich and influential men who—being on good terms with the local <term>mandarins</term>—feel sure of winning their case if the offended party should call for the intervention of the officials to correct the wrong. In such cases, nothing remains for the family but to beat a humble

But, should the two parties possess an equal, or nearly equal, amount of social influence, or have no influence at all, a complaint is soon filed with the chief local magistrate. Our readers might naturally suppose that this official will simply dismiss the case, since written law and the Government—as we have stated on page 1017—have denounced modern Fung-shui in contemptuous terms as a heap of nonsense, and its practitioners as a set of deceivers. However, regarding geomancy, theory and practice in China are two different things; for should a mandarin refuse to hear such cases, his secretaries, constables, police, and other attendants would be deprived of many a fine opportunity to make money easily. These underlings, by leaving the accusation ignored after it has been entered, compel the plaintiff—who is anxious to save his Fung-shui from imminent death by loss of blood—to bribe them to act quickly. But however hard this may make his lot, that of the defendant is still harder. If he has any money to lose, he lives in constant fear of being taken into custody, for the common people, no matter how innocent, are always liable to immediate imprisonment if an accusation has been filed against them with the authorities. And as the Yamen officials take good care to remind the defendant of this danger, he pays them generous fees, and pays them over and over again. And yet all these fees are not always sufficient to protect him from a terrible dungeon, a literal hell of cold, filth, starvation, and torment.

Not until they have wrung the last penny out of their victims do these underlings rouse the magistrate from his inactivity. He is then carried in state to the graves in his official palankeen, escorted by his usual attendance of soldiers, retainers, and lictors. Arrived at the spot, maps of the locality, submitted by the plaintiff, are unrolled and compared with the deeds of sale for the property; with a dignified air, the mandarin surveys the country, and usually, he is convinced in a few moments that his subordinates were quite justified in persuading him that the party which paid them best is in the right. Otherwise, judgment is usually given in favor of the plaintiff; but many mandarins stubbornly refuse to do this when the distance between the two graves exceeds a certain number of

# FUNG-SHUI QUESTIONS DECIDED BY THE AUTHORITIES.

Such a "Fung-shui inspection" or *khàm hong-suí* <note>1 勘風水.</note>, as the Amoy Chinese call it, must of course be paid for by the party on whose behalf it is made. A large sum is extorted from them for the men who have accompanied the magistrate and carried his sedan chair. Furthermore, the same party must offer refreshments and delicacies to the great man while he makes his inspection, and they must spread a piece of red cloth over the top of his palankeen to protect him from harmful influences; this cloth is then kept by him (compare pages 97 and 219). Last, but not least, they must send him a sum of money along with a selection of costly presents, lest their case be lost at the last moment by the mandarin ultimately changing his mind in favor of the other party.

It follows from this that poor people, whose graves’ Fung-shui has been disturbed, must swallow the injustice in silence. The Amoy Chinese are quite right when they say:

> ->*Gé-mng pat dzi khai,*<-
> ->*Bô tsîn m sái lái* <note>2 衙門八字開、無錢無使來.</note>,<-

which means: "Mandarins' offices stand open as wide as the character 八 (eight); but those who have no money need not enter."

The abuse of litigation by petty officials for the purpose of extorting money is very common in China and is systematically tolerated in all cases, both criminal and civil. We say "systematically" because, while the Government—as readers know (see page 541)—acts on the principle that each individual or family should have their affairs regulated by their own clan and not trouble the higher authorities, those who are unwise enough to call for official interference may expect to suffer, primarily in their pockets. This method is very practical for the moral education of the people, teaching them to be mild and patient and to avoid litigation. Mandarins are sometimes honest enough to issue proclamations in which the evils resulting from litigation are depicted in vivid colors, thus openly confessing that extortion by police officers and clerks is, as a matter of course, inseparably connected with lawsuits.

<page-num>1038</page-num>

# THE GRAVE.

Much strife and contention regarding graves is created by the foul intrigues and frauds of certain brokers, who earn a living by assisting people in acquiring suitable burial grounds. These men possess, or are thought to possess, a thorough knowledge of the locations where suitable burial sites can be found, and they know better than anyone else who the owners are and the conditions under which they are willing to sell. In Amoy, the people refer to them by the unflattering terms of *soaⁿ-kúi* <note>1 山鬼.</note>, "mountain spectres," and *soaⁿ ka-tsoáh* <note>2 山 〇 〇.</note>, "mountain cockroaches," because they haunt graves like ghosts and rummage through every spot and corner of the open country like cockroaches in a house. When a client approaches such a grave broker, the client is taken out to see the land; the broker’s primary goal is to ask for the highest possible price and to persuade the owners to sell cheaply, quietly pocketing the difference. As is generally the custom with brokers in China, the "mountain cockroach" settles the transaction without allowing the buyer and seller to see each other, or even to know one another's name. For the sake of his own wallet, he maintains very friendly terms with all the Fung-shui professors in the district; these individuals are able to assist him greatly in the sale of any land by declaring, for a fee, that the geomantic influences under which they are situated are good, or even excellent.

The "cockroaches" are generally described by the people as a reckless group, nearly as unscrupulous in their methods of making money as thieves and robbers. It is primarily they who commit frauds such as those addressed in the fourth and fifth supplementary articles of the Law on Burial (pages 878 and following). They target their victims especially among those who do not have enough money or influence to get a hearing from the magistrates, should they apply to them for a remedy for their grievances. One of their most common tricks is as follows: within the boundaries of a grave belonging to such a family, the broker stealthily builds a grave mound that is barely visible. When the family notices it, they do not dare to remove it, fearing that the wicked unknown person who built it might be cruel enough to denounce them as grave robbers, thereby bringing upon them all the suffering that an accusation—whether false or not—usually entails. Having now demonstrated its lack of power and influence by

<header>MALVERSATIONS OF FUNG-SHUI BROKERS.</header>

By not reporting the matter to the authorities, after a couple of years the broker sells the mock grave to a third party, telling them that it is his legal property from which he has, for some reason or another, removed the bones. Up to this point, all goes well. But no sooner do the purchasers proceed to burying their dead, than the real owners come forward to interfere. A scene ensues such as we have described on page 128; quarrels, arguments, and lawsuits follow. In most cases, however, both parties have the good sense not to start a legal suit, and the legal owners are persuaded to give up their claim to the disputed ground for a small sum paid to them by the broker. The broker, of course, is most interested in hushing the matter up as quickly as possible.

With a view to check practices of this sort, pious people—anxious to keep the moral condition of their countrymen at the highest possible level—sometimes erect slabs or small columns of granite in the grounds where people are accustomed to bury their dead. These are engraved with this inscription: "If you desire to find the beneficial influences of the earth (<term>Ti li</term>), then first gain those of the heavens (<term>T’ien li</term>)" <note>1 "If you seek earthly principles, first seek heavenly principles." 要求地理、先求天理．</note>, which can only be done by the cultivation of virtues (p. 1013).

In many other ways, <term>mountain-cockroaches</term> cause serious burial disputes to arise. Such individuals, not considering it beneath their dignity to misappropriate other people’s grave grounds and sell them, can, of course, have no qualms of conscience about selling grounds which, when converted into graves, entirely disturb the <term>Fung-shui</term> of other tombs. Neither will they shrink from misleading the buyers so as to cause them to build their <term>omega-shaped fence</term> over the grave of another, thus inflicting a mortal blow upon the <term>Fung-shui</term> of that grave, or a dagger stroke which causes an incurable wound. This stirs up the indignation of the owners to the highest pitch. If they do not have enough money or influence to place the matter in the hands of the magistrates, and their protests and threats remain without effect, they vent their anger under the cover of night by knocking to pieces the inscribed stone of the grave belonging to the encroachers. This stone is considered the place where the <term>geomantic</term> influences are chiefly concentrated and, moreover, the seat of the <term>manes</term> <note>the spirits of the dead</note> of the occupant of the grave. The next night, they find their own grave

In the countryside, such feuds generally entail the desecration of several more graves, open fights, destruction of crops, and arson. Men, women, and children are waylaid and ensnared, captured and mistreated, or held as hostages, to be either ransomed for money or exchanged; in short, civil war, which is always smoldering in China, breaks out in the locality with all its disastrous consequences.

When matters have reached such a point, the mandarins sometimes resort to rigorous measures. Soldiers are stationed in both villages and soon restore order by extorting money and food from the inhabitants so mercilessly that within a few weeks not a bushel of rice, nor a handful of copper coins is to be found in either of the villages. While everything of value is thus being eaten up, carried off, or gambled away by the "peacemakers," the magistrate paternally corrects those who have taken an active part in the desecration of the graves by making liberal use of sticks both long and short, punishing some, if he deems it fit, with the utmost rigor of the Burial Law.

Since social life has not undergone any radical change in China since culture was established there, we have no reason to suppose that conflicts about graves requiring the interference of the authorities are exclusively peculiar to modern times. The passage in the *Cheu li*, which we have reproduced on page 830, gives evidence that already in the pre-Christian era certain high-ranking officers were appointed to attend to litigation of this kind and to settle them by a judicial decision. That they have sometimes assumed enormous proportions is proved by the History of the *Sung Dynasty*, according to which, in the thirteenth century, one

> "Lü Hang, in
> the capacity of prefect of Wu-cheu, managed to settle by judicial
> decision a lawsuit which had been pending about some fields for
> forty-two years between Mr. Chu and a certain Chang, and also
> a contention about graves which had lasted twenty-nine years
> between two gentlemen with the surnames of Wu and Wang" 1.

<page-num>1041</page-num>
<header>CONTENTIONS ARISING FROM FUNG-SHUI QUESTIONS.</header>

disarrangement of the Fung-shui of an extensive tract of country. A slight alteration made in the course of a brook for agricultural or other purposes; the modification of the brow of a hill or the outlines of a rock by the erection of a house or shed; in short, any little trifle may seriously disturb the Fung-shui of villages or valleys, which is usually evidenced by a decline in their prosperity, bad crops, calamities, etc. Attacks upon the Fung-shui of a landscape are often made for malignant purposes. There are instances on record of the whole male population of a village having worked hard for several days to destroy the good fortune of a hated neighbor by digging away a knoll, leveling down an eminence, or amputating a limb from a Dragon or Tiger <note>Dragon and Tiger refer to specific mountain or hill formations in geomancy.</note>.

Quarrels and litigation arising from Fung-shui questions are of daily occurrence in towns. The repairing of a house, the building of a wall or dwelling—especially if it overtops its surroundings—the planting of a pole or cutting down of a tree; in short, any change in the ordinary position of objects may disturb the Fung-shui of the houses and temples in the vicinity and of the whole quarter, and cause the people to be visited by disasters, misery, and death. Should anyone suddenly fall ill or die, his kindred are immediately ready to attribute the cause to somebody who has ventured to make a change in the established order of things, or has made an improvement in his own property, which he had a perfect right to do. Instances are by no means rare of their having stormed his house, demolished his furniture, or assailed his person; sometimes they place the corpse in his bed, with the object of extorting money and avenging themselves by introducing the influences of death into his house <note>Compare pages 840 and following.</note>. No wonder Chinese people do not repair their houses until they are ready to fall and become uninhabitable.

Fortunately, much animosity and contention is prevented by the fact that Fung-shui, when disturbed, can be restored in various ways. Professors, if consulted in time, are generally able to suggest some remedy. When a dwelling house is endangered, they usually order the erection of certain fences capable of keeping off or absorbing the *shah* <note>Harmful geomantic influences or "killing breaths."</note> which are, they think, encroaching upon the good geomantic influences. Among such fences, slabs of granite inscribed with the sentence: "This stone dares to resist them" <note>Shi Gandang (石敢當).</note>, are considered the best, if placed at a proper spot on the premises.
