Also, when the <term>Fung-shui</term> of a village, town, or valley has been disturbed, there are many means of remedying the evil. We have already stated on page 958 how the disastrous contours of rocks, mountains, or plains may be rectified by skillful adjustments and turned into sources of blessing. If an elevation is not high enough, it can be made higher; a disastrous watercourse may be given a favorable turn; groves may be planted at the back or on the sides of villages and towns as screens; tanks and ponds may be dug to counteract harmful breaths by the aquatic influences they hold (pages 946 and 958); pagodas may be erected for the same purpose, or piles of stone may be made to represent such structures (pages 941 and 958). Temples for the worship of mighty guardian divinities and even large Buddhist convents generally owe their existence to a desire of the people to strengthen the <term>Fung-shui</term> of the surroundings. However, we reserve the particulars on this topic for other parts of this work, where such sanctuaries will be described.

After this digression, let us return to the Fung-shui of the resting places of the dead: a wound inflicted on a grave does not necessarily result in the death of its Fung-shui. The Fung-shui of some graves is so vigorous that it can sustain many an injury without being seriously damaged—even, in fact, the amputation of a <term>Dragon</term>'s or <term>Tiger</term>'s limb. In others, on the contrary, the Fung-shui is so frail that the slightest wound is sure to affect its operation and bring the whole machine to a standstill. Only professional experts are capable of determining whether the wound is dangerous, and whether a cure is possible. They assert that, as with the human body, the severity of the injury chiefly depends upon the part affected. The stone, for instance, on which the grave inscription is carved, and the <term>tumulus</term>, are especially vulnerable, as they are—as stated before—the primary seat of the <term>manes</term> of the occupant of the grave. Whether a wound is fatal is inferred from its consequences. Should the family be visited by sickness, death, or a decline in business, or suffer any considerable financial losses, then, after long consultation with one or more learned professors, the death of the Fung-shui is taken for granted. It is then useless to remove the object which caused the wound, to repair the violated <term>tumulus</term>, or to set up a new gravestone in the place of the one that has been destroyed. Indeed, as people argue, neither pulling a dagger from the body of a murdered man, nor patching up his wounds, can ever restore him to life.

When enough evil has befallen the family to convince them that the wound inflicted on their grave is fatal, they generally conclude that the best thing they can do is to ask their professor to look for another grave site and rebury the corpse. It frequently happens that a professor, eager for business and profit, makes a family believe that one of their graves has entirely lost its good Fung-shui, claiming the corpse has fallen prey to termites, the skeleton has been turned upside down, or the bones are lying in disorder or topsy-turvy in the coffin. He tells them it is their duty to break the grave open and give the soul a better resting

But no sooner does a disaster occur than the professor’s argument gains attention; and a few more mishaps suffice to make the family surrender themselves, bound hand and foot, into his power. When the grave is opened—fortunately for the credit of the Fung-shui and the professor—the correctness of the latter’s statement is often verified by facts. In truth, it is a very common occurrence in China for termites to build their nests in coffins, or for foxes, rats, or other beasts to nestle there; besides, the stick of a "mountain cockroach" <note>likely a derogatory term for a local scavenger or a specific type of grave-meddler</note> or of the professor himself can secretly disarrange the bones so as to ensure the triumph of the latter. And even if everything in the grave should be in the best condition, and the bones dry and hard, and the coffin but little affected by decay, the professor has plenty of arguments to prove that the Fung-shui was thoroughly bad.

It is not necessary to elaborate further on Fung-shui and its influence upon social life. The above pages will suffice to show what it really is: the product of egotism under the guise of filial piety; a sure sign that this highest among the national virtues of the Chinese, so often highly praised by European authors, is much less sincere than is generally supposed; that it is not spontaneous, but calculating; not generous, but thoroughly selfish. Fung-shui is fetishism applied to the dead and their physical remains. It is a hybrid monster, born of the union of filial devotion in its vilest form with blind gropings after natural science. At the outset a numbed viper, it has, carefully fostered by the nation, developed into a horrid hydra suffocating the whole Empire in its coils and drenching it with its venom throughout its length and breadth.

In fact, as we have stated, wielding its cruel scourge with vigor, it disturbs social peace and order, sowing endless discord among families, clans, and villages, and giving rise to quarrels, lawsuits, conflict, arson, and bloodshed. It causes the ruin of many families, wasting their fortunes under the pretext of building them. It compels the people to keep their dead unburied for months, or even years, in spite of epidemics and contagious diseases, and to exhume them before the process of decay is complete, thus increasing mortality. with industry and commercial enterprise, as it is the basis for refusing many improvements that would be of the greatest advantage to the people. The cutting of a new road or canal, the construction of a new bridge, almost always involves the amputation of a limb of some Celestial Animal, intercepts good aquatic influences, or affects the calculations of geomancers in some way or another. This causes entire clans, wards, villages, and towns to rise up as one man against the reckless individual whose enterprising spirit dares to bring misfortune upon them all. "When," says Dr. Eitel <gloss>1</gloss>, "it was proposed to erect a few telegraph poles, when the construction of a railway was urged upon the Chinese Government, when a mere tramway was suggested to utilize the coal mines of the interior, Chinese officials would invariably make a polite bow and declare the thing impossible on account of Fung-shui. When, thirty years ago, the leading merchants of the Colony of Hongkong endeavored to place the business part of the town in the so-called Happy Valley, and to make that part of the island the center of the whole town, they ignominiously failed on account of Fung-shui. When the Hongkong Government cut a road, now known as the Gap, to the Happy Valley, the Chinese community was thrown into a state of abject terror and fright, because of the disturbance which this amputation of the Dragon's limbs would cause to the Fung-shui of Hongkong; and when many of the engineers, employed at the cutting, died of Hongkong fever, and the foreign houses already built in the Happy Valley had to be deserted on account of malaria, the Chinese triumphantly declared it was an act of retributive justice on the part of Fung-shui. When Senhor Amaral, the Governor of Macao, who combined a great passion for constructing roads with an unlimited contempt for Fung-shui, interfered with the situation and aspects of Chinese tombs, he was waylaid by Chinese and his head cut off <gloss>2</gloss>, and the Chinese called this despicable deed the revenge of Fung-shui."

"...people of rank and influence appropriate the place for themselves, or agriculture is practiced there" <note>1</note>. As a consequence of this, Fung-shui causes an immense waste of labor in China; since it prevents the construction of good canals and roads in most parts of the empire, ships, beasts of burden, or carts can only be employed in limited numbers. This necessitates a great use of human shoulders for the transport of persons and merchandise along paths that are barely passable. Nor is it rare to see hundreds of ships and vessels taking a long, roundabout, and difficult detour, simply because Fung-shui has forbidden a bridge to be built high enough to allow them to pass underneath.

The question will be asked: how is it possible that so large a portion of the human race—though imbued since childhood with sacred awe for the mysteries of the Universe—has grown up to adulthood and extreme old age without arriving at even an elementary knowledge of the true laws of Nature? How is it that the Chinese never built up anything better than a speculative system based upon ancient formulas and mystic diagrams, amounting to little more than a mechanical play of idle abstractions—a system so unscientific and childish that it can only make us smile?

The answer must primarily be sought in the educational system of the nation. This has always been grounded on an unbounded reverence for everything that could claim an ancient origin. Whatever the ancients thought, taught, and created was always, in everyone's eyes, the highest truth—sacred and inviolable. Beyond it, no other truth ever existed. Thus, the classical books, transmitting the ideas and actions of the ancients to posterity, naturally became the exclusive starting point of instruction, both public and private. And because the government was recruited, regularly and systematically, from the classes educated in this way, it could do nothing but disparage—and even formally forbid—any doctrines and studies arising from other principles. On the other hand, it never occurred to anyone among the people to pursue another line of study, because only the old method opened up any prospect of being admitted into the ranks of the ruling party, which is the highest ambition of every true Chinaman.

# NO TRUE NATURAL SCIENCE EXISTS IN CHINA.

So nobody in China has ever thought of studying Nature in that independent, objective way which alone can reveal the secrets of the Universe to man; nor have the Chinese tried to make instruments to aid them in the observation of the canopy of heaven, the study of the atmosphere, or the laws of gravity and hydrostatics. Instead of this, they have dulled their wits upon speculative theories, developing an entire system of natural science from their religious superstitions regarding the dead in connection with a few rough guesses about Nature occurring in the Classics; the result being a monstrous mixture of religion, superstition, ignorance, and philosophy, more strange than anything ever produced by the human brain. It seems never to have occurred to anyone, not even to the wisest of the wise, that methodical, independent research might be a better foundation for large books than the ignorance of the ancients. Chinese sages, by extending the dogmatic formulas of ancient tradition to an infinite length, have succeeded in proving that oceans of wisdom lie hidden in those formulas. Thus the position of the ancients has been strengthened, so as to render it unassailable, but in the mountains of reasoning, not a single grain of common sense is to be found; and though these sages have obtained places of worship for themselves in the government temples dedicated to Confucius and the great disciples of his school of learning—thereby gaining the highest honors ever awarded in their country to the human intellect—not one of them has ever enriched the Empire with the simplest fundamental of real, useful knowledge.

Even at present, the educational system of China is based, as firmly as ever, upon the principle that the Classics are the sole repositories of true science; and everything which is not built upon the principles laid down there is ignored or labeled as unorthodox. And the Government is in the hands of the learned class, as it has always been. Hence, Feng Shui is still at the peak of its power, holding influence in the mansions of emperors and princes just as in the cabins of the poor. The palace grounds in the capital and the magnificent mausoleums of the Imperial Family, as well as the graves of the lowest class, are laid out in accordance with its decrees. That Feng Shui has a legal status we have seen from the fact that the authorities hear the claims and give judgment when complaints about the disturbance of Feng Shui are placed before them.

Feng Shui even has a political status. "When a rebellion breaks out in any one of the eighteen provinces, the first step taken by

Historical books mention that emperors, undoubtedly for similar reasons, destroyed the graves of the dynasties they had overthrown. Chwang Tsung, for instance, the first sovereign of the short-lived posterior T'ang dynasty, "having destroyed the House of Liang, desired to dig up the grave of T'ai Tsu (the founder of that House), to hack open his coffin, and to mutilate the corpse. He argued that the breaking open of a coffin and the mutilation of a corpse was not a noble measure for a sovereign to take as a warning example to the world. There is little doubt that it was not merely greed that inspired insurgents to destroy so many imperial tombs over the centuries, but also a desire to weaken the Throne by stripping it of the indispensable protection of its ancestors. We have already drawn our readers' attention to this point in Chapter V (p. 441) and, furthermore, stated (see pp. 427 *and following* and p. 436) that to minimize such dangers, walled cities have been built near the imperial mausoleums since the Han dynasty; these tombs remain walled and garrisoned to the present day. Should European armies have to march on Peking for a second time, it would be worth trying whether the campaign could be shortened and loss of life spared by a military occupation of the burial grounds of the Imperial Family. Indeed, should the Court receive an ultimatum that these tombs will be successively destroyed by foreign explosives, its belief in Fung-shui will without a doubt force it to submit completely to the foreign demands.

# GREAT GEOMANTIC SKILL ASCRIBED TO FOREIGNERS.

By thus making use of Feng Shui doctrines to harm their enemies, foreign powers would merely be wielding the same weapon that Chinese statesmen have so frequently and cunningly used against them in times of peace. 

"When land had to be ceded to the hated foreigner along the coast of China, as a so-called foreign concession, the Chinese Government invariably selected ground condemned by the best experts in Feng Shui as combining a deadly breath with all those indications of the compass which imply dire calamity to all who settle upon it, even to their children’s children. If the spot did not have to be ceded by treaty, it would have been pointed out to the unsuspecting foreigner as the only one available for sale, and in any case, the ignorant barbarian skeptic would be made the supposed dupe and laughingstock of the astute Chinese. 

Witness, for example, the views held by intelligent Chinese in regard to the island of Sha-meen, the foreign concession of Canton. It was originally a mudflat in the Canton River in the very worst position known to Feng Shui. It was conceded to the imperious demands of the foreign powers as the best available place of residence for foreigners; and when it was found that the Canton trade, once so important, would not revive and would not flourish there, despite all the efforts of its supporters—when it was discovered that every house built on Sha-meen was overrun with termites as soon as it was built, boldly defying coal tar, carbolic acid, and all other foreign appliances—when it was noticed that the English Consul, though a special residence was built for him there, preferred to live two miles away under the protecting shadow of a Pagoda—this was a clear triumph of Feng Shui and of Chinese statesmanship." <note>1 Eitel, *cited work*, pp. 80–81.</note>

Afterward, when the "barbarians" had been settled long enough in the several ports for the Chinese to witness the rise of flourishing mercantile houses, surrounded by buildings and villas which must have appeared to them as palaces when compared with their own huts and houses, then a decided change in their ideas as to the stupidity of foreigners in Feng Shui matters occurred. Did not the fact that there were never any paupers to be found among them, and that most of them became rich enough to pay their lowest-ranking clerks salaries which, if earned by a Chinese man, would mark him as a man of wealth, sufficiently prove that they knew all about that noble art? The only power capable of overthrowing it, or weakening its all-pervading influence, is sound natural science. However, seeing that neither the ruling classes nor the people have ever shown the slightest inclination to study Nature through an experimental and critical survey of its laws, and that a national stagnation has kept their mental culture at such a low level, it seems hopeless to expect that sound views of natural science will ever be acquired by the Chinese on their own initiative. Perhaps foreigners may be able to shed some rays of the light of their science upon the <term>Middle Kingdom</term>. But where are the men to be found who are willing and able to take upon themselves the Herculean task of educating such a nation, and who are capable of writing clear and popular explanations of the laws of Nature in that idiomatic, attractive Chinese style which alone finds favor in the eyes of the educated? And even if such men were found, their attempts would most likely be shipwrecked by the national ignorance of the written language; for, because this language is extremely difficult to learn, only very few men in every hundred or, more correctly speaking, in every thousand, are able to understand a book. # CHAPTER XIII.

## ON THE CUSTOM OF RE-BURYING BODIES IN OTHER GRAVES.
## URN BURIALS.

In the preceding chapter we have briefly introduced the reader to the custom of transferring buried corpses to other graves in certain cases. We stated that this is frequently done when a family sees its fortunes declining as a consequence of the supposed disappearance of the <term>Fung-shui</term> of a parent's or grandparent's grave, or because a deadly blow may have been struck against that <term>Fung-shui</term>. We must now consider this matter in detail and deal with some other cases in which re-burial takes place.

When the <term>Fung-shui</term> of a grave is believed to be harmful to the fortunes of the family, the exhumation is seldom delayed for long, and is even performed before a new grave has been found. The reasoning is that an ancestor lying in a grave beyond the reach of the good influences of Nature is entirely at the mercy of evil, as that evil is neither countered nor destroyed by anything. No doubt, then, his wrath will descend upon his descendants unless he is immediately rescued from his painful position by them. To dwell in a bad grave is only one degree worse than not being buried at all.

Naturally, a long time must pass before it can be convincingly proven that the <term>Fung-shui</term> of a grave is bad, inactive, or dead. Therefore, it seldom happens that a corpse is disinterred before it has become a skeleton and the coffin is too decayed to be used for the second grave.

Once disinterment is decided upon, an auspicious day is selected for the work, for reasons explained on pages 103 and following. When this day arrives, some grave-diggers, guided by a few members of the family and a <term>Fung-shui</term> professor of their choice, open the grave and then the coffin. They take the bones out of it, starting at the feet, and arrange them in their natural order upon a large wicker tray, such as is in general use in China for winnowing rice by throwing it up in the wind. The hair and the <term>cue</term> <note>A long braid of hair, also known as a queue, traditionally worn by Chinese men during the Qing Dynasty.</note> are thrown away, being considered useless, as no substance of the

During these proceedings, an open umbrella belonging to the family stands at the head of the pit on behalf of the soul, should it desire to take shelter underneath; and when the workmen have finished their task, they may take it for themselves as a perk. Finally, all the bones are placed in their natural order in a tall, wide-mouthed earthenware jar. The skull, which is placed last, is first wrapped in paper marked with the rough outlines of a mouth, nose, and eyes. To better preserve the bones, the jar is frequently filled with bits of charcoal and sealed with an earthen pan, which is fastened into the mouth using lime.

Should the bones, when exhumed, be solid and hard, with none missing, and should the grave, moreover, show no signs of termites, the family generally concludes that the <term>Fung-shui</term> is by no means as bad as they were led to believe from the professor’s description. Pained by the idea of having to give up a grave so dearly bought, they bury the jar in the same spot if they can succeed in persuading the professor to agree with their opinion, selecting a lucky day and hour for the purpose with the usual Chinese foresight. But in the vast majority of cases, another grave is sought and the old ground is sold. This sale does not necessarily cause a financial loss, for, as the geomantic doctrines affirm that a <term>Fung-shui</term>—though disadvantageous to one—may be extremely beneficial to another, eager buyers are often easily found.

Since the wealthy generally have high demands regarding graves, a new burial place for the remains of an exhumed corpse is, as a rule, not found quickly. While waiting to acquire one, the jar is stowed away somewhere in a location where some <term>Fung-shui</term> is supposed to remain—*for example*, under an overhanging rock, or in a grotto or cavern, of which there are many between the huge granite boulders that crown the hills and dot the valleys in the coastal districts. Dilapidated granite tombs of solid construction are very often used for this purpose, as are sheds or cottages in which <term>encoffined corpses</term> are preserved for burial <note>see pages 127 *and following*</note>, and the small buildings erected by benevolent men as conservatories for the <term>soul tablets</term> of deceased people who have no offspring to attend to their worship <note>Plate XXVIII</note>. # RE-BURIAL OF BONES IN URNS AND COFFINS.

When putting the urn away, one of the relatives, taking a couple of burning incense sticks between his fingers, makes a slight bow toward it and begs the soul to be content for a time with this humble home, as the family will soon find a new grave of excellent quality for it. "Potted Chinese," as foreigners have ridiculously called these urns, are quite safe everywhere. To a great extent, this is due to their worthlessness; they are of very plain construction, unglazed, without decoration, and therefore hardly worth stealing. But even more so, the aversion felt by all classes toward any unfriendly encounters with disembodied spirits protects them from sacrilegious hands. Nevertheless, it is advisable not to place charcoal inside the urns. For it is a fact that the Flowery Kingdom harbors many reckless individuals who, as poor as Job, will not shrink from the dangerous task of emptying them of combustible material and selling it for a few copper coins; but even such low characters will carefully avoid cooking their own food over it, for the same reason that prevents everyone from using old coffin boards for such a purpose (see p. 329).

Once a new grave has been found, the family usually leaves it to the <term>Feng-shui</term> expert to decide whether the urn with the bones should be buried in it, or whether a coffin is necessary. Our readers will remember that <term>geomancers</term> attach great importance to the five elements and their influence on the resting places of the dead. Thus, because urns used for bones happen to be called *kim tāng* $^1$ ("urns of metal") in Amoy and the surrounding districts—though only earthenware urns are currently in use—these men, if they are talented and clever, use them to increase the metallic influences on the grave. If they find that metal is not present in the surrounding hills and rocks in a sufficient quantity to counterbalance or neutralize the dangerous presence of the element fire, which conquers and subdues metal (see page 957), they advise urn burial. But if there is a superabundance of metallic power in the surrounding area, so that the element wood (which is conquered by metal) becomes insufficient to counterbalance it, they strengthen the wood element by burying the bones in a coffin. They also do this if there is too much of the earth element in the neighborhood, as this element is subdued by wood.

Coffins used for second burials are generally much smaller than ordinary coffins and are little better than mere wooden boxes. The Chinese of Amoy call them <term>siáo bók</term><note>Small wood (小木). Coffins for burying young children are also called *bók*, with the diminutive affix *á*; see page 330.</note>, or "small coffins." In the written language, they are denoted by the characters <term>sui</term> (檖) and <term>tuh</term> (櫝), which, as far as we know, appear with this meaning for the first time in the *Books of the Early Han Dynasty*. It is stated there that Emperor Kao Tsu, in 199 B.C., ordered the remains of the warriors who had died in the armies to be sent back to their native places in such <term>sui</term> (see page 845). It also states that:
"the Emperor Cheng, in the fourth year of the Ho-p‘ing period (25 B.C.), dispatched eleven officials—namely Kia, who was the Chief of his Court of Entertainment, and some other Doctors of that court—with orders to report to him about the condition of the regions along the Yellow River (Hwangho). There they were to distribute assistance among those who had been ruined by the floods or reduced to such misery that they could no longer support themselves. The various local governments were ordered to grant <term>sui</term> and <term>tuh</term> for the burial of those who had been swept away by the waters and whose own relations could not afford to bury them."<note>Emperor Cheng, Ho-p‘ing period, fourth year. Eleven officials, including the Court of Entertainment's Chief Doctor Jia, were sent to inspect the prefectures along the river. They provided financial aid and loans to those ruined by the water or too impoverished to survive; for those drowned or crushed by the water whose families could not bury them, the local governments were ordered to provide <term>sui</term> and <term>tuh</term> for their burial. Chapter 10, line 6.</note> Yen Shi-ku, commenting on this passage, explicitly declares that "those <term>sui</term> and <term>tuh</term> were small coffins."<note>*Sui* and *tuh* refer to small coffins.</note>

On placing the exhumed remains in a "small coffin," the skull is often patched up with a kind of felt made of cotton and silk fibers and daubed with a rough outline of eyes, nose, and mouth. A piece of paper is wrapped around every bone; the vertebrae of the spine are strung on a cord or a piece of rattan, and the whole skeleton, reduced to the size of a child's, is arranged inside one or more suits of clothes. These garments scarcely differ from ordinary grave suits except in size and are made of silk for the wealthy. The same items are put into the coffin as in ordinary burials. But second burials in coffins are reasonably rare; people almost

# RE-BURIAL OF BONES IN URNS AND COFFINS.

...always preferring to use the cheaper urns, if <term>geomancy</term> does not object.

Re-burials always take place on a lucky day and hour. Some close relatives are present and never fail to offer incense and a few dishes of food to the spirit, though they do so without excessive ceremony. On these occasions, they wear a few items indicating light mourning, following the decree of the *I Li* mentioned on page 532, which states that the lowest degree of mourning should be worn when a burial is repeated.

In this way, human bones are dug up and buried again several times in a row by families who are deeply obsessed with the <term>Fung-shui</term> fad. However, more ordinary people generally lose interest in the remains of their ancestors after a few generations have passed. Thousands upon thousands of buried and re-buried bodies—as well as countless unburied skeletons in urns—suffer the same fate as the millions of poor people for whose graves little or no money is spent on <term>Fung-shui</term>. In a short time, they follow the unchanging law of Nature: "To dust you shall return." There are very few families who can brag about owning an ancient grave that has escaped being forgotten or slowly destroyed; such graves only survive because of constant repairs made by those who believe the grave is the main source of their wealth and success.

Re-burials also occur for people who died and were buried far from their hometowns and are then brought back for reasons explained in Chapter X (pages 833 and following). As a rule, the family in these cases waits to dig up the body until enough time has passed for it to decay into a skeleton, because the bones can then be easily and cheaply sent home in a box or package. Many sets of bones are handled this way every year. Customs officers in the Treaty Ports have told me that they have had to inspect the suitcases of returning emigrants which were partially filled with this strange luggage. Those living abroad who cannot afford to send the bodies of their relatives home in coffins often bury them first—using poor-quality coffins to speed up the process of decomposition—and then send the bones home later. It is almost unnecessary to state that, in many cases, the main reason for sending human bones or coffined bodies home for a second burial is the desire to make them sources of blessing by burying them in ground located under favorable <term>geomantic</term> influences.

# THE GRAVE.

Among re-burials may be ranked the cases mentioned on pages 1033 and following, in which corpses for which no suitable graves have been found—and which cannot be kept at home because of the poor quality of the coffins—are provisionally buried in a careless manner, and afterwards permanently entombed in a proper grave under favorable celestial and terrestrial influences. We may finally class among re-burials the practice of depraved individuals who, with the intention of selling the burial lands of their relatives merely for the sake of profit, dig up the remains and re-bury them in a cheaper place, or put them in an urn and deposit them somewhere in the mountains or under the open sky. The reader does not need to be told that such a proceeding is unanimously condemned as a hideous crime and the height of depravity. Sons or grandsons who make themselves guilty of this are threatened by the laws of the Empire with "slow death by the knives" <note>Also known as death by a thousand cuts or lingchi.</note>, as the article quoted on page 887 shows.

It now remains for us to review the several forms of re-burial of the dead in their historical aspect.

Re-burials have been in fashion in China since very ancient times. In its record of events for the year 721 before our era, the *<term>Tso ch'wen</term>* states:

> "In winter, in the tenth month, the ruler Hwui
> (of Lu) was re-buried in another grave. When he died, the state of
> Sung was at war (against Lu) and the crown prince was young,
> so that then some omissions were made in the burial rites. Hence
> they now buried him in another grave" <note>1</note>.

The ruler Chwang also was, according to the same chronicle, taken by his people out of the grave in which his murderer had buried him with little ceremony, and transferred to another; but we have already presented this case to our readers on page 841. That a repetition of burial was a common occurrence in pre-Christian times may be inferred from the fact that the *<term>I li</term>* formally prescribes the dress to be worn by those who attend such ceremonies (see page 532).

The historical books of every dynasty so frequently make mention of emperors, imperial consorts, princes, high officials, and commoners whose interment was repeated for various reasons, that it seems a matter beyond dispute that re-burials under a variety of circumstances have always held a place among the established customs of

# RE-BURIAL LEGALIZED BY SEVERAL DYNASTIES.

Because the ancients sanctioned re-burials by performing them themselves, the ethical and political leaders of the nation have generally shown themselves well-disposed toward them, provided that they are properly justified by the circumstances. Commenting on the rescript of the *I li* stating that mourning dress of the fifth degree should be worn at such burials (see page 532), Ching Khang-ch'ing wrote in the second century:

> » This rescript refers to cases in which the
> » grave has caved in, or has somehow or other fallen to ruin, so that
> » the coffin with the corpse is in danger of being destroyed or
> » lost " $^1$.

Reasons such as those based on Feng-shui speculations were evidently excluded without reservation by this authority. The emperors of the Tang dynasty legalized re-burials by establishing elaborate rescripts in the *Ritual of the Kaiyuan period* regarding how the relatives, after having opened the grave, should place the corpse on a couch in a white linen tent pitched near the grave, how they should dress its hair, lean upon it in wailing, re-coffin it, and sacrifice to the soul, and finally re-inter it with the usual funeral ceremonies. The Ming dynasty enacted similar rules, both for the official class and the people, giving them a place among its *Collective Statutes* $^2$. Both dynasties prescribing that the preparation of the

***

On the evening of the burial, the sons-in-law, perhaps thirty or more, assemble at the house of the head of the clan. They wear hats made of hollowed corn stalks called *mao-sui* (grass plumes), and each carries a bamboo pole about ten feet long, with the top three or four feet still bearing branches and leaves. Their ranks move forward and backward in rhythm, and their songs and shouts also follow a specific melody. Tradition says that when Pan Hu first died, he was placed in a tree, and they used bamboo and wooden poles to poke him down. Thus, this has been passed down to the present as an established custom. They conceal the true nature of the matter by calling it "poking the Northern Bushel" (the Great Bear).

After the burial is completed and the sacrifice is set, both close and distant relatives wail. When the wailing ends and the family members have arrived, they simply drink joyfully and return home, and do not sacrifice or wail again.

The people to the left (the east) are different. They do not wear deep mourning clothes and do not perform the ritual to recall the soul. When someone first dies, the body is placed in a building. The young men of the neighborhood each hold a bow and arrow and circle the body while singing, using the arrows to strike the bows to keep time. Their song lyrics describe the happy events of the person's life until their death. In general, these are like the dirges of today. After dozens of stanzas are sung, the body is dressed and placed in a coffin, then sent to the mountains or forests. They set up separate huts to house the coffins, though some are buried near the village. They wait for twenty or thirty burials to accumulate and then bury them all together in a stone cave. <note>Books of the Sui Dynasty, chapter 31, l. 23.</note>

# EXHUMING AND WASHING OF HUMAN BONES.

In the works of Jü-chʻing <note>1 Huang Ru-cheng (黃汝成).</note>, the following statement occurs: 

> » Recently, there were still people living throughout the entire region
> » of Kwang-sin, in Kiangsi province, who practice a custom which
> » they call ‘the burial of washed bones.’ Two or three years after the
> » burial, they open the coffins without any obvious reasons, wash
> » the bones until they are clean, place the bones of each corpse
> » separately in an earthen jar, and bury it in the ground. One
> » consequence of this custom is that people, while fighting over
> » auspicious burial sites, often become guilty of the theft of human
> » bones; if discovered, this leads to lawsuits.” <note>2 In recent times, in the Kwang-sin region of Jiangxi, there has been a practice called "bone-washing burial." Two or three years after the burial, the coffin is opened, the bones are washed clean, stored in a clay jar, and reburied. Because of this, those competing for lucky burial sites often resort to stealing bones, which leads to legal disputes. (Chapter 15, line 24).</note>

This extract serves as evidence that re-burials involving the washing of skeletal remains were still common in China barely two centuries ago. Therefore, it is quite possible that the practice continues to this day. This assumption is supported by the fact that the Code of Laws includes an article forbidding it—specifically, the one for which we provided the text and translation on page 882. Like most of the supplementary articles regarding burial laws, it was probably enacted during the present century. It suggests that human bones are sometimes dug up for the specific purpose of using them for divination. To our great regret, we have not been able to find any more details on this subject, either from modern Chinese life or from native literature.

## CHAPTER XIV.

### DESCRIPTION OF TOMBS AND MAUSOLEA.

A work such as this, which aims to provide an account of the principal subjects, customs, and practices connected with the resting places of the dead in China, certainly ought above all else to contain details about the shape and construction of graves and tombs—ranging from the smallest and simplest built for the lower classes, to the large, even gigantic mausolea that protect the bodies and souls of magnates, nobles, and emperors. Although the details we have collected on this subject and set down in this chapter are numerous, they do not cover the entire Middle Kingdom, as our travels extended over only six provinces. However, we hope to make clear in the following pages all the principal features of grave construction, especially those revealed by a comparison of the tombs and graves in Fuhkien and the adjacent mountainous regions with those in the central and northwestern provinces of the Empire.

Unfortunately, we can only rarely lead our readers into an archaeological field. No important graves older than the fourteenth century have been found by us in a state of preservation that allows for any reproduction of their original shape and structure (compare page 441). Furthermore, although Chinese books often refer to significant ancient and medieval sepulchers, we can find no regular descriptions sufficient to form a general picture of them that would be of value or interest. Our readers will, therefore, have to be content with descriptions of tombs and mausolea built during the reign of the current House of Ts’ing <note>The Qing Dynasty (1644–1912).</note> and the Ming dynasty; however, we shall often intersperse these descriptions with information drawn from older works when it helps trace the antiquity and history of matters related to graves.

#### **1. Concerning Graves of the Common People, the Nobility and the Mandarinate.**

# ANCIENT AND MODERN NAMES FOR GRAVES.

The term already appears in the *Classic of History* (*Shu Jing*), in the account of the achievements of the founder of the Zhou dynasty <note>Section "The Completion of the War" (*Wu cheng*).</note>. It also occurs in the *Classic of Poetry* (*Shi Jing*) <note>The Odes of Chen, section "The Gate of the Grave" (*Mu men*).</note>, but it is used more regularly in the *Book of Rites* (*Li Ji*), the *Rites of Zhou* (*Zhou Li*), and other ancient books. Another term now in very common use is 墳 (*fen*). This also occurs very often in the literature of pre-Christian times, though almost exclusively in the sense of a hillock or mound, and in the sense of height and size; therefore, the meaning of "grave" was undoubtedly attached to it at a later period, and its first use with this meaning was restricted to graves with a burial mound. The *Book of Rites* confirms this by stating in a passage we quoted on page 664 that "anciently *mo* <note>Graves (*mu*).</note> were made, but no *fen*" <note>"Anciently there were graves, but no mounds" (*Gu ye mu er bu fen*).</note>—that is to say, there were graves, but no graves with mounds.

Most often, however, ancient books denote graves and sepulchers with the character 冢 (*ch'ung*). Medieval and modern authors also use it extensively, but they often place the radical 土 ("earth") at its side (塚) to define its meaning more clearly. We already stated on page 442 that this word originally signified a high place, and that it consequently refers, strictly speaking, to a burial mound. On the same page, we provided four other terms of ancient origin that denote both an elevation and a grave. Still, we must add the character 瑩 (*ying*) to the list; its widespread use seems to date from the Han dynasty. In the literature of that era, and in all subsequent periods, it occurs chiefly in the sense of a tomb of considerable area, or a grave with its surrounding grounds and related buildings, or a family graveyard or mausoleum. Sometimes we find the expression 封墓 (*fung mo*) as a synonym, meaning "a graveyard in which a mound or several mounds are raised." Characters that are now somewhat antiquated and obsolete include: 墦 (*fan*), which we believe appears for the first time in the works of Mencius (specifically in the excerpt provided on page 385); and 垠 (*lang*), 堉 (*yü*), and 堟 (*ts'ai*), mentioned in a small vocabulary titled "Local Terms" <note>The *Fangyan*, Chapter 13.</note> composed by Yang Xiong <note>Yang Xiong (53 BC – AD 18) was an ethical philosopher and statesman.</note>.

In addition, there are various expressions for graves that are merely descriptive phrases. For example, *hwang ts'üen* (黃泉) or "yellow

In Amoy and the surrounding districts a grave is styled *bōng* or *bō*, which words are the local pronunciation of the above-mentioned character 墓. Also the word *hún*, representing the character 墳, is popular there, but almost always in combination with *bōng* or *bō*, namely as *hún bōng* or *hún bō*, "grave with a burial mound". But, owing to the influence of the Feng Shui theories, these terms are at Amoy almost totally replaced by the word *hong-súi*, which, as our readers know, is the local form of the word Feng Shui; the beneficial influences of Nature, which everyone is sure to concentrate upon his graves, are thus used to denote the graves themselves. This fact, though insignificant at first sight, is yet of some interest, as showing that the people are accustomed to connect Feng Shui so inseparably with their burial places, that a grave without some Feng Shui is to them an unimaginable thing. <page-num>1075</page-num>
# GRAVES OF CHILDLESS PEOPLE AND CHILDREN.

Therefore, it is not surprising that our proverb, "All his geese are swans," has a standard equivalent in common Amoy speech, which runs: *Pat láng ê hong-súi khah m̄ hó*¹: "Other people's graves never have a Fung-shui like that of our own."

Nevertheless, a considerable number of graves exist in which Fung-shui calculations have played no part. These belong to forlorn people without children, on whose last resting places no one's fate depends, and whom benevolent men—anxious to accumulate merit—have buried in urns or poor coffins without much ceremony. Similarly, Fung-shui theories do not exist for the graves of young children. Their bodies are placed in a jar or a cheap wooden box (see page 330), which a workman unceremoniously carries on his shoulder, or in some other way, to the open country, along with a hoe to dig the grave pit. No relatives escort him on his way. At best, the sorrowing mother sees him out into the street, giving vent to her grief by piteous wailing and loudly protesting against her child leaving her. The body is buried anywhere at a depth of a few inches, and the rest of the earth is heaped up over it. Within a short time, the dust returns to dust, or, as is very often the case, the remains are devoured by dogs and crows. No legal ownership of the ground is secured, nor is any attention paid to the spot afterward. Many babies are not buried at all; the urn or box is merely set aside in the open country, where it likewise soon falls prey to birds and starving dogs.

Some care is, however, bestowed upon the graves of children approaching the age of puberty, especially if they are male. Indeed, because their bones are solid enough to resist decomposition for a long time, they may be advantageously used to bring blessings to the nearest relatives through the medium of Fung-shui. It is therefore worth the trouble and expense to bury them with a ceremony approximating that of adults, in grounds where ownership has been duly acquired, and in graves proportionate to the wealth of the family. The case is nearly always treated this way when it concerns an only son on the verge of manhood; his parents are then compelled by the laws of social life to adopt a son for him to continue his lineage and the worship of his ancestors, and

# THE GRAVE.

Even when Confucius lived, it was common practice to bury minors in a careless manner. There is evidence of this in the interesting passage of the *Li ki*, which we translated on page 240; furthermore, the same classic narrates the following incident from the life of the Sage (chapter 27, line 40):

> “Tseng-tszě asked: ‘Children who die between the ages of eight and twelve are buried in the fields by surrounding them with earth on all sides. If the relatives follow the vehicle serving as a carriage to that spot, they do so because the burial place is nearby. But now, if the grave is far away, how should the burial be performed?’
> 
> Confucius said: ‘I have heard Lao Tan say: “Formerly (that is, in the twelfth century B.C.), the recorder Yih had a son who died prematurely, and the grave was far away. The ruler of Chao said to him: ‘Why not place him in a coffin and dress him in your palace?’ The recorder answered: ‘Would I dare to do so?’ The ruler of Chao spoke about it to the prince of Cheu (see page 691), who said: ‘Why not?’—and the recorder did so. The custom of using coffins for boys who have died between the ages of eight and twelve, and placing them inside after having dressed them, dates from the recorder Yih.”’ <note>1</note>

The right to use land for a grave is generally acquired through purchase. That is to say, for a certain sum, the proprietor—who may be an individual, a family, a clan, or a village—grants ownership of it to another man and his offspring, or to a family and their descendants, either forever or for as long as the ground is used for the purpose for which it was granted. Since this latter condition is stipulated in almost every case, or silently understood, time usually cancels the transaction after several generations, when the grave falls into oblivion or is cleared away because it is no longer maintained. # CONTRACTS FOR THE PURCHASE OF GRAVE GROUNDS.

After the transfer, the sellers hand the buyers a written deed, called in Amoy *soaⁿ koan*<note>1</note>, "a deed for land," or *hong-súi khoè*<note>2</note>, "a deed for a grave." The wording of such a document is as simple as the transaction itself. Formal language and wordiness are omitted as unnecessary, because the universal respect for the dead and the laws protecting their resting places are considered effective enough to prevent any attempts by dishonest people to swindle the legal owners out of their property. Here is the text and translation of a *soaⁿ koan*, the original of which we possess:

In ancient times, before paper was invented—or, at any rate, before paper was in universal use—deeds and bonds of all kinds in China were carved on small wooden boards, which are denoted in native books by the character 券, <gloss>quan</gloss>. This word appears with this meaning as early as the *Shuowen*, making it certain that wooden bonds were common in pre-Christian times. It is undoubtedly true that, in ancient times, contracts for grave sites in China were written on wood, just like any other transaction. Regardless, we have documentary evidence that this remained the custom as late as the fourteenth century, even though paper was likely manufactured on a large scale and in general use by then; however, old customs are very persistent. We read in the *Guixin zazhi*, a work written at the beginning of the fourteenth century (see page 399):

> » Today, when people prepare a grave, they do not neglect
> » to draw up a written contract for the land; and they
> » make it of Rottlera wood, upon which they write in red
> » characters that such-and-such a plot has been bought for a sum of
> » 99,999 coins, etc. This is a custom prescribed by village
> » priests and is therefore quite absurd. In the Continuation

However, observing the *Supplement to the Records of the Strange* by Yuan Yishan, in the Qing-yang embankment of Yen-chwan in Khü-yang, someone opened a grave and found an iron contract with gold characters saying: “By imperial decree, bury the loyal official Wang Chu-tsun, granting 99,999 strings and 999 coins.” This was during the time of Emperor Ngai of the Tang; therefore, this practice has existed for a long time. *Gujin Tushu Jicheng*, section on Geography, chapter 140.</note>.

We are unable to provide the reasons for this strange practice of stating in such certificates an amount of money composed exclusively of the number nine, as we have not found any explanation for it in Chinese books. The wording of the above extract, however, suggests that this practice was far from universal, as the author presents it as a mere curiosity, appearing ridiculous to many. The conservative spirit of the Chinese regarding everything connected with the treatment of the dead makes it probable that this custom still exists somewhere or other in the Empire; however, we never heard the people speak of it during our stay in China. As for the custom, also mentioned in the quotation above, of placing contracts engraved in metal within graves, this must undoubtedly have been a common occurrence, since the Song dynasty considered it important enough to officially sanction it. Indeed, among its statutory decrees concerning funerals for the <term>mandarinate</term>, we read: » There shall be used, besides » a stone bearing a record of the life of the deceased, one stone » on which the deed is engraved, and one copy of the latter » in iron”<note>One memorial stone, one contract stone, and one iron contract. *History of the Song Dynasty*, chapter 124, line 14.</note>.

<page-num>1080</page-num>
<header>THE GRAVE.</header>
<page-type>text</page-type>

The essential part of every grave in Amoy and the surrounding countryside is a <term>tumulus</term>—a mound smoothly rounded on the top, slightly longer and wider than the coffin buried beneath it. Graves without a mound are extremely rare, though the mounds of the poor are often so low that they are barely distinguishable from their surroundings. In many cases, the coffin is buried at a considerable depth. Much more often, however, it is scarcely below the level of the surrounding soil—indeed, it is often partly or entirely above it, with only the mound covering it from view. This method reminds us of the way in which, in ancient times, encoffined corpses were stored under a layer of clay inside the house (pp. 363—365). However, such shallow burials—or "burials by heaping up the earth (around the coffin)"¹ as they are called in books—have no connection whatsoever with those house burials of bygone days. They are simply required by <term>geomancy</term>; enlightened practitioners of this art revealed many centuries ago the remarkable physical fact that in many parts of eastern Fuhkien, and particularly in the departments of Chang-cheu and Ts'üen-cheu, the <term>Terrestrial Breath</term> (see page 948) "is floating on or near the surface." Shallow burials also have the advantage of protecting the coffin from groundwater. Moreover, they are frequently ordered by geomancers because, according to their theories, the outlines of mountains and other landscape features are only valuable for a grave if they can be "seen" from the spot where the corpse is placed.

At nearly every burial, it is the <term>Fung-shui</term> professor who determines the depth of the grave. He also fixes the direction of its longitudinal axis in connection with the decrees of the almanac and the bearings he takes (compare page 974). He regulates the construction and finishing of the tomb in all its details, as geomantic art has, over the course of years, applied its theories to every essential part of these dwellings of the dead.

On page 213, we stated that coffins in the grave are generally covered with oiled paper, straw, matting, or similar material, and then embedded in a layer of earth mixed with lime. This mixture, becoming hard and solid, forms a vault that keeps out rainwater and protects the coffin from being crushed when the wood decays. No solid foundation is placed underneath the coffin,

<page-num>1081</page-num>
<header>THE USE OF LIME FOR THE CONSTRUCTION OF GRAVES.</header>

For no beneficial effects can be expected from a grave unless the <term>Terrestrial Breath</term> has access to the coffin and can freely exert its influence upon the corpse. The earth of the <term>tumulus</term>, too, is often mixed with lime, particularly if the grave pit is shallow.

In many families, the conviction prevails that it is the duty of the married daughters to pay the cost of the lime required for their parents' graves. Indeed, since they must mourn for their father and mother in the second degree (see page 552, no. 13), it is naturally appropriate for them to provide the second covering in the grave; the first one, namely the coffin, must be bought by the sons and the other mourners in the first degree. The same considerations make it a duty for the married daughters to provide the second layer of grave clothes, as we stated on page 63.

Books teach us that lime was already used for the construction of graves many centuries before the Christian era. In a passage we quoted on page 725, the *<term>Tso ch'wen</term>* relates that lime prepared from sea clams was used at the burial of <term>Wen</term>, a ruler of <term>Sung</term>, who died in 587 B.C.; and it is interesting to read, in connection with this, in the *<term>Cheu li</term>*:

> "The Officer for Sea Clams directs the gathering of bivalve animals and clams, and thus provides the clams needed for closing burial pits" <note>掌蜃掌斂互物蜃物、以共壙之蜃. Ch. 16, line 38.</note>.

In the Middle Ages, the use of lime for graves must have been very common; otherwise, it would hardly have occurred to <term>Chu Hi</term> to issue a formal decree making its use almost obligatory. We indeed read in his *<term>Rituals for Family Life</term>*:

> "Make a partition wall (of boards around the coffin in the grave) for the lime, then put a (wooden) cover into the pit, fill the space around it with lime, and finally fill the pit with earth" <note>加灰隔、內外蓋、實以灰、乃實土. Chapter 6.</note>.

Commentators explaining this passage say that a layer of charcoal dust must be placed at the bottom of the pit, and over it, a thick layer of lime mixed with sand and clay. They add that a similar double protection against termites, moisture, tree roots, and robbers should be constructed around and over the coffin using wooden boards. However, these directions are far from being followed to the letter by the <term>Fuhkienese</term> of the present day.

We believe it is no exaggeration to say that at least nine graves

...out of ten merely consist of a <term>tumulus</term>, at best with a four-sided granite tablet engraved with characters, standing upright at the shortest side or foot end. By far the majority of the people are indeed too poor to do more for their dead; and many wealthy people use no better graves when the requirements of <term>Fung-shui</term> compel them to follow the "stealthy" method of burial, of which we have spoken on page 1033. At many graves of this simple description, the said inscribed gravestone is fixed into a small wall, which, as a rule, is a little lower and slopes down in a curved line on both sides, as can be seen from those represented in the background on Plate XXIV, inserted at page 941. Generally, this wall is a mixture of sand and clay, well-mixed with lime, packed into a solid mass and plastered over with white mortar. In a few cases, it is made of white-plastered masonry.

Only the graves of the upper class have an omega-shaped ridge of earth, the purpose of which we explained on page 942. Indeed, such a <term>bōng moa</term> covers an area of ground much larger than the small plot required for a <term>tumulus</term> alone, thus requiring an expense that the poor cannot afford. On page 942, we also stated that some graves have a double bank—one of granite or brick, and one of earth on the outside. This latter bank, if it is large and broad, is often called <term>bōng ch'iú</term><note>1 墓手 (grave-arms).</note>, "the grave-arms," because it extends along both sides like arms hanging down from the human body. Now, just as a person is utterly helpless if they lose the free use of their limbs, it is extremely disastrous for a grave if its arms are "wounded" (compare page 1035). Like a fortress with crumbling defenses, its <term>Fung-shui</term> must inevitably succumb to any attack by harmful powers, which are always lurking about to destroy good influences.

Since grave banks are especially common in the southern provinces of China, they are also a distinctive feature of Chinese graves in the <term>Straits Settlements</term>, the <term>Malay Archipelago</term>, and other overseas colonies where natives of those provinces have settled. Some explanations of their meaning given by European authors may be dismissed as fanciful and ridiculous. Some writers have claimed that they are literal representations of the legs of <term>Mother Earth</term>, from whose womb man is born and to whose womb he returns at death!

<page-num>1083</page-num>

# GRAVE EMBANKMENTS AND TUMULI.

At Amoy, the common name for a <term>tumulus</term> is *<term>bōng tui</term>*<note>1 墓堆 (grave heap)</note>, meaning "grave heap" or "grave mound." Its shape is often ellipsoidal, which must be attributed to the form of the coffin buried beneath it (compare page 941). When surrounded by a *<term>bōng moa</term>*, the <term>tumulus</term> is generally low and reminds us of the shape of a tortoise; for this reason, it is popularly called *<term>bōng ku</term>*<note>2 墓龜 (grave tortoise)</note>, or "grave tortoise." Some say that tortoises are often intentionally imitated because, as we stated on page 56, they are a popular symbol of longevity. The ability to reach a great age is thus concentrated within the grave and passes from it to the descendants of its occupant. It is also likely that we are dealing here with an attempt to place the grave under the influence of the <term>Celestial Tortoise</term>, the spirit of the northern quadrant of the heavens. Indeed, the <term>tumulus</term> is, in theory, the northern part of the grave, and an ancient decree requires the dead to be buried in the northern suburbs with their heads facing north (see page 984). We have seen many graves where the <term>tumulus</term> was entirely coated with plaster in light and dark colors, imitating the lines and patterns of a tortoise shell.

It is a fairly common custom to plaster grave mounds over their entire surface with white mortar. At Amoy, these are then called *<term>he bōng</term>*<note>3 灰墓 (lime grave)</note>, or "lime graves," in contrast to the *<term>tô bōng</term>*<note>4 塗墓 (earth grave)</note>, which are covered with turf. Some *<term>he bōng</term>* are round and low, especially when they cover urns or small coffins containing bones that have been exhumed and re-buried for the reasons explained in Chapter XIII.

Complete tombs, such as those the wealthy class in Amoy are accustomed to build for their deceased relatives, are generally laid out on the same plan as the dwellings of the living. In the first volume of this work, opposite page 16, we inserted a plate showing how mansions used to be built in ancient China, according to the opinions of Chinese authors in general and <term>Chu Hi</term> in particular<note>5 See his "Explanation of Mansions" 釋宮, reprinted at the beginning of the Imperial Khien lung edition of the *I li*.</note>. Most palaces, homes of the wealthy, and temples of the gods are planned similarly at the present day; therefore, it can hardly be doubted that they have also been designed this way throughout the many centuries that separate ancient from modern China. If the reader keeps the outlines of that plan in mind, he will understand every detail of the construction of Chinese tombs. Plates XXIV, XXV

and XXIX, which represent complete tombs of the simplest kind, may help the reader in this matter.

The chief part of the grave, namely the <term>tumulus</term> covering the coffin, corresponds to the back chamber of the house, in which, in ancient times, its inmates passed away and were washed and prepared for the grave. In front of the <term>tumulus</term>, separated from it by a wall in which the gravestone is fixed, we have the <term>*bōng tng*</term>¹ or "grave hall," corresponding to the "hall" of houses and temples. As we have stated on page 5, such a house hall contains an altar bearing the soul tablets of the ancestors, which is erected against the wall opposite the door; in a similar situation, there is an altar in the hall of the grave, which serves for sacrifices to the soul of the buried man. It is the so-called <term>*bōng toh*</term>² or "grave table": a square slab of granite, either placed on the ground or upon a massive table-shaped pile of masonry; sometimes it is made entirely of granite and carved in front with characters or emblematic figures, such as those we mentioned on page 979. As this altar is attached to the wall of the gravestone, it apparently supports the latter; this makes its resemblance to a house altar as close as possible, the said stone being, as we shall see shortly, considered to be—like the wooden soul tablets at home—a seat for the <term>manes</term>. Let us add here that in temples dedicated to the worship of the dead, or to gods and saints of any sort, the altar with the tablets or images stands in a very similar position in the main hall.

That grave altars can be traced back by the Chinese to the dawn of their history, we have already explained on page 385.

The next essential part of a complete tomb is a <term>*bōng tiâⁿ*</term>³ or "grave court," corresponding to the paved *tiâⁿ* or courtyard of houses and temples. Just like the latter, it is a depression in front of the "hall." Directly before it we have the <term>*tan tí*</term> (*tan ch'i*), the important reservoir which, whether it be empty or filled, is expected to bless the grave with an abundance of aquatic influences. Having explained in detail on page 946 the role such tanks play in grave building, and having stated there that they are also constructed before large mansions and temples, we may now pass over them.

# THE SEVERAL PARTS COMPOSING A TOMB.

It corresponds with the walls surrounding the site and forming a row of apartments on either side with a veranda, or a covered gallery without apartments, called <term>wu</term> ¹ or <term>lang wu</term> ²; — indeed, the term <term>bōng moa</term> essentially means the gallery or side gallery of a grave (see page 942). So much for complete tombs of the simplest construction. Although modeled on the same plan, they are, as our illustrations show, by no means all alike in shape. A great many, for example the one represented in Plate XXIX, have no tank, as some gully nearby makes it unnecessary; others have no court, with the whole space in front being occupied by the tank. Almost always, everything, including the floors of the hall, courtyard, and tank, is made of a mixture of clay, sand, and lime, packed into a solid mass, over which comes a coating of white plaster. But in the course of time, this coating tarnishes, giving the tomb a dirty and ruined appearance unless it is kept in constant repair. Hence, some people prefer mixing the plaster with blue-gray coloring material.

Tombs such as those described above are often very large when they enclose the remains of a high mandarin, or a person with a high titular rank. We have seen many occupying an area twenty or more times as large as the graves represented in our illustrations, and providing room for the construction of a dozen good-sized European houses. Some of these large sepulchral monuments have one or two flights of steps leading from the tank up to the grave court, and other flights connecting the grave court with the hall, if the latter is a few feet higher. Some large tombs also have, set into the floor in front of the altar, a <term>pài tsióh</term> ³ or "stone for reverences," which is a square slab of granite serving, as the name indicates, for the relatives to make prostrations upon when they worship the buried man. Such a stone is to be found also in front of the altar in many a temple and many a dwelling house. Several large graves have a low wall encircling the entire front beyond the tank (compare Plate XXVII), with an opening for an entrance, which is called a <term>bōng mng</term> ⁴, or "the grave gate." Our readers will immediately recognize in it the gate erected in front of the courtyard of temples or mansions, in both modern and ancient times (compare Plate I, on page 16). Families wealthy enough to afford tombs of such dimensions generally also possess the means to build them from a material more durable than a mixture of earth and lime. To better protect the coffin, they have a brick vault constructed over it or have it covered with granite slabs resting on other slabs that line the pit; in this way, the grave is permanently prevented from caving in and is reasonably safe from robbery. They make the outer parts of the tomb, either partially or entirely, of granite and brick, almost always plastering the brickwork but never the granite. In many cases, only the low pillars at the corners of the tomb are made of granite and carved at the top into a lion, a flame, a lotus flower, or some other ornament (compare Plate XXIX). However, it would be incorrect to claim that granite plays any significant role in modern grave construction. Nearly all the granite graves still existing in Fuhkien province were built during the Ming dynasty. This fact suggests a significant decline in tomb building; we believe this decline must be attributed to a general decrease in wealth, as there is no reason to suppose that respect for the dead is diminishing or that the art of stonecutting has declined, since the Chinese everywhere are still capable of producing excellent work in this trade.

These old granite tombs are fairly numerous in the surrounding areas of Amoy. Many are in good condition, but a far greater number are badly dilapidated because the descendants have died out or, having become impoverished, no longer take an interest in them, leaving them to be scavenged by anyone who needs good pieces of stone for building or other purposes. It is certain that they will soon share the fate of the many thousands that have already been swept out of existence. Therefore, we include in these pages pictures of some of the best examples we have seen, specifically directing our readers' attention to the one shown in Plate XXVII, opposite page 979; because it is hidden in a mountain recess on the island of Amoy, far from human sight, it has remained intact and is undoubtedly one of the finest to be found in Fuhkien. Its gravestone indicates that it was built in 1587.

We do not need to dwell long on those ancient monuments; for, as our readers will see at a glance, they are planned like modern graves. However, attention must be drawn to the fact that straight lines are more common in them than in modern tombs, and that the walls are generally higher than those of the latter. The walls

However, it would be incorrect to claim that granite plays any significant role in modern grave construction. Nearly all the granite graves still existing in <term>Fuhkien</term> <note>Modern Fujian</note> province were built during the Ming dynasty. This fact suggests a significant decline in tomb building; we believe this decline must be attributed to a general decrease in wealth, as there is no reason to suppose that respect for the dead is diminishing or that the art of stonecutting has declined, since the Chinese everywhere are still capable of producing excellent work in this trade.

These old granite tombs are fairly numerous in the surrounding areas of <term>Amoy</term> <note>Modern Xiamen</note>. Many are in good condition, but a far greater number are badly dilapidated because the descendants have died out or, having become impoverished, no longer take an interest in them, leaving them to be scavenged by anyone who needs good pieces of stone ...

<summary>This page describes the construction of wealthy Chinese tombs using durable materials like brick and granite to prevent collapse and robbery. The author notes that high-quality granite tombs mostly date back to the Ming dynasty, suggesting that modern economic decline, rather than a lack of skill or respect, has led to less substantial grave construction.</summary>

<meta>Continuing from the previous page's discussion of tomb layouts and materials, this section examines the architectural features of Ming dynasty tombs, specifically their resemblance to residential palaces and temples, and the use of stone sheltering structures.</meta>

<page-num>1087</page-num>
# TOMBS BUILT UNDER THE MING DYNASTY.

On the right and left of the grave hall and the grave court, the walls are covered with blocks of stone carved into the shape of roofs. This again shows that tombs and human dwellings are closely connected, for during the Ming dynasty it was—as it is today—an established custom to place tiled roofs upon the walls surrounding the grounds of palaces and important buildings. These blocks often bear a crouching lion or a lion's head in stone on their front; such figures are also sometimes seen in front of the tomb, where they flank the ground on both sides like a pair of sentinels (see Plate XXXI).

A special feature of many tombs dating from the Ming dynasty is a square sheltering structure of granite, raised on pillars over the gravestone. In many cases, it covers the altar or even the entire grave hall (Pl. XXX). This structure is another link connecting tombs with houses and temples; indeed, it makes their resemblance almost perfect. Its roof is generally double-layered, which is also the case with the roofs of several buildings of any architectural significance. In many cases, the gravestone it shelters is not fixed into the back wall of the grave hall, but stands separately on a square granite pedestal, in the same way as the large stone tablets shown in Plate XXXVI on page 1141; similarly, wooden soul tablets are usually set into wooden blocks.

We have never seen these so-called *bōng am* <note>1. 墓庵.</note> or "grave sheds" on tombs constructed during the current reigning dynasty. It can hardly be questioned that they were in style before the rule of the House of Ming, as they are actually small grave temples. Grave temples, as we showed on page 388, can be traced in Chinese records back to pre-Christian times. We may finally conclude that the method of building graves exactly on the plan of houses is directly connected with the ancient Chinese practice of "house-burial," which we discussed in an earlier chapter (pp. 363 onwards). Even though we look in vain for written evidence to support this suggestion, we believe that probability prevents us from flatly rejecting it as impossible.

As already stated in our discussion devoted to grave decorations, many graves of the Ming dynasty feature stone images of men and animals in front of them—or animals alone—if the occupant was a member of the mandarinate or the nobility.

The author suggests these designs are a continuation of ancient Chinese "house-burial" traditions and notes that such elaborate structures are largely absent in the current dynasty.</summary>

In the official regulations of both dynasties, they are called <term>wang chu</term>¹ <note>1. 望柱: pillars to look at.</note>, "pillars to look at." This name reveals their purpose: they are intended to serve the soul as beacons by which it may find its way back to its resting place when it has wandered from the tomb. To make them better serve this purpose, the top is pointed to imitate a flame; this emits an imaginary light, which also has the advantage of increasing the vitality of the soul. Consequently, the role these pillars play at the tomb is the same as that of candles or lamps burning near a deathbed <note>Compare pages 21 and following.</note>. In Amoy, they are usually called <term>tsiôh tsik</term>² <note>2. 石燭: stone torches.</note>, "stone torches," even if, as is often the case, they bear a decorative lion at the top instead of a flame.

It is reasonable to connect these stone grave-lights with the stone torch-bearers which, according to an ancient book we quoted on page 811, stood in the crypt of a king in the seventh century before our era and were undoubtedly placed in many graves of distinguished people at that time. They can be traced back to very early times. We find them mentioned in an old description of a mausoleum from the Han period, which we translated on pages 445–446; this supports the statement of Wang Jui that their use dates from the Ts'in and Han dynasties (see p. 825). In later writings, they are mentioned regularly; for example, in the description of a fifth-century mausoleum, which we translated on pages 440–441, and in a note regarding the tomb of Chao Siu, who lived in the sixth century (p. 814), besides several other passages that are unnecessary to quote. However, it must be noted that their construction was officially regulated in the sixth century of our era, as shown by the excerpt we quoted on page 814 from the *Books of the Sui Dynasty*. In medieval times, they clearly held a place among the decorations of imperial tombs; as we showed on page 815, the emperor T'ai Tsu ordained in his last instructions that the pillars to be erected on his tomb should be made of brick and not of stone. Public officials were officially permitted to have them on their graves during the Sung dynasty, as the government regulations regarding the burial of such distinguished people then prescribed that:

> "One pair of stone sheep, one
> pair of tigers, and one pair of <term>wang chu</term> should be placed
> on their graves; but the officers of the first, second, or third
> degree may add two stone images of men." <note>1. 墳所有石羊虎望柱各二、三品以上加石人二人. *History of the Sung Dynasty, chapter 124, l. 14.*</note>

And we shall see later that they are also found in the mausoleums of the Ming dynasty emperors and in those of the current reigning House.

Large tombs are generally surrounded by a tract of private land large enough to prevent others from building graves nearby and spoiling the <term>Fung-shui</term>. The boundaries of these adjacent grounds are marked by small granite slabs, planted upright in the soil and engraved with characters indicating the name of the owners, such as 陳界, "boundary of (the family) Ch'en," or something similar. If there happen to be rocks or boulders on the boundaries, the inscription is usually carved directly onto them. These adjacent grounds are generally called <term>mo yin</term> <note>2. 墓蔭 (mù yìn)</note>, "the grave shade," referring to the so-called "shade trees" <note>3. 蔭樹 (yìn shù)</note> which are supposed to grow there. <header>THE GRAVE.</header>

Despite the fact that having trees on tombs represents a time-honored custom which can be traced back to the dawn of Chinese history; and despite the circumstance that the planting and keeping of grave trees has always ranked among the primary duties of virtuous wives and children, as we have demonstrated elsewhere (pp. 460 and following), they are nowadays rare in the south of the Empire, and seldom seen there even on graves of the largest sort. In the main, as we have stated before (p. 945), this is owing to <term>Fung-shui</term>, which, condemning the presence of trees in the front of graves, only allows them to be planted there if there are no other tombs behind. Besides, only a few tombs have adjacent grounds so large that trees may grow in them without the roots undermining the masonry and destroying the corpse. Most experts set very little value on trees as shields, for, unless they are planted in considerable numbers so as to form a foliage of great density, they can scarcely prevent the harmful effects of the atmosphere from penetrating to the <term>tumulus</term> and the gravestone. In many cases, grave trees are planted because of geomantic speculation about the elements, when calculations have determined that an increase of Wood is urgently demanded by the surrounding landscape. Here and there, the traveler comes across a grave built under the <term>Ming</term> dynasty which—owing to the care of descendants who regard it as the safeguard of their prosperity—is shielded on both sides of the avenue of animals and at the back by groves and underwood of a considerable size. But such mausoleums are rare, and we have not seen half a dozen in the course of so many years. It caught our attention that graves planted with trees are more numerous in the northern half of <term>Fuhkien</term> than in the southern parts of that province.

Apart from the above reasons, it is not improbable that the total absence of trees from the graves of the common people is a survival of ancient times when, according to the extracts from the *Cheu li* and the *Li ki* quoted on page 461, sepulchral trees were planted exclusively on the tombs of the higher classes. It is, however, doubtful whether those extracts are to be relied upon implicitly, as they are contradicted by the *Poh hu t'ung i*, a book which is generally believed to date from the first century of our era.

"...eight feet, and Lwan trees were planted around it. That of an ordinary office-bearer was four feet and planted with Sophora trees. Commoners had no grave mounds, and the trees planted around their tombs were willows" <note>The Emperor's mound is three ren high, planted with pine.
