But, whatever the truth may be, it appears certain that the ancient Chinese planted trees primarily around the remains of distinguished people, simply because the graves of the latter covered more ground than those of the common people, and also because customary law—as we learn from the extract from the *Cheu li* just mentioned—prescribed that their number must be proportionate to the rank of the deceased.

Although the current inhabitants of south-eastern China hardly ever plant sepulchral trees, they still regard them with great awe and respect. The conviction that they protect the soul, which rests under their shade, from harmful influences and prevent decay from reaching the coffin and the remains, is still as vividly alive as ever; nor has the belief in a mystical relationship between those trees and the soul—into which they continuously infuse new vitality—diminished in the least. To chop them down is considered a heinous crime for which the Laws of the Empire inflict heavy punishments, as we have shown on pages 902 and following. And in Amoy, the expression *boē bōng-ch'iū* <note>To sell grave trees</note>, "to sell grave trees," is frequently used by the people as a metaphor representing the height of filial ingratitude. The nation's conscience is constantly urged to respect grave trees by the *Li ki*, which declares that "no worthy man chops down any trees from his grave mounds when he has to build a mansion or dwelling" <note>See page 461.</note>; moreover, many centuries before our era, the *Shi king* pronounced a curse against the destruction of such trees in these terms: "At the gate of the tomb there stood jujube trees, and they were cut away with an axe: that man was not virtuous. The people of the kingdom knew he would do it, and yet they did not stop him" <note>At the gate of the tomb are jujube trees, chopped with an axe; that man is not good. The people of the country know it, and yet they do not stop him. The Odes of Ch'en, section Mu-men.</note>.

<page-num>1092</page-num>
<header>THE GRAVE.</header>

Mention was made of an altar, built at many tombs, for presenting sacrifices to the local divinity of the Soil (see page 219), in order to propitiate its favors on behalf of the body and the soul entrusted to its care. Such an altar is hardly ever missing from tombs whose construction required considerable expense, but it is also found near many which consist of nothing but a burial mound with a gravestone. In most cases, it is built on the left-hand side of the occupant of the grave, as this deity is higher in rank than he is, and etiquette requires that persons of lower rank should stay to the right of those in a higher position. Hence, Chao Ki-ming has also prescribed that, in family burial grounds, the altar erected for all the graves in common shall be on the northeast (see page 833), as it is there on the left of all the principal dead who lie with their heads to the north. The rule is not, however, without exceptions; many altars are on the right side, or to the northwest, southwest, or southeast, because, as the god of the Soil is considered to dominate the Fung-shui of graves, the practitioners deem nothing more important than placing its seat under a confluence of excellent geomantic influences.

The altar (see Pl. XXXIII) consists of a rectangular slab of granite, seldom higher than one or two feet, fixed perpendicularly in the ground. On the front of this slab are carved the characters 后土, "Ruler of the Earth"; 土神, "God or Spirit of the Earth"; 山靈, "Active Animus of the Ground"<note>This superscript 1 refers to the footnote at the bottom of the page.</note>¹; 福德神, "Spirit of the Felicitating Agencies," or some other title denoting the divinity for whose worship it is erected, and whose spirit, being identified with the stone by means of the inscription, is believed to reside within it. In some cases, this divine soul tablet is, like a gravestone, fixed in a small masonry wall built against a little mound of earth, which is sometimes covered with white plaster and sometimes not, the whole resembling a grave in miniature. Not infrequently, this resemblance is enhanced by a square slab of granite lying at the base of the inscription, forming a small sacrificial table that brings to mind the "table" of a grave.

# ON OLD GRAVES, AND CAVE-BURIAL.

...nothing was left but a burial mound with a gravestone; and even these poor remains would long ago have disappeared, had the owners not been accustomed for generations to regard them as the safeguards of their wealth and fortunes, sacrificing regularly to the ancestral spirits supposed to dwell there, even after the last atoms of the corpse and the coffin had mixed forever with earthly dust. We have never seen such an ancestral grave converted into a funeral monument worthy of the powerful family deity inhabiting it. Apparently, the owners had steadfastly refrained from building or digging on the spot, for fear that such a procedure might disturb the <term>Fung-shui</term> and destroy their fortunes. Families who possess such a "grave of a first ancestor"¹ are generally very proud of it, as it ensures them a reputation for being of ancient descent and, consequently, of indisputable respectability.

Since this description of tombs and graves is based on those in the province of Fuhkien, our readers should not consider it applicable to the whole Empire. No doubt, every province and region has its own peculiarities regarding grave construction, which it is impossible for us to detail individually, but which may be illustrated by the following short notes from our diary. Almost everywhere in Fuhkien, when brooks or rivulets are nearby, the tombs are built of large gravel cemented together with lime; this material combines strength with low cost and is affordable for everyone, even the poor. In the regions watered by the Min River and its tributaries, a type of cave burial is practiced; the dead are often placed in vertical cliffs of reddish-yellow loam, formed by brooks or rivers that have eroded their way through the soil. The cave is made at the base of such a cliff, the coffin is slid into it headfirst, and the opening is sealed with gravel, in front of which is placed the gravestone or other masonry or stone structures like those described in the preceding pages. We saw a curious instance of cave burial at Ho-kheu², a town with significant traffic in the district of Yen-shan³ in Kiangsi, and a hub for river craft of every description. Amid a cluster of barren red sandstone rocks on the bank opposite that place, there was a strange grotto in a vertical boulder rising high above, about twenty meters from the ground, consisting of a collection of small shafts, likely formed by water that had filtered through the stone and eroded it (see Pl. XXXIV). Some of the lowermost shafts had been cut

# THE GRAVE.

...away and a coffin had been inserted in the spot. The decaying foot-end of the coffin was entirely visible when we visited the place, because the masonry that originally hid it had fallen apart and crumbled away. Holes chiseled into the rock beneath this grotto showed that scaffolding had been used to place the coffin in that "eagle’s nest."

Grave mounds are not shaped the same everywhere in the Empire. In the northwestern districts of Fuhkien, the conical form <image-desc>a small hand-drawn triangle</image-desc> is the most common. In Kiangsi province and the areas surrounding Nanking, we have seen such burial mounds (<term>tumuli</term>) over three meters in height. On tombs of this description, we hardly ever saw any stone or brick structures, nor a protective bank of earth. In Shantung, conical mounds are also common. Many graves in this province have a vertical gravestone standing separately in front, and, furthermore, a "grave table"—a square slab lying on the ground or resting on two or four stone legs. This table is placed either against the gravestone or a few feet away. Sometimes it holds a stone incense burner, flanked by a pair of stone candlesticks and flower vases of the same material. In other cases, these objects are placed on the ground in front of the table; in others still, there is nothing but a censer. Since all these items are solid, they are not functional and serve merely as decoration and to maintain the idea of perpetual sacrifices offered to the soul in the grave. Such mounds, gravestones, and associated decorations vary greatly in size according to the wealth of the families who own the graves. We have seen gravestones over two meters high and mounds of four meters, though the average height of the latter does not exceed one meter.

Aside from the conical shape, many grave mounds in the central and northern provinces are semi-spherical <image-desc>a small hand-drawn semicircle</image-desc>, or resemble upright cylinders with vaulted tops <image-desc>a small hand-drawn tall arch</image-desc>. These latter shapes are a characteristic feature of the numerous tombs and mausoleums that dot the plains around Peking. They house the bodies and souls of noblemen and officials (<term>mandarins</term>) who spent their lives serving in the Boards, Courts, and Offices surrounding the <term>Son of Heaven</term> to maintain his glory and supreme authority throughout the Empire and its vast territories. Generally, these mounds are entirely covered in grass. Many are plastered with lime; others are enclosed with gray bricks, either all the way to the top or up to a certain height, to prevent the earth from sliding away. In some cases, a slab is fixed into the front, carved to represent a closed door, which is perhaps a survival of ancient

# SEPULCHRES OF NOBLEMEN AND MANDARINS.

...times, when the dwellings of the living were used to bury the dead; but we have already spoken of this on page 374.

The sepulchres of these Pekingese grandees are especially deserving of a description because they differ greatly from the graves in the South, of which we have tried to convey an idea in these pages. They are remarkably simple, although the area of ground they occupy is large. There are no brick or stone structures around the tumulus, but it stands isolated in an unpaved plot, usually with a few smaller mounds on the right and left, which cover the remains of the wife and the principal descendants. A bank of earth runs in a straight line behind this row of tumuli, protecting them from harmful *shah*. With two similar banks on the right and left respectively, it forms a walled square that is open in front; in many cases, the bank runs in a curved line, embracing the spot like a *böng moa* and gradually diminishing in height at the ends. These banks vary greatly in size. Many are barely one meter high, but we have seen others over five meters.

Thus, when such *ying* (see page 1073) contain more than one corpse and one tumulus, they are in reality family graves. The main feature that distinguishes them from the graves in the South is that they are richly covered with trees. It is, indeed, by means of trees that <term>geomancers</term> usually try to remedy the disadvantage of lacking mountains, hills, or rocks, which elsewhere protect the graves from evil influences. A shady grove of pines and cypresses, planted in parallel rows, forms a dense protection at the back and sides of the tumuli. Rows of oaks and other trees surround this grove on the outside, enhancing its protective qualities. In front, too, there is a rectangular arbor of pine and cypress trees and, in many cases, a second grove of a similar shape; the mausoleum thus has the appearance of a four-sided park, which is particularly beautiful if it is old enough to contain trees of a stately size. The row of tumuli, concealed in a somber grove of evergreens, gives the spot a druidical appearance; this illusion is often enhanced by gravestones, a stone table with sacrificial implements standing alone in the middle of the open plot in front of the tumuli, and one or more large stone tablets displaying the names and titles of the buried persons, erected on the spot on stone pedestals or on the backs of huge stone tortoises of the same material.

A drainage ditch extends along the four sides of the park to keep it dry. Further out in the fields, small stone landmarks mark the furthest boundaries, as well as those of the adjacent

<meta>This page continues the description of the large burial grounds (*ying*) in Peking, specifically focusing on the families who maintain them and the eventual decay of these parks when their geomantic value is lost or the families fall into poverty.</meta>

->THE GRAVE.<-

grounds set apart for the sustenance of the families who act as keepers of the sepulcher in the numbers fixed by the institutions of the State. They regularly till these grounds, dwelling there in humble huts which contrast strikingly with the splendor of the adjacent park of death.

These numerous grave parks of evergreens pleasantly break the monotony of the Peking plains, especially in winter and early spring, when they resemble countless oases in a boundless, dreary desert. Their attractiveness is enhanced by stately pines with milk-white bark, which are a peculiar feature of the landscape in this part of the world. But many *ying* are mere symbols of neglect and ruin. They can lose their <term>geomantic</term> value for a hundred reasons, and the owners consequently feel no more interest in keeping them in good condition; or the proprietors may be reduced to poverty and sell the ground, this not being forbidden by law if it does not entail the destruction of the graves (see p. 896); or the family may die out, with nobody preventing the keepers and the farmers in the surrounding areas from gradually felling the trees and converting the grounds into fields for themselves. In China, too, the dead among the great of this earth and the most magnificent monuments erected in their honor are finally engulfed in the abyss of oblivion. Thus it is that many *tumuli* stand alone and desolate in the midst of cultivated fields, surrounded only by a small open grass plot, with nothing testifying to the former grandeur of the spot except the large stone tablets and the debris of the grave altar.

Among such sepulchral parks, there are many in which the central part—containing the *tumuli*, the gravestones, the altar, the stone tablets, and a portion of the trees—is surrounded by open-work brick walls that take the place of the earthen banks. These walls generally run in straight lines along the front and the sides, or along the front only, and in a curve along the back. Sometimes the wall in front has an opening in the middle that serves as an entrance. In point of size and grandeur, these sepulchers stand next to the most magnificent *mausolea* ever erected for the subjects of the <term>Sons of Heaven</term>, namely, those of princes of Imperial lineage, the description of which we will postpone until the third section of this chapter. We must now speak of the official <term>rescripts</term> regulating the dimensions and ornamentation of graves.

It is hardly necessary to recall the characteristic feature of the Chinese nation, traceable throughout all ages known to us from its books, of burying the dead in graves

# OFFICIAL RESCRIPTS CONCERNING GRAVES.

In November 1858, it was stipulated that one <term>ch'ih</term> should be considered equal to 14.1 inches English, which would equal 0.358 meters French. There is some doubt, however, whether the <term>ch'ih</term> referred to in the dynastic Ordinances and Laws is of this length. Williamson says that, according to the Board of Works, it measures 13 1/8 inches <note>1 Journeys in North China, I, xix.</note>. The official <term>ch'ih</term> differed considerably under various dynasties. The <term>pu</term> does not seem to be commensurate with the <term>ch'ih</term>, and measures about 66 English inches or 1.675 meters <note>2 Chinese Repository, X, p. 651; Journal of the North China Branch of the Royal Asiatic Society, XX p. 93, and XXIV p. 95.</note>. If these figures are at all correct, the length of grave walls—supposing the ground they enclose to be a regular square—is, in the case of a <term>mandarin</term> of the highest rank, about 31 meters on all sides, and the length and breadth of the whole ground about 300; while for <term>mandarins</term> of the lowest class and members of the <term>gentry</term>, these figures are about 11 and 67 meters.

These regulations are not established to force the nation to make the graves of noblemen and officers of the size and height stated; rather, they provide the maximum limits which must not be exceeded. Our readers have seen that only a small number of those <term>sepulchres</term>—in the South, hardly any—are enclosed by walls. Neither is it obligatory to erect the stone figures which, according to the ordinance translated on page 821, may be placed on the graves of distinguished nobles and public functionaries; and our readers know they have hardly ever been placed on a tomb during the reign of this dynasty (p. 1088). But the privilege, also guaranteed by the institutions of the State, of having a large stone tablet in those grounds, inscribed with the name and titles of the deceased and, occasionally, with some details about his career, is seldom neglected. We shall deal with this subject in the next section of this Chapter.

On page 412, we mentioned a custom of China's ancient rulers of bestowing burial requisites and money upon deceased statesmen, in order to enable their families to bury them in a manner worthy of their merits and careers. Numerous passages in the records show that emperors of later ages have not abandoned this custom; they have finally come to consider such care for the burial of their servants not merely as a gift, but as a binding duty toward a class of men whose lives have been devoted to supporting their sovereigns in supreme power and maintaining them on the throne. During the Ming dynasty, the graves of civil officers were still built at the expense of the state; indeed, a certain sum, varying according to the rank of the deceased and the number of years he had spent in state service, was awarded for that purpose from the treasury, and a certain number of workmen were placed at the disposal of the family.

The same dynasty also established in its *Collective Statutes*² a long decree regulating the gifts to be made in cases of the death of military officers. These gifts included bricks and lime for the tomb, a wooden vault, stones inscribed with a eulogistic biography, workmen assigned from among the prisoners, objects for the <term>Netherworld</term>, embroidered needlework, and horse harnesses and saddles. The nature and quantity of these gifts depended on the rank of the man upon whom they were bestowed.

### 2. Inscriptions placed upon and in the Tombs.

*Grave Stones.*
Like other nations that have made progress in the noble art of writing, the Chinese attach much importance to decorating their tombs with inscriptions. Characters intended to attract happiness to the buried person and transmit it through him to his descendants are frequent on graves of considerable size and solid construction, as we have stated elsewhere (page 979). Besides, every tomb—except those of the very poor, who cannot afford such an expense, and those of infants and neglected individuals who have no one to care for them—has a granite slab at the foot of the mound, on which are carved some characters, sometimes painted red, or partly red and partly green, which identify the man or woman buried behind it. We have spoken of such stones on pages 1082 and 1084; but we must still give our readers some details respecting them to clearly explain the important position they hold at graves.
In Amoy and the surrounding districts, they are generally called <term>bōng pái</term>², “grave tablets.” Serving to point out who

Consequently, the title *jü-jen*¹, which pertains to the wives of title-bearers of the three lowest degrees, occurs more often on gravestones for women than any other, and all the more so because the people are accustomed to placing it on the graves of women upon whom no rank was ever conferred. This custom of making the graves an exhibition of ranks and titles has led to a great variation in the inscriptions on the graves of the upper class, with which the soil of the Empire literally teems. It is unnecessary to say that many a gravestone, if placed on a tomb of considerable size, is several feet high.

Gravestones which mention both the date of erection and the names of the children by whose care they were set up are, relatively speaking, rare. More common are those which only state, on the right side of the central column, that "The filial sons So-and-So have erected it." The birthplace or ancestral home of the deceased is hardly ever carved into the stone when the grave is situated within that locality or close by.

On page 1084, attention was directed to the fact that the gravestone, owing to the position in which it is placed on the altar of the grave, is an actual pendant or counterpart of the wooden soul tablet of the buried man, which is displayed for worship on the altar in his home. Another important point of similarity between the two objects is that the inscriptions they bear are almost identical. Our readers can see this for themselves by referring to our description of soul tablets, included in the Second Book of this work. Because of the inscriptions, both the gravestone and the tablet are, according to popular belief, inhabited by the <term>manes</term> of the deceased for whom they are erected. It is, in fact, the inscription which, by describing the deceased, *identifies* him with his gravestone and his soul tablet, making either of them an *alter ego* of him—an artificial body to which his frail, vaporous soul may cling as a firm support that shall prevent its dissolution. Consequently, the part that gravestones play in the religious worship of the dead is also analogous to that of the temporary soul tablets described on pages 70 and following.

Being an embodiment of the <term>manes</term> of the buried man, his gravestone is deemed to exert a greater influence upon the well-being and misfortune of his family than any other part of his grave. Hence, it is by no means a matter of indifference how many characters it

<page-num>1105</page-num>
# ARITHMANCY APPLIED TO GRAVE INSCRIPTIONS.

Existence, the Chinese say, is a chain of birth (生), old age (老), disease (病), death (死), and misery (苦). Only the first and second of these five stages possess a lucky character; producing many male offspring and achieving longevity rank among the greatest blessings ever bestowed on man in the Middle Kingdom. Consequently, the grave will confer these blessings upon its owners if the inscription contains either one or two characters. Should it consist of three, four, or five, the family will be visited with sickness, death, or woe. Six characters again bring childbirth, seven longevity, and so forth; in short, the total number of characters should certainly be fixed at one or two, six or seven, eleven or twelve, or sixteen or seventeen. In most cases, the same rule is observed regarding the columns on the right and left, if there are any. However, many assert that these side columns do not influence the lucky qualities of the grave, as only the central column represents the buried person.

This learned <term>arithmancy</term> explains why so many gravestones of the poor bear only two characters, even though there might be room on them for three, four, or five. It also causes grave inscriptions in general to be more varied in tone than they would be if this rule did not exist. For instance, in some cases, it requires placing the name of the reigning dynasty at the top of the column. It may also happen that, in order to obtain the required number of characters, the birthplace—which is otherwise generally carved in the top corners—must be placed within the column itself. Or, as in the second grave inscription given on page 1103, the character 諱 (meaning "the personal name which may not be pronounced") must be shifted a little to the left so that it forms no essential part of the column. Again, the number of characters may have to be restricted by simply writing 考 or 妣 ("deceased father or mother") instead of 顯考 or 顯妣 ("illustrious deceased father or mother"), or by omitting the private name of the dead person. On the other hand, the characters may have to be increased by inserting the genitive particle 之 above the word 墓 ("grave"), or by replacing this latter word with a synonymous term composed of two characters, and so forth.

It may now reasonably be asked how this popular five-part division of human fate came into existence. None of the Chinese people to whom we have applied for information were able to answer the question. Feeling that this division had a Buddhist tone to it, we have sought for a solution in the writings

Both these examples teach us that, during the Ming dynasty, it was customary for a married couple buried in the same grave to share a single gravestone. This custom still exists today. On such a stone, the inscription for the wife forms a separate column of characters, always placed to the right of her husband's column because, as our readers know, the right is the less honorable side, and the wife is buried to the right of her husband. called in Amoy *siang khòng* <note>雙壙</note>, "double grave-pits." Relatively speaking, they are rare in Fujian, as Feng Shui masters there find it difficult to discover spots where the geomantic properties align with two different horoscopes; besides, they entertain serious fears that when a grave is opened to receive a second body, the manes already settled there may be disturbed, and the Feng Shui "wounded" or "killed." Therefore, graves in which a husband rests with his wife and one or more concubines are even rarer.

The importance of the gravestone as an embodiment of the soul is openly declared by Feng Shui doctrines. No less than the corpse—the principal seat of the manes—that stone ought to be a focus in which the good celestial and terrestrial influences converge; and consequently, the geomantic bearings are primarily taken from it. If it is damaged or broken, the Feng Shui itself is maimed and doomed to inactivity; for how can a human soul possibly exert any energy on behalf of its offspring if the body it inhabits is seriously impaired? Because of this, destroying their gravestones is the worst blow an enemy can inflict on a family whose fortunes he wishes to ruin (see page 1039). On the other hand, also because they are inhabited by the soul, such stones can be used to great advantage for the improvement of the Feng Shui of graves. The masters, indeed, frequently resort to them to rectify the influences of the Five Elements or Planets. Should one element or another be insufficiently represented in the landscape surrounding a grave, they simply give the top of the stone the shape of that element, in accordance with the theory of forms discussed on page 956; or they make it represent an element which, according to ancient philosophical speculation, has the capacity to produce the missing one (see page 957). Conversely, if a certain element prevails too much in the surrounding landscape, the stone is given the form of an element that destroys it. Such transformations of the gravestone have a powerful effect, as the primary active power of the grave—namely, the soul joined with the stone—is immediately affected. Frequently, the wall in which the stone is set is also given a planetary form, and two elements are thus combined to work together to rectify the Feng Shui of the location. ## *Eulogistic Biographies in Stone, buried in the Tombs.*

Grave inscriptions of quite another kind, but of no less importance than those described above, are the so-called <term>mo chi-ming</term><note>1: 墓誌銘</note> (Amoy dialect: *bōng tsì-bîng*), "sepulchral biographies with inscriptions." They are engraved on rectangular slabs of smooth slate of equal size, often measuring about thirty centimeters by twenty and two centimeters thick. They consist of a <term>chi</term> or "biography"—that is to say, a summary of the chief events in the life of the deceased—and a <term>ming</term> or "inscription," which is a eulogy of his good qualities and excellence, written in the grandiloquent, flowery language that Chinese literati consider to be the height of elegance in style. The characters are of the same style as those found in the best printed books and are coated with red paint or gilded. A <term>mo chi-ming</term> generally covers more than one slab, sometimes four, five, or even more; the inscription is consistently continued from one slab to the next, covering both sides, so that when placed upon each other in regular sequence, the slabs form an unbound stone book of a few leaves. This resemblance to a book is by no means accidental; it is intentional. Like the title page of many fine books, the first side of the first slab bears the title of the biography, or the so-called "cover,"<note>2: 蓋</note> in tall characters of <term>chwen</term> writing (seal script),<note>3: 篆字</note> which is supposed to have been popular during the Zhou dynasty; a knowledge of this script is now considered a proof of high literary attainment.

The stone book is placed in the grave of the person whose life is described therein. As we have stated on pages 166 and 213, it should, in theory, be carried there in the funeral procession by a special vehicle, and it is buried between the coffin and the gravestone; in some cases, however, it is placed at the head of the coffin. Before sending it to the grave, the relatives have a number of facsimile copies made from it on paper in the following way: a wet sheet of white paper is laid out over the surface of the slabs, pressed down into the characters with a soft wad of wet linen, and rubbed over with black ink. After being removed from the stone, the sheet bears the characters in white on a black ground. It is then folded up so as to resemble

a thin Chinese book with double leaves, as may be seen from Plate XXXV, which is the exact reproduction of a specimen. Such facsimiles are made for distribution among relatives and friends to spread the fame of the deceased. Generally, they are also sold in bookshops as models of style and handwriting, being much sought after by students and schoolboys; indeed, sepulchral biographies are always composed by local scholars of high repute and written out by renowned calligraphers, and the carving in the stone is likewise entrusted to the ablest hands to be found.

Employing men of prominent scholarship and capacity requires a considerable outlay in presents and pecuniary remuneration. Therefore, only people of wealth and distinction are able to have sepulchral biographies composed. The poor must content themselves with tiles or flat bricks on which they write in ink a few dates of the events in the life of the deceased, covering them with a coating of transparent varnish to prevent them from being effaced by the moisture from the grave.

The great care bestowed by the Chinese on these necrologies in stone indicates their belief in their importance to the dead. In fact, the reputation of their ancestors is dear to all, and devotion demands that the living should establish their fame both in the realm of Death and in this world. Therefore, they place in their tombs an indelible record of their commendable and glorious feats, while at the same time spreading their fame by a liberal distribution of copies on paper. By thus expressing their filial feelings, they also greatly benefit themselves, for the ancestors cannot do otherwise than reward them by showering down blessings. These blessings may be shared by the composer of the document and the calligrapher who have done their work so well. Therefore, to direct the attention of the dead to themselves, they take good care to place their names on the stone, with all their official titles—their boast and glory—either at the head of the "biography" or at the end of the "inscription." This adds much to the reputation of the family of the deceased, showing both in this world and the next how distinguished its members are, who count such noble men of rank among their kinsfolk, friends, or acquaintances.

The people generally consider one of the great advantages connected with the placing of stone biographies in the graves to consist in their identifying the buried corpses forever, even after

He died at the hour of the Tiger [3–5 a.m.] on the sixteenth day of the twelfth month of the *Jiwei* year of the Xianfeng era [January 9, 1860]. He reached the age of fifty-nine. He married Lady Cai in Dichi and Lady Lin in Xiamen. His concubine, Lady Chen, bore him eight sons. The eldest, Longwen; the third, Dewen; the fifth, Yangwen; and the seventh, Huanwen, were all born to Lady Lin. Dewen was given in adoption to the senior branch of the family. The second, Qinwen; the sixth, Fengwen; and the eighth, Tongwen, were all born to Lady Cai. The fourth, Fangwen, was born to the concubine Lady Chen and was given in adoption to the seventh branch of the family. On the fifteenth day of the eleventh month of the *Gengshen* year of the Xianfeng era [December 26, 1860], he was buried at the plateau of Hujingshan in Andou village, positioned on the Yi-Xin axis with an orientation toward the Chen-Xu divisions.

<column-break/>

The people's hearts were greatly calmed, and as the rice continued to arrive, the famine caused no harm. The gentleman's actions in this regard demonstrate how extraordinary he was. In the *Wuwu* year [1858], when rebels caused disturbances upstream, the provincial government daily planned for military supplies. Contributions were urgently required. The gentleman was the first to donate funds and encouraged the public to do the same. As a result, he was recommended for the rank of Candidate <term>Daoyuan</term> <note>Circuit Intendant</note> with an additional three levels of merit, and was granted the title of <term>Tongfeng Dafu</term> <note>Dignitary of the Second Rank</note>. Three generations of his ancestors were posthumously granted the same rank as he. The gentleman's wisdom and intelligence surpassed others, yet he was so cautious and soft-spoken that he seemed almost incapable. His family was wealthy, yet he conducted himself with the simplicity of a poor scholar. Looking at the gentleman's deeds, they sprang from his natural character and were rooted in his appreciation for the Classics; they aligned perfectly with the conduct of a noble scholar. Because he was such a man, he deserves this inscription. The gentleman was born on the twentieth day of the sixth month of the *Xinyou* year of the Jiaqing era [July 30, 1801]...

<column-break/>

During the grain shortage, the price of crops rose higher every day, and the people cried out in hunger. The gentry member Lin Shubei urgently established an office to stabilize prices through government sales, but he was frustrated because no rice was arriving. The gentleman spoke with various foreign merchants, arranging for them to sail their ships to request grain from other countries. Previously, although Xiamen had been recovered, many rebels still hid in foreign territories, spreading rumors daily so that the people grew increasingly fearful. The gentleman said, "The people are already suffering from hunger within; if the rebels sprout up again from without, we will be in great danger. We must quickly unite with the foreigners and have them guard the sea for us." He took charge of this matter personally, inviting the various foreign merchants to the Nanputuo Temple. He explained the risks and benefits to them, making them restrain the people in their employ, and he summoned warships to the harbor to prevent external threats. The foreigners had long respected and deferred to the gentleman, and they all followed the agreement.

<summary>This epitaph honors a man born in 1801 who stabilized Xiamen during a famine by negotiating with foreign merchants and donating to military funds. It details his official titles, his large family, and his burial in 1860.</summary>

# Epitaph of Mr. Yang, Posthumously Awarded the Title of Grand Master for Thorough Service, Expectant Circuit Intendant with Three Merit Ranks
## Epitaph

->Recipient of the *Jinshi* degree<-
->Posthumously awarded the title of Grand Master of Palace Leisure, rewarded for military merit with the peacock feather, expectant Circuit Intendant of Sichuan, former Secretary of the Ministry of War, and Recorded Censor<-
->By Imperial Command, Superintendent of the Meeting House for Foreign Envoys, Director of the Wulan School, Director of the Bureau of Regulations of the Ministry of War, awarded three additional ranks plus one additional rank, your humble younger family friend, Zhuang Zhiqian, bows his head and writes this text<-

->Posthumously awarded the title of Grand Master of Palace Leisure, Secretary of the Fengtian Bureau of the Ministry of Punishments, General Manager of the Autumn Review Office, Attendant of the Grand Council, Associate Editor of the Military Strategy Bureau, Co-examiner of the *Gengxu* [1850] Metropolitan Examination, awarded three additional ranks plus one additional rank, your humble younger brother, Xie Qianheng, bows his head and writes the calligraphy and the seal script for the cover<-

Wudao <note>A poetic name for Xiamen</note> produces many extraordinary men. Among them was **Mr. Yang Xianzhou**, who possessed great strategic wisdom, was capable in his duties, and was skilled at managing his livelihood. I had long heard of his reputation, but I had never met him. In the year *Wuwu* [1858], while I was resting at Yuping, Mr. Yang’s son, **Jiemei**, along with his disciple **Yang Qinwen**, came to request to become my students. Upon inquiring about his family background, I discovered he was indeed the son of Mr. Yang Xianzhou. Jiemei is an upright man; since the gentleman was able to choose such a teacher for his son, was he not perhaps a merchant who possessed the conduct of a scholar? Upon the gentleman’s death, his sons presented a record of his life and, weeping, bowed and requested an inscription for his tombstone. Therefore, I examined the record of his deeds to write this account.

The gentleman’s given name was **Jichuan**, and his courtesy name was **Changtuan**; **Xianzhou** was his pseudonym. His family had lived for generations in Tingdian Village, south of the prefecture. His father was **Tianxi**, and his mother was of the **Zhuang** family. They first moved to Xiamen. Tianxi had seven sons, but only the gentleman and his brother, **Yanxiu**, survived. The gentleman was the third son. Even as a child, he was exceptionally intelligent and stood out from ordinary children; he could recite the Classics from memory after a single glance. However, his family was extremely poor, so he could not complete his studies and followed his father as a petty trader.

At age fifteen, he lost his father, and his poverty deepened. An old friend of his father, the elder **Mr. Hou Puyuan**, returned from Luzon <note>The Philippines</note> and comforted him, saying: "How can a child as sharp and alert as you remain in poverty and low status?" He then invited the gentleman to the port to assist in trade, instructing all his associates to follow the gentleman’s direction. The gentleman responded with sincerity and diligence. Within a few years, he had mastered the local dialect, foreign script <note>likely Spanish or Latin letters</note>, and the methods of trading with various foreign groups. After assisting the Hou family for over a decade—during which time the Hou family prospered—the gentleman began his own trade using his family's resources. 

He arranged a marriage for his younger brother early on. When people asked about it, he replied, "It is so he may have a household early to reverently carry on our ancestral line." Later, he returned to purchase sacrificial land for the clan and provided for his kinsmen and the village. He was involved in every righteous undertaking. In the *Dingsi* year [1857], Xiamen suffered a great famine, and the Taiwan region also <column-break/>

During the military turmoil, army supplies were insufficient. The Lady repeatedly instructed her sons and grandsons to provide rations and donate funds to recruit soldiers to serve the country. When peace was restored, the local authorities intended to repair the Tong’an Academy and the examination hall. She again instructed Shui-shu to contribute funds, leading the way for the local gentry. She was selfless in private matters and diligent in public service.

Her nature was strict, but her heart was truly broad. In the summer of the *ji-si* year, Shui-shu was falsely accused by an enemy. Those who heard of it were indignant, but the Lady cautioned him to endure and settle the dispute, encouraging him to exert himself rather than get involved in a major lawsuit; everyone admired her. In the twenty years after Longshi passed away, whenever disputes arose among the clan members, a few words from the Lady always resolved them immediately.

As she approached the age of a hundred, she did not easily wear fine silks or eat delicacies. She still personally performed hard labor to show her descendants the importance of avoiding idleness. Alas, the Lady's virtuous conduct can truly serve as a model for the women's quarters.</gloss>.

tracing out important matters of Chinese society and family life. It would therefore be very satisfactory if some Sinologist would make a choice selection of such documents and edit them, after careful sifting, with correct translations and explanatory notes.

Placing eulogistic biographies, engraved in stone, in the graves of the dead is by no means a modern custom. The common opinion in China, which is apparently well-founded and supported by documentary evidence, is that it dates from high antiquity, being based upon a practice, frequently mentioned in the Classics, of making eulogies to glorify the dead.

Originally, homage seems to have been paid in this way exclusively to officials of considerable rank. We read, indeed, in the *Li ki* (ch. 9, l. 35):

> » When Ruler Chwang of the kingdom
> » of Lu fought a battle against the men of Sung at Shing-
> » khiu, Hien Pen-fu drove, and Puh-kwoh was the man on his
> » right. The horse took fright, the harness broke, and the Ruler fell
> » down. Hien Pen-fu said: ‘On no other day did the harness break;
> » that such a disaster occurs today is owing to my want of courage.’
> » Immediately he was killed (by the king?). When the groom was
> » bathing the horse, a stray arrow was found sticking in the
> » flesh under the flank, upon which the Ruler said: ‘It was not his
> » fault,’ and he immediately honored him with a eulogy. The practice
> » of making eulogies for lower officials dates from this time” <note>¹ 魯莊公及宋人戰于乘丘、縣賁父御、卜國爲右。馬驚、敗績、公隊。縣賁父曰、他日不敗績而今敗績、是無勇也。遂死之。圉人浴馬有流矢在白肉、公曰、非其罪也、遂誄之。士之有誄自此始也。Section Tan-kung, I, 1.</note>.

This passage teaches us that the custom in question was in practice as early as the seventh century before our era; the battle of Shingkhiu was fought, according to the *Ch'un ts'iu* <note>² The tenth year of Ruler Chwang's reign.</note>, in 683 B.C. This is confirmed by the fact that funeral eulogies are, as we shall see on page 1124, mentioned more than once in the *Cheu li*. This ancient constitution dates, according to the prevailing Chinese belief, from the thirteenth century before our era.

Like the *ming*, or eulogies proper, on the current *mo chi-ming*, they were composed of only a few lines; and their commendatory character apparently consisted of expressing the profound grief felt by the survivors because of the departure of the deceased. They were, in fact, short elegiac encomiums—eulogistic death-dirges. This may be seen from the *lei* made upon the death of Confucius:

> » conduct’ ” <note>¹ 夏四月孔丘卒、公誄之曰、旻天不弔、不憖遺一老俾屏余一人在位。焭焭余在疚。嗚呼、哀哉、尼父、無自律. *Tso ch'wen*, the sixteenth year of Ruler Ngai’s reign. See also the *Historical Records*, ch. 47, l. 27.</note>.

> » support my throne. Alas! woe is me! Oh, Father Ni!” <note>² 天不遺耆老、莫相予位焉。嗚呼、哀哉、尼父· *Section* 檀弓, I, 3.</note>

Since the homage paid to the dead by such panegyrics consisted chiefly of expressions of grief, it necessarily follows that their value for the deceased kept pace with the social position of the men who composed them. A deceased man could, indeed, not be better honored than by having profound regret for his departure openly expressed by men of much higher rank. It is therefore natural to read in the *Li ki* (ch. 27, l. 18):
> » A man in a low posi-
> » tion does not write a eulogy for another in a higher position, nor does a younger
> » man compose it for an elder of his family—this is the rule.
> » In the case of a Son of Heaven, Heaven alone can be appealed to
> » for his eulogy. It is even against the ceremonial institutions for
> » feudal Princes to eulogize each other” <note>³ 賤不誄貴、幼不誄長、禮也。唯天子稱天以誄之。諸侯相誄非禮也. *Section* 曾子問, II.</note>

It actually happens, in fact, that people of humble status create them; but in such cases, the names and titles of officials and *literati* are, with their consent, featured on the stone as if they were truly the composers and writers.

It is quite natural that funeral eulogies in ancient China played a part whenever and wherever it was deemed appropriate to honor the deceased; for example, when prayers were chanted or recited at the burial and at the sacrifices offered to the soul on that occasion. In the *Cheu li* we read: »The Great Invoker prepares six »kinds of formulas to maintain communication with »the beings above and below (that is, of Heaven and Earth), with »the near and distant ancestors, and the spirits far away and nearby; »the sixth kind includes the funeral eulogies$^1$. The Great Annalist »recites the eulogy at Great Funerals on the day when the corpse »is sent away»$^2$ — that is to say, as the extracts quoted on pages 151—152 from the *I li* and the *Li ki* show, at the farewell sacrifice offered to the deceased before sending them to their last resting place; — »and at the funeral of a Great »officer, a Sub-Annalist delivers the posthumous name and recites »the eulogy»$^3$. Since the eulogies were thus clearly formal addresses recited in mournful terms at the moment when the dead were sent to the tomb, we may call them »mourning addresses» or »funeral addresses».

At imperial funerals during the Han dynasty, they also served this purpose. They were called at that time »elegiac bamboo slips»$^4$, being, no doubt, scratched or written on bamboo, the common writing material in those times. When the imperial remains were placed on the bier or hearse, as we read in the Record of Rituals contained in the Standard History of the Han dynasty, »the Great Annalist, holding the elegiac »bamboo slip on the palms of his hands, stands behind »the hearse. The Grandmaster of the Sacrifices kneels down, ex- »claiming: ‘Come forward!’ The Emperor obeys this order; the »Commander of the Army reads the bamboo slip, engraved

"...composed a disquisition on eulogies, in four sections" <note>Books of the Later Han Dynasty, chapter 110, first section, lines 14 and following: 所著賦論誄哀辭雜文凡十六篇。時三輔多士、扶風曹曄伯師亦有才學、著誄書論四篇。</note>. Nor did the *lei* fall into disuse in subsequent ages. It is recorded, for instance, of one Khih Ch'ao <note>郄超</note>, who lived in the fourth century, that "on the day of his death, men of all ranks and conditions took up their writing brushes, and more than forty persons each composed a eulogy for him; such was the general esteem in which he was held" <note>Books of the Tsin Dynasty, chapter 67, line 22: 及死之日貴賤操筆而為誄者四十餘人、其為衆所宗貴如此。</note>. "And Ho Ch'ing-sui, a native of Ch'i-cheu, who had cured his sick father by giving him some flesh to eat which he had cut from his own thigh, prostrated himself on the grave upon the old man's death. He wailed and stamped his feet countless times, and died from emaciation. He was called the filial son of Ts'ing-yang, and scholars wrote a very great number of eulogies for him" <note>New Books of the T'ang Dynasty, chapter 195, line 14: 有何澄粹者、池州人、親病刲股肉進親、疾為瘳、後親沒伏于墓、哭踊無數、以毀卒。當時號青陽孝子、士為作誄甚衆。</note>.

In books of later times, elegies commonly appear under the name of "sacrificial writings" <note>祭文</note>, that is, offertories addressed to the dead during the celebration of the funeral. That this term, in fact, already denoted an elegy during the Liang dynasty is proved by the following extract: "When Sü Fei died while holding the office of prefect of Tsin-ngan, his corpse was sent back to the capital (the present Nanking), and his consort then wrote a *sacrificial writing* in very sad and mournful terms. Mien (his father) first intended to write the *elegy* for him; but when he had seen that sacrificial writing, he laid down his writing brush

<note>When Xu Fei died while serving in Jin’an commandery, his remains were returned to the capital. His wife composed a sacrificial piece, the language of which was extremely mournful. Ever since, sacrificial writings have been mentioned very frequently in books, and to this day they are generally used at the funerals of prominent people. Original specimens have been placed before our readers on pages 147 and 225. Just like the *lei* of the ancients, they bear the twofold character of elegy and eulogy and are recited at the funeral; the fact that they are then burned (see pages 149 and 226) also connects them with the *lei*. Indeed, these latter were, during the Han dynasty, placed in the grave (see pages 1125 and 1131), and, as we have demonstrated on pages 711 and following, the ancient custom of burying articles with the dead gradually gave way in later times to offering them up to the manes by converting them into flames and smoke.

Also the songs which, as we have suggested on page 189, were chanted in ancient China by the gagged drawers of the hearse, were, in the opinion of native scholars, nothing other than elegiac eulogies, and, as such, were most closely allied to the *lei*. The Record of Rites of the Han dynasty <note>Books of the Later Han Dynasty, chapter 16, line 5.</note> states that, during the reign of this House, there were in the funeral procession of an Emperor no less than three hundred so-called <term>wan</term> 挽 or "car drawers," in six rows of fifty each, who dragged the cumbersome hearse by means of six thick ropes of white silk, thirty <term>chang</term> long. All these men, and also the officials accompanying them, had gags in their mouths to reduce their chanting to a monotonous hum; besides, there were six files of ten singing men, and each file was preceded by eight military officers carrying clappers. In the third century, while the Tsin dynasty occupied the throne, it was—as we have shown on page 188 by a long extract from the Official History of that era—called into question by high servants of the State whether such singing at the bier-ropes should, on archaeological grounds, be granted a place among the ritual institutions of the Government, and it was decided to maintain it. No doubt it is to a great extent owing to this Imperial decision that it has kept its place in the institutions of later dynasties. As for the present reigning dynasty, neither its Collective Statutes nor its *Tongli* make mention of funeral chanters. From this, we must infer that, as such men are not explicitly mentioned in the Classics, this dynasty has deemed it incorrect to sanction their presence in funeral processions. In the numerous burial processions that have passed before our eyes, we never saw any chanters, though many of those processions were for men and women of high social position and official rank. Yet, the ancient custom, observed during so many centuries, survives in another form. In Fujian and some parts of Guangdong, the elegiac eulogies, instead of being sung at the coffin on the way to the grave, are carried aloft in the funeral procession, each of them being inscribed on a large sheet of colored cloth or silk, hanging down from a horizontal wooden strip which is fixed to the top of a pole. We have spoken of these banners already on page 199. They are specifically used when the great Buddhist mass for the repose of the soul has been celebrated; for, since this ceremony is specially devoted to enriching the deceased with sacrificial offerings, all friends, relatives, and admirers take the opportunity to pay homage to the soul by presenting eulogistic banners, in addition to food, mock money, etc. Sometimes a pair of banners are offered, each inscribed with one line of a...

These eulogistic funeral banners most clearly demonstrate their origin by the names they bear. In literary style they are generally called *wan* 輓, “car drawers,” the same word which, as we stated on page 1128, denoted the men who pulled the Imperial funeral car to the mausoleum during the Han dynasty, and which has ever since denoted them in the dynastic books of rites and in general literature. Often the banners are also called *chuh* 軸, a word which denotes the axle of a vehicle, or the axle-arms; that is to say, the instrument by means of which a funeral car is pulled forward. A third name, also in frequent use, is a combination of the two words above into the compound term *wan-chuh*. As to the inscriptions on these banners, the standard expression by which they are denoted at present is *wan ko* 輓歌, “car-drawers’ chants,” the same term, indeed, which is used in the Books of the Tsin dynasty—namely, in the extract which was given, with a translation, on pages 188–189 of this work—and afterwards in the literature of all ages, to denote the songs of the hearse drawers. In literary style, those

<header>EULOGIES BURIED IN THE TOMBS.</header>

Inscriptions are, moreover, called *wan shi*¹ or *wan ts’ze*², "car-drawers' verses," and *tsi wan*³ or *tsi chuh*⁴, "sacrificial car-drawers" or "sacrificial car-axles." We must also observe that it is very common to find in books the character 輓 interchanged with 挽, which is a homonym for the first—or we might say a synonym—having the meaning of pulling or drawing in a general sense.

After this digression, we must again focus our attention on the eulogistic biographies in stone placed in the graves. They, too, represent a form that the *lei* of the ancients has assumed over the course of ages.

It was seen on page 1125 that, during Imperial burials in the Han dynasty, the elegiac eulogy, inscribed on bamboo, was deposited in the crypt. Liu Chao⁵, who lived during the Liang dynasty, informs us in the commentary he wrote for the *Books of the Later Han Dynasty*, that:

> "During the reign of the House of Tsin, there was found at the foot of Mount Sung-kao a slip of bamboo, inscribed with two columns of tadpole-shaped characters. They passed from hand to hand in that table-land and beyond it, with people showing them to each other; but nobody could understand them until Chang Hwa, Superintendent of Works, consulted the learned scholar Shuh Cheh. He declared that he was dealing with the slip that had been placed in the Hien-tsieh Mausoleum of Emperor Ming (who died in A.D. 75). On further investigation, this was found to be factually correct."⁶

It was also during the Han dynasty that there lived a man who, as recorded in the Standard Histories, had an engraved stone put into his grave, which strongly reminds one of the modern <term>mo chi-ming</term>. In the fifth century of our era, the nobleman Chang Yung, while opening an old grave found near Lake Hüen-wu, discovered a copper peck with a handle. When inquiries were made about this object among the scholars at Court by Emperor Wen, Ho Ching-t'ien said: "This is a peck of...

Reliable references to eulogistic biographies in stone, buried in the tombs, do not appear in national literature before the fifth century. Regarding P'ei $^1$, the consort of the heir-apparent of the first Emperor of the Southern Ts'i dynasty, we read: "She died in the second year of the Kien yuen period (480 A.D.). At that time, while the proposal to create a stone biography (*chi*) for her was being discussed, (the minister) Wang Kien made the following statement: 'Stone biographies do not owe their existence to ancient ritual institutions and did not come into fashion until the Sung dynasty, in the Yuen kia period (424–454), when Yen Yen-chi created one for Wang Khiu. The Imperial clan has not used any engraved bamboo slips for tombs until now and must continue to act in accordance with that same line of conduct. In the past, its members have collectively observed the customs of their ancestors; if an additional practice is now observed for this secondary consort, the rules of conduct that have been constantly practiced until now will be abandoned. In any case, since an elegiac bamboo slip is used for her, we must not trouble ourselves over a stone biography.' This advice was followed" $^2$. This excerpt is also important because it demonstrates that, in those times, there were men who truly considered the ancient bamboo elegies to be essentially identical to the modern stone biographies of that day.

So, for instance, upon the death of the magnate <term>Ch'ü Siang</term> <note>Ch'ü Siang.</note> of the Liang dynasty, in the third year of the <term>Ta t'ung</term> period (529), "his brother <term>Sié-kü</term> composed his sepulchral inscription (<term>mo ming</term>), of which the following is a summary: 'A man whose glorious rule produced so many flowers and seeds that the size of Mount Sung <note>Located in Honan province, it is considered by the Chinese to be the highest mountain peak in the Empire.</note> is insufficient to estimate their quantity; a man from whose fame under the moon the pure harpsichord tunes arise—with such a man, this person may, according to those who speak of him, be freely compared'" <note>His brother Sié-kü created the tomb inscription for him, an excerpt of which says: "The greatness of his rule spread like blossoms; even the height of Mount Sung is not enough to measure it. His fame is like the pure sound of a lute under the moon; people say he can be compared to the best of men." *Books of the Liang Dynasty*, chapter 41, page 5.</note>. 

The *Books of the Northern Ts'i Dynasty* mention a certain <term>P'ei Tseu-chi</term> <note>P'ei Tseu-chi.</note>, a scholar of great wit and learning, who, "when the various members of the house of <term>Yang Yin</term> were moved to other graves, was entrusted with reverently creating more than ten sepulchral biographies (<term>mo chi</term>)" <note>When the Yang Yin family was reburied, Tseu-chi was asked to write more than ten tomb inscriptions. *Books of the Northern Ts'i Dynasty*, chapter 35, page 2.</note>.

> Two slabs shall be used. The one forming the "cover" shall bear this inscription: "Grave of Mr. So-and-So, who lived under this or that dynasty and was appointed to such-and-such an office"; if the deceased held no office, it shall bear his courtesy name. On the other slab, which forms the "bottom," his official rank shall be engraved, along with his family name, his taboo personal name, his courtesy name, his department and district, the name and office of his father, and the family name and honorary title of his mother. Furthermore, it shall include the year, month, and day of his birth; the official posts to which he was successively appointed; the year, month, and day of his death; the village or ward where the burial takes place; his age; the name of his wife and that of her father; and the offices held by his sons, as well as the offices and names of the men whom his daughters married. On the day of the burial, the inscribed sides of the two slabs must be placed against each other, and the slabs must be fastened together with iron bands. Thus they shall be placed in the front part of the burial pit, only three or four feet from the surface of the soil; for if the contours of the ground should later change, the grave might be disturbed by mistake. In such a case, these stones, being the first things seen, will inform the intruders of the names and persuade them to cover the grave again. <note>1. Use two pieces of stone. One is the cover, inscribed: "Grave of Lord So-and-so, official of such-and-such a dynasty"; if there is no office, write the courtesy name. The other is the base, inscribed: "Lord So-and-so, official," followed by his taboo name and courtesy name, his district and county of origin, his father's taboo name and office, his mother's family name and title, birth date, career history, date of death, place of burial in such-and-such a village and ward, age, wife’s family name and father, sons' offices, and daughters' husbands' names and offices. On the burial day, place the two stones face-to-face and bind them with iron. Place them before the burial chamber, three or four feet from the surface... [The text ends here].</note>

<header># RESCRIPTS OF THE MING DYNASTY.</header>

The Ming dynasty enacted decrees that differed little from those mentioned above. In the fifth year of the Hung-wu period (1372), the first monarch of this family decreed as follows:

<margin>Kia li, chapter 6. Fearing that if the landscape changes over time or the grave is accidentally disturbed, the presence of this stone will allow someone to identify the deceased and rebury them.</margin>

> "Two flat biographical stones are to be used for all mandarins of any rank. The one, forming the cover, shall be inscribed with the words: 'Grave of the mandarin So-and-so'; the other, forming the base, shall bear the family name, the name, and the residence of the deceased; his ancestors up to the third generation; the year of his birth; the month and day of his death and burial; his sons and grandsons; and the location of his grave. In the case of a married woman, the stone shall bear the title conferred upon her in accordance with the rank of her husband, sons, or grandsons (compare page 767). The two faces of the stones shall be placed against each other, fastened together with iron bands, and buried in the grave." ^1

<margin>History of the Ming Dynasty, chapter 60, line 15. 1. Regulations for the two biographical slabs used by officials: one as a cover with the title, and one as a base with detailed personal and genealogical records, bound with iron and buried.</margin>

From a summary provided by the *History of the Ming Dynasty* regarding the decrees that were in force during that era for the burial of members of the gentry, we learn that for these individuals as well:

<margin>Chapter 60, line 20. 2. Instructions to carve a biographical stone and place it in the burial pit along with the soul banner during interment.</margin>

> "biographical stones were to be carved, which were to be placed in the grave at the interment, together with the soul banner." ^2

Finally, the edict of the fifth year of the Hung-wu period directed that the common people should also use "biographical stones in two slabs, made in accordance with the rules in force for mandarins." ^3 Also, in the *Collective Statutes of the Ming Dynasty*, "the carving of a biographical stone" ^4 is mentioned among the necessary preparations for the burial of officers, and "the placing of such a stone in the grave" ^5 is included among the burial rites for commoners.

The dynasty now on the Throne has made very similar decrees. In the *Ta Tsing t'ung li* (General Rituals of the Great Qing), we read that upon the death of Princes of the Imperial lineage—of whose titles we provided a list on page 453—after the coffin is placed in the grave, "the biographical stones shall be hidden within it"¹; furthermore, in the case of a mandarin of any rank, "two stones shall be used for carving the funerary biography. One is to be inscribed like the stone tablet outside the grave (see pages 1147 and following), and the other should state in detail the surname of the deceased; his personal name that may not be spoken; his posthumous name; his courtesy name; his district, town, village, and place of residence; the offices he held and the posts to which he was successively transferred; furthermore, the year, month, day, and hour of his birth and death; the location of his burial place and the compass points denoting the direction in which it lies; and the sons and daughters he left behind. The stones must be fastened together by means of iron bindings in such a way that the characters face inward."² Also for the <term>shi</term>³, that is to say, the officers of the eighth and ninth degree and the gentry, "a funerary biography shall be carved, following the rules found among the decrees for the funerals of mandarins"⁴; and for the common people "there shall be a biography, but no stone tablet."⁵

Knowing now that the celebratory biographies placed in the tombs of the dead have evolved from a sacred institution of the ancients; knowing also that they have been a matter of concern to the State for over a thousand years—decrees relative to their use having been laid down in the ritual codes of four of the great dynasties that have ruled the Empire since the seventh century—we may be sure the modern Chinese also consider them of the highest importance in the disposal of their dead. It is remarkable that none of these four dynasties has granted such biographies a celebratory character; indeed, their official decrees designate them

# OLD SEPULCHRAL BIOGRAPHIES.

These records are referred to by the terms "stone biographies, biographical stones, or sepulchral biographies"<note>Shi-zhi, zhi-shi, or kuang-zhi.</note>, and never by the word *ming*, which, as our readers will remember, denotes the actual eulogies currently engraved on stones after the biography. Perhaps this fact is attributed to the circumstance that the most ancient records mentioning the placement of *lei* in tombs—specifically the Books of the Han Dynasty—only mention this practice in connection with Imperial graves. Thus, the sovereigns of later times have refrained from devaluing this honor, which belonged to the ancient ancestors of the Throne alone, by officially allowing it for mere officials and commoners. Nevertheless, as we have seen, the whole nation has always used stone biographies for the purpose of praising the dead; however, this is probably attributed to the tolerance of the Government.

Chinese authors have preserved many sepulchral biographies from past ages in their writings. Some of these documents are from the hand of Chu Hi, the favorite of modern scholars, and are therefore viewed with special admiration. Some earlier examples have also found their way into books, but it is doubtful whether they are all correctly represented as having been placed inside the graves. Indeed, many may have been displayed upon the tombs on large stone tablets, to which we shall soon devote a few pages. None of the sepulchral biographies from those earlier ages that we have encountered in books consisted of both a *chi* and a *ming*. However, there is clear evidence that some of that kind were composed during the time of Chu Hi. We are told in the *Yung-chai wu pih*<note>Yung-chai wu pih (Five Collections from the Yung Studio).</note>, the fifth and final collection of a series of miscellanies published by Hung Mai<note>See the note on page 1078.</note>—who lived from 1123 to 1203 at the same time as Chu Hi—that in 1197, a stone slab was discovered in the ground. It was engraved with a notice of the life of one Ts'ao Yin<note>Ts'ao Yin.</note>, the son of a court official under the first Emperor of the T'ang dynasty. This notice was followed by a *ming*, which read: "His life was in accordance with the principles of Heaven, and his death was in conformity with the same; since he thoroughly identified himself with those principles, why should we waste any words to mournfully summon back his soul?"<note>The original reads: "Qi sheng ye tian, qi si ye tian, gou da ci li, ai fu he yan." See the Ku kin t'u shu tsih ch'ing (Imperial Encyclopedia), Literature section, chapter 178.</note> The truth of this tale is subject to

See the work and place previously cited.</note>, though with a change of names and date; but it is evident that it would not have occurred to the mind of Hung Mai to write such a tale unless sepulchral biographies followed by a <term>ming</term> did exist in his time. Still, we recollect, as stated on page 1134, that an Emperor of the sixth century is said by historical books to have composed for his own son a <term>chi</term> followed by a <term>ming</term>.

After all, it can hardly escape the reader's notice that the <term>mo chi-ming</term> are related to gravestones. Indeed, they contain the same facts as the latter, though in a more elaborate form and with the addition of many particulars. In some parts of China, the similarity is very obvious—for instance, in the province of Kiangsi, in the regions around P'o-yang Lake. There, we have seen many gravestones made of the same slate stone of which the <term>mo chi-ming</term> are made, displaying, in addition to the ordinary inscription, the dates of the birth and death of the deceased in small-sized characters, as well as the chief particulars concerning his offspring, his age, and the location of his grave. Of course, these biographical gravestones, as we may call them, are of considerable size, as so many characters are engraved on them. We have seen many whose tops we could scarcely reach with our hands.

### *Large Sepulchral Tablets of Stone.*

We now come to a third category of sepulchral inscriptions, namely, the so-called <term>pei</term> or <term>pi</term><note>碑 (*Pei*).</note>, which are rectangular slabs of granite, dolomite, marble, or other natural stone. These are high and broad, standing apart in an upright position near the tombs of actual or titular officials and those of their wives, located either exactly in the middle of the open ground in front or a little to the right or left. They display in large characters the names and titles of the occupant of the grave, or of both occupants if a husband and wife are buried together.

If raised for an official of one of the three highest ranks, such a tablet stands on the back of a huge stone tortoise (see Fig. 25), called "a tortoise pedestal"<note>龜趺 (*Kuei-fu*).</note>; in all other cases, it is fixed in a so-called "square pedestal"<note>方趺 (*Fang-fu*).</note>, which is a single block of stone, the four sides of which

Furthermore, the crowning border of many a *pei* is decorated with a *ki-lin* or unicorn, a monster with which our readers are already acquainted (pp. 819, 822 and following). Finally, some bear a *t'ien-luh* $^3$ and a *p'ih-sié* $^4$, two mythical animals about whose true character the Chinese seem to know very little. The *t'ien-luh*, or "celestial good fortune," we have not been able to trace back any further than the standard chronicles of the reign of the Emperor Ling of the Han dynasty: "In the third year of the Chung-p'ing period (A.D. 186) they repaired the Jade Hall Palace, and cast some *t'ien-luh* and frogs" $^5$. An additional note, taken from a commentary written during the T'ang dynasty, says: "The *t'ien-luh* is a quadruped. These *t'ien-luh* and frogs vomited water outside the P'ing gate. At present there exists in Teng-cheu, in the north of the district of Nan-yang, a *pei* for one Tsung Tszĕ,

# THE T'IEN-LUH AND THE P'IH-SIÉ.

> " ...and at the side of it stands a pair of stone animals, on the
> thighs of which characters are engraved, namely <term>t'ien-luh</term> on the
> one, and <term>p'ih-sié</term> on the other; this proves that both these
> terms denote quadrupeds. The House of Han possessed a t'ien-
> luh corridor, which was named after the animal" <note>1: **天祿獸也。天祿蝦蟆吐水於平門外。今鄧州南陽縣北有宗資碑、旁有兩石獸、鐫其膊、一曰天祿、一曰辟邪、據此即天祿辟邪並獸名也。漢有天祿閣、亦因獸以立名．** (The t'ien-luh is a beast. T'ien-luh and frogs vomited water outside the P'ing gate. Now at Nan-yang district in Teng-cheu, there is a stela for Tsung Tszĕ; at its side are two stone beasts with characters engraved on their shoulders, one called t'ien-luh and the other p'ih-sié. Based on this, t'ien-luh and p'ih-sié are both names of beasts. The Han had a T'ien-luh Pavilion, also named after the beast.)</note>.

In early works, the word <term>t'ien-luh</term> is sometimes written <term>天鹿</term>, "celestial stag." It is uncertain whether we are dealing here with a simple play on sounds—<term>祿</term> and <term>鹿</term> both being pronounced *luh*—or whether "celestial stag" is the correct name and the animal originally represented a type of stag that was seldom seen and consequently became shrouded in a vague myth by the people. In a "Memoir on Vehicles and Dress" <note>2: **輿服志 (Yü fu chi).**</note> used during the reign of the House of Han—which was compiled by Liu Chao, who lived during the Liang dynasty and whom our readers have already encountered on page 1131—we read that the Empresses, when they visited the temples of their ancestors, wore pendants in the shape of bears, tigers, celestial stags, and <term>p'ih-sié</term> on their head-dresses <note>3: Books of the Later Han Dynasty, ch. 40, l. 13.</note>. This statement, just like the passage cited above from the T'ang commentary on the *Books of the Later Han Dynasty*, shows that in the first centuries of our era, the <term>t'ien-luh</term> and <term>p'ih-sié</term> were generally paired together in the minds of the nation; and this explains why we find them joined today on the decorative top borders of the <term>pei</term>.

As for the <term>p'ih-sié</term>, it is evident from the name itself that this animal is a mythical one. In fact, the word means: "something that wards off evil influences, a charm." It was undoubtedly in the capacity of a charm that, as the previously cited *Memoir on Vehicles and Dress* states, "the Imperial Princesses, the Princes granted a fief, and all those of even higher rank, were accustomed to wear a buckle on their sash in the shape of a golden <term>p'ih-sié</term> head, decorated with white pearls" <note>4: **自公主封君以上皆黃金辟邪首為帶鈎、飾以白珠．** Op. et cap. cit., l. 14.</note>. We believe it was likewise because of their evil-dispelling

### ->THE T'IEN-LUH AND THE P'IH-SIÉ.<-

A reference to the sixth century is provided by the following passage in the *Books of the Sui Dynasty*:

> "In the twelfth year of the Ta t'ung period of the Liang dynasty (A.D. 546), in the first month, two *p'ih-sié* were sent to the Kien mausoleum. The two-horned one, which was to be placed on the left side, arrived safely at the site; but the other with one horn, which was to stand on the right, became unstable on the carriage when they were about to move it forward. It leaped three times, so that both shafts broke and the carriage had to be replaced by another. And again, before the latter arrived within two miles of the mausoleum, the beast skipped three times, and the men surrounding the carriage fled in great alarm at every motion it made. At three or four feet from its destination, the wheels of the carriage sank into the ground to a depth of three inches" <note>1: 梁大同十二年正月送辟邪二于建陵。左雙角者至陵所、右獨角者將引、於車上振、躍者三、車兩轅俱折、因換車。未至陵二里又躍者三、每一振則車側人莫不聳奮。去地三四尺車輪陷入土三寸。Chapter 22, l. 28.</note>.

That during the T'ang dynasty there still stood a *p'ih-sié* on a grave in Nan-yang, alongside a *t'ien-luh*, is explicitly stated in a commentary on the *Books of the Later Han Dynasty*, as we saw on page 1143. Moreover, another author of that period, namely Wang Jui (see p. 825), says:

> "Since the Qin and Han dynasties, stone unicorns, stone elephants, *p'ih-sié*, stone horses, and other images have been erected in front of the mausoleums of Emperors and Princes. Before the tombs of officials, stone tigers, sheep, men, pillars, and the like were placed, all serving to decorate the grave mound like a bodyguard arrayed as if for the living" <note>2: 秦漢以來帝王陵前有石麟石象辟邪石馬之屬、人臣墓前有石虎石羊石人石柱之類、皆以飾壟如生前之儀衛。See the *Chih kuh tszě luh*, quoted in the *Ku kin t'u shu tsih ch'ing*, sect. 坤輿, ch. 140.</note>.

We cannot say whether *p'ih-sié* or *t'ien-luh* have been erected on tombs in more recent ages, as we find no statements to this effect in native books. Perhaps they have gradually become obsolete, with their figures being carved thereafter in the crowning borders of the *pei* (stone tablets), as is the case at present.

<page-num>1146</page-num>
# THE GRAVE.

We think it is doubtful whether the *p'ih-sié* plays a role in the decoration of sepulchral tablets for any reason other than the power of its name, which, as we have seen, means "to charm away evil influences." Because of this name, its image ensures the absence of dangers and misfortunes for the individual whose names and titles are carved into the "body" of the tablet. From him, the desirable situation created in this way passes to his living descendants through the mediation of the grave. Nor can it be doubted that the *t'ien-luh*, when carved on a tablet, serves to bring blessings down upon the buried man and his descendants for similar reasons. We have indeed seen that *t'ien-luh* means "celestial good fortune." However, it also signifies "blessings or favors bestowed by the Emperor," or "Imperial salary derived from an official position." As our readers know, nothing is as highly desired by the Chinese as government posts for themselves and their descendants. If the name *t'ien-luh* means "celestial stag," similar blessings are thereby ensured; for, as we demonstrated on page 56, the stag represents them because of its name and is, moreover, an emblem of delight and enjoyment. Regarding the *ki-lin*, as this animal foretells the appearance of perfect rulers (see page 824), its presence on a *pei* promises that virtuous descendants will be granted official honors as long as their destiny is tied to the tomb. A hornless dragon showers upon the buried man and his descendants all the blessings that dragons generally pour onto graves in their role as the primary bearers of the universe's beneficial influences (pp. 949 and following). Finally, the stone tortoise that supports the *pei* ensures a long life for everyone and perpetuates the family's existence, as tortoises symbolize vital power and longevity (see page 56).

Not all sepulchral tablets are decorated with animals. If erected on the tombs of officers of the six lowest ranks, they have only a so-called "round head" <note>1</note>, which is a crowning border that is rounded at the top. In the countryside around Peking, where tablets are especially numerous because this city was once full of nobles and dignitaries of every class and rank, these "round heads" are shaped like a lily or a lotus; they are very thick and heavy, bulging out significantly in front. Elsewhere, they are shaped as shown in Plate XXXVI. Tablets of this description usually have a "square pedestal." Although they are often called *pei*, their correct name is *kieh* <note>2</note>,

---

<note>1: 圓首.</note> ->           <- <note>2: 碣.</note>

> "At the beginning of the reign of the Ming dynasty, a decree existed by which the Emperor was to be petitioned, upon the death of a high minister, whether civil or military, to order the officers of his Hanlin College to prepare an epitaph and to erect a *pei* on the Road of the Soul (the avenue to the tomb).
