Rules to the same effect are to be found in the Collective Statutes of the Ming dynasty¹.

We should also note that, according to the institutions of the currently reigning dynasty, upon the death of every nobleman belonging to one of the three highest ranks, and of every mandarin of the first degree, the inscription for the grave tablet is composed by the Imperial Chancery (Nei-koh) or the Han-lin College, in the event that a posthumous name is conferred upon the deceased by the Emperor². It goes without saying that this honor, just as all others bestowed either by the Son of Heaven or his chief departments of central administration, is considered by the entire nation to cast a brilliant halo of glory around the memory of the deceased and his family.

Since the *pei* and *kieh* are generally erected in front of the tombs, they often stand on the spot where the path leading to the grave branches off from the nearest public road. On the island of Amoy and in other parts of the Ts'üen-cheu department, this path is called *bōng tō*³, "grave road," and the tablet is also referred to by this word because it marks the place where the path begins; and it is very common to see this word carved in the stone as a part of the inscription. This, for example, is the case with the *kieh* represented in Plate XXXVI (facing page 1141); its inscription reads: "Road to the grave of Mr. Lin Kiün-hwui, upon whom, after his death, the Imperial Ts'ing dynasty conferred the honorary title of General of the Hwai-yuen region; and of Mrs. Wang Tszĕ-king, buried at his side, upon whom the Imperial Ts'ing dynasty bestowed, during her life, the female honorary title of the third degree." The words "Imperial Ts'ing dynasty" are placed on the crowning border. This is due to the consideration that respect requires the name of the family of the reigning monarch to be raised high above the rest of the inscription; moreover, the superstitious calculation based upon the quinary division of human fate (see page 1105) has evidently required the removal of a couple of characters from

# TABLET-HOUSES.

The same plate also shows that stone tablets are sometimes decorated on the front with margins of carved figures, reminding us of a wreath of twigs and leaves, and that it is not unusual to adorn the pedestal of a <term>kieh</term> with some mystic animal <note>1</note>.

In some mausoleums on the Peking plains, the <term>pei</term> is sheltered underneath a pavilion. But the right of having the tombs decorated in this way is, as we shall see on page 1176, a prerogative of Imperial Princes of the two highest ranks, granted to them by the written institutions of the State. Consequently, such tablet-houses are very rare in the provinces. Plate XXXVII is a picture of the only specimen to be found in the outskirts of Amoy. It is made entirely of granite. The style of honorary gates is repeated here, as may be seen at a glance from the pictures we have given of these monuments in the Second Volume. The inscription on the tablet shows that it was built for a married couple bearing no higher title of honor than that of the fourth rank. Hence, we must infer that a license to erect it was, for some reason or other, granted by special favor, or that pavilions of such small dimensions and plain construction once were, or still are, tolerated by the authorities. The structure bears some inscriptions. On a tablet upheld by a dragon, placed underneath the highest roof, we read: "Glory conferred by Imperial favor" <note>2</note>, and on the lintel, under the lower roof: "Imperial favors he has received over and over again" <note>3</note>. A couplet, placed on the two posts in front, reads:

> "If an official, while maintaining respect for the authorities with a firm hand, performs from the very beginning actions which proceed from exemplary virtue,
> "His variegated pheasant feathers (a symbol of official dignity) shall emit streams of perfume, and he will forever carry with him the certificates of appointment to honors granted by the Emperor’s grace" <note>4</note>.

# THE GRAVE.

We must now provide the origin and history of the sepulchral tablets. The fact that, during the Ming dynasty, the <term>pei</term> and <term>kieh</term> were matters of great concern—being subject to minute official rules—leads us to believe they were considered ancient in that era. On this account, they were deemed to deserve a place among the institutions of the State, alongside everything else of ancient origin. They are, in truth, as old as the Han dynasty, and Chinese authors trace them as far back as the reign of the House of Cheu.

In the *Li ki* (chapter 13, line 34) we read:
> "At the death of the mother of Ki Khang-tszĕ, Kung-shu Joh was still young. When the body was dressed for the coffin, Pan (that is, Kung-shu Joh) asked permission to bury the corpse by means of a mechanical device. They were about to agree, when Kung-kien Kia said: ‘This must not be done. According to the ancient practice in the state of Lu, the ruling House uses "great <term>pei</term>" for this purpose, and the three principal families use wooden posts arranged in a square. Pan, you have tested your skill on other people’s mothers; shouldn't you also test your skill on your own mother? Would that distress you? Bah!’ They did not allow him to carry out his plan" <note>1. Section Tan-kung, II, 2.</note>.

On another page, the same Classic states (chapter 58, line 44): "In burying the Ruler of a State, they use four coffin ropes and two <term>pei</term>; in burying a Great Officer, they use two ropes and two <term>pei</term>; and in burying an ordinary officer, they use two ropes and no <term>pei</term>" <note>2. Section Sang-ta-ki, II.</note>. It appears from these two extracts that it was customary during the Cheu dynasty to lower princes and magnates into their graves using posts called <term>pei</term>, which were planted at the edge of the pit. In the second century of our era, the famous Ching Khang-ch'ing wrote: "The 'great <term>pei</term>' were carved from large tree trunks and shaped like the stone <term>pei</term> (tablets). Soon after, he was destroyed by Huan Wen. *Books of the Tsin Dynasty*, chapter 72, lines 12 and following.</note>.

It should be remembered that speculations of this sort are not out of fashion at present; geomancy attributes various metallic properties to gravestones in connection with their shape, as we have seen on page 1108.

In the *Books of the Han Dynasty*, as far as we know, there is no mention of any measures taken by the government to officially regulate the construction of sepulchral tablets. However, in the era immediately following the fall of that House, official decrees to this effect seem to have been enacted and strictly enforced.

> "Since the Han dynasty, the dead throughout the Empire have been sent to their graves with extravagant wastefulness," we read in the *Books of the Sung Dynasty*. "Stone buildings, stone animals, eulogistic inscriptions carved on tablets, and other monuments were created for them on a large scale. Consequently, in the tenth year of the Kien ngan period (205 AD), Emperor Wu of the Wei dynasty (Ts'ao Ts'ao), considering that the Empire's resources were being depleted, issued an order stating that it was no longer permitted to bury the dead with great expense and prohibited the construction of stone tablets. During the reign of Kao-kwei-hiang-kung (of the same dynasty), in the second year of the Kan lu period (257 AD), Generalissimo Lun, Prince of T'ai-yuen, died. His elder brother Tsun wrote an essay to glorify his virtues, wishing to record the fame he left behind. However, fearing that the official regulations established for Princes did not authorize him to engrave a eulogistic essay in stone, he composed a simple account of the deceased man’s career and had it engraved on the northern side of the tomb. This event suggests that the prohibition against stone tablets was strictly upheld at that time."

Later, a period of relaxation occurred. But under the Tsin dynasty, Emperor Wu issued the following decree in the fourth...

# THE DISTINCTION MADE BETWEEN PEI AND KIEH.

> "At seven or more miles from the city walls, a *pei* with a hornless dragon at the top and a tortoise as a pedestal might be erected, but it should not rise more than nine feet above the pedestal. For officers from the seventh rank up to the third, a *kieh* four feet high might be raised, with a top resembling that of a scepter and with a square pedestal; and for persons who, though not holding official titles, had obtained a reputation for perfection in modest solitude, or for simple and pure filial devotion and sense of duty, a permit to erect a *kieh* might be requested from the Throne and could be granted by it" <note>1. For those buried at the capital, seven miles or more outside the city walls: for those of the third rank and above, a *pei* with a hornless dragon head and a tortoise pedestal may be erected, with the height above the pedestal not exceeding nine feet. For those of the seventh rank and above, a *kieh* four feet high may be erected with a scepter-shaped top and a square pedestal. For those known for their reclusive life, purity, or exceptional filial piety and righteousness, even if they have no rank, a petition may be submitted to request the erection of a *kieh*. Books of the Sui Dynasty, chapter 8, line 7. 在京師葬者去城七里外三品以上立碑螭首龜趺、趺上高不得過九尺。七品已上立碣高四尺圭首方趺、若隱淪道素孝義著聞者、雖無爵、奏聽立碣.</note>.

Here we have, I believe, the oldest printed reference to stone tablets with a tortoise pedestal and a hornless dragon on the crowning border, and also the first passage in which such tablets are officially distinguished, by the name of *pei*, from the *kieh* with a simple square pedestal.

This distinction between the two types has evidently been maintained ever since, and both the *pei* and *kieh* have been consistently made in the same shape and similarly decorated as they are at present. We read, for example, that in an inscription which Liu Yü-sih <note>2. 劉禹錫.</note>, a poet who lived between 772 and 842, wrote for the tablet of the high official Hi Chih <note>3. 奚陟.</note>, this passage occurred:

> "This crowning border, decorated with a hornless dragon, and this pedestal, shaped like a tortoise, record the radiant glory of his virtues" <note>4. "The hornless dragon head and tortoise pedestal record the radiance of his virtue." *Pei wen yun fu*, chapter 7, II, line 149. 螭首龜趺德輝是紀.</note>.

Sü Shi-tseng states categorically that

> "during the reign of the Tang dynasty, the *kieh* had a square pedestal and a round head and were erected for officers of the fifth rank and those of lower degree" <note>5. "The Tang system for the *kieh* used a square pedestal and a round head; they were used by officials of the fifth rank and below." *Wen t'i ming pien*, quoted in the *Ku kin t'u shu tsih ch'ing*, Literature section (文學), chapter 177. 唐碣制方趺圓首、五品以下官用之.</note>;

and finally we read that the following couplet was engraved on the *kieh* of one Yao Sui <note>6. 姚燧.</note>, a significant high official during the Yuan dynasty:

> "Square is its pedestal, and sculpted its crowning border; the place where the *kieh* stands in the paved

"The avenue to the tomb shall not decay, even when a thousand sacrifices have been offered to this soul" <note>1. That the Ming dynasty sharply distinguished the two kinds from each other is demonstrated by its ordinances reproduced on page 1149; and the current reigning dynasty, which, as we have stated, maintained those ordinances with almost no modifications, does the same.

Ordinances of the same tendency having been passed by successive dynasties, almost from the very beginning of the custom of erecting such tablets, it is clear enough that the nation and its Rulers have always regarded these monuments as objects of the highest importance for the worship of the dead. Nowadays, the Government certainly does not regard them from a less serious point of view, even going so far as to pay, in the case of certain nobles and public servants, the expenses connected with their erection, apart from the allowances which, as stated on page 1101, it grants for the construction of their graves. 

"In the second year of the Khang hi period (1663), it was stipulated that, in the case of officials to whom a posthumous name was granted (by the Emperor), the Board of Works should appoint an officer to erect the tablet. And in the fourteenth year of the same period (1675), a proposal was approved, according to which 400 taels should be paid for that of a nobleman of one of the three highest ranks; for an officer of the first rank, the same sum as for an Imperial Prince of the ninth order (namely 350 taels); for an officer of the second rank, as much as for a Prince of the tenth rank (300 taels); and for an officer of the third rank, 250 taels. As for the building of graves and the erection of tablets: in case officers of the first or second rank become ill and die, the Board of Rites shall submit a proposal to the Throne; and if only half the ordinary allowance be granted for the burial, no payment shall be made for the tablet. <header>TABLETS ENGRAVED WITH A BIOGRAPHY. 1163</header>

We must now direct our attention to the fact that a small number of these sepulchral tablets also contain an account of the life of the deceased, and for this reason, they are closely allied with the *mo chi-ming*. This account is mostly engraved on the reverse of the stone. It seems that such biographical tablets did not come into use before the sixth century, and that the *pei* and *kieh*, previously erected, only displayed names and titles, either with or without an eulogy; for we find in the national histories the following statement concerning P'ei Tszě-yé <gloss>1 裴子野.</gloss>, a Minister who died in A.D. 528:

> "When he was buried, the Prince of Siang-tung made a *mo chi-ming* for him and placed it in his grave; besides, a sepulchral biography (*mo chi*) was erected by the Prince of Shao-ling on the path leading to the tomb. From this time dates the custom of placing biographies in such avenues" <gloss>2 及葬、湘東王為之墓誌銘、陳于藏內、邵陵王又立墓誌、堙于羨道。羨道列誌自此始焉. History of the Southern Part of the Realm, ch. 33, l. 23.</gloss>.

In connection with this passage, it may be remarked that, in the early references to the tablets, the inscriptions carved on them are often called *ming* or *lei*, but never *chi*, and that the decrees of the present dynasty, quoted on pages 1147 and following, explicitly declare that the tablets shall only bear the names and official titles of the dead for whom they are erected. Hence, it seems probable that the sparse biographies preserved in books as copies from sepulchral tablets of bygone ages are exceptions, and have appeared on graves only by special Imperial license.

The *pei* and *kieh*, the inscriptions of which are commemorative of the celebrity of the dead, are, from the very first, often denoted in the books by the name *mo piao* <gloss>3 墓表.</gloss>, "sepulchral marks of distinction." We read, indeed, of Yen Tuh, a dignitary of whom we have spoken on page 639, who lived in the second century of our era:

> "When he had arrived in the country the administration of which was entrusted to him, he erected an eulogistic inscription (*ming*) as a mark of distinction to the grave of—"

<header>THE GRAVE.</header>

"...Kung Sui, and presented a sacrifice on the spot"¹. That the *mo piao* did not, however, actually form a distinct species of tablets, we may admit on the authority of Sü Shi-tseng. "The *mo piao*," he says, "began to be erected during the Eastern (Later) Han dynasty, when the Emperor Ngan raised such a monument, in the first year of the period Yuen ch'u (114 AD), to King Kiün, an officer charged with the reception and entertainment of the guests of the Court. Those tablets bore characters of the same shape as those on the *pei* and *kieh*; they might be made for office-bearers and non-official persons indiscriminately, and were not, like the *pei* and *kieh*, subject to decrees concerning grade and rank. Being erected on the Road of the Spirit, they were also called: 'marks of distinction on Spirit-roads'"². Another name for such tablets, likewise of rather frequent use in the books, is *pei piao*³: "stone tablets serving as marks of distinction."

In conclusion, we note that the stone tablets erected at the tombs are mentioned in the books of every period by two terms alluding to their origin—namely, "great *pei*"⁴, and "marks of distinction in the shape of wooden posts"⁵. Both these terms are derived from the extract of the *Li ki*, which we provided on page 1152. Even the *T'ung li* of the present dynasty denotes the tablets erected for the principal members of the Imperial Family (see page 1174) by the name of "great *pei*."

<page-num>1165</page-num>
<header>-># ON MAUSOLEA FOR PRINCES OF THE HIGHEST RANK.<-</header>

The pages we will now devote to this subject will show that such monuments, even the largest and most gorgeous, are very similar to the sepulchres of the common people and the mandarinate. This is because they, too, are laid out on the same plan as the dwellings of the living.

The Princes of Imperial lineage are divided into twelve classes, the titles of which are given on page 453 of this work. These classes correspond with twelve generations in the male line of descent. Their mausolea are spread over the vast plains around the Metropolis and over the hills that bound those plains to the west and north. Some are situated elsewhere in the Empire, but not in any great numbers, as the general custom of conveying the dead back to the place where their ancestors lived and where they were born is observed with special strictness regarding the members of the Imperial Family.

Among those mausolea, the largest and grandest are, of course, those of Imperial sons—Princes of the first or highest rank, entitled <term>Ts'in wang</term>¹, "Princes or Kings of the nearest Generation, or of the nearest Blood." They cover many acres of ground. A vast quadrilateral plot of about two acres in size, surrounded on all four sides by a thick, solid wall, forms the main part, the so-called <term>fen yuen</term>² or "grave enclosure." The wall, called <term>wei ts'iang</term>³, "enclosing wall," is, in many cases, over four meters high. It consists of large, hard grayish bricks. Over its whole length, it is covered with a narrow span-roof with glazed tiles of a beautiful green color, glistening and shining in the rays of the sun. An idea of the shape of such wall-roofs is conveyed by Plate XLVI, facing page 1217, where the reader can see them to the right and left of the gate. As is the case with the roofs of large temples and palaces generally, a layer of tiles or a ridge of limestone runs over the top, and on both facades, the eaves rest on thick wall-plates of white limestone or painted wood. The tiles are made of coarse porcelain, very solid and heavy, and are of the same kind and make as the tiles that cover many buildings within the vast Imperial Altar grounds in the suburbs of the Metropolis and many temples likewise connected with the State religion located within its walls. They are slightly curved and arranged in rows, the intervals between which are covered with reversed semi-tubular tiles, so that the roof looks like a file of parallel...

The bottom tile in every row ends in a rounded border, decorated with embossed ornamental figures; these borders together form a beautiful scalloped edge along the eaves. Access to the enclosure is gained through a broad roofed gate, called <term>ta men</term><note>1 大門.</note>: "great gate, or main gate," located exactly in the middle of the side which, either actually or in theory, faces the South. It is of the same type as the main entrance to large mansions and public buildings. It stands on a raised rectangular substructure of thick slabs of marble or dolomite of considerable length, which greatly aids in bringing out its stately appearance. Both in front and at the back, this stylobate has steps for ascent, protected sometimes by elaborately wrought balustrades of limestone or marble. The gate has three openings, closed by folding wooden doors and decorated with paint of many colors. The high span roof is supported by wooden pillars and covered with green glazed tiles, similar to those which decorate the walls of the enclosure. they in turn support brackets longer than the second, which are also fastened at right angles over them, with one lying near the end; and so on, until the eaves are reached. This increases the breadth at the top to support the roof. This complex timber construction is the most decorative part of the roof; it is painted in red and other bright colors, and the ends of the brackets are adorned with handsome carvings. It produces a massive yet elegant effect and is a prominent feature of Chinese architecture throughout the Empire; all buildings with any claim to beauty are adorned with such a unique frieze.

Passing through the gate, the visitor immediately enters the *t'ing* <note>1 庭.</note> or courtyard. On the opposite side, he sees a freestanding building called the *hiang t'ang* <note>2 享堂 or 饗堂.</note> or *hiang tien* <note>3 享殿 or 饗殿.</note>: the "sacrificial hall" (see Fig. 39). A road paved with slabs of marble or stone runs in a straight line from the gate to that temple. Over a small arched marble bridge with handsome balustrades, it leads across a Feng-shui tank lined with rectangular blocks of stone, which is situated in the middle of the court. Two lion-like stone monsters, crouching on pedestals, watch over this bridge on either side; their jaws are turned toward the gate as if to drive away all spirits that might attempt to approach the temple or the burial mounds with malicious intent. Pines, cypresses, and other trees are planted on the right and left of the courtyard, enhancing the impressive atmosphere of this home of the dead.

The temple is made of wood and is rectangular in form. Its front, which faces the courtyard, is considerably longer than its side walls—in some cases almost twice as long—and contains the main entrance exactly in the middle, directly opposite the bridge. When viewed from the front, the temple closely resembles the "great gate," being built in the same style and likewise standing on a rectangular stone platform with steps in the front and back; sometimes it is just as wide as the gate, and in other cases it is considerably wider. The green-tiled roof, supported by wooden pillars arranged within the building and by wooden pilasters set within the walls, rises significantly higher than the gate. On every side, the eaves rest on a bracket construction exactly like that of the gate. Upon entering through the main door, the visitor faces an altar which bears

# TABLET-HOUSES IN THE MAUSOLEA FOR PRINCES.

Now retracing our steps to view the adjacent parts outside the wall, our attention is drawn to a square, pavilion-like building, raised directly in front of the main gate. It is the *pei t’ing*¹ or "tablet pavilion," built on a low terrace of brick or solid stone that has an ascent of a few steps on all sides. The red-plastered brick walls, about six meters long, each have an arched entrance exactly in the middle; these have no doors but are sometimes closed by a wooden railing. In many tablet houses, these entrances are formed by a pair of wooden pillars placed on either side like doorposts, which serve at the same time as supports for the roof (see Pl. XXXVIII). The walls have a massive base of large limestone slabs and bear carved limestone plates on top, upon which the roof rests. This roof is generally double-tiered, and the eaves project boldly on all sides. The building's main attraction is concentrated in the roof; indeed, the blue glazed tiles contrast charmingly with the double wooden architrave—elegantly ornamented with multi-colored painted arabesques—and with the bright red of the overlying bracket frieze. The marble tablet is visible through all four entrances, as it is placed exactly in the center of the building. It is a large monolith, inscribed with a few characters that state the name and title of the noble buried in the mausoleum, such as: "Mien Hien, Banner Prince of Shui and Hwai, of the closest Imperial kin"². The tortoise, on whose back the tablet stands, is likewise carved from a single piece of limestone and is of large dimensions. We have seen such stone monsters measuring a full four meters from snout to tail.

The grounds, in the midst of which the tablet house displays its glistening roofs, constitute a vast forecourt, planted on all sides with stately evergreens. This yard ends at the front at an artificial tank or moat, built of stone blocks and passable by means of a stone bridge that lies exactly in the same line as the tablet house, the main gate, and the temple. A pair of lions, crouching on their haunches, flank this bridge. In some instances, the forecourt is surrounded by a low wall of simple construction. A large tract, covered

with cypresses, pines, and oaks, the extent of which is not limited by any dynastic laws or decrees, encloses the mausoleum on all sides.

The royal funeral parks of evergreens, amidst which bright, green-glazed roofs charmingly sparkle in the rays of the sun, do not always match the description above in every respect. The tablet-house, for example, often stands inside the main gate and is sometimes adorned with elegantly carved balustrades, extending along the borders of the platform and the four flights of steps. In the courtyard between the main gate and the temple, one may also see two plain, one-story wooden buildings, one on either side. Their humble appearance, when contrasted with the gate and the temple, proves that they were not strictly built for the honor of the <term>manes</term> <note>the spirits of the dead ancestors</note>. They serve to accommodate the relatives when they visit the place to worship and sacrifice, and are called, respectively, <term>fan fang</term>¹: "eating-room," and <term>ch'a fang</term>²: "apartment to take tea in."

In the same courtyard, on the left of the temple, there often stands a rectangular <term>liao lu</term>³, meaning an "incineration furnace." This is intended for burning silk fabrics and paper mock money, which are presented in the temple on sacrificial days; these articles are thrown into it through an arched opening in the front. The solid stone base and the walls of this structure are, either partly or entirely, covered with bricks and plates of glazed porcelain. These display raised figures of various colors, among which green is the most prominent. The roof resembles that of the temple and the main gate, being covered with tiles of the same form, color, and dimensions; even the bracket construction is repeated in porcelain. The reader can obtain a good idea of such furnaces from Plate XXXIX, though they are by no means always so large and beautiful. Their maximum height averages between three and four meters.

Some mausoleums of Princes have a pair of stone pillars in front. However, at no site have we seen any stone statues of men or animals, except for the lions on the bridge. The clay huts of the guards are in the outer grounds, near a small door built into the wall, which they are not easily persuaded to open for foreign tourists. The main gate always remains closed, except when the family visits the place to worship and to sacrifice.

At first sight, it would appear that these gorgeous sepulchers of Imperial Princes of the nearest kin differ *entirely* from the graves

# MAUSOLEA FOR PRINCES OF INFERIOR RANK.

...in the South, described in the first section of this chapter. A little attention, however, is enough to convince us that just the opposite is the case, as both categories are laid out on the plan of large mansions, palaces, and temples. Our readers may easily verify this by reading what is written on pages 1083 *ff.* A comparison shows that, except for the tumuli and the tablet-house, a Prince's mausoleum resembles a mansion or a temple almost perfectly, since the sacrificial hall corresponds, in both location and purpose, to the main building of a residence or of an ancestral temple; such a building is likewise furnished with an altar and soul tablets.

Now that we are acquainted with the mausolea of the highest Imperial nobility of the present day, the reader will be much better able to understand the ancient native descriptions of some mausolea of the grandees of the Han dynasty, of which we have given translations on pages 445 *ff.* Indeed, these descriptions show that those ancient burial places must have resembled the current mausolea in almost every essential point. Consequently, Chinese monarchs, in building graves for the members of their family, have not greatly deviated from the path laid out by their ancestors; and if any novelties have been introduced, they only affect matters of minor importance. According to the same descriptions, the construction of temples on the graves of high-ranking officials was common practice at the beginning of our era. But the fact that their origin must be sought in pre-Christian times has been stated already on page 388.

The mausolea of Princes of lower rank are generally not as large or beautiful as those of Princes of the first rank. The Government has, indeed, enacted a sliding scale for their dimensions and decoration. Those of Princes of the four lowest degrees have no temple and, in many cases, no walls; as a result, they are hardly distinguishable from those of nobles and mandarins among which they lie scattered, so that a regular transition from one category to the other can be traced. They are by no means all kept in equally good and constant repair. We have seen many where the temple, gate, and walls were nothing but heaps of desolate ruins, overgrown with weeds and entirely bare of trees.

Sovereigns who, as we have stated on page 1101, have the graves of their Ministers and officers built at their expense, may reasonably be expected to take upon themselves the costs of the mausolea of their own kindred as well. Indeed, we read in the collections of dynastic ordinances:
> "Regarding the allowances to be paid for works connected with the construction of graves: in the tenth year of the Shun-chi period (1653) a proposal, presented to the Throne, was approved, according to which 5,000 taels of silver should be granted for a Prince of the first rank; 4,000 for his eldest son by the principal consort; 3,000 for a Prince of the second order; 2,000 and 1,000 respectively for Princes of the third and fourth order; and 500 for a Prince of the fifth, sixth, seventh, or eighth rank. And in the fourteenth year of the Khang-hi period (1675), a proposal, having been duly deliberated upon, was approved, according to which the same subsidy as for an officer of the first rank should be granted for a Prince of the ninth order, and for a Prince of the tenth order the same as for an officer of the second rank^8."

"...ornamented with a *t’ien-luh* and a *p’ih-sié* <note>mythical guardian creatures</note>, and the pedestal shall have the shape of a tortoise; the tablet of a Prince of the 12th order shall have a round head and a square pedestal" <gloss>1</gloss>. This matching of the four lowest classes of Princes with the four highest classes of mandarins is also carried out in respect to the length of the enclosures of their sepulchres, as shown by the data given on pages 1098 and 1172 onward.

The great importance attached to grave tablets in general sufficiently accounts for the reason why the dynastic Ordinances prescribe paying out subsidies from the Treasuries for their erection in the mausolea of Princes, and why these subsidies are exceedingly high compared with the sums granted for their graves (see page 1173). "As to the allowances for such tablets, in the tenth year of the Shunzhi period (1653), it was proposed to the Emperor and sanctioned by him that for a Prince of the first order, 3000 taels of silver should be paid; 2500 taels for the eldest son of such a Prince born of the principal consort; and 2000 for other Princes of the second order; 1000 and 700 taels respectively for Princes of the third and fourth order; and 450 for a Prince of the fifth, sixth, seventh, or eighth rank. In the fourteenth year of the Kangxi period (1675), a project to the following effect was approved, namely, that for Princes of the ninth and tenth order, the allowance should be 350 and 300 taels respectively" <gloss>3</gloss>.

In most mausolea of Imperial Princes, the stone tablet stands unsheltered in the open air, as it is a fundamental decree, laid down in the Collective Statutes of the dynasty, that "a tablet-house may be erected only for a Prince of the second or of a higher degree" ². Generally, the inscription for the tablet of a Prince of one of the eight highest orders is, like that for a high nobleman or a mandarin of the first degree (see p. 1150), composed by the Han-lin College ³.

Special mausolea for Princesses must be rare, since, as our readers know, it is an old established custom to bury women by the side of their husbands. It must further be noted that not every son and daughter of an Emperor rests in a mausoleum built in accordance with the general statutory rules. Occasionally, special ordinances have been issued by the Throne for their sepulchres, fixing the dimensions of the temple, the gates, the furnace, and the apartments for the warders, and regulating some other points on which the statutory rules are silent. The length of the enclosure wall was in nearly all these special cases fixed below the standard maximum length of one hundred chang; but a length of 130 chang was prescribed for the wall of the mausoleum in which Twan Hwui ⁴, heir-apparent of Kao Tsung, was buried in 1742 ⁵, so that this sepulchre belongs to the largest

### 4. The Imperial Cemeteries of the Ming Dynasty.

From the mausoleums of Imperial Princes, the highest-ranking figures in the Empire, we naturally pass to those of the Sons of Heaven, which are the only funerary monuments that surpass them in size and grandeur. Aside from those of the Ts'ing dynasty, who currently occupy the throne—which are naturally kept in good repair with devoted care because they are the dwelling places of Imperial ancestors on whose help and favor the prosperity and hardship of the Crown and the Realm depend—only those of the House of Ming can be adequately described. The Ming, who were dethroned by the Ts'ing in 1644, left tombs that are still in a condition that allows us to obtain a clear idea of their original shape and magnificence. All those from earlier times have either vanished completely or been reduced to a mere shadow of what they once were; only some parts of them have been patched up by the current Government, following the example set by previous dynasties. The simple fact that only these Ming tombs have survived the passage of time so well fully entitles them to a detailed description in this work.

However, they also merit description for other reasons. Because extreme conservatism in matters of religion, ceremonies, and rites has dominated the Chinese people throughout the ages, we are justified in our belief that these tombs were built according to the same plans that were passed down through successive dynasties as an heirloom from the ancients. Thus, they present a clear image of the Imperial tombs of every era, beginning with those of the Ts'in and Han. This fact, to which we have already drawn attention on page 441, marks them as monuments whose historical and archaeological value is almost impossible to overrate. The currently reigning dynasty, having taken them as a proto-

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the necessity of documenting Ming dynasty tombs due to the potential decay and instability of the current Qing government. It transitions into detailing the specific burial sites of the Ming emperors, starting with the founder in Nanjing and moving to the imperial cemetery near Beijing.</meta>

<page-num>1178</page-num>
<header>THE GRAVE.</header>

As the model for their own mausoleums, which are inaccessible to foreigners and consequently very poorly described, the Ming tombs are a valuable way to gain a good understanding of their shape and construction. Furthermore, documenting them is urgent. Indeed, their preservation depends merely on the whims of the current government, which—as the whole world knows—is established on a decaying and unstable throne. Their decay and eventual ruin, resulting from imperial indifference, greed, or financial troubles, is a constant threat. Additionally, rebellions or political considerations based on Feng Shui <note>Fung-shui</note> theories may at any moment lead to their demolition or, at the very least, reduce them to a condition that would forever make it impossible to describe them properly.

Tai-tsu <note>太祖</note>, the founder of the Ming dynasty, was buried outside the walls of Nanjing <note>Nanking</note>, which was the residence of the court and the capital of the Empire during his reign. His mausoleum cannot serve as a model for description, as it is entirely in ruins except for the avenue of stone figures, of which we have given a short account on page 821. For such a model, we must use the mausoleum of Cheng-tsu <note>成祖</note>, the third monarch; having moved his seat to Beijing <note>Peking</note>, he was buried almost due north of this city in the department of Chang-p'ing <note>昌平州</note>. His burial place there became the center of a vast family cemetery where, over the course of more than two centuries, twelve other Emperors—all his direct descendants in the male line—were laid to eternal rest in separate cenotaphs. These were built in the same style but on a smaller scale and with less magnificence; furthermore, a much greater number of Empresses, imperial concubines, and princes were interred there.

No mausoleum was ever built for the second Emperor of that dynasty, known in history by the name of Hui <note>惠</note>. He was a grandson of Tai-tsu and the son of the Heir Apparent I-wen <note>懿文</note>, who died in 1392 <note>History of the Ming Dynasty, chapter 3, line 10, and chapter 115, line 4</note>, six years before his father's death would have called him to the throne. Four years after Hui had ascended the throne in obedience to his appointment by his grandfather, his fourth paternal uncle, who was granted the fief <note>enfeoffed</note> of the principality of

<page-num>1179</page-num>
<header>THE SECOND EMPEROR OF THE MING DYNASTY.</header>

Yan¹ <note>Yen</note> in the present province of Hebei <note>Peh-chihli</note>, raised the banner of revolt and boldly marched on Nanjing <note>Nanking</note>. "This metropolis," says the historian, "fell into his hands; a fire broke out in the palace, and it is unknown how the Emperor perished." The King of Yan <note>Yen</note> sent court servants to recover the remains of the Emperor and his consort from the fire, and he buried them eight days later; however, some say that the monarch escaped through an underground passage. In the fifth year of the Zhengtong <note>Ching t'ung</note> period (1440), a Buddhist priest traveled from the province of Yunnan to that of Guangxi, and there claimed to be the Emperor of the Jianwen <note>Kien wen</note> period (that is, Hwui). Cen Ying <note>Ch'en Ying</note>, prefect of the department of Si'en <note>Szĕ-ngen</note>, informed the court of this; the man was put on trial and turned out to be one Yang Xingxiang <note>Yang Hing-siang</note> from Junzhou <note>Kiün-cheu</note>, a man over ninety years old. He was sent to jail for further examination and died in the fourth month of that year. Twelve priests who had been his accomplices in the plot were banished to Liaodong <note>Liao-tung</note>. Since that time, traditions have been common among the people in Dian <note>Tien; Yunnan</note>, in Qian <note>Khien; Guizhou</note>, and in Ba and Shu <note>Pa and Shuh; Sichuan</note> regarding the time when that Emperor is supposed to have lived there as a priest. — In the Zhengde <note>Ching teh</note> (1506–1521), Wanli <note>Wan lih</note> (1573–1620), and Chongzhen <note>Ch'ung ching</note> (1628–1644) periods, high-ranking officers requested that titles of honor be conferred upon the descendants of that Emperor, and that a posthumous name might be bestowed on him to be used in the ancestral temple; however, although those proposals were all forwarded to the Boards for discussion, they were never carried out" ².

The *Xu wenxian tongkao* <note>Suh wen hien t'ung khao</note> recounts the same particulars.

Whatever may have been the final fate of Hwui, there existed reasons enough for Chengzu <note>Ch'ing Tsu</note> and his successors to permanently deprive him of the honor of being buried in an Imperial mausoleum. First of all, filial piety and the laws of ancestor worship never prescribed that an uncle should bury his nephew with the same honors that everyone must bestow upon his own father. And subsequent Emperors never regarded Hwui as a lawful heir to the throne, as proven by their stubborn refusal, mentioned above, to grant titles of nobility to his descendants. In this respect, Chengzu <note>Ch'ing Tsu</note> had set the example, even going so far as to disavow the name of Jianwen <note>Kien wen</note>^2, which Hwui had adopted to designate his reign.

It strikingly characterizes the boundless influence Feng-shui exercises over the Chinese nation that even this Imperial burial ground was selected under the guidance of geomantic experts. Most of the above information is also recorded in the *Ming t'ung ki*: see the *Ku kin t'u shu tsih ch'ing*, section 禮儀, ch. 66. Comp. also the *Suh wen hien t'ung khao*, ch. 133, l. 15.</note>.

Our readers might easily be tempted to believe that the mountain range was thus named by Ch‘ing Tsu with the object of increasing, by the power of the name, its capacity to bestow—through the graves to be laid out at its foot—longevity upon his line of descendants and thus to perpetuate the dynasty. But his intention did not go so far. "The name Mounts of Imperial Longevity," says Sü Hioh-mu<note>3 徐學謨．</note>, "dates from Ch‘ing Tsu. When he stayed in that locality, he held a drinking party; and as the day happened to be his birthday, so that all his ministers offered him their good wishes for the prolongation of his life, those mountains were thus named by him. The fiction, current nowadays, that this name was given to those hills because they were to serve for the burial of Imperial remains, is erroneous"<note>4 天壽山名始於成祖。蓋嘗駐蹕於此飲酒、是</note>.

It also clarifies that the name "Imperial Longevity Hills" was chosen due to a birthday celebration held there, rather than as a geomantic charm for the dynasty's longevity.</summary>

As stated on page 1177, the mausoleums of the Ming dynasty owe their preservation exclusively to the care of the now-reigning House of Tsʻing. Since the conquest of the Empire, it has included them among the numerous sepulchers of rulers, statesmen, sages, and other paragons of the nation. The State raised these to the rank of objects of official attention, as respect forbade them being left to fall into ruin and obliteration. # THE MING TOMBS PROTECTED BY THE TS'ING DYNASTY.

Shing Tsu <note>3 聖祖 (the Kangxi Emperor).</note>, the next Emperor, in the fourteenth year of his reign (1675), ordered the Board of Rites by a special edict not to be neglectful in having the mausoleums carefully <note>4 Memoirs concerning Shun-t’ien, *loc. cit.*</note> looked after. That his successor, Shi Tsung, likewise took their preservation seriously to heart, the reader may see from the decree issued by him in 1729, of which we have provided a translation elsewhere (see page 932). Edicts for the same purpose were issued in 1786 and 1787 by Kao Tsung <note>5 高宗 (the Qianlong Emperor). See the same work, ch. 26, l. 28.</note>; and succeeding Emperors, down to this day, have followed that example.

Perhaps a question arises for our readers: Were not such measures for the preservation of those tombs very dangerous to the dynasty that took them, since geomancy teaches that graves create and promote the fortunes of the descendants of those who lie buried within? Did that dynasty not fear that they might endanger its throne by causing obscure descendants of the former House to stir up rebellions, and that seditious attempts at re-establishing the Ming family might be crowned with ultimate success through the powerful help of those tombs?

The answer is that the Manchu conquerors could not help but be convinced that the Feng-shui of those tombs was incurably damaged—indeed, killed forever—by the destruction of a considerable number of buildings and trees within their boundaries. Besides, the very overthrow of the Ming dynasty had proved to them either that the geomantic influence of its chief cemetery was entirely gone or, at any rate, that no significant spiritual power issued from it anymore. It was, no doubt, because of these considerations that in 1699, during a temporary stay in Nanking, Shing Tsu did not hesitate to order that the descendants of the extinct family be traced, so that he might appoint one of them as chief sacrificer at its tombs and grant him an official title <note>6 See his edict to this effect in the *Shing hiun*, ch. 56, l. 2.</note>. In 1724 he endowed the chosen man, a certain Chu Chi-lien <note>7 朱之璉.</note>, with

Consequently, Emperor Shing Tsu even appointed a Ming descendant, Chu Chi-lien, to oversee sacrifices at the ancestral site.</summary>

See the Memoirs concerning the Department of Shun-t'ien, ch. 26, l. 29.</note>; and his descendants still live in Beijing at the present day <note>2 Dr. Edkins states that the present reigning dynasty has erected geomantic walls northwest of Beijing, in the Kin-shan—specifically on the hillsides facing north-northeast on the way to Heh-lung T'an (Black Dragon Pool) 黑龍潭 from the Metropolis—thinking thereby to check the pernicious influences from the power that watches over the last resting-place of the Ming. See *The Chinese Recorder and Missionary Journal*, IV, p. 292.</note>.

Before the dethronement of the dynasty whose Emperors lie buried there, the Ming tombs in Ch'ang-p'ing undoubtedly formed one of the largest and most gorgeous royal cemeteries ever laid out by the hand of man. They are surpassed by the Egyptian pyramids in size, but certainly not in style and grandeur. The various palatial buildings, erected within their precincts, are highly interesting for our knowledge of the architectural achievements of the Chinese more than five hundred years ago. It is no wonder that they have been one of the great attractions for travelers and globe-trotters of every nationality ever since European cannon and diplomacy made the country generally accessible. Foreign tourists mostly visit them on their excursion to the Great Wall where it is nearest to Beijing and easiest to reach, namely at the Nan-k'ou Pass, the tombs being situated only a few miles northeast of the southern end of this defile. Having passed the night there in the village of Nan-k'ou <note>3 南口.</note>, the visitor may reach them in a few hours and stay for the next night at Ch'ang-p'ing, a small walled town due south of the cemetery; this town is the capital of the department of the same name, which encompasses within its borders the entire valley containing the tombs.

Because those Ming tombs have been visited so often, they have also been frequently described in books, periodicals, and magazines. Unfortunately, these descriptions are generally the result of hasty visits—some even of no visits at all—and, consequently, they are extremely defective, superficial, and inaccurate. None of them convey a clear and accurate idea of the appearance of the Cemetery and its various details, but merely give, in a very few pages, a bare list of some of the principal buildings and structures belonging to the Ch'ang-ling, the mausoleum of Ch'ing Tsu, which is the oldest and largest of all. But,

<meta>This page continues the critique of previous scholarship on the Ming tombs and initiates a detailed geographical description of the site's layout near Beijing.</meta>

### SUNDRY DESCRIPTIONS OF THE MING TOMBS.

What is worse, even those short accounts are full of errors, stemming from the fact that the authors have not seriously tried to find out the meaning and *purpose* of the various parts of the mausolea, and that their personal observations *on site* were not guided by what Chinese books have to say about those monuments. Furthermore, no attempt has ever been made to reconstruct the original layout of the cemetery using information provided by native authors. In short, all those descriptions are purely amateurish; they are of no real scientific use and, for the most part, of little value even to the general reader <note>1 The account by M. W. Lockhart in his "Notes on Peking and its Neighborhood," which was published in the *Journal of the Royal Geographical Society* for 1866, vol. 36, pp. 150 and 151, and that of William Simpson in a paper on "The Architecture of China," included in the *Transactions of the Royal Institute of British Architects* for 1873, pp. 36—38, are undoubtedly among the best that have been written; however, they are extremely brief and contain many errors. The sketch provided by Dr. Edkins in *Williamson's Journeys in North China*, vol. II, pp. 386—389, is a little more detailed; but it is so confused and vague, and even somewhat imaginary in many points, that no clear idea of the cemetery in general, nor of the thirteen mausolea in particular, can be formed from it unless the reader has visited the spot himself. The notes included by Dr. Bretschneider in his valuable essay on "The Peking Plain and the Neighboring Mountain Region" (see *Petermanns Mittheilungen* of 1876, Supplement no. 46) are too short and insignificant to be called a description. More details are contained in a paper by Camille Imbault-Huart, entitled "The Ming Tombs near Peking," published in the *T'ung-pao* for 1893, vol. IV, pp. 391—400, and illustrated with three zincographical reproductions of photographs. It is regrettable, however, that this author has diminished the value of his paper by wildly mixing his personal notes made on-site with extracts, often mistranslated, from Ku Yen-wu's *Ch'ang-p'ing shan-shui ki*. Such second-hand accounts of the mausolea as those appearing in semi-scientific periodicals like the *Globus* and the *Tour du Monde* are too insignificant to deserve attention, and are therefore left unnoticed here.</note>. Therefore, it cannot be said that our work here is redundant by providing in these pages a more detailed account of the tombs than has been published before—an account which, we hope, may be useful as a guide for anyone who might undertake a further study of those invaluable relics before the destructive hand of man or the changes of time reduce them to ruins or sweep them out of existence.

The thirteen Imperial mausolea lie in a wide valley, bounded on the north, the west, and the east by a range of hills, and accessible on the south through four passes or defiles, separated from each other by clusters of low hills. Under the Ming dynasty, the official approach to the tombs was the road leading

# THE GRAVE.

The reasons why the sovereigns of the Ming dynasty gave their mausoleums the names mentioned above are unknown to us, as the native books we consulted contain no information on this topic. Therefore, we do not venture to attempt to translate those names into English. The only thing we can confirm is that all of them were used for various imperial sepulchers of previous dynasties. Perhaps we must infer from this fact that the monarchs of the House of Ming, when choosing names for their tombs, were guided by the well-known spirit of imitating ancestral actions, which has characterized the Chinese people in every era and under every dynasty. The following is a list of older mausoleums with the same names, including the names of some emperors who were buried in them. Other names of sovereigns could be added, but we think it would be a mere waste of time to search the Standard Histories for more—

## THE QUINQUEPARTITE DECORATIVE GATE.

On leaving the northern gate of Ch'ang-p'ing city, an unpaved road—extremely muddy in rainy weather but covered with dust in the dry season—takes us over flat, gently rising land. Its monotonous, dreary appearance is broken by nothing that attracts the attention. The inquisitive eye instinctively turns to the north, continually expecting to see the first stages of the Imperial Cemetery; but the rising ground, though hardly noticeable, blocks every view in that direction. However, our impatience is not tested for long. In about half an hour, the first monument on the road leading to the Ch'ang ling catches the eye. It is a large, five-span decorative gateway, standing stately against the blue sky, right in front of us where the horizon is bordered by a rise in the ground.

This gate (see Pl. XL) is made entirely of solid natural stone. It rests upon six square pillars, placed in a straight line and connected at the tops by lintels or <term>architraves</term> resting on stone <term>corbels</term> that jut out from the sides of the pillars, thus forming five passages or portals of different heights. The middle portal is the highest; those to the right and left of it are lower by the thickness of the lintel, and the two outermost portals are lower than those in the same proportion. Over each lintel is a frieze, above which is placed a second lintel supporting a roof. All these lintels, as well as the tops of the pillars, are uniformly carved with linear <term>basso-relievo</term> figures; the five friezes, being intended exclusively for decoration, are engraved with seven square figures in bold <term>mezzo-relievo</term>, which give great prominence to the ornamentation of the monument. Every pillar, every lintel, and every frieze is a <term>monolith</term>. Each portal is covered with a roof, the shape of which—including the underlying bracket construction—matches the description we gave on pages 1166 *and following* regarding the roofs of mausoleum buildings in general. But, on closer inspection, we see that each roof, apart from a stone ridge placed over the top, is one monolithic mass of the same white, marble-like stone of which almost the entire monument is composed. Height is given to each roof by another frieze, likewise enriched with <term>mezzo-relievo</term> sculptural ornaments and framed in stone; and as these friezes are shorter than the width of the spans over which they stand, they leave room for smaller roofs with bracket construction to crown the pillars.

The square pedestals of the pillars are very attractive due to the fine embossed sculpture with which they are adorned. They are the only

parts of the gate which are not made of white, marble-like limestone; they are of a deep-blue kind of stone, finely polished, very hard, and durable, with the sculpture showing no signs of decay or weathering. They measure 15 decimeters in width on all sides. Those supporting the two outermost pillars are sculpted on each of the four faces with two lion-like animals, rampant and playing with a ball; the four other pedestals display, on every face, an Imperial Dragon soaring in the midst of the usual emblems accompanying this divine bringer of life-giving rains—namely, clouds and stars. Each pedestal has a cornice carved with figures representing a lotus flower and bearing, on either façade of the monument, a four-legged animal crouching on all fours, which faces the central portal. Of these twelve animals, those resting on the two innermost pedestals appear to represent unicorns; the others are lion-like beasts with collars around their necks, from which hangs a round instrument like a rattle-bell.

The two façades of the gate are exactly alike in shape and decoration, as is generally the case with memorial gates (see page 779). Since there is no inscription on the monument, we do not believe it was erected for the glorification of the Imperial occupants of the mausoleums; indeed, we have shown elsewhere (pp. 786–788) that the <term>p'ai-fang</term> or <term>p'ai-leu</term> often serve as decorative monuments. There may, however, have formerly been some inscription of praise painted over the central portal on the highest frieze, as this section is perfectly smooth in the middle <note>¹ Of a similar gate decorating the tomb of Confucius, we have provided a picture on page 788, which our readers may compare side by side with Plate XL.</note>.

Though the architectural style of this five-part gate is not likely to suit European tastes, it never fails to impress the visitor because of its size and majesty. Its entire length is only a few inches under thirty-four meters, which gives a sufficient idea of the bulk and weight of the enormous blocks from which it is composed. Its structural integrity is unquestionable. Indeed, though it was erected in 1540 during the reign of Shi Tsung <note>² See the *Yen-tu yiu lan chi* 燕都游覽志, "Account of what I saw on an Excursion to the Capital of Yen (Peking)," by Sun Kwoh-mi 孫國敉. This work contains a short account of a visit paid to the Ming tombs before the overthrow of the dynasty, which is reprinted in the *Tuh li t'ung khao*, ch. 93, l. 12.</note>, it is perfectly intact; the blocks have not shifted in the least,

nor have they visibly suffered from atmospheric influences. The fact that the fine, white dolomite is not even browned by the weather suggests that it has been kept for many ages under a layer of paint, some faint traces of which are still discernible in the ornamental sculpture. The latter was probably decorated in bright colors, as is still the case today (see page 787) with similar monuments at the entrance to some Imperial Altars and government buildings in Peking.

The ground beneath the monument is carefully paved with large rectangular slabs of white limestone, forming a broad platform with a slanting ascent of blocks on both sides. The square scalloped plinths of the pedestals of the pillars rise a few inches above the level of the platform and are the tops of foundation stones, sunk into the earth, no doubt, to a considerable depth. There was probably a time when the platform was larger than it is now; many slabs have, as people claim, been carried away from the mausoleums under the currently reigning dynasty for the construction of various Imperial buildings in and around the Metropolis.

Beyond this monumental entrance to the outer avenue of the mausoleums, the plain slopes almost imperceptibly, so that the platform commands a wide view to the north, allowing us to catch a first glimpse of the T'ien-sheu Mountains, dimly visible against the horizon. The various mausoleum parks along the foot of this chain may be seen from here as several black spots against a yellowish background of barren, treeless slopes.

In his *Description of the Mountains and Waters in Ch'ang-p'ing*, Ku Yen-wu states that "to the north of the gate there was a triple bridge of stone." <note>¹ Further north there is a three-arched stone bridge. Leaf 3.</note> No traces of this structure now remain, but the gully still exists over which it was built. After crossing through it, an unpaved path—either dusty or muddy depending on the weather—leads us through a flat countryside, well-cultivated in summer but offering a dreary, desert-like appearance during the dry winter season. Hardly a single tree now breaks its monotony; but when Sun Kwoh-mi visited it, he says there stood:

» Gate”¹. This building forms the actual entrance to the Cemetery and is about one kilometer distant from the decorative gate. It is a rectangular structure of massive masonry, thirty-seven meters long and eleven meters wide, pierced by three arched, tunnel-like passages, and placed upon a platform of large rectangular blocks of limestone. The span-roof is covered with yellow glazed tiles, just like the gates and buildings within the Palace grounds in Peking and many Imperial buildings both inside and outside the city. Stone sockets or hinges, inserted in the masonry, indicate that each passage used to be closed on the inside, not far from the back outlet, by means of folding doors, of which no trace is now left. The central passage is more spacious than those on the right and left, being five meters and thirty centimeters in width.

In a short summary given in the *History of the Ming Dynasty* regarding the several parts of this Imperial Cemetery², this gate is called <term>Hung men</term>³: » The Red Gate ”. By this name it is also known, both officially and popularly, at the present moment. It is, in fact, covered on every side with a coating of red plaster, and red is the color predominating in the bracket construction that supports the eaves⁴. On either side, a low wall covered with yellow tiles is connected to this gate. These walls are now only a few meters long; but they may once have extended much farther, or perhaps they had an extension in the form of palisades, as the closable Red Gate proves that the Cemetery was inaccessible from this side. It may even be supposed that such fences extended as far as the hillocks that flank the pass in the midst of which the Red Gate stands; but no evidence testifying to the correctness of this suggestion was visible to the eye.

As the Red Gate marked the boundary of the sacred grounds, respect for the Imperial spirits obliged all servants of the Crown to dismount from their horses before entering it. To remind them of this duty, two stone tablets stood a few paces in front of it, with this inscription: » Public officials and other persons, dismount

here"¹. These tablets are still in perfect condition, but the current dynasty has perhaps restored them from time to time. It is a general custom for the government to place such inscriptions at temples and altars dedicated to the worship of state divinities—a custom apparently based on an ancient maxim laid down in the *Li ki* (ch. 13, l. 40) in these words: "Tszĕ-lu (a disciple of Confucius) said: 'I have heard that, when passing by a grave, a man should bow, and when passing by a place of sacrifice, he should dismount'²." During the Ming dynasty, it was strictly forbidden to pass by or through the Red Gate without obeying the command expressed on the tablets; for "in the twenty-sixth year of the Hung wu period (A.D. 1393), it was ordained that those passing by the mausolea in carts or on horseback—as well as the officers and subjects charged with the care of the mausolea who might intend to enter them—must dismount before coming within one hundred *pu* [paces], and that violators of this ordinance should be sentenced for 'great irreverence'³." The Ts'ing dynasty has, with respect to its own imperial tombs, the same law in its Code in precisely the same wording, with the addition that the punishment shall be one hundred blows with the long stick⁴.

The scanning eye scarcely discerns any human dwellings in these dreary, sparsely populated plains. A few humble huts on the right and left of the road north of the Red Gate form the only hamlet visible, as far as the eye can see. Perhaps its inhabitants are the descendants of the families who were once appointed by imperial command to live on the spot as gatekeepers and mausoleum warders, and who have ever since earned their livelihood by tilling such parts of the adjacent land, outside or inside the gate, as were set aside for their support.

The unpaved avenue now leads us for about half a kilometer over level ground, in the same straight direction, to a colossal tablet-house with a double, yellow-tiled roof, resting on a wooden bracket frieze and projecting considerably beyond the walls (see Pl. XLI). In 1890, during our last excursion to the cemetery, it had suffered much from wind and weather, and the timber was in an advanced state of decay; many rows of tiles were displaced, and most of the ornamental figures rising above the gable corners and the upper stone ridge had fallen down. The building is square and measures twenty-six meters on each side; its four facades are exactly similar. It stands on a low platform of white limestone and has a massive basement of red-veined marble or dolomite, which, wherever visible—that is to say, on the four facades and in the tunnel-like passages which run crosswise through the building—shows, like the pedestal of a column, a plinth-like base, a die, and a cornice. The walls are made of large bricks and covered with red plaster, which has, however, peeled off in many places.

> "The stone images of men, horses, etc., at the east and west of

> Tsung, the Emperor Wen; but it was erected so late because no
> ruthless use was made of the labor of the people" <note>This quote is from the *Ch'ang-p'ing shan-shui ki*, a historical record of the geography and history of the Changping district.</note> $^1$.

Without placing any trust in this pathetic boast of generosity by those despots regarding the forced labor imposed upon their people, we learn from this passage that even their unlimited command over the bodies and lives of everyone under the sky could not save them from a shortage of manual labor in that sparsely populated region.

Under the heading: "Thirty elegiac rhymes concerning the Ming tombs" $^2$, the back of the tablet displays a series of poems which, according to an inscription at the end, are of recent date—namely, the fiftieth year of the Khien lung period (1785). Several of the mausoleums, if not all, are mentioned there. We are inclined to believe these verses were written by Kao Tsung's own hand, whose long and brilliant reign spanned that era; indeed, like his two predecessors, Shing Tsu and Shi Tsung, he was a man of high achievement in the poetic arts and produced large collections of verses and rhymes highly esteemed by the scholars. The presence of those poems on Ch'ing Tsu's grave tablet is especially noteworthy, as it clearly illustrates the spirit of reverence shown by the Emperors of the current reigning dynasty for the spirits of the family they dethroned.

The Ming dynasty was not the first to provide examples of grave tablets commemorating the "divine feats and sage virtues" of an emperor. We read in the History of the Liao Dynasty that a certain statesman and scholar, Li Hwan $^3$, lost the favor of his

It is also recorded in the History of the Kin Dynasty that Han Fang <note>韓昉</note>, a learned statesman of high repute, in the twelfth century composed the tablet commemorating the sage virtues and divine feats of T‘ai Tsu, and that this product of his hand was highly commended at the time <note>He composed the tablet for T‘ai Tsu's wise virtues and divine achievements; it was praised by his contemporaries. As Ch‘ing Tsu’s funeral tablet bears an account of his feats and virtues, and thus embodies his Imperial life and career, it is no wonder that those who erected it should have respectfully surrounded it with the emblems of Imperial dignity—that is to say, with images of the god of clouds and rains, who, by making the fields and grounds fertile, blesses mankind with food and clothing in abundance. There stand, indeed, four detached tall columns along the extensions of the diagonals of the tablet-house, at equal distances from its corners (see Pl. XLII), and the shaft of each is carved with a gigantic dragon, coiling itself around it as if climbing the skies. These monuments, similar in shape and dimensions, are octagonal monoliths of white marble. During the Ming dynasty they were officially known as <term>king-t‘ien chu</term> <note>擎天柱: "columns bearing the sky"</note>; indeed, their height being considerable, they appear to be holding the dome of heaven over the Imperial tablet-house. broad octagonal pedestal, composed of a plinth and base, a die, and a cornice. Since the upper border of the plinth and the lower border of the cornice are worked all around into a row of leaves, the pedestal is evidently modeled on the lotus-throne of the Buddhas, indicating Buddhist influence in architecture. Its eight façades are sculpted with small dragons soaring in the midst of clouds, and clouds are also carved on the shaft wherever it is not covered by the dragon. The column is crowned by a capital consisting of two horizontal stone disks with a diameter larger than that of the shaft; upon this capital is placed a dragon-like animal, squatting on its hind legs. Under the capital, we see two flat, perforated pieces of stone enriched with carved figures of straight and curved lines; they stand out to the right and left like a pair of wings, the broadest of which points toward the tablet-house. We believe they represent the imaginary clouds produced by the dragon on the shaft.

The marble decorative gate, the Red Gate, and the tablet-house all face exactly the same southern direction, and the central openings in all these structures are placed precisely in the same straight line along which the avenue they stand across is traced. Since the openings in the tablet-house were not intended to serve as passages, the avenue forks out in front of it and, running along the two side façades, reunites at the back of the building to form what the *History of the Ming Dynasty* designates by the name *Tsung shen-tao*$^1$, "the Spirit's Road for the Mausoleums in Common." As we have seen on page 1157, the author Sü Shi-tseng states that the term "Spirit's Road" was already in use in the fourth century of our era, but it can be traced back to a much older time. Specifically, we read in the *Books of the Early Han Dynasty* that when the nobleman Ki Sin-ch'ing$^2$ "was found guilty of an offense in the fifth year of the period Yuen sheu (118 B.C.), the Minister Tsung, Grand Master of Sacrifices, judged his Spirit's Road to be forfeited and degraded him to the rank of an inferior official"$^3$. Avenues to tombs are sometimes indicated in books by the characters **阡** or **仟** (*qian*). At the beginning of our era, they simply signified, as the *Shuowen Jiezi* teaches us, “a road lying from south to north” (路南北爲阡); and that many authors use it in the first sense seems to be due to an episode recounted in the *History of the Former Han Dynasty* in the following words:

> “When Ts’ao, the Governor of the Metropolis during the reign of Emperor Wu (140—87 B.C.), was buried near the Mou mausoleum, the people called the road leading toward it: the *Qian* of the Metropolis. Yuan She, coveting a similar honor for his father, purchased a plot of ground near the grave of the latter, built a road in it, and set up a sign on the spot inscribed with the words: ‘*Qian* of Nanyang’ (that is, the region where his father had been Governor). But the people would not follow suit and simply called that road the *Qian* of Sir Yuan”: 初武帝時京兆尹曹氏葬茂陵、民謂其道爲京兆千。[原]涉慕之、迺買地、開道、立表、署曰南陽仟。人不肯從、謂之原氏仟。Chapter 92, l. 14.</note>. Another term denoting such avenues is *shen lu* <note>**神路**.</note>, which has exactly the same meaning.

The Road of the Spirit is one of the most interesting features of the Ming Cemetery. At the tablet-house, the inquisitive visitor perceives in the distance two long parallel rows of figures of animals and men, the furthest of which are so far off that their forms are hardly discernible to the naked eye; a little further on, a blank wall with three openings (see Pl. XLIII) closes this curious alley. First, at three hundred and fifty paces from the tablet-house, we pass between two hexagonal columns of white stone which flank the road; they are perfectly similar in shape and size, and each is raised on a six-sided pedestal adorned with a cornice. The monolithic shafts taper slightly upward and are crowned with a top, the profile of which is represented by the annexed figure. These

tops are, we think, intended to represent a flame; for, as our readers know (see page 1088), the purpose of these grave-columns is probably nothing other than to light the disembodied soul along its path and to intensify its vitality. The *History of the Ming Dynasty* <note>Chapter 60, l. 6.</note> calls them *wang chu* <note>**望柱**.</note>, “columns to look at.” They stand in the same lines as the animals, so it may be said they form the southern terminus of the avenue of statues.

<page-num>1205</page-num>

# THE DRAGON-AND-PHOENIX GATE.

At about ninety paces from the last pair of statues, the <term>Road of the Spirit</term> meets a solid wall with three openings, depicted in Plate XLIII. It is built of very large bricks and covered with red plaster which has flaked off extensively, and it was originally roofed with yellow tiles, as some fragments scattered over the ground on both sides unmistakably indicate. The foundation, which is considerably thicker than the wall itself, is covered on top—both on the front and the back of the wall—with smooth slabs of white stone. The three openings are exactly alike in shape and dimensions and are constructed as follows: Two square pillars of white stone are fixed in the wall like a pair of door-posts and rise considerably above it. They are connected by a square stone cross-beam, the ends of which are firmly fitted into square holes pierced through the pillars a little way from the top. In the center of this cross-beam stands a lotus-shaped socle, supporting an oval piece of stone pointed at the top and carved all over with ornate decorations apparently representing a peach, the symbol of longevity (see page 56). As the hinges still present show, the passages were originally closed by folding doors. Consequently, there is in each of them a stone doorframe with a sill of the same material; the lintel of this doorframe bears an architrave, and the space between it and the previously mentioned cross-beam is filled by a frieze carved with linear figures. All the parts described so far are solid pieces of limestone. Just like the four columns that flank the tablet-house, the six gate-posts all bear, near the top, a pair of stone clouds pointing to the right and left like wings; moreover, the top of each post is covered with a square block of stone, sculpted with clouds, and topped with a dragon crouching on a socle which exactly resembles those supporting the stone peaches; each pair of these monsters faces the passage over which they are placed. Finally, each pillar is reinforced at the base, on both sides, by a square stone counter-fort, resembling the pedestal of a column, as it is composed of a plinth or base, a die, and a cornice. It supports an upright slab of white stone in the shape of a right-angled triangle; the vertical side of this slab is set into the pillar, and the hypotenuse is carved with undulations, some of which form parts of spirals engraved on the two flat sides of the stone.

This curious triple gate is called <term>Ling-sing men</term><note>1 櫺星門.</note>, or "Linteled Star Gate," probably because the passages, not being roofed,

The *History of the Ming Dynasty* does not mention it in its list of the structures on the avenue; but from Ku Yen-wu, we learn that it certainly existed in his time, and that "it was then popularly called Lung-fung men: Dragon-and-Phoenix Gate" <note>Popularly called the Dragon-and-Phoenix Gate. *Ch'ang-p'ing shan-shui ki*, leaf 3.</note>. Specimens of the same style and shape, either single or triple, are a common feature of almost all the Altar grounds of Peking connected with the State Religion, such as those for the worship of Heaven, Earth, the Sun, the Moon, the Gods of Land and Grain, etc. They generally stand at the four cardinal points, being parts of the single or double enclosures immediately surrounding the Altar.

Before the fall of the House of Ming, the Road of the Spirit must have made a deep impression on the minds of visitors, as it was then flanked by stately evergreens; a vast forest of them also covered the surrounding grounds to their furthest limits. The tablet-house with the four columns probably stood in a large, open square or yard in the midst of that park, offering a comfortable resting place to the Sons of Heaven and the high officials of the Empire when visiting the tombs; indeed, Ku Yen-wu wrote: "There was once a traveling palace on the east side, but it has now disappeared" <note>To its east there was a traveling palace, now gone. *Op. et loc. cit.*</note>. Today, not a trace of that vast forest remains, and during the cold season there is hardly anything for the eye to see in any direction except land and sky, and a chain of barren hills in the distance. It is then only a dreary, extensive plain, where not a single blade of living grass is visible. But in summer, it is covered with an immense expanse of food crops, such as wheat, barley, and tall millet, as well as sorghum growing so high that a horse and rider are lost to sight in the midst of it, with the plow doing its work every year right up to the bases of the stone animals and men.

The destruction of those forests was carried out at an early date; indeed, Ku Yen-wu wrote at the beginning of the reign of the current dynasty: "Several hundred thousand dark pines and green cypresses, which studded the inner grounds beyond the great Red Gate in numbers beyond imagination, have now disappeared, having been cut down to the very last one" <note>From the Great Red Gate inward, dark pines and green cypresses were so numerous they could not be counted—hundreds of thousands—but now they have been completely cut down. *Ch'ang-p'ing shan-shui ki*, leaf 4.</note>. The greed with which the people seized upon the trees of the Ming tombs for timber and fuel — two articles always precious in those treeless regions — as soon as the downfall of the House of Ming gave them a chance to do so unpunished, accounts for the rigid measures which this dynasty took for their protection during its rule.
> "In the
> second year of the period Ching t'ung (1437) the Court of

> should be subjected to heavy punishments, and their families
> should be relegated to a distant region for perpetual banishment.
> Placards should be immediately issued to forbid such crimes; the
> officers of the Guards with Embroidered Uniforms should make

> set out landmarks all around, only outside which the people
> might collect fuel" <note>In the second year of Zhengtong, an edict was issued to the Court of Censors: anyone daring to cut trees where the ancestral tombs of the T'ien-sheu Mountains are located shall be punished with heavy penalties, and their family members shall be sent to the frontiers for military service. Proclamations must be issued as a ban; furthermore, officers of the Embroidered Uniform Guard shall patrol the area. The Board of Works, together with officials from the Directorate of Astronomy, shall establish boundaries around the mountains, and only outside these boundaries may the people gather firewood. *Ta Ming hwui tien*, chapter 83, leaf 9. See also the *History of the Ming Dynasty*, chapter 60, leaf 3, and the *Suh wen hien t'ung khao*, chapter 133, leaf 20.</note>.
