Our readers may see on page 902 that this article is still in force today for the mausolea of the Ts‘ing dynasty, as that House adopted it word-for-word in its own Code of Laws.

The Road of the Spirit runs between the two clusters of bluffs which, as we stated on page 1196, flank the tract of flat ground that forms a broad natural entrance into the valley in the background of which the mausolea are built. Thus, this entrance was properly guarded by stone men and animals, and barred at the southern extremity by the Red Gate, and on the north by the Linteled Star Gate. Beyond this latter, the treeless plains, gently sloping upward, afford an unobstructed view of the row of mausolea scattered along the foot of the mountain chain; the glittering yellow roofs of the walls and buildings are now perfectly discernible among the dark green trees. Not all thirteen grave parks are visible, as a few are hidden from view by others.

A walk of more than half an hour is still required before we reach the Ch‘ang ling, the oldest mausoleum and the most magnificent of all. The path, occasionally strewn with the debris of a pavement of large stone slabs, leads us over the scattered remains of marble bridges and through three brooks coming from the west and north. These converge further on to form a tributary of a stream called the Sha-ho <note>沙 河 (Sand River)</note> or Sand River, which empties into the Pei-ho very close to T‘ung-cheu <note>通 州 (Tongzhou)</note>, a walled town half a day’s journey eastward from Peking. <page-num>1211</page-num>
# THE MAIN GATE, AND THE TEMPLE GATE.

The approach to the <term>mausoleum</term>, paved for a considerable distance with stone slabs, leads the visitor straight to a triple main gate, built exactly in the middle of the roofed wall which forms the front of the enclosed area. This gate has a single span-roof covered with yellow tiles, bearing a ridge of white limestone on the top; it closely resembles the roof that covers the walls over their entire length but exceeds it considerably in width and height. The three gateways are closed by wooden folding doors. A square platform, very long and broad, extends in front of the gate; this platform is built of rectangular slabs and is ascended at the front by a broad incline of the same material. On the right and left, several dozen majestic cypress trees vividly recall the antiquity of the <term>mausoleum</term>, many of them unmistakably being remnants of the forests which once covered the whole Cemetery. Some humble huts of clay here form a hamlet, inhabited by the families which, as is expressed in the Imperial edict translated elsewhere in this volume (p. 932), "are charged with strictly keeping the place in good condition, with offering sacrifices there, and preventing people from gathering fuel and timber, and to whom fields are assigned for their sustenance." The brickwork of the gate and that of all the walls enclosing the two courts is plastered on both the outer and the inner façade with red plaster, and it rests everywhere on a high base of rectangular blocks of limestone.

The width of the courts is a little over one hundred and thirty meters. The main gate opens upon a yard more than forty meters deep, bounded on the opposite side by another triple gate of stately appearance. This is the <term>Ling-ngen men</term><note>1 祾恩門.</note>, "Gate of Blessings and Favors," so named because the blessings and favors sent forth from the temple behind this gate by the spirits of the occupants of the <term>mausoleum</term> were expected to find their way through it straight to their heirs to the throne. A wooden tablet affixed under the eaves, over the middle passage, is inscribed with the three characters representing that name. The sculptured frame of this tablet juts out considerably on either side and over the top and represents a dragon, indicating that the blessings and favors alluded to in the inscription emanate from an Emperor. The <term>Ling-yen men</term> has a single roof covered with tiles of the Imperial yellow color. It is placed upon a rectangular platform of white stone with three flights of steps

> » Ch'ang ling and all the Imperial mausolea built after it, as

Passing through the Gate of Blessing and Favours, we immediately see, straight ahead, the entire facade of an enormous rectangular temple, which is the most imposing feature of the whole cemetery. It is built on a rectangular terraced platform of white stone, consisting of three stages that decrease in size by two and a half meters on each side. Each stage or terrace exactly resembles the platform of the Gate of Blessing and Favours, being protected by balustrades of the same shape. It is ascended, both at the front and at the back of the building, by three flights of steps placed side-by-side; the middle one has an inclined stone plane in its center, sculpted with dragons. There are five steps in the flights of the two highest terraces and eight in those of the lowest. To drain the rainwater that flows freely from the temple eaves, stone gargoyles representing monstrous animal heads are designed all around each stage, with one gargoyle jutting out at the base of each baluster.

The temple covers the entire upper surface of this platform, except for a narrow passage between its walls and the balustrades and a broad space in front of almost the entire facade. The platform has a rectangular projection there of about twelve meters, which brings forward the triple tiers of steps and greatly enhances the majesty of the whole structure. The picture in Plate XXII, which we have placed as a frontispiece at the beginning of this volume, will hardly convey an adequate idea of the grandeur of this finest and largest specimen of Chinese architecture. The intricately crafted balustrades of beautiful marble are too small in the picture to create an effect, and the red color of the walls and the bright yellow of the roofs are lost.

The length of the temple exceeds that of the transept of Westminster Abbey, being over sixty-eight meters. It is somewhat more than thirty meters deep and, consequently, has about half the length and breadth of Cologne Cathedral. The double yellow-tiled roof extends several feet from the walls and is crowned with a marble ridge bearing a voluted ornament at each end;

History of the Ming Dynasty, ch. 60, l. 4; see also the *Ta Ming hwui tien*, ch. 83, l. 3.

# THE TEMPLE OF CH'ING TSU'S MAUSOLEUM.

It has the same shape as the roof of the great tablet house at the avenue of animals, and the eaves rest upon a similar timber construction placed on architraves. The three entrances in the front facade of the temple correspond to the three flights of steps, and each can be closed with a wooden folding door. Over the main entrance, which is exactly in the middle of the front facade, a wooden tablet is affixed under the eaves of the upper roof, bearing the inscription *Ling-ngen tien*¹, "Temple of Blessing and Favors." Like the tablet suspended over the *Ling-ngen men*, it has a frame depicting a dragon. It should be noted in passing that this name for the temple and the gate dates from 1538; it is recorded that "in the seventeenth year of the Kia tsing period, the name 'Mausoleum Temple' was changed to *Ling-ngen tien*, and the gate was named *Ling-ngen men*"². For the rest, the front facade consists of a series of wooden lattice windows, unglazed but covered on the inside with white paper; consequently, when the doors are closed, only a very dim light can penetrate the building.

As is the case with the main gate (the Gate of Blessing and Favors) and the walls surrounding the courts, red is the prominent color of the temple. Its side and back walls are made of red-plastered brickwork and have a sturdy, high basement of white stone. Upon entering the building, we see twenty-four bulky, round wooden pillars supporting the upper roof (see Plate XLV); each is cut from a single trunk and averages three meters and seventeen centimeters in circumference. They are arranged in three straight rows parallel to the long sides of the temple. At either end of each row, another wooden pillar with a smaller diameter is inserted into the side wall like a pilaster, serving as a support for the lowest roof. A fourth row of ten round pillars supporting this roof forms the framework in which the frames of the doors and windows of the front facade are fixed; these are visible from the outside. Consequently, there are forty pillars in total inside the hall.

We cannot describe the construction of the timber frame of the roof, as it is entirely hidden from view by a wooden ceiling made of small square panels, each painted with a circular figure in

A red square railing of wood surrounds the shrine. In front of this railing, exactly in the center of the middle row of pillars, stands a large sacrificial wooden table, bearing an incense burner flanked by two flower vases and candle supports, all likewise made of wood. Otherwise, there is no furniture of any kind in the hall.

# THE SACRIFICIAL FURNACES, AND THE LING-TS'IN GATE.

Wood was brought from Pegu, through Yunnan, and then overland to Peking; but these authors do not provide any evidence for this claim. Bretschneider suggests they may be of the so-called **nan-muh**¹, a durable, rot-resistant variety of the *Laurus*, growing in the southern provinces; and indeed we saw on page 1181 that Ch'ing Tsu commissioned some high-ranking officers to collect timber in Szĕ-ch'wen, Hukwang, Kiangsi, Chehkiang, and Shansi. However, certain indications regarding the origin of those columns are completely missing.

Since the temple has served from the beginning for the presentation of sacrifices to the Imperial spirits <note>manes</note>, there are two furnaces in the court between it and the Gate of Blessing and Favours, one on each side, for converting the offered silk and mock money into smoke and ashes. They are made of yellow glazed porcelain and roofed with yellow glazed tiles. Inside there is no grate; the articles are simply burned on the stone floor, which is level with the sill of the arched opening in front. Both structures are of exactly the same shape and dimensions, and their ornamentation and colors do not differ in the least. One of them is represented in Plate XXXIX, opposite page 1170; we also refer the reader to the description of such fireplaces in general given on that page. The mentioned Plate will show that those of the Ch'ang ling are very elegant pieces of workmanship, from the Chinese perspective, of course. The court in which they stand measures about sixty meters between the platform of the temple and that of the gate, and is planted on both sides with pines and cypresses. A broad stone path connects the middle ascents of the two platforms and is of exactly the same width; its center is laid with cross flags that are just as long as the width of the slopes carved with dragons.

Leaving the temple by the above-mentioned exit in the back wall, a similarly paved path, twenty-five paces in length, leads us to a broad yellow-tiled gate bounding the temple court on the north (see Pl. XLVI). This building has three tunnel-like passages, five and six-tenths meters deep, which correspond in position with the three tiers of steps in the rear of the temple platform; its walls are plastered red, and its basement is made of white stone. A transverse red wall, covered with yellow tiles, is connected with the gate on either side and extends as far as the wall which surrounds the mausoleum, thus entirely separating the temple court from the rest of the grounds.

# THE GRAVE.

...second great court. This gate is called Ling-ts'in men¹, the “Gate of the Ts'in of the Mausoleum.” To understand this term, we must remember that the word *ts'in* anciently denoted the apartment in a house situated behind the main hall (compare Plate I, opposite page 16), and that this “back chamber” performed—as many passages cited by us from the *Li ki* and the *I li* have shown—a most important part in the rites and ceremonies connected with the disposal of the dead. Remembering further that graves are planned like human dwellings, and that a mausoleum-temple with its Imperial soul tablets corresponds, in consequence, with the main hall at home in which the family tablets are worshipped, it is self-evident how the name *ts'in* has come to be applied to the court behind the temple, to which the gate in question gives access.

The aspect of this court is impressive. It is planted with stately evergreens and other trees, the gnarled trunks of many of which bear evidence of great age. A solemn silence reigns in these sacred precincts of death, and nothing is heard but the chirping voice of some solitary bird and the whispering of the wind through the foliage. The court is about eighty-five meters deep. Emerging from the Ling-ts'in men, the eye is attracted to a decorative gate about twenty meters off, across the marble-paved path which leads straight on to the tomb. It is in a thoroughly ruinous condition, the roofs having entirely disappeared, and hardly anything remains of it but two square marble pillars, connected by two horizontal cross-pieces of wood, which formerly supported the roof. In another mausoleum, we found such a monument perfectly preserved, and we place a picture of it before our readers in Plate XLVII. The two pillars each bear on the top a scaled quadruped resembling a unicorn, and, as is the case with the Linteled Star Gate, they are strengthened at their base by means of voluted counterforts of stone. The two cross-pieces, between which a frieze is inserted, are of wood and painted with figures in various colors; the triple, yellow-tiled roof, suspended over them between the pillars, resembles in shape the roofs of the other buildings and gates in the Cemetery, and the wooden bracket construction recurs three times within it. The tiles on the lowest eaves are considerably larger than those of the other two roofs. There being no transverse fence whatever on the right or left of this beautiful gate, the visitor is tempted to conclude that it has served for decorative purposes only. But, considering that

## THE SOUL TOWER WITH THE GRAVESTONE.

The passage between the two pillars is closed by a folding door flanked by two wooden panels; it is likely that the gate was also intended to block harmful influences moving toward the tomb. Indeed, the stone path that passes through it leads straight to the mouth of the tunnel, which forms the only entrance into the crypt. Readers will remember that it is an established geomantic principle that roads running in a straight line toward a tomb may have very harmful effects on it.

Beyond this gate, we obtain our first full view of the curious tower-like building. We had frequently caught glimpses of its yellow-tiled double roof, standing out above all the other buildings and the surrounding foliage, while approaching the mausoleum (*Pl. XLVIII*). This is the so-called <term>Ming leu</term> <note>Ming Lou (明 樓)</note> or "Soul Tower," built on top of an unplastered brick terrace. This terrace was built in front of the gigantic burial mound under which the Imperial remains rest, and it hides the mound entirely from view. This terrace is perfectly square and tapers slightly upward; at the top, it measures thirty-one meters on each side. It has a base of white blocks, which precisely resembles that of the tablet house standing at the beginning of the avenue of stone statues. The top, which is about fourteen meters from the ground, has a crenelated parapet or <term>ch'ing tieh</term> <note>Cheng die (城 堞)</note> along the front and the sides, composed of bricks half a meter in length. In the center of the top stands the Tower: a square, red-plastered building sheltering the gravestone. It may be described as a massive piece of masonry raised on a marble platform and pierced at right angles by two arched tunnels. The gravestone is raised at the intersection of these tunnels, making the tower resemble the previously mentioned tablet house in nearly every respect; however, it is considerably smaller, being only eighteen meters long and wide. A wooden board, inscribed with two characters expressing the name <term>Ch'ang ling</term>, was formerly suspended from the facade under the eaves of the upper roof <note>*Ch'ang-p'ing shan-shui ki*, l. 5.</note>, but it has now disappeared. In many of the other mausoleums, however, a corresponding object can still be seen in the same place.

The gravestone is an enormous vertical monolith of fine marble, no less than ninety-four centimeters thick and one hundred and sixty-two centimeters wide, rising high into a vaulted cupola in the ceiling. The front, which precisely faces the southern direction

The most interesting part of the terrace on which the Soul Tower stands—a part attracting the curiosity of the visitor more than anything else—is the *yung tao* <note>埵道 or 甬道</note> or "earthed road," a vaulted tunnel through which the Imperial remains were introduced into the crypt. It is pierced straight through the terrace, exactly coinciding with the longitudinal axis of the mausoleum. It is an oblong table of white stone, measuring six meters and sixty centimeters by one meter and eighty-three centimeters; it is worked all around in the same style as the pedestals of the "sky-bearing" columns that stand around the great tablet-house, namely, with a plinth and base, a die, and a cornice; and the base and cornice are likewise carved with a row of leaves, in imitation of a lotus flower. On entering the tunnel, we perceive it is entirely lined and paved with bare grey bricks and rises at a gentle incline. Our steps resound mysteriously in the dim background, which, as our eyes become adjusted to the darkness, turns out to be a brick wall totally closing the tunnel and ruining our hopes of making our way to the crypt. Formerly there was, according to Ku Yen-wu, "a yellow glazed screen in the tunnel" <note>1. 甬道內爲黃琉璃屏一座. "Inside the tunnel was one yellow glazed screen." *Op. cit.*, l. 4.</note>, but we saw no trace of it. This cave-like passage called up thoughts of ancient China—reminiscences of the mystic tombs of the monarchs before and during the Han dynasty, which likewise had an underground passage giving access to the crypt (see page 425).

At its bricked-up end, the tunnel branches off at right angles on either hand, forming two other tunnels of quite the same construction, one meter and seventy-five centimeters wide by two and a half meters in height, which lead at a sharp incline up to the crenelated top of the terrace. On emerging from these passages, we find ourselves nearly on a level with the top of the grave hill, and perceive at a glance that this eminence consists of a high wall of grey bricks, crowned with a crenelated parapet of the same material, and encircling a vast area entirely filled with earth which lies against the wall as high as the foot of the parapet, rising from there toward the center, so as to form a top with gentle slopes entirely covered with little cypresses and other young trees. The burial mound wall starts at right angles from both sides of the terrace at about four meters from the back of the terrace, and the battlements crowning both structures form together an unbroken, uniform row, being all of the same shape and dimensions. At the two points where the wall starts from the terrace, it slopes down immediately at a considerable drop, about four and a half meters in all; subsequently, it describes an irregular circle nearly twelve hundred paces long, or almost a kilometer, so that the diameter of the burial mound is much longer than twice the breadth of the two large courts in front.

<meta>This page continues the detailed architectural description of the Ch'ang ling mausoleum, focusing on the exterior walls of the tumulus and comparing them to defensive fortress structures and other Ming tombs.</meta>

<page-num>1222</page-num>
<header>THE GRAVE.</header>

When viewed from the outside, the crenelated, unplastered wall resembles a Chinese fortress in every respect, and the Soul Tower resembles the gate of such a structure. Indeed, city walls in China are also generally made of large grayish bricks and have crenelated parapets made of that material, as well as gates topped with roofed buildings. Under the Ming Dynasty, the tumulus wall of an Emperor was called *Pao ch'ing* <note>1. 寶城 (Precious City).</note>, "City of the Precious Relics." We may recall here that as early as the Han dynasty, the imperial mausoleums took on the character of strongholds, being formally intended for the armed defense of the sacred remains from sacrilegious attacks (see pp. 427 *sqq.*).

Making our way along the parapet of the tumulus wall through thorny brambles and obstructive shrubs, we see that this wall actually consists of two parallel concentric walls, two meters apart from each other, the outer one of which supports the parapet. We could discover no crumbling or damaged spots that might allow us to determine whether the space between those walls consists of masonry or is merely filled with earth. Only the top of the inner wall peeps out all around from the tumulus, showing that it is as thick as the length of the bricks of which it is composed—namely, five decimeters. The earth of the tumulus rests heavily against the back of the terrace of the Soul Tower, perhaps covering an underground passage connecting the tunnel with the crypt. But perhaps there is no such passage at all, and the earth may have been placed there after the burial of the imperial corpse and the bricking-up of the tunnel. This suggestion is raised by the fact that in the King ling—the mausoleum of Süen Tsung—the mound stands quite detached from its wall and the Soul Tower, and the tunnel is bricked up in exactly the same way as it is in the Ch'ang ling, without any earth covering its outlet. Nor does the crypt of that mound have a visible entrance, so there can be no doubt that the opening providing access to it was blocked with earth after the burial.

Because Ch'ing Tsu's tumulus stands on a low spur of the T'ien-sheu chain in undulating ground, it is uncertain whether it was entirely raised by human labor. Perhaps it is a natural eminence, modified more or less by human hands; but we have found no statements at all on this matter in the books. Nor is it certain whether the imperial couple, buried underneath,

With this, we may finish our description of Ch'ing Tsu's enormous and stately tomb. The only point we still have to address is that formerly there stood somewhere in front of it a building, or set of buildings, for an Inspectorate created during the reign of Wu Tsung and officially titled: Inspectorate for the Dwellings of the Manes (see page 1213). "For each of the twelve mausoleums," says Ku Yen-wu, "there was such an Inspectorate established at its base, either on the right or the left. It had two gates, one in front of the other, followed by a main hall and apartments occupied by officials associated with the interior parts of the mausoleum. At the Yung ling, the Chao ling, the Ting ling, and the Khing ling, the number of rooms in those buildings totaled more than three hundred. A Captain was appointed for the interior of each mausoleum as Inspector-in-Chief, as well as a Seal-keeper of the Inspectorate and twelve Inspectors" <note>5. Twelve mausoleums each had a Spirit Palace Inspectorate (*Shen-kung kien*), located at the foot of the tomb, either on the left or the right. It had double gates, a hall, and chambers where the inner officials resided. In the four tombs of Yong, Zhao, Ding, and Qing, these buildings contained more than three hundred rooms. One eunuch was appointed as Internal Commandant for each, along with twelve seal-keeping eunuchs for the Spirit Palace Inspectorates. — *Ch'ang-p'ing shan-shui ki*, book 12.</note>. Based on the extract on page 1209, it appears that the various inspectorates had a common head office somewhere in front of the Ch'ang ling. Additionally, "every mausoleum had an audience chamber at its base, either on the right or the left" <note>6. Each had audience chambers at the base of the tomb, either on the left or the right. — In the same work and place mentioned above.</note>.

Undoubtedly, there was a time when the Ch'ang ling was surrounded by a substantial park; the stately trees now growing outside the walls of the courtyards and around the walled tumulus bear witness to this. It is even almost certain that the entire cemetery once formed a vast forest, as large trees can also be seen around many of the other mausoleums. At present, the valley is under cul-

Passes are labeled: Chui-shih Pass, Lao-kiün-t'ang Pass, Si-shan Pass (with the small Red Gate), and Tung-shan Pass. Features like the "Tien-sheu Mounts," a "Five-arched Bridge," and a "Seven-arched Bridge" are marked along a central path leading "To the Avenue of Animals."</image-desc>

->Approximate Sketch of the Situation of the Ming Tombs and their Spirit's Roads.<-

The thirteen mausoleums cover an area more than an hour’s walk from east to west. From their distribution over the valley, we see at a glance that they do not form a cemetery laid out in strict accordance with the old orthodox rules of the <term>Cheu li</term>, which we have translated on page 421, as they are not arranged in the order of family descent. No doubt we must attribute this fact to the circumstance that for every Emperor, the <term>Fung-shui</term> doctrines required a burial place located amidst configurations of hills and brooks specifically compatible with his horoscope. It is probably also for this reason that not all the mausoleums have a southern exposure. The <term>Khang ling</term>, having the protecting mountains on the west, faces almost due east; the <term>Ting ling</term> and the <term>Chao ling</term> have a southeastern aspect, and the <term>King ling</term> and the <term>Yung</term>

# THE MOUNTAINS IN THE REAR OF THE CEMETERY.

...ling a south-western, the Teh ling a western. The hills at the rear of the mausoleums, though collectively called the T'ien-sheu Mountains, are distinguished by various names. The Ch'ang ling, the Hien ling, the Khing ling, and the King ling are considered to be placed in the T'ien-sheu Mountains proper; the Yü ling rests against the Shih-men Shan¹ or "Stone Gate Mountain"; the Meu ling against the Tsü-pao Shan² or "Mountain of Accumulated Valuables"; the T'ai ling against the Pih-kia Shan³ or "Pencil Stand Mountain," which is so named because of its shape and also bears the name of Shi-kia Shan⁴, "Mount of the Shi family." The Khang ling has at its rear the Kin-ling Shan⁵ or "Mount of the Gold Range"; the Yung ling has the Shih-pah-tao Ling⁶ or "Range with Eighteen Roads," a name that was officially changed to Yang-ts'ui Ling⁷, "Range of the Southern Kingfisher (?)" in 1536, when orders had been issued for building this mausoleum. The Chao ling and the Ting ling respectively stand against the Ta-yuh Shan⁸ and the Siao-yuh Shan⁹, or "Great Valley Mountain and Small Valley Mountain"; the Teh ling against the T'an-tszĕ Yuh¹⁰ or "Valley of the T'an Trees," and the Szĕ ling against the Kin-p'ing Shan¹¹ or "Decorated Screen Hills"¹².

Each mausoleum had its own special <term>Spirit's Road</term>, branching off either directly from the main one leading to the Ch'ang ling, or from that of the mausoleum nearest it, as is pointed out approximately by the lines in Fig. 41. Most of those roads have now entirely disappeared, as farmers have obliterated them while tilling the ground, and some have become narrow footpaths. Almost every mausoleum also has a special tablet house, resembling that which stands south of the stone images, but of much smaller dimensions, being hardly larger than those now to be seen in front of the mausoleums of Imperial Princes (see p. 1169). It stands straight in front of the main gate, at a short distance from it, and has a double yellow-tiled roof. In most cases, if not in all, the tablet

...of fine white stone bears no inscriptions and is supported by a tortoise, adorned with a crowning border engraved with dragons. In a few instances, the tablet stands under the open sky, the building that once sheltered it having disappeared due to vandalism, neglect, or because no such building ever existed.

Apart from the Szĕ ling, which we will discuss later, the smallest and plainest of all the mausoleums is the Hien ling. The monarch buried in it occupied the throne for no more than nine months. It is recorded that "it was being built when (his son) Süen Tsung ascended the throne, and that this new monarch then desired to practice economy regarding it, in obedience to his father’s last will. He consulted Kien I and Hia Yuen-kih on this point, and both these men praised him enthusiastically for it, saying: 'This plan of Your Majesty is sublime and lofty; it is a product of filial piety of the highest order, which will bear fruit for ten thousand generations.' The Emperor himself designed the plan of the mausoleum; it was finished in three months and did not equal the Ch‘ang ling in beauty. Succeeding Emperors followed his example and used that mausoleum as a model; but when Shi Tsung built the Yung ling, extravagant prodigality began to be practiced again to a much greater extent" <note>1</note>. This passage may account for the fact that the courtyard between the temple and the Soul Tower of the Hien ling is not leveled, but still contains a broad elevated area of ground, so that the pathway connecting those two buildings turns westward.

The King ling, the sepulcher of Süen Tsung, though larger than the Hien ling, likewise ranks among the smaller mausoleums. As we noted on page 1222, the burial mound stands quite detached from the wall that surrounds it and does not cover the bricked-up exit of the tunnel; this may perhaps be attributed to the fact that it was never raised to the height originally intended.

The statement in this long extract—that separate underground passages were made for the three bodies buried in the Yü ling—is a strong indication that there are also two or even more tunnels in some other mausoleums. However, we must by no means take this for granted. The concerns raised by the Imperial geomancers of that period regarding the construction of open entrances are also noteworthy. They seem to explain why the tunnel is bricked up in some mausoleums or why, as in the case of the King ling (see page 1226), it has no extension behind the Soul Tower. They even clarify why some mausoleums have no tunnel at all. This is the case, for example, with the Yung ling, the magnificent sepulcher of Shi Tsung, which we will discuss briefly on page 1232.

But the excerpt above is especially important for what it adds to our knowledge of Imperial burial customs. # THE MEU LING.

But, as we have stated on page 444, it had been customary during previous dynasties to also accord the same prerogative to Empresses proper, even though they had not given birth to an Heir Apparent. Hence, no doubt, it is that in the case of the Empress Hiao Chwang the servants of the Crown felt it so incumbent upon them to join in a stubborn opposition against any refusal to execute the last will of her own Imperial spouse regarding her. As the list on pages 1189 and following shows, it was not a prerequisite for enjoying the privilege in question that Chief Consorts, or Concubines who had given birth to a successor to the throne, should have lived during the reign of their husband. Hiao I, in fact, the Chief Consort of Muh Tsung while he was Heir Apparent, died before his accession; and the Chief Consort and the two Concubines buried in the Khing ling had likewise died when their husband was called to the throne. The biographies of these women <note>Contained in chapter 114 of the *History of the Ming Dynasty*.</note> teach us that Hiao I was invested with the posthumous title of empress on her husband’s accession, and that Hiao Yuen received the same title from Hi Tsung when he assumed the Government. In connection with those customs it may be remarked, that every Concubine who gave birth to an Emperor was, on the accession of the latter, endowed by him with the title of empress, whether she was still alive or not <note>See the biographies of those women in chapters 113 and 114 of the *History of the Ming Dynasty*.</note>, so that, considered from the Chinese point of view, all the women interred in the mausolea are in reality Empresses.

The Meu ling deserves special attention on account of its being also the tomb of Hiao Hwui, the ancestress of the collateral line of sovereigns who, commencing with Shi Tsung, have occupied the throne during the latter half of the sway of the Ming dynasty. Down to the period of Wu Tsung no difficulty in regard to the succession had presented itself in the Imperial line, every monarch having left a son to succeed him. Wu Tsung, however, was without male issue, and therefore deemed it proper to bequeath the throne to the nearest heir according to national ideas, namely, the eldest son of his father’s younger brother, who at that time was hardly fourteen years old. The father of this lad was Yiu Yuen <note>祐杬.</note>, King of Hing <note>興王.</note>, fourth son of the Emperor Hien Tsung by the Concubine

The mausoleum of Shi Tsung, the Yung ling, surpasses all the other mausoleums, except the Ch'ang ling, in size and magnificence. Its construction took many years, and it is recorded that already thirty years before his death, namely "in the fifteenth year of his reign (1536), the Emperor gave orders for its construction”⁴.

In the official annals of his time, many visits he paid to the burial valley are chronicled, with the goal of personally inspecting the progress of the work. We found this mausoleum especially worth visiting because the woodwork and paint were in better preservation and repair than in the Ch'ang ling. Otherwise, like the other tombs, it is in almost every respect a copy of it on a reduced scale. The temple, in the first place, is much smaller than that of the Ch'ang ling, but the terrace on which it stands projects much further forward. No trace of a tunnel is to be seen at the Soul Tower, and access to the top of the building's terrace is reached by means of a broad, sloping brick walkway built against its two sides. The tumulus does not quite equal the size of the Ch'ang ling—its diameter being about one-fifth shorter—but it exceeds it in detail and finish. Indeed, the two concentric walls that surround it (the space between which is, as at the Ch'ang ling, entirely filled with earth),

# THE YUNG LING AND THE KHING LING.

The earth of the mound (tumulus) rests against the innermost wall as high as the top of the wall itself, and against the terrace of the Soul Tower it is only slightly lower. The rounded top of the mound is heightened by a small, truncated conical mound, perhaps placed there for some mysterious geomantic reason.

The Khing ling, which contains the remains of Kwang Tsung, is also of some interest, as it was built upon the foundations of another mausoleum laid some one hundred and seventy years earlier. As Kwang Tsung died exactly one month after his accession, he did not have the opportunity—as his predecessors did—to build or partially build a mausoleum for himself during his lifetime. We read in a local work on the country northeast and east of the Imperial Cemetery:

> "A longevity mausoleum had formerly been built during the King t'ai period; but Ying Tsung deposed Emperor King (for whom it was intended) and buried him at the foot of the Western Mountains, so that this mausoleum remained vacant. When Kwang Tsung died, no special burial ground could be selected because death took him away so early and unexpectedly. Therefore, they converted that tomb into a mausoleum for him." <note>先是景泰中建爲壽宮、英宗復辟景皇帝、遂葬西山之麓、陵基遂虛。光宗上賓、旣速倉卒不能擇地。乃用此爲陵. *Khin-ch'ing siao chi* 芹城小志, "Small Memoirs concerning Khin-ch'ing," written by Li Yin-tuh 李因篤; quoted in the *Tuh li t'ung khao*, ch. 93, l. 27.</note>

# THE GRAVE.

It is hardly necessary to draw our readers' attention to the interesting information this extract provides regarding the construction and furnishings of that tomb's crypt. If it is trustworthy—and we have no reason to doubt it—it fills a gap we were forced to leave in our description of the Ch'ang ling and the other mausoleums; for we may well suppose that their crypts also correspond to the description above, as these mausoleums closely resemble the Szĕ ling in all other respects, as we shall presently show. A short description of this mausoleum is also of some importance because it teaches us everything that can now be learned about the tombs that the Ming family used to construct for imperial consorts of lower rank; indeed, it is the only one of this class of sepulchers that has survived in good condition, as the currently reigning dynasty has kept it in constant repair, along with the other twelve mausoleums.

It is located in the southwestern part of the valley and is the first that a traveler reaches when coming from the Nan-khao Pass. Like the twelve imperial mausoleums proper, it consists of a tomb mound within a round crenelated wall; on the front side, there is a Soul Tower with a square walled court before it, followed by another court containing a Temple of Blessing and Favors and a gate bearing the same name, directly in front of which there is a tablet-house. The dimensions of these squares and buildings are small—even very small—compared to the other mausoleums.

Next, Empress Zhou was laid to rest on the left side of the stone bed; afterward, they requested that the late Emperor Chongzhen’s coffin be placed in the center. Consort Tian had been buried during a time of peace, so both her inner and outer coffins were already prepared. The burial supervisors and I, a minor official, saw that the late ruler had an inner coffin but no outer casket, so we moved Consort Tian’s outer casket to use for him. In front of the three coffins, incense altars and sacrificial vessels were each placed. When this was finished, I personally lit the everlasting lamp, then closed the two stone doors and immediately covered them with earth. The ground was level, as a tomb mound had not yet been raised. On the sixth day, I led the village elders and others who had donated to the burial to offer sacrifices; their weeping shook the heavens and only stopped after a long time.

I dispatched men to recruit a hundred laborers from the nearby West Mountain Pass, each equipped with shovels and baskets to carry earth. When the construction was finished, I and the scholar Sun Fan-chi also donated five taels to buy bricks and build a surrounding tomb wall over five feet high. Fortunately, the Ts'ing dynasty established its rule and specifically sent the Board of Works to rebuild the three-section incense temple and the surrounding walls of the late Emperor’s mausoleum from the Ch'ung ching period, ensuring that the former ruler of the Great Ming would not be lost in the wild countryside, and that the Emperor and Empress could still receive sacrificial offerings in the afterlife.

*Chapter 34, ll. 26 seq.*

### SHORT DESCRIPTION OF THE SZĔ LING.

The tumulus is a circular mound of earth, barely forty meters in circumference and four meters high, surrounded all around with a wall about one meter high and made of gray bricks which are half a meter in length; its top, gently rounded, is planted with a few small pine trees. It stands isolated within the unplastered crenelated wall, which is about twelve meters distant from it all around, and about three meters high, one brick's length thick, and also made of gray bricks of half a meter. The crenelated terrace of the Soul Tower is just as high as the crenelated wall. No tunnel runs through this terrace, and access to its top is gained by two brick-paved sloping paths constructed at its back, along which they run up from the right and left. The double-roofed house for the gravestone exactly resembles that of the Ch'ang ling, but it measures only eight meters and nine decimeters on each side. The gravestone of white marble is one meter sixteen centimeters broad, and stands on a "square pedestal" of the same material, about one meter high and adorned with relief sculptures, namely: dragons on the front, unicorns on the back, and lion-like monsters on the two sides. The front of the tablet and its crowning border are carved with dragons and characters, in the same way as in the Ch'ang ling (compare p. 1220), and the inscription reads: "Grave Hill of Chwang Lieh, the Emperor Min, of the Great Ming Dynasty" <note>1: Tomb of the Zhuanglie Min Emperor (莊烈愍皇帝之陵).</note>. Chwang Lieh and Min are his posthumous names, bestowed by the first sovereign of the Ts'ing dynasty.

> "In the sixteenth year of the Shun chi period," thus we read, "in the eleventh month, this monarch issued an edict of the following nature to the Board of Rites: The Emperor who reigned in the Ch'ung ching period of the Ming dynasty applied himself for seventeen years to governing the Empire with energy and skill, ultimately sacrificing his life to the Spirits of the Land and Grain when his House was so unfortunate as to be destroyed by rebellion. Upon examination, it has been found that he had no significant shortcomings during his life. Since a pitiable fate fell upon him so suddenly, he really deserves compassion; and therefore We ought to confer on him posthumous titles which may clearly show what his conduct really was, namely: Chwang Lieh and Min Hwang-ti" <note>2: In the 11th month of the 16th year of Shunzhi, an imperial edict was issued to the Board of Rites, saying: The Ming Emperor Chongzhen... (順治十六年十一月上諭禮部曰、明崇禎帝)</note>,

*that is*, "Stern and energetic," and "the Compassionate Emperor."

# THE GRAVE.

The circular area containing the tumulus communicates with the square court in front of the Soul Tower by means of two small doors, built into the tumulus wall on either side of the terrace that supports the tower. This court, which is no more than sixty paces deep, is planted with pines and has, directly in front of the Soul Tower, an altar of solid stone bearing the usual five massive sacrificial stone implements. Next follows the second court of about the same size, which contains the temple. This building resembles the temple of the Ch‘ang-ling so closely that we might call it a miniature copy of it. However, the low square platform of solid stone on which it is raised has neither balustrades nor any flights of steps. The triple Ling-en Gate stands on a similar platform. Finally, directly opposite the middle entrance of this gate, about fifteen paces away, is the tablet-house. It has an entrance only in the front and back facades and contains a tablet with no inscription other than: "Erected by Imperial Command" <note>1: Chih-chien (勅建).</note>, placed on the upper border.

Before the House of Ming had lost the throne, several more small tombs of this description were scattered among the Imperial mausoleums, as every monarch kept a selection of consorts of various ranks in his harem, and the remains of several of them were granted a final resting place in the Imperial Cemetery. However, those who sacrificed their lives upon the death of their lord to follow him into the Realm of Shadows—that is to say, before Ying Tsung ended the practice (see pp. 733 *et seq.*)—do not seem to have had separate mausoleums. Indeed, Ku Yen-wu writes:

> » The decree that the ladies of the palace were to be buried
> » along with the Emperor was not abolished until Ying Tsung’s
> » reign; this is why the Ch‘ang-ling has two pits, one
> » to its east and the other to its west. The Eastern Pit is
> » located southeast of the Teh-ling and south of Cake
> » Mount, and faces the west; the other stands northwest of the

He worked diligently to govern for seventeen years; unfortunately, due to rebel disturbances, the nation fell and he sacrificed his life for the state. Examining his life, he had no major moral failings. Meeting such a disastrous fate is deeply pitiable; it is appropriate to grant a posthumous title to reflect his actual conduct. He is now posthumously named the Zhuanglie Min Emperor. <gloss>Sheng-xun; edicts of Shi-zu, chapter 4, line 3.</gloss>

### SEPULCHRES IN THE EASTERN AND WESTERN MOUNTAINS. ###

With the aid of the sketch given on page 1224, we may see from this extract that the Imperial Cemetery extended considerably to the southwest. Probably it was not quite unintentional that so many consorts were buried on that side, as Chinese social laws of etiquette prescribe that women—being naturally inferior in rank to their husbands—have their places on the right side of the latter, or the theoretical west. There were nevertheless a few graves on the opposite side of the valley, that is to say, in or near the Tung-shan <note>1</note>, meaning "the Mountains on the East."

> "Eastward from the
> Tung-shan Pass," says Ku Yen-wu, "we have the sepulchre of
> Ying Tsung's concubine of the sixth rank bearing the surname
> Liu, and eight miles further eastward, in Mount Mien, those of
> Chwang Hien, King of Khi, and Hwai, King of T'ing, sons of
> Jen Tsung. In general," he adds, "the outer walls of the Im-
> perial mausoleums and the sepulchres of the concubines, Crown
> Princes, and Princes, as also those of the temples that are objects
> of Imperial care, are plastered red" <note>2</note>.

We need hardly tell our readers that the "Eastern and Western Mountains" were important factors of the Feng Shui of the Imperial Cemetery, forming, as they did, a protecting Dragon and Tiger which sent down an abundance of water influences, accumulated—to the advantage of the mausoleums—in numerous brooks and gullies.

While the Ming dynasty held the reins of government, the sepulchral valley was encompassed by a series of closures, placed in the principal passes and defiles providing access to it.

> "There
> are ten such passes in the mountains around," says Ku Yen-wu.
> "Starting from the Great Red Gate, we have, three miles

> » when these troops had nothing else to do, they were trained on
> » the drill ground of the department's chief city, but when-
> » ever there was an alarm, they rushed to all
> » the passes and exits of the valley to block and defend them ” $^1$.

It was, undoubtedly, the thousands of families of mausoleum serfs mentioned in this extract who carried out, under the whip of the soldiers, the work connected with the construction and repair of those numerous cenotaphs, in accordance with the Chinese principle that everything existing under the sky, including the bodies and labor of his subjects, is the property of the Son of Heaven. That the Imperial sepulchres have generally come into existence under the same system since early pre-Christian times, and that this system has not seldom been enforced with ferocious intensity resulting in the loss of countless lives; also, that strong military garrisons have been stationed in the mausoleums since the reign of the House of Han, and walled cities and strongholds founded for their protection—these are all matters we have already discussed at length in Chapter V (pp. 427—436).

Monarchs who had the burial places of their ancestors thus carefully guarded against intrusion may easily be assumed to have had heavy punishments in store for those who dared to enter them without a valid official permit. » Those who enter the gate of the Imperial ancestral temple, or the grounds of a mausoleum without authorization ”, we read in the Code of the Ming dynasty, » shall receive a hundred blows with the long stick ” $^2$.
» Nor might the foot of the hills surrounding the mausoleums be stepped upon
» for the purpose of cutting timber, making kilns or pits for baking
» bricks and pots, or building graves ” $^3$. We have already shown on pages 1207 and following that rigorous laws and decrees also existed then for the protection of the trees in the Imperial cemeteries.

<page-num>1249</page-num>

<header>THE ORCHARDS. — THE TRANSPORT OF STONE BLOCKS.</header>

Chinese authors mention a dozen orchards <note>1 Orchard.</note>, one for each mausoleum, distributed mostly over the countryside outside the circle of passes, near the great Red Gate, or even close to the gates of Ch'ang-p'ing city <note>2 The location of all of them is given in the *Suh sung luh*, and reprinted from this work in the *Jih hia kiu wen*, chapter 34, leaf 31.</note>. Although we are told nothing about their purpose, we cannot doubt that they served to produce the fruit required for sacrifices to the Imperial ancestral spirits during their various days of worship. We believe they will have disappeared by this time, or fallen into the hands of people living nearby.

We are also indebted to the invaluable treatise of Ku Yen-wu for our knowledge of the place of origin of the marble or dolomite, of which such enormous quantities were used in the construction of the mausoleums. 

> "The white stone and the black mortar used for
> the mausoleums and other important works were," he says, "all
> obtained from the northwestern mountains of Shun-i" <note>3 "All the white stone and black mortar used for the great work of the imperial tombs were taken from the mountains northwest of Shun-i." *Ch'ang-p'ing shan-shui ki*, chapter 2, leaf 3.</note>,

that is to say, the district that borders the Ch'ang-p'ing region on the east. If we add the quarrying work to the difficult transport of countless unwieldy blocks over such a great distance, across bad roads and hilly ground, the burdens laid upon the people for the sake of the mausoleums must have been truly immeasurable. It would be interesting to know the means by which the largest blocks, such as those for the statues of the elephants and camels, were transported to the spot where they were placed and carved into shape. Unfortunately, Chinese books leave us in the dark here, but it is highly probable that it was done in much the same way as it is today; therefore, it may be useful to reprint here what two foreign residents have written about the matter. Mr. Rennie, a staff surgeon to the British Legation in Peking after the war of 1860, wrote: 

> "At the beginning of February 1862, I received a
> letter from Peking giving me an account of a large block of
> white marble, weighing sixty (?) tons, which was at that time

> "...an elephant to form one of the decorations of the mausoleum of the late Emperor Hien Fung (Wen Tsung). Its dimensions were fifteen feet long, twelve feet thick, and twelve feet broad. Horses and mules were harnessed to two immense hawsers, running parallel with one another from the truck; the length of each of them was nearly a quarter of a mile. On the block was hoisted the Imperial flag, and on the truck a mandarin and some attendants were seated. One of the latter had a gong, which he sounded after each halt when all was ready to start. Other gongs were then sounded along the line, and at a given signal the carters simultaneously cracked their whips, and off started the horses with their unwieldy load. The line was led by a man bearing a large flag, and all orders were given by signals made with flags. Several other large blocks of marble have already gone to the Eastern Tombs for the same purpose as the one in question, and others are to follow. The sums of money must be enormous which are expended in connection with the death of an emperor of China" <note>1 *Peking and the Pekingese*, vol. II, ch. IX, pp. 256 onwards.</note>.

> "The limestone quarries of the Fang-shan district <note>2 房山縣.</note>, situated about fifty miles (westward) from Peking, furnish the blocks which are carved into the shapes traditionally consecrated to the guardianship of the tombs; and for the completion of the mausoleum of Hien Fung it was necessary to transport masses of stone, estimated as weighing no less than six tons each, to a distance of about ninety miles eastward from Peking, or about one hundred and forty miles in all. The huge square blocks are so quarried out as to be allowed, when finally detached, to sink to rest upon two longitudinal beams, which are subsequently raised to a sufficient extent to allow two sets of wheels, consisting of solid blocks of wood, roughly hewn into a circular shape, to be placed beneath them and connected by axles. To these axles are attached two enormous parallel hawsers, hanging but a few inches above the ground and extending for many yards in front of the truck. On either side of the hawsers there are fastened, at short distances apart, transverse lengths of drag-rope, to each of which a pony, mule or donkey is harnessed, and by these means one hundred or one hundred and fifty animals may be brought to bear on the task of conveying the..."

# THE HIGH ROAD BETWEEN PEKING AND CHʻANG-PʻING.

» monolithic mass to its final destination. Special roads are prepared,

The numerous visits for the purpose of sacrifice and for other ends, regularly made every year to the Imperial tombs by the highest officials and dignitaries, and even by Emperors and Empresses themselves, naturally caused the high road leading from Peking to Chʻang-pʻing to be kept in a better condition than Chinese roads generally are, and led to the construction of several good bridges. At the point where it crossed the Tsʻing-ho <note>2 Tsʻing-ho.</note>—a small stream coming from the Kin-shan and flowing almost due eastward until it flows into the Sha-ho, which originates in the burial valley (see page 1208)—there stood in the time of Ku Yen-wu "a stone bridge across the stream, which was built in the Yung lo period" <note>3 "There is a stone bridge spanning it, built in the Yung lo period." *Chʻang-pʻing shan-shui ki*, leaf 1.</note>. It was probably not far from the present town of Tsʻing-ho, where we now find a stone bridge about which the *Memoirs relating to the Department of Shun-tʻien* say: "The Broad Ferry Bridge spans the Tsʻing-ho twenty miles north of the capital. Formerly there was also a Tsʻing-ho Bridge there, built in the Yung lo period" <note>4 "The Broad Ferry Bridge is twenty miles north of the city, spanning the Tsʻing-ho. It was also known as the Tsʻing-ho Bridge, built in the Yung lo period." *Ch. 47, leaf 1.*</note>. Further on to the north, about halfway between Tsʻing-ho and Chʻang-pʻing, the road ran past Kung-hwa <note>5 Kung-hwa.</note>, now generally called Sha-ho city <note>6 Sha-ho city.</note>, which, as we learned on page 1247 from Ku Yen-wu, was a stronghold with a large garrison when the Ming dynasty held the throne. The road here passed across the two main sources of the Sha-ho, which flow respectively from the northern slopes of the Kin-shan and from the Nan-khao Pass, meeting not far to the east of Kung-hwa. Two beautiful bridges, which still exist today, were built along the road over these streams during the Ming dynasty; the southern one was then called the Quiet Ferry Bridge <note>7 Quiet Ferry Bridge.</note>, and the other the Bridge of the Ancestry of the Dynasty <note>8 Bridge of the Ancestry of the Dynasty.</note>. "Orders for their construction were given in the thirteenth year of the Ching

The location was enclosed with walls in the first month of the nineteenth year and named Kung-hwa. It measured two miles from south to north and two miles from east to west, and it had four gates. The southern gate, called 'the Gate Reverently Bowing to the Metropolis,' was modeled after the south gate of the Palace. The traveling mansion stood inside the city. ### *The Cemetery in the Kin-shan.*

We must now leave the main burial ground of the Ming family and turn our attention to other cemeteries of the same House, one of which was situated in the same department, and three in various parts of the Empire.

The first mentioned we might call an accessory cemetery to that of Ch'ang-p'ing, as the tombs of several Princes and Princesses of Imperial lineage and of some Imperial Consorts were placed in it. It was situated within the boundaries of the present district of Yuen-p'ing <note>2 Wanping District (宛平縣).</note>, in the Kin-shan <note>3 Jinshan or Golden Mountains (金山).</note> or Kin Mountains, which are so frequently referred to in these pages. These mountains form the extreme northeastern spur of the so-called Si-shan <note>4 Xishan or Western Mountains (西山).</note> or "Western Mountains," which, as their name indicates, extend along the Peking plains on the west side and border the T'ien-sheu Range in the north, near the Pass of the Western Mountains or the small Red Gate mentioned on page 1244. The Kin-shan lie to the northwest of the capital, at barely half a day's journey from it, and almost due south of the town of Ch'ang-p'ing, from which they may be easily reached in a day.

Some well-known features of it are the Imperial pleasure grounds Yuanmingyuan <note>1 圓明園</note>, Xiangshan <note>2 香山</note>, Wanshou Shan <note>3 萬壽山</note>, and Yuquan Shan <note>4 玉泉山</note>, situated at its foot to the south and southeast.

The Emperor Jing <note>Emperor King, the Jingtai Emperor</note> is the principal member of the Ming family who was buried there. We have seen on pages 1233 and following that he occupied the throne for some years instead of his elder brother Yingzong, and that, upon being dethroned by the latter, he was demoted to the rank of Prince and denied a burial in the great Imperial Cemetery. His mausoleum was laid out in the so-called Jinshan Kou <note>5 金山口</note> or "Jinshan Passage," a defile leading from the plains in a northwestern direction, right across the Jinshan to its northern slopes, where we find the Heilong Tan <note>6 黑龍潭</note> or "Black Dragon Pond," a well-known Buddhist temple much frequented by foreign tourists. According to Gu Yanwu, "it had three gates, each with three passages, as well as a temple with five divisions, a wall surrounding the ground, and a tablet-house within the gate" <note>7 門三道三重、殿五間、周垣、門內有碑亭一座. *Changping shanshui ji*, book 11.</note>. Jinghui <note>8 貞惠</note>, Jing’s repudiated Consort—who, as we have related on page 734, had a narrow escape from being sacrificed at his death to his ancestral spirits—was buried by his side upon her death in 1506 <note>9 History of the Ming Dynasty, chapter 113, page 17.</note>. Undoubtedly, those of his concubines who followed him in death (see page 733) were likewise buried in his mausoleum or in its vicinity.

The *Yitongzhi* <note>10 一統志</note> or "Memoirs concerning the whole Empire," an exhaustive work on the geography of China published under Imperial patronage about a century and a half ago, quotes the following passage from the *Changan Kehua* <note>11 長安客話</note>, a work by Jiang Yikui <note>12 蔣一葵</note>: "In the depressed area in front of that mausoleum are planted several white aspen trees and *Chu* trees (*Ailanthus glandulosa*). The Princes and Princesses of Imperial lineage who died before puberty were also generally buried at the Jinshan Passage, in grounds forming one tract with those of the mausoleum of the Emperor Jing; and the Imperial Concubines likewise were for a large part buried..."

### *The Nanjing Mausoleum.*
This sepulchre, which we mentioned on pages 821 and 1178, contains the remains of Taizu <note>T'ai Tsu</note>⁵, the first Emperor of the Ming dynasty. Having seized the Empire by force of arms from the Mongol Yuan <note>Yuen</note> family, this monarch was enthroned at Nanjing <note>Nanking</note> in 1368, and ruled there under the reign title Hongwu <note>Hung wu</note>⁶ until his death in 1398. In that year, he was buried a few miles from the city, at the foot of Zhongshan <note>Chung-shan</note>⁷ or the "Bell Mountains."

Zhongshan <note>Chung-shan</note> is a treeless range of hills to the northeast of Nanjing <note>Nanking</note>, forming the Blue Dragon of the Feng-shui <note>Fung-shui</note> of the city. <meta>This page continues the discussion of Ming dynasty imperial burial grounds, transitioning from the cemeteries in the Western Mountains near Beijing to the first Ming emperor's mausoleum in Nanjing, specifically focusing on the history and naming of the mountain range where it is located.</meta>

<page-num>1257</page-num>
<header>ANCIENT AND MODERN NAMES OF THE ZHONGSHAN <note>CHUNG-SHAN</note>. 1257</header>

During the period of the Jin <note>Tsin</note> dynasty (A.D. 307), a bell descended there from the sky; upon being recovered from a brook, it was found to bear an inscription showing it to be a musical instrument made during the reign of the House of Qin <note>Tsʻin</note>. The range is still known by other names. One of the oldest among these is Jinling Shan <note>Kin-ling Shan</note>¹: "Golden Hill Mountains," or, in an abbreviated form, Jin-shan <note>Kin-shan</note>²: "Golden Mountains"; this was derived from the name Jinling <note>Kin-ling</note>, which Nanjing <note>Nanking</note> bore in ancient times. Furthermore, we have Jiang-shan <note>Tsiang-shan</note>³: "Mountains of Jiang," named after one Jiang Ziwen <note>Tsiang Tszĕ-wen</note>⁴, a Governor of Nanjing <note>Nanking</note> at the close of the Han dynasty. Having perished in an engagement against an army of insurgents, he was an object of extensive worship in the locality for many centuries. The chain is also often styled Zijin Shan <note>Tszĕ-kin Shan</note>⁵: "Purplish Golden Mountains," a name which, according to tradition, was given to it after Emperor Yuan <note>Yuen</note>⁶ of the Jin <note>Tsin</note> dynasty—who established the Imperial Court at Nanjing <note>Nanking</note> in the fourth century of our era—had seen it in a reddish haze. Even nowadays, it is well-known among both the Chinese and the foreign residents in the town for its many changes of color, which are especially observable on bright and sunny days. Finally, in 1531, the chain received from Shizong <note>Shi Tsung</note> of the Ming dynasty the name of Shenlie Shan <note>Shen-lieh Shan</note>⁷: "Mountains Burning by Spiritual Power" ⁸; this monarch intended, we think, to invigorate by the power of that name the beneficial geomantic influences which he expected the hills to pour out over Taizu's <note>Tʻai Tsu's</note> grave, to be converted there into blessings for the descendants of this Emperor.

During the Ming dynasty and ever since, Taizu's <note>Tʻai Tsu's</note> mausoleum was styled the Xiaoling <note>Hiao ling</note>⁹. We do not venture to offer any suggestion as to the origin of this name, as Chinese books are silent on the point. Xiaoling <note>Hiao ling</note> means "Mausoleum of Filial Piety," but this does not explain the secret; nor is the mystery solved by the fact that the same name was borne many centuries before by the mausoleum of Wu ¹⁰ of the Zhou <note>Cheu</note> dynasty, who died in A.D. 578 ¹¹.

Like the Imperial mausoleums in the Changping <note>Chʻang-pʻing</note> district, the

### THE GRAVE.

Xiao Ling <note>Hiao ling</note> was taken under official protection by the present reigning dynasty. In an edict which Shengzu <note>Shing Tsu</note> sent in 1684 to the Governor-General of Jiangnan <note>Kiangnan</note> and Jiangxi <note>Kiangsi</note>, we read:

> "In regard to the mausoleum of Taizu <note>T'ai Tsu</note> of the Ming dynasty, situated at the foot of the Zhongshan <note>Chung-shan</note> belonging to Jiangning <note>Kiang-ning</note>, an Imperial rescript has hitherto been in force, ordaining that the magistracy shall offer a sacrifice there every spring and every autumn, and strictly forbid the gathering of fuel, as also that they shall appoint families to guard the mausoleum and to go their rounds there in the morning and in the evening, to see that everything is in order. But this rescript being of ancient date, it is executed in all its parts with neglect. On the tour of inspection We are now making through the Jiangning <note>Kiang-ning</note> region, We have personally visited the spot to worship and to offer libations to the ancestral spirits <note>manes</note>, and have seen the walls in ruins, the trees withered and destroyed, all because ignorant people had not obeyed the restraining rescripts. By ruthlessly trampling down everything and continually moving up and down the grounds, they have seriously transgressed the laws. From this moment, you yourself as Governor-General and all the local authorities, must make frequent tours of inspection to that place and use all your powers to cause the keepers to take assiduous care of it, lest the Bannermen and the people of the neighborhood persist in trampling down and destroying it, as they have hitherto done" ¹.

Thus the State papers themselves teach us that the now reigning dynasty took measures for the protection of the Xiao Ling <note>Hiao ling</note> already at an early date, without, however, being thereby able to prevent its being in a most lamentable condition hardly forty years after it had enthroned itself at Beijing <note>Peking</note>. Manchu soldiery, pursuing the conquest of the provinces, probably laid violating hands upon

## PROTECTION OF THE XIAO LING <note>HIAO LING</note> BY THE QING <note>TS'ING</note> DYNASTY.

...it with the object of destroying its Feng Shui <note>Fung-shui</note>, and thereby breaking the resistance of the last champions in the cause of a family for whose welfare <note>weal</note> and fortunes it had been a protective shield <note>palladium</note> for more than two centuries. And the people, no longer restrained by that family, did more, gradually demolishing the mausoleum for fuel, or for timber, bricks, and stone for their own building purposes. Shengzu <note>Shing Tsu</note> still allowed many years to elapse before he took steps to restore this monument of death to something of its former glory. "In the thirty-eighth year of the Kangxi <note>Khang hi</note> period (1699)," we read, "permission was granted to delegate a local assistant magistrate of Jiangning <note>Kiang-ning</note> to the Xiao Ling <note>Hiao ling</note> of the Ming dynasty, in order to specially direct the repairs of its ruined parts" $^1$. But those measures did not, of course, restore the mausoleum to its pristine grandeur. Nor may we expect that such a result was achieved by the edict issued in 1729 by Shengzu's <note>Shing Tsu's</note> successor, which we have translated in its entirety on pages 930 *and following* <note>sqq</note>. In China, Imperial orders are often a dead letter or very laxly obeyed, especially if they tend to drain the treasuries of provincial Viceroys and other officials <note>mandarins</note>; moreover, all those edicts were certainly not intended to involve a thorough restoration. In 1744, repairs were ordered again. "In the ninth year of the Qianlong <note>Khien lung</note> period, permission was granted to delegate officials to make estimates of the expenditure that would be required for the mausoleum of Taizu <note>T'ai Tsu</note> of the Ming dynasty—namely, for the ruined parts of the Halberds' Gate (*that is*, the temple gate), the walls of the enclosed area, the audience chamber, the side buildings, the tumulus wall, etc.—with orders that the rebuilding and restoration should be started with funds drawn from the Provincial Treasury" $^2$.

It may be assumed that, since that time, the Xiao Ling <note>Hiao ling</note> has been in a passable state of repair, as have the mausolea in Changping <note>Ch'ang-p'ing</note>. The great Taiping <note>T'ai-p'ing</note> rebellion <note>insurrection</note> was its doom. In an edict which the late Emperor Muzong <note>Muh Tsung</note> issued in 1864

This plausible-sounding edict simply accomplished nothing. When we visited the mausoleum in 1886, we found it in a most desolate and dilapidated condition. Leaving Nanking through the eastern city gate, the main road leads past an upright stone tablet, engraved with the three characters which express the official name of the mountains: <term>Shen-lieh Shan</term>. It is here that the approach to the mausoleum forks off.

Quite close by is a pair of stone posts, connected at the top by a stone lintel, carved with six characters which read: "Officers of every class or rank, dismount!" <note>The original Chinese characters are 諸 司 官 員 下 馬.</note> At the same time, the eye beholds a stone tablet on a sloped pedestal of the same material; it displays an ordinance from the year 1641, forbidding all quarrying in the mausoleum grounds, the felling of trees, etc., and also threatening with punishment all those who might dare to approach the spot without dismounting when a hundred paces away, in order to reverently pass by on foot.

From this point we see, at about a ten minutes’ walk, the remains of a triple gate of brick: the counterpart of the great Red Gate of the <term>Changping</term> <note>Ch‘ang-p‘ing</note> mausoleums. Its walls no longer bear any traces of plaster or ornamentation, nor of a roof, but fragments of yellow tiles may be picked up all around in the level fields. Through this gate we come in a few minutes to the ruins of the great tablet-house, likewise showing nothing but bare brick walls, the roofs having entirely disappeared, and the huge tortoise which bears the large monolith commemorating <term>Tai Zu's</term> <note>T‘ai Tsu</note> "divine feats and sage virtues" being thus exposed to the open sky above. This building once undoubtedly bore a great resemblance to its counterpart in the <term>Changping</term> Cemetery, its walls having on the four sides similar tunnel-like openings, no less than eight meters in depth.

At this point the approach makes a rectangular turn to the left, having to avoid a rise in the ground, which until now kept the mausoleum hidden from our view. Wading a brook—once, no doubt, spanned by a stone bridge of which there are now no remains—we soon reach the avenue of stone images, which is the only part of this cemetery that has preserved its original appearance undamaged. We have described it on page 821. The double row of animals is separated from the stone men by a pair of stone columns forming the counterpart of those at the beginning of the avenue of animals in the northern Cemetery (page 1203). At the point where these columns stand, the avenue turns sharply to the right, winding around the aforementioned elevation, and immediately revealing the mausoleum in the distance. The avenue probably once ended at a triple gate resembling the Linteled Star Gate of the northern tombs; six stone plinths, placed in a straight line across it, show that the same number of gateposts must have stood here.

Only a few hundred paces now separate us from the mausoleum, a distance certainly very small when compared with that which lies in the <term>Changping</term> <note>Ch'ang-p'ing</note> Cemetery between the Linteled Star Gate and the <term>Changling</term> <note>Ch'ang ling</note>. Having crossed some arched stone bridges lying side by side, we soon perceive that the mausoleum consists of three successive enclosed squares of different widths, the original walls of which have disappeared and been replaced by poor walls of debris and rubbish, which are neither roofed nor plastered. Those of the foremost square are only a few feet high, as if built for no other purpose than to mark the site of the original walls. No doubt this square once connected with the open area before it by means of a gate; but no trace of such a building is now to be seen.

From this square we enter the second and largest court through the poor, roofless remains of a portal patched up with rubbish, which no longer gives an idea of its original appearance. Here we find, forty paces onward, the large platform of solid stone which formerly supported the gate of the temple; but even the last traces of this gate are now wiped out. The ramps and some remains of balustrades indicate that this terrace once closely resembled that of the temple gate in the <term>Changling</term>. Upon it we find a stone tortoise, bearing an upright stone tablet with this inscription:
> "His reign was as glorious as that of the dynasties of *Tang* and *Sung*" <note>The original Chinese characters are 治隆唐宋.</note>.

It was placed there by order of <term>Shengzu</term> <note>Shing Tsu</note> of the now-reigning House, who wished to give the highest possible praise to <term>Taizu’s</term> <note>T'ai Tsu's</note> memory by proclaiming his fame far and wide at his tomb. On either side of this praising monument we see the remains of two stone tablets fixed in pedestals carved with dragons in *relief* <note>relievo</note>; but they are very mutilated, and the inscriptions are hardly legible. Behind this row of tablets, two similar monuments of smaller dimensions stand side by side, but only one of them is in good condition, having probably been restored in recent times. It records that <term>Shengzu</term> in the thirty-eighth year of his reign (1699) visited <term>Nanjing</term> <note>Nanking</note> while carrying relief to the province of <term>Anhui</term> <note>Ngan-hwui</note>, which was harassed by tremendous floods, and that he ordered his Ministers to offer a sacrifice in the <term>Xiaoling</term> <note>Hiao ling</note>, deeming it unnecessary this time to perform the ceremony personally, as he had already done so on two previous occasions. Besides, the inscription goes on to say, he ordered that some new repairs should be done. We believe that the other five tablets were erected in commemoration of similar

<page-num>1263</page-num>
# DESCRIPTION OF THE RUINS OF THE HIAO LING.

Imperial visits occurred frequently, with Shing Tsu <note>the Kangxi Emperor</note> visiting Nanking six times. On the first and second occasions, in 1684 and 1689, he offered a libation in the mausoleum in person 1; in 1703 he dispatched a <term>Grand-Secretary</term> from the town with orders to sacrifice in the mausoleum as his proxy; two years later he was there himself, and in 1707 he went up as far as the temple 2.

Behind the platform of the temple gate, at a distance of about sixty paces, we find a stone terrace of three levels that formerly supported the temple. In the broad staircases at the front and back, we count twenty steps flanked by finely crafted balustrades; the middle staircase has an inclined monolithic slab carved with dragons in the center, similar to those in the <term>Changling</term> <note>Ch'ang ling</note>. However, the terrace is smaller in size than that of that mausoleum, barely measuring forty meters in length at the top. The stone bases that once supported the wooden pillars of the temple can still be seen upon it; otherwise, there are no remains of this building at all, except for chips of bricks and heavy yellow tiles lying thick all around. Square granite foundations on either side in front of the terrace mark the spots where two sacrificial furnaces once emitted clouds of smoke from the silks and paper money offered to the <term>manes</term> <note>spirits</note> of the deceased monarch.

The square containing the two platforms is nearly two and a half times as wide as the next one, which we enter through the roofless ruins of a gate located a short distance behind the temple terrace. The three tunnel-like openings of this gate, which strongly remind us of the <term>Ling'en Gate</term> <note>Ling-ts'in men</note> of the Changling, still exist. This third square measures approximately sixty meters in width, making it much narrower than the <term>inner court</term> <note>ts'in</note> of the Changling, to which it corresponds; however, it is more than twice as deep, as the distance from its gate to the <term>Soul Tower</term> is about two hundred meters. No stone altar is found within it. In front of the <term>Soul Tower</term> is an arched stone bridge, about twenty-five meters wide and nearly fifty meters long. Its balustrades have disappeared, except—

...a small portion just sufficient to show how nicely carved and elaborately wrought they were. The channel underneath the bridge traverses this square at right angles and is entirely lined with large rectangular stone blocks; doubtless, it was intended from the beginning to ensure a rich supply of blissful aquatic influences for the grave and for the Imperial progeny.

The <term>Soul Tower</term> (see Pl. XLIX) differs from the corresponding buildings in the Ch'ang-p'ing Cemetery especially in this: that the terrace on which it stands is not made of bricks, but of large rectangular blocks of solid stone. Moreover, the terrace is not square, measuring about sixty meters along the front and the back, and somewhat over thirty-two on the flanks; consequently, it covers twice as much ground as that of the Ch'ang ling. Nearly the same proportion between length and breadth exists for the tower, which measures about forty-six meters by twenty-six, thus being likewise more than twice as large as that of the Ch'ang ling. The bricks of which it is made are more than four decimeters long; its walls are over three meters thick. The roofs are now entirely gone. The projecting eaves once rested all around the building upon wooden columns; stone plinths, which evidently served to support the columns, can still be seen on the borders of the high stone ledge on which the tower stands. There is one vaulted opening in the back of this edifice, and one in every flank, but the front facade has three such entrances, which is the case with none of the <term>Soul Towers</term> in the Ch'ang-p'ing Cemetery. The <term>pargeting</term> <note>decorative plasterwork</note> has entirely disappeared, as has the gravestone; it probably lies in pieces within the tower under the debris of the roof, overgrown with grass and weeds, out of which startled pheasants flutter up lazily at the approach of visitors. Even the last traces of the terrace's parapet have now vanished.

Access to the top of the terrace is gained by a broad, brick-paved sloping footway constructed against its two flanks, as in the Yung ling in the Ch'ang-p'ing Cemetery (see p. 1232). The tunnel runs upward with a considerable gradient, and its outlet is quite open at the back of the terrace; immediately behind this, as in the King ling (p. 1226), lies the green foot of the <term>tumulus</term> <note>burial mound</note>. This latter is surrounded by a wall of large-sized gray bricks, originally crowned with a <term>crenelated parapet</term> of blocks of solid stone, as some still-existing portions show; in the rear, this wall slopes up against the Chung-shan, at the very foot of which the <term>tumulus</term> was raised. The <term>tumulus</term> resembles a truncated cone of an irregular shape, measuring approximately sixty paces across at the top. It is covered all over with brambles.
