### THE HISTORY OF THE HIAO LING.

and small trees, which do not, however, grow so dense as to prevent the visitor in the least from moving up and down it in any direction.

As the top of this gigantic <term>tumulus</term> <note>A burial mound.</note> stands out high above the roofless remains of the <term>Soul Tower</term>, it provides a broad bird's-eye view over the walled enclosures and the vast plain beyond. This plain is now treeless but was undoubtedly, like the <term>Ch'ang-p'ing Cemetery</term>, once planted with countless burial trees. A few simple cabins inside the enclosures indicate that the Government has not entirely withdrawn its protection from this ruined <term>cenotaph</term> <note>A monument honoring a person whose body is elsewhere.</note>, for they are inhabited by warders officially appointed to look after it. For the rest, the eye hardly discerns any human dwellings, as the population was wiped out by the terrible scourge of war which passed over the area in 1853, when the <term>T'ai-p'ing insurgents</term> captured <term>Nanking</term>, and again in 1864, when they had to surrender the city to the Imperial armies.

<term>T'ai Tsu's</term> mortal remains were solemnly entombed here in the intercalary month <note>A month inserted into the calendar to harmonize the lunar and solar cycles.</note> following the fifth month of the year 1398, only six days after his death <note>History of the Ming Dynasty, chapter 3, line 15, and chapter 4, line 1.</note>. The tumulus had already been constructed many years before, for we read that his consort <term>Hiao Ts'ze</term> <note>孝慈</note>, the ancestress of the whole dynasty, was buried in the <term>Hiao Ling</term> in 1382, forty-five days after her death <note>History of the Ming Dynasty, chapter 3, lines 1 and following, and chapter 113, line 6.</note>. It is further stated in the Official Annals that the temple was finished in 1383 and solemnly inaugurated with a sacrifice, presented within its walls by the Heir-Apparent and his retinue of Imperial Princes <note>Cited work, chapter 60, line 2.</note>. Concerning the completion of the avenue, we do not find any data recorded. However, we believe it existed prior to the removal of the Court to Peking; its grandeur and the great size of the stone images support the assumption that it was not originally intended to serve for a single mausoleum, but rather for a whole Imperial graveyard which was then expected to be developed there over the course of centuries, as has actually happened in the Ch'ang-p'ing region.

During the reign of the Ming dynasty, the Hiao Ling was officially ranked among its most important places of worship and sacrifice. "An Inspectorate for the Dwelling of the <term>Manes</term> <note>The souls of deceased ancestors.</note> shall be established there," so say the Statutory Ordinances of that Dynasty, "as also a special garrison, and an Office for Sacrificial

### *The Tombs of the Ancestors of the Ming Dynasty.*

In the province of Ngan-hwui, which extends along the western borders of Kiangsu (where Nanking is the capital), two cemeteries exist containing the remains of the four immediate ancestors of the founder of the Ming dynasty.

> » After this monarch had offered a sacrifice to Heaven and Earth in the southern suburbs on the day *yih-hai* of the first month of the first year of the Hung wu period, he ascended the Imperial throne. He decided that the name for the empire should be Ming and that the era of his reign should be called Hung wu. He bestowed honors on his deceased great-great-grandfather by conferring on him the title of Emperor Yuen, with the temple name of Teh Tsu; to his deceased great-grandfather, he gave the title of Emperor Heng and the temple name of I Tsu; to his late grandfather, the title of Emperor Yü and the temple name of Hi Tsu; and to his late father, the title of Emperor Shun and the temple name of Jen Tsu. Their wives were all raised by him to the rank of Empresses <note>2</note>.

T'ai Tsu's first act of sovereignty was thus to elevate his immediate ancestors to a rank equal to his own, in obedience to the laws of filial piety and in imitation of what the founders of former dynasties had done. It was only reasonable for him also to convert their graves into sepulchers worthy of their high titled position, and he was not slow in doing so.

T'ai Tsu's father moved his residence to the department of Feng-yang <note>Fung-yang</note> ², which borders Si-zhou <note>Szě-cheu</note> to the south. Afterward, he was buried not far from the chief city of that department; and it was likely for this reason that T'ai Tsu resolved to establish the capital of his newly acquired Empire there and began to carry out the plan. "In the ninth month of the second year of his reign," we read, "he began building the walls of a Central Metropolis westward from the old chief city of that department; these walls were finished in the twelfth month of the following year and measured fifty miles and 443 <term>pu</term> <note>paces</note> in circumference. In the center, an Imperial City (for the Palaces) was built, nine miles and thirty <term>pu</term> in circuit, with a gate called the Southern Gate, located exactly on the southern side" ³. Although this new Metropolis never served the Court as a residence, yet, as we shall see on page 1275, it was carefully maintained, probably because it provided excellent accommodation for the troops appointed to protect Jen Tsu's grave.

> The mausoleum of Hi Tsu, located in Sze-cheu in the present department of Fung-yang, north of Pin-ch'ing, was granted the honorary designation of Tsu ling (meaning the "Mausoleum of the Grandfather") in the first year of the Hung-wu period. > "And the mausoleum of Jen Tsu, located at the Central Metropolis in the department of Fung-yang, near the village of T’ai-p’ing, was granted the honorary name of Hwang ling (that is, the Imperial Mausoleum) in the same year of the Hung wu period. <header>THE TSU LING AND THE HWANG LING.</header>

accessory to it. It is worth noting that the number of families appointed for the protection of this burial ground only amounted to about one-twelfth of those appointed for the Hwang ling, and that, unlike the latter, it was not garrisoned; also, the officer appointed to perform sacrifices there was not assisted by three subordinate officers. All of these facts clearly show that it occupied a much lower position than the Hwang ling among the objects the dynasty deemed worthy of its attention. "The temple of the Tsu ling," we further read, "was erected in the fourth year of the Hung wu period (1371). It was modeled after the temples of the T’ang and Sung dynasties, in that (the three ancestors) had one common main hall in it, and each had a special compartment to himself. The front hall and the back hall of this edifice each contained fifteen pillars, two of which formed an extra compartment on the eastern as well as on the western side. This arrangement had been proposed by Suh, the Prince of Tsin. The compartment for the worship of the soul tablet of Teh Tsu, which was also intended for the general family sacrifices, was between the three central pillars; I Tsu was worshiped at the eastern pillar, and Hi Tsu at the western. In the nineteenth year of his reign, the same Emperor ordered the Heir Apparent to travel to Szě-cheu to undertake the restoration of the Tsu ling, and also to bury crowns and ceremonial robes on the spot on behalf of the three Imperial Ancestors and their chief Consorts" ¹. This statement that the three Ancestors had one temple in common implies, we believe, that their remains rested in one mausoleum.

And in reference to the Hwang ling we read: "T’ai Tsu, upon visiting Hao-cheu (that is, Fung-yang), resolved to transfer the remains of his father (to the Chung-shan); but this plan was not carried out. He heightened the burial mound with earth and ordered the people who had lived since olden times around the mausoleum—namely, the families named Wang, Wen, Liu, Ying, and others, twenty in all—to watch over it."

"In the second year of the Hung wu period, he conferred on it the honorific name of Ying ling, which he afterwards changed to that of Hwang ling" $^1$. This mausoleum was a true family cemetery. Close to it, there were also five sepulchres containing the remains of Jen Tsu's brothers, to whom T'ai Tsu had granted the title of Imperial Prince (Wang) at the beginning of his reign; three of them were interred there with their consorts. The spirits of all were worshiped regularly by officers appointed for that purpose $^2$. We briefly note that another cemetery, containing the remains of ten personages elevated to the rank of Prince upon T'ai Tsu's accession, and of four of their spouses, was located twenty-five Chinese miles north of Fung-yang in the so-called White Pagoda Grounds $^3$. An Office for Sacrificial Services was also established for this burial ground, and families were appointed to guard it $^4$.

As long as the Ming dynasty held the throne and the realm, its two oldest cemeteries were just as much objects of its tireless care as the mausoleums of the Emperors who had actually reigned; they were nonetheless regarded as cornerstones of the <term>Fung-shui</term> and fortunes of the Crown. We read of repairs ordered by various Sons of Heaven; of solemn sacrifices they personally performed at the Hwang ling while passing by on their frequent journeys between Peking and Nanking; and of edicts ordering rigorous measures to be taken against the violation of those sacred grounds. So, for example, "it was ordained in the fifteenth year of the Ch'ing hwa period (A.D. 1479) regarding the forbidden hills and grounds of the Hwang ling, the Imperial City, and the Tsu ling in Szĕ-cheu: the civilians and military personnel appointed to patrol there shall apply themselves with zeal and care to the work of inspection and watching; and nobody shall be allowed to cut down any trees there, or to carry away soil or stones, or to build kilns for pottery or bricks, or to burn the vegetation on the hills. It is hard to imagine that in those days, precarious as they were, the other Imperial ancestral tombs in that region could have remained undamaged, as internal peace never returned in the nine years that passed before the Ming dynasty was finally overthrown. And the House of Ts'ing does not seem to have concerned itself much with the restoration of those monuments; we have found no mention of any such measures in any collection of Imperial Ordinances issued during its reign. We cannot say whether any remains or ruins of those mausoleums still exist, as we have not explored the part of the Empire where they would be located. The absence of a description from these pages is not a major drawback, however, as it would undoubtedly provide little more than a shortened repetition of our accounts of the Ming tombs in Ch'ang-p'ing and near Nanking.

### *The Mausoleum of the Titulary Emperor Hien.*

Under the Ming dynasty, it seems that enfeoffed Imperial Princes were often buried in their feudal kingdoms. This was also the case with Yiu Yuen², the younger brother of Emperor Hiao Tsung. Appointed in 1487 as the feudal Ruler (<term>Wang</term>) of the state of Hing³, in the province of Hupeh, he died in 1519 and was buried in the hills north of Ngan-luh⁴. This city, the capital of his fief, still exists today on the left bank of the Han River⁵ as the capital of a department of the same name. Two years later, the son of this nobleman inherited the Imperial throne from Wu Tsung, the son of Hiao Tsung, who died without a male heir (see p. 1231); he is known in history by the temple name Shi Tsung. As one of his first acts, he conferred the posthumous title of Emperor upon his father, who was thereafter styled Emperor Hien of Hing⁶; the honorary name "Hien" had been bestowed on him at his death by the then-reigning sovereign. Shi Tsung » elevated his father’s burial park » to the rank of a <term>ling</term>, and appointed inspectors and guards for it » from among the members of the Imperial clan, in accordance

» He ordered Kwoh Hiun, King of the principality of Yih, to oversee the measures to be taken regarding a mausoleum for his Imperial mother; but when he had traveled to the Great Valley himself and seen the spot, he ordered arrangements to be made for the transportation of the Empress Dowager to the south, for burial there beside her husband. » This officer returned the following year, reporting that the Hien ling was not an auspicious tomb. We learn this from a short description of this tomb which M. Michaelis gives in his account of a journey he made in 1879–81 through central and western China ¹. This description, illustrated by a sketch plan of which *Fig. 42* is a reproduction, shows that this sepulchral monument, though not differing essentially in plan from the other mausoleums of the Ming dynasty, possesses some features which make it worthwhile to reproduce here what its author mentions of *it*.

Including the avenue, it is situated within a vast, walled area of almost two kilometers by one, which has been to a great extent converted into rice fields. The front half of this enclosure is nearly square, with rounded corners; the back half, which contains the tumuli, is rounded off at the rear. The brick wall is approximately six meters high and is roofed with yellow and blue glazed tiles. In the middle of the front wall, which faces the south, is a large brick gate built on a solid sandstone base with three passages, eight meters deep. Behind it, a path, partly paved with stone slabs, leads across a triple stone bridge with balustrades of the same material to a detached gate, which we do not doubt is the counterpart of the Red Gate of the Ch’ang-p’ing Cemetery; nearby stands a hamlet where, we think, the descendants of the families appointed in times long past to guard the grounds still live. Moving onward in a straight line, we again cross a triple bridge, arriving then at a tablet house measuring eighteen meters on every side and built entirely of stone blocks. Each facade has a lofty, arched entrance, over which are stone slabs sculpted with curling dragons; the roof is destroyed, and the tablet has fallen to the ground.

Behind the tablet house is another triple bridge, giving access to an avenue lined with life-sized, clumsy stone images of animals and men. It is almost two hundred meters long. First, we have a pair of octagonal pillars covered with sculpture; then follow two lions, two tigers, two camels, two pairs of unicorns, and two horses, all crouching, and finally two standing horses, two pairs of military officers, and two pairs of civilians. About 250 meters onward, we pass a triple bridge, beyond which we see a round pond lined with stone blocks. We suppose this is intended to ensure the prosperity of the temple and the burial mounds that are situated further on. The diameter of this pond is about thirty meters. After passing through a triple gate raised on a stone platform, we enter a walled court paved with slabs and see in the background a platform that formerly supported a temple, which is now almost entirely destroyed. A cross-wall with a gate in the middle separates this court from a second yard, bounded at the back by a square Soul Tower. In front of this building stands a stone altar, before which we see a tripod and two columns made of the same material. The terrace of the Soul Tower connects to a circular area surrounded by a wall three meters thick, in the center of which stands a round burial mound, nine meters high. This enclosure is followed by another of similar form, which also contains a round burial mound in the middle; both are connected by a raised open passage, nine meters wide, formed by two parallel walls and entered at either end by a flight of steps. We suppose the front mound contains the remains of the Emperor, and that the one in the rear contains those of his wife. These tombs alone are in good condition, but everything else is in a state of neglect.

### 5. The Burial Grounds of the Present Reigning Dynasty.

#### a. The two Cemeteries in Peh-chihli Province.

The Manchu founder of the Ts'ing dynasty, who ascended the throne of China upon the conquest of Peking by his armies in 1644, and most of his successors down to the present day, are—together with their chief Consorts and Concubines—buried in a valley or a series of valleys in Tsun-hwa ¹, one of the departments of the province of Peh-chihli bordering on the west with the department of Shun-t'ien, where Peking is located. Officially and popularly, those tombs are designated by the name of Tung ling ²: "the Eastern Mausolea," because of their location east of Peking. They stand against a broad chain of hills called the Ch'ang-shui Shan ³ or "Hills of Radiant Felicity," over which the Great Wall runs from east to west, forming the northern boundary of the

<header>THE GRAVE.</header>

Concerning the location of these mausoleums relative to one another, we read that:
> "the Xiaoling lies in the center, the Zhaoxiling to the southeast, and the Xiaodongling to the east of it; and that the Jingling is situated eastward from the Xiaodongling, and the mausoleum of Empress Xiaoxian (the Yuling) is westward from the Xiaoling"¹.

The same Qing dynasty which—as our readers will remember from our chapter on Feng-shui—deems it its duty to earnestly warn its subjects against the dangerous delusions of this system, nevertheless had the selection of its own principal cemetery entirely governed by geomantic considerations. In the surrounding hills, its eagle-eyed experts discerned a combination of qualities able to ensure the dynasty’s everlasting possession of the throne, and eternal peace and prosperity for the nation.

> "On the four sides,"

thus we read,
> "the place is enclosed by hills rising range upon range, producing a prosperity based on nature which may support us for ten thousand years to come. Originally the Changshui Mountain bore the name of Fengtai Ling: 'Chain of the Terrace of Abundance', and Fengtai Shan: 'Mountains of the Phoenix Terrace'. Their pulses (compare page 953) come forth from the Taihang Mountains (which extend between Peh-chihli and Shanxi); their double chains and accumulated peaks represent a phoenix soaring in the sky (that is, the Bird of the Southern Quadrant), and the windings of a dragon. The undulating peaks are several hundreds of *jen* <note>A traditional Chinese unit of length, often roughly equivalent to 8 feet or a fathom.</note> in height. In front arise the peaks of the Planet of Metal (Venus); in the rear, the site is encompassed by the lofty hills of the chains which form the watershed. On the left we have the Nianyu Pass and the Malan Valley; on the right the Guantian Vale and the Huanghua Hills. Thus the Imperial Clan is embraced on every side by a thousand peaks and ten thousand water streams; two rivers from the watershed wind closely along it on the right and left respectively, and meet in the Dragon and Tiger Valley. The glory and prosperity (which the site thus ensures) are firm and solid; it is propitious ground which shall confer happiness on this Dynasty for myriads of years"².

<header>THE EMPEROR AND EMPRESSES BURIED IN THE HIAO LING.</header>

The first time burials took place in this valley was in the sixth Chinese month of the year 1663. Shing Tsu then deposited the remains of his father Shi Tsu in the crypt of the <term>Hiao ling</term>, together with those of two of the latter’s consorts: namely, Hiao Hien, a concubine of the first rank, who was granted the title of empress upon her death three years before; and Hiao Khang, a concubine of the third rank, who—because she had given birth to Shing Tsu—was granted the rank of empress by him upon his accession, and only held this titular dignity for a few months^1. In the very same year, Shing Tsu changed the name of Phoenix Terrace Mounts—which, as we have seen, had until then been the name of the hills around the valley—to the Hills of Radiant Felicity^2, which has remained the official name to the present day. No beginning seems to have been made on the construction of the <term>Hiao ling</term> during the reign of Shi Tsu himself; for it is explicitly stated that in the year 1661, the year in which he died, his successor "issued orders to erect a sacrificial temple and an underground crypt for Shi Tsu, the Emperor Chang, and to carefully appoint for the purpose persons well-versed in <term>geomancy</term>. When the day of the burial had arrived, Shi Tsu’s coffin was reverently placed exactly in the middle of the stone couch erected in the crypt; that of the Empress Hiao Khang was placed on his left, and that of the other Empress on his right"^3.

<term>Hiao Hwui</term>, <term>Shi Tsu</term>'s primary Empress, who was his concubine until 1655, survived him until 1717 <note>1. *Wen hien t'ung khao*, chapter 240, lines 23 and following.</note>. They feared, moreover, that such a reckless act might disturb the fortunes of the unfilial descendants who committed it. "The custom of burying Emperors with their Empresses in the same grave," as we read, "has been observed in a perfect and well-accomplished way from the beginning (of this dynasty). <term>Yen Shen-szě</term>, a Minister of the <term>T'ang dynasty</term>, has demonstrated that when one of higher position is buried first, no one of lower rank may enter his grave; moreover, the practitioners of the <term>geomantic art</term> are averse to having superiors disturbed in their rest by inferiors. Therefore, the question of whether an Empress was to be entombed at the side of her spouse has, in strict accordance with the rules of propriety, been made to depend, in each particular case, on the time (of her death). Since the burial of Emperors with their Empresses in the same tomb is practiced regarding the mausolea of our present dynasty according to this ancient method, it follows that the <term>Chao-si ling</term>, the <term>Hiao-tung ling</term>, and the <term>T'ai-tung ling</term> owe their origin to a respectful adherence to the decrees of former times. This example (set by the dynasty) of letting the ancients regulate the behavior of the moderns is worthy of being imitated for ten thousand generations to come" <note>3. 至於合葬之義昉自成周。唐臣嚴善思又言、尊者先葬卑者不得入、以卑動尊術家所忌、故合葬與不合葬惟義所在各因乎時。我朝列聖山陵循古合拊之制、而昭西陵孝東陵泰東陵之建則仰承先制憲。古準今允堪垂法萬世者也。 *Wen hien t'ung khao*, chapter 150, lines 2 and following.</note>.

> “...grand and prosperous.”... This memorial was not submitted to the Throne.<note>I respectfully note that according to the burial methods in the *Tianyuan Fanglu*, if a superior person is buried first, an inferior person should not follow by reopening the tomb. Empress Wu Zetian was lower in status than the Great Emperor Gaozong; therefore, opening the Qianling mausoleum for a joint burial would mean disturbing a superior for the sake of an inferior. This practice is unconventional and potentially dangerous. Furthermore, I have heard that the gate to the Qianling crypt is blocked with stone and the gaps are filled with molten iron to secure it. Opening the mausoleum would require carving and drilling, and since the way of the spirits is subtle and mysterious, I fear that such heavy labor would cause great offense. If a new entrance were made to the crypt, the spiritual positions established during the original burial would be altered, causing even deeper harm. Additionally, since the construction of Qianling, the nation has faced frequent difficulties, which only subsided during the twenty years that Empress Wu Zetian held power. I fear that undertaking new construction now might cause these troubles to arise again. Joint burial is not an ancient practice; although it is mentioned in the *Classic of Rites*, it is based on personal sentiment and lacks a firm standard for compliance. During the Han dynasty, Empresses were usually not buried in the same tomb as the Emperors; it was only from the Wei and Jin dynasties onward that joint burials began. The Han dynasty lasted for over four hundred years, whereas the dynasties following the Wei and Jin did not enjoy such longevity. Since the peace of a tomb relies on a superior location to bless its descendants, any unrest at the site makes it difficult for successors to enjoy a long reign. I humbly hope that the Han example is followed and the flawed traditions of the Wei and Jin are avoided; that another auspicious site be chosen near Qianling to build a separate tomb according to the proper methods. This would satisfy the rituals of burial while securing the foundation of the state. The essence of mountains and rivers corresponds to the stars above; if a burial is in the right place, the spirits are at peace and their descendants will prosper. If it is misplaced, the spirits are endangered and their descendants will suffer. For this reason, the ancient sages provided examples in the *Burial Classic* to ensure the living are secure and the spirits of the dead are at rest... This memorial was not accepted. *Old Books of the Tang Dynasty*, chapter 191, lines 15 and following. See also the *New Books of the Tang Dynasty*, chapter 204, line 10.</note>

The doctrine that an Emperor, once entombed, may no longer be disturbed in his rest—and that his widow must consequently be buried in a separate mausoleum of her own—has placed heavy costs upon the Imperial Court. The construction and constant repair of so many special cenotaphs has required enormous expenses in both money and labor. No special names were given to any of these sepulchers. Each is officially designated by the name of the mausoleum of the Emperor to whom the occupant was married, with the addition of the word *tung* (“east”) or *si* (“west”), depending on whether it is located to the left or the right of the Emperor’s tomb.

<summary>This page concludes Yen Shen-szĕ's failed memorial against reopening the Qianling mausoleum for Empress Wu Zetian, citing spiritual and political risks. It also explains the resulting expensive tradition of building separate "east" or "west" mausoleums for Empresses.</summary>

Shing Tsu never elevated her to the dignity of empress; but her son, in obedience to the demands of filial respect, did so upon her death, which occurred in the fifth month of the first year of his reign <note>¹ *Wen hien t'ung khao*, chapter 240, line 40.</note>. ...therefore, We ordain Our Grand-Secretaries and nine Directors of the Courts to carefully examine this point, hold a meeting to discuss it, and report their conclusions to Us."

The Grand-Secretaries and the said Ministers deliberated on the matter on the *wu-wu* day of the same month and reported as follows: "If we carefully consult the *Genealogical Register of Emperors and Princes* (see p. 434), the *General History* <gloss>1</gloss>, and the *Wen hien t'ung khao*, we find that the sovereigns of successive dynasties have sometimes had their tombs situated in grounds more than a thousand miles away, and hardly ever nearer than two hundred or three hundred miles. The question of whether the <term>pulses of the earth</term> will produce felicity depends on the prosperity-producing factors and indicators that dominate the natural destiny of the person concerned (compare page 1013); and favorable spiritual operation is not, of course, monopolized by a single place among the many good grounds, spanning hundreds or thousands of miles, that contain felicity. 

The spot in question in the T'ai-p'ing Valley at the T'ai-ning Mountains, which promises felicity for ten thousand years, is indeed several hundred miles from the Hiao ling and the King ling; however, the departments of Yih and Tsun-hwa are close to the Capital and really not far away. The T'ai-ning Mountains are bold and lofty, and their peaks emit pulses whose origin lies in the Kwan-ch'en Mountains (in the north of Shansi) and in the Hing Mountains (in the southwest of Pehchihli, on the Shansi borders). The spot is encircled by a hundred streams, and the watershed with the Kü-ma-hu River forms its boundary on the north. 

If we observe the spots where those surrounding configurations concentrate their influences, we come to the conclusion that we are dealing here with the very best of shelters in a sublime tract of ground; and if we examine such sections of the standard works as refer to the subject, we find that the matter is perfectly consistent with what the three dynasties of antiquity have done. Hence we humbly pray Your Majesty to carry this out with reverence and care and in keeping with the established institutions, in order that the pure, unalloyed felicity naturally stored up on the spot may...

¹ <note>In the seventh year of his reign, Shizong (the Yongzheng Emperor) issued an edict to the Grand Secretaries and others, saying: "My original intention was to select a future auspicious site near the Xiaoling and Jingling tombs. However, the geomancers all believed there was no place there where construction could be undertaken. Later, a lucky site at Nine Phoenixes Facing the Sun Hill was selected and proposed. I thought this place was suitable as it was near Xiaoling and Jingling, matching my first wish. Now, according to the report from Prince Yi, Governor Gao Qizhuo, and others, they have surveyed a 'ten-thousand-year lucky ground' at Taiping Valley in the Taining Mountains within the borders of Yi Prefecture. It is truly a region where the beauty of heaven and earth converges, a place where Yin and Yang harmonize. The appearance of auspiciousness in the <term>earth pulses</term> is related to the unfolding of heavenly luck and the historical destiny of the era. A region of blessing that spans hundreds or thousands of miles is not something that only one area can monopolize. 

Now, although the ten-thousand-year lucky ground at Taiping Valley in the Taining Mountains is several hundred miles from Xiaoling and Jingling, both Yi Prefecture and Zunhua are close to the Capital and are not actually far away. Moreover, the Taining Mountains are grand and high, with peaks drawing their pulses from the Guancan and Heng Mountains; they are surrounded by many rivers, with the Juma and Hutuo rivers serving as boundaries. Observing its configuration, it is clearly a place of concentrated great blessings; examining the records, it also matches the standards of the Three Dynasties..."</note>

These women, by virtue of their maternal power, carried on the supreme government with great vigor and determination during the whole of Muh Tsung’s reign. Ts'ze Ngan received the temple-name of Hiao Ching upon her death in 1881, and was buried in 1888 in a mausoleum built specifically for her to the east of Wen Ts'ung’s.

According to Mr. Bourne, there is in the Eastern Cemetery, northwest of Shi Tsu's tomb, on the banks of the stream running in front of it, the site of a mausoleum that was built by the Emperor Süen Tsung for himself, and afterwards destroyed by him under curious circumstances.

> "This tomb", he writes (page 30), "was prepared before the death of the Emperor. By the direction of a Grand Secretary named Ying Hwo, the elaborate and costly drainage arrangements, which formed a part of the plan, were omitted; through this, Ying Hwo is said to have made 100,000 taels or £30,000. The Empress died first and was buried in the tomb, but the stone door was not finally closed until the Emperor joined her. On one of his visits to sacrifice at the tombs, he expressed a wish to see his own future resting place. Upon his ordering the stone door to be opened so that he might enter the mound itself, he was horrified to see that there were several feet of water in the chamber—enough to reach the level of the stone bed on which the coffin lay. Ying Hwo was banished, and his possessions were forfeited. The Emperor decreed that a new mausoleum should be constructed at the western tombs, 180 miles away. The building was leveled to the ground; some of the materials were removed to the new site, but most of them were left, and we noticed pieces of finely carved stone that formerly belonged to this tomb, carelessly thrown together to form makeshift bridges. There are many believers in Fung-shui <note>Feng shui</note> who attribute the misfortunes of the current dynasty, even the untimely death of the late Emperor, to this unfortunate incident and the mistake made in changing the site of this tomb."

These lines, which show evidence in themselves of being based on mere hearsay, arouse our curiosity for some reliable, authentic information. Unfortunately, the collections of state papers which have guided us until now do not cover the reign of Süen Tsung, and no documents shedding official light on this incident are at our disposal, except for three imperial edicts issued in 1828, which the compilers of the *Shing hiun*<sup>1</sup> have considered inter-

<note>1. In the tenth month, on the day of *Gengwu*, an Imperial Edict was issued to the Grand Secretariat. I-shao and others jointly and strictly investigated Ying-ho and his associates for their negligent management of the construction at the auspicious site <note>the mausoleum</note>, and submitted a report detailing their proposed sentences. Ying-ho was in charge of the important works at the *Baohuayu* auspicious site from start to finish, and should have been cautious and thorough. However, knowing that the stone base of the burial chamber was leaking water because it was made of discarded materials, he consulted with Mian-ke and Dai Junyuan and used soil to cover it up. Furthermore, fearing that the "Dragon Whisker" drainage ditch might leak the "Earth Qi" <note>geomantic energy</note>, he reported that he had stopped its construction. Yet, he suggested adding stone lattices next to the stone vaults, only to later order that work to stop as well. Regarding the stone masonry for the walls and paving, whenever there were chips or cracks, they simply used a mixture of rosin and white wax with stone dust to patch them. Moreover, he ordered Niu Kun to rush the project and set a strict deadline for completion. Ying-ho relied solely on Niu Kun for such vital work, resulting in a rushed job that eventually led to flooding.

I-shao and the others conducted a clear investigation and, according to the established statutes, proposed the sentence of execution with a stay of enforcement. This was the deserved punishment, but considering that Ying-ho once served as a Minister and Associate Grand Secretary, and since this investigation found no evidence of bribery or personal gain, We may show a shred of mercy. Furthermore, the construction of the auspicious site is Our own personal affair, and We are unwilling to execute high ministers because of mismanagement. Since We have not sentenced him to death, there is no need to keep him in prison for a long time. Ying-ho is granted the grace of being sent to Heilongjiang to serve as a laborer, demonstrating Our mercy beyond the law. Since he is currently ill and has not recovered, his sons Khwei-chao and Khwei-yao do not need to be handed over to Jing-zheng and others to be taken to the construction site for labor; instead, they shall accompany their father to Heilongjiang. His grandson Yin-sheng, an Expectant Second-Class Secretary named Sih-chi, is to be stripped of his office immediately. Niu Kun was appointed as the General Supervisor, stationed permanently at the site to monitor the work—a responsibility much heavier than that of other supervisors. Although the investigation showed no signs of embezzlement or corruption, his failure to properly supervise is a grave offense. He is to be sent to Ili to labor and atone for his crimes.

The dismissed supervisors Poh Sheu and Yen Feng were not found guilty of theft or embezzlement. However, they had personally committed to finishing the project within seven years in their contracts; yet they failed to plan properly and became desperate as the deadline approached, allowing the craftsmen to perform sloppy repairs. Both are to be sent to Urumqi to labor and atone for his crimes. The dismissed construction supervisors Ding-shan, Chang-chun, and Ma Yanbu were specifically responsible for oversight; having witnessed the sloppy construction, they failed in their duties. They are all to be sent to military posts to labor and atone for their crimes. The dismissed supervisor Qing-yu, who arrived to take over the work after the ground level was completed, is exempted from being sent to a military post but is ordered to serve at the construction site.</note>

<page-num>1305</page-num>
# SÜEN TSUNG’S FIRST MAUSOLEUM.

Even now the matter was not ended. In the next month, another Imperial edict arrived at the Chancery, with the following contents: 
"The survey of the mountain formations at the Pao-hwa Valley was initially the work of Tai Kwun-yuen, Muh-khoh-teng-ngoh, and O-khoh-tang-o. The property of the first-named has been traced and confiscated, and the other two have been condemned to pay a certain amount in taels. This serves as a warning that neglecting one's duty leads to punishment. 

However, We will take into consideration that, although those three men visited the valley together and selected the spot in question, a distinction should be made between them based on whether or not they were involved in the actual execution of the works. Tai Kwun-yuen was present for nearly three years and never reported a single word about the water oozing through the stones, until Siang T'ung had to cover the leakage with earth. Therefore, his possessions have been (justly) identified and seized, and he himself has been brought to trial. 

O-khoh-tang-o attended the works for more than half a year, and likewise failed to report the truth about the matter; for this misconduct, he fully deserves the fine that has been imposed on him. But Muh-khoh-teng-ngoh merely accompanied them on their surveying excursion and did not manage any of the works at all; therefore, some discrimination must be made in his case. 

We are reducing the fine of 30,000 taels of silver that was imposed on him by 20,000 taels, and he is ordered to pay the remainder by the appointed deadline. In this way, by imposing fines proportionate to the crimes committed, We demonstrate that Our strength lies in a resolute will to be just and fair." <note>1</note>

-># THE GRAVE.<-

It is quite impossible to provide a description of the two Imperial Cemeteries based on personal observation. For they are jealously guarded against intrusion by Chinese soldiers and Manchu Bannermen, and no foreigner can enter these mysterious grounds without risking injury, or even his life. Locals are also carefully excluded, and the Code of Laws states:

> » Whoever enters the gates of the area containing the mausolea without valid 
> » reasons or authorization shall receive one hundred blows with the long stick. 
> » And if anyone goes no farther than a gate, without passing the limit fixed 
> » by it, the above punishment shall be reduced by one degree. Should the 
> » officers of the guard have willfully allowed the intrusion, they shall 
> » be punished in the same way as the trespassers; and should the 
> » intrusion be attributable to their mere lack of vigilance, they shall 
> » be punished three degrees less severely than the offenders" $^1$.

Nevertheless, there is a way to gain a fairly good idea of the appearance of those grounds. Familiarity with the cemetery of the Ming dynasty in Ch'ang-p'ing is sufficient for the purpose, as every mausoleum located there resembles the Eastern and Western Tombs in all the main features. We know this for certain from the general rules for their construction, which the Ts'ing dynasty itself has laid down in its fundamental

On the Spirit’s Road south of the bridge, there shall be a "dragon-and-phoenix gate" (p. 1206), standing exactly in the middle of the grounds, with a guardhouse consisting of three rooms in front of it on either side; and further, a line of stone images arranged on the left and right, namely: civil ministers, military officers, unicorns, lions, elephants, horses, camels, and others. The front part of the Spirit's Road shall be occupied by a "Great Red Gate" (p. 1196), featuring three passages and decorated with various colors; the rafters of the roof of this building shall slope downward on all four sides. A decorative stone gate shall stand here to the south (p. 1193) and two such structures to the east and west, as well as a stone slab on either side ordering riders to dismount. 

Within the "Great Red Gate," there shall be a hall on the left for the preparation of ceremonial robes, consisting of three rooms and surrounded on all sides by a wall with a single gate. This three-room hall shall contain an altar facing west, and it—as well as the gate and the wall—shall be roofed with yellow glazed tiles. This place shall serve the Emperor for boarding his carriage and changing his clothes (compare page 1198). <page-num>1309</page-num>
# SUPPLEMENTARY ORDINANCES FOR THE MAUSOLEA.

These fundamental ordinances prove in the clearest possible way that the Ts'ing dynasty has entirely modeled its mausolea on the plans of those of the House of Ming. Indeed, almost every building and structure prescribed has its counterpart in the old Ch'ang-p'ing Cemetery and bears the same name there, with only a few minor exceptions. Since the general plan of the Ts'ing tombs is so strikingly uniform with that of the Ming tombs, we may infer that the buildings and structures composing them will also differ very little from those in the Ch'ang-p'ing Cemetery in style, decoration, elaboration, and finish. This becomes even more probable if we consider that the Manchus never possessed any solid architecture of their own and, consequently, resorted to mere imitation of what they found worth copying in this field after the conquest of the Empire.

The ordinances issued by the Throne at different periods to supplement the fundamental decrees mentioned above—in the case of each mausoleum in particular—are the only authentic sources still in existence from which we may gain a more accurate knowledge of the Imperial

---

<margin>*Ta Ts'ing hwui tien* (Collected Statutes of the Great Ts'ing), chapter 76, lines 2 and following. See also the *Rules and Regulations for the Board of Rites*, chapter 143, lines 5 and following.</margin>

Establish warm chambers and sleeping rooms according to the system of the Imperial Ancestral Temple. There shall be five rooms in each of the eastern and western side-galleries. There shall be one ritual furnace each on the left and right. In front shall be the Gate of Eminent Grace (Long’en Gate), consisting of five rooms and three passages. It shall be surrounded by a red wall. Outside the gate, there shall be five rooms each in the eastern and western side-wings, and three rooms each for the guardhouses of the duty officers and soldiers on the east and west.

In front shall be a Spirit Road Tablet, inscribed with the posthumous title and temple name, and covered by a pavilion. These shall all be painted in five colors and decorated with gold. In front of the pavilion are three stone bridges. To the left and right of the bridges stands a stone tablet ordering riders to dismount. The slaughterhouse pavilion, the divine kitchen, the divine storehouse, and the well pavilion shall all be painted in various colors.

South of the bridges, in the exact center of the Spirit Road, stands the Dragon and Phoenix Gate. Outside the gate on both sides are three guardrooms. Civil officials, military officers, and stone statues of unicorns, lions, elephants, horses, camels, and other animals are arranged in rows on the left and right. In front of these are two viewing columns, and further forward is a single stone bridge. In front of the bridge is a Tablet of Sacred Virtue and Divine Merit covered by a lofty tower, with two "pillars that support the sky" <note>sky-bearing columns</note> in front and two at the back. At the front of the Spirit Road is the Great Red Gate, featuring three passages, decorated with colors, and having a roof with four slopes. There are two corner gates on the left and right. South of the gate is one stone archway, with two more archways to the east and west, and a stone dismounting tablet on each side.

Inside the Great Red Gate to the left is the Hall for Changing Ceremonial Robes, consisting of three rooms and surrounded by a perimeter wall with one gate. This hall has three rooms with an altar facing west; the hall, gate, and wall are all covered with yellow glazed tiles. This serves as the place for the Imperial carriage to stop and for the Emperor to change his clothes. Along both sides of the Spirit Road, trees shall be planted in rows of ten, each spaced twenty feet <note>two zhang</note> apart. Outside the perimeter wall, red posts shall be planted to mark the boundaries and to prohibit the gathering of firewood, farming, or gardening.

tombs. They tell us very little about the exact architectural style, contours, and ornamentation of the buildings, but they provide nearly everything regarding their dimensions and layout. This offers many new proofs of their close resemblance to the mausoleums of the Ming dynasty. These ordinances, like the fundamental decrees, were drafted to guide the Administrative Bureau for the Government Reservations¹, a subdivision of the Board of Works. This bureau is responsible for the construction and restoration of the tombs of the Imperial Family, nobles, and high officials (<term>mandarins</term>), as well as the graves of rulers, sages, and worthies from previous dynasties. It also manages the fuel required for Imperial service². As readers are aware (see p. 1097), the *Ta Ts‘ing hwui tien shi li*, published in 1818, is the largest existing collection of supplementary ordinances for executing the statutes established in the *Ta Ts‘ing hwui tien*. The ordinances regarding the two Imperial Cemeteries, found in its 711th chapter, cover up to "the mausoleum of Empress Hiao Shuh"—that is, the Ch‘ang ling. This tomb did not receive that name until the death of Jen Tsung, which occurred after the work was published. The Supplementary Edition of the *Ta Ts‘ing hwui tien*, also published in 1818 (see p. 1173), covers the same period; however, the *Ta Ts‘ing hwui tien tseh li* (ch. 137) only goes as far as the Yü ling, as this collection was published before the other two. Unless we specifically mention other authorities, the information in the following pages is drawn from the *T. Ts. h. t. shi li*. For reasons we do not fully understand, the dimensions it provides are, in most cases, slightly different from those found in the *T. Ts. h. t. tseh li*. We will review only the four oldest Imperial mausoleums, as the regulations for the Ch‘ang ling show that it differs so little from them that it does not require special attention.

The Hiao ling of Shi Tsu, being the first one built, has become the center around which all the mausoleums of the Eastern Cemetery are grouped, just as the Ch‘ang ling was in the great Ming Cemetery. However, its <term>tumulus</term> (burial mound) is much smaller than that of the Ch‘ang ling, standing only 1.5 <term>chang</term> high. Calculating the <term>chang</term> as 3.35 meters, this is a little over five meters.

while its circumference is barely 54.9 *chang* or about 184 meters. It seems to be a rule with the reigning Imperial House to have <term>tumuli</term> of moderate size; the height and circumference of those of the three next Emperors measure, according to the ordinances, 2 *chang* by 62.8, 1.3 by 66.4, and 1.5 by 64.9 respectively. The term by which the ordinances invariably denote the tumuli is Pao ting <note>寶頂: "Precious Top" or "Precious Dome."</note>, apparently meaning: "Crown or top of the Precious Relics."

In the Hiao ling, the Pao ch'ing <note>寶城: "Precious Wall."</note>, that is to say, the wall encompassing the tumulus, exceeds the latter only slightly in circumference, its entire length being given as 63 *chang*. This leads us to the conclusion that the space it encloses is entirely filled by the tumulus, for, assuming the latter and the wall both to be circular, their respective radii will be almost equal, differing by only 1.3 *chang* or about 4 meters—a figure representing perhaps the thickness of the wall. The reader may remember here that the tumulus wall of the Yung ling in the Ming Cemetery is even five meters thick (see p. 1233). In the King ling, as well as in the T'ai ling and the Yü ling, the radius-length of the wall likewise only slightly exceeds that of the tumulus, namely, by no more than 0.78, 2.62, and 1.35 *chang* respectively. In each of the four mausolea, the tumulus is considerably lower than the wall; the latter measures 2.4, 3.7, 2.1, and 2.6 *chang* in height respectively, leaving out the inches or hundredth parts of a *chang*.

The *T. Ts. h. t. shi li* and the Supplementary *T. Ts. h. t.* mention a yueh-ya ch'ing <note>月牙城: "Moon-crescent wall" or "Crescent city."</note> or "moon-tips wall," placed in each mausoleum behind the terrace bearing the Soul tower. It is either 2.1, 2.2, or 2.3 *chang* high; that of the T'ai ling has the same height as the tumulus wall, and in the other three mausolea, it is a few feet lower than the latter. It is perhaps a projection from the terrace, connected with the tumulus wall, and it may have something to do with footways or steps giving access to the top of the terrace. Its name is a puzzle to us. "Precisely in the middle," so we read, "is a glazed reflection wall" <note>正中琉璃影壁一座: "One glazed spirit screen (or shadow wall) exactly in the center."</note>, the position of which, however, is not described more definitely. We can only refer the reader to the "yellow glazed screen" stated by Ku Yen-wu to have stood within the tunnel of the Ch'ang ling of the Ming dynasty (p. 1221). tien (see p. 1307), every Soul tower is adorned with the name of the mausoleum in which it stands, painted or carved on a board affixed, no doubt, in the same place as the corresponding object in each Ming tomb. We read that Shing Tsu ordained in the same year in which he buried his father, "that the tower of the Hiao ling should henceforth be designated as a ‘Soul tower,’ and that a board inscribed with the characters Hiao ling should be suspended at the top of it" 1. Such a board was also affixed in each of the other three mausolea upon the burial of the Emperor for whom it was built 2. We read in the Rules and Regulations for the Board of Rites: "The Imperial Chancery shall propose a name for each mausoleum and present it to the Throne. After its approval by the Emperor, the Board of Rites shall request that the boards to be suspended against the Soul tower, the temple and its great gate, as well as the inscriptions to be placed on those boards in Manchu, Mongol, and Chinese, be delivered over to the office established in the mausoleum in question (as a branch of that Board), with orders to further do what is necessary. And after this office has reported that the boards are finished, the Bureau of Astrology shall select an auspicious day on which to reverently suspend them in their places. On that day, a President or Vice-President of the Board of Rites shall present a sacrifice on the sacrificial table before the Imperial coffin, and thereby inform the Soul of what is to take place; the written offertory for this occasion shall be composed by the Han-lin College, and the articles to be offered be prepared by the Court of Sacrificial Worship" 3.

One can only guess what is meant by this term, not knowing what to make of the Chinese characters representing it. It may denote the sealable mouth of the tunnel, but the regulations make no mention of tunnels at all. Mr. Bourne, however, asserts that they do exist; but we must take into consideration that he only saw a very small part of the Eastern Cemetery and that he does not categorically state that he saw any tunnels with his own eyes. He says that the entrance to the tomb is beneath the Soul tower, and that this building is connected by a descending passage with the burial mound <note>tumulus</note> within which the coffin lies <note>1 Proceedings of the Royal Geographical Society, vol. V, p. 26.</note>. That the coffins are placed within the crypt upon a ledge or couch, which is probably made of stone, and that the entrance to the crypt is closed by a door of the same material, the reader has seen on page 1290. According to Bourne,
> "there is
> behind the door, inside, a round hole cut in the stone of the
> floor; and when the door is shut, a large stone ball follows it
> and, falling into the hole, its protruding top prevents the door
> from ever opening again. The door itself is made of solid stone, and
> once shut, it may be smashed to pieces if enough force is applied,
> but it cannot be opened. When this door has been shut, the deceased 
> Emperor is said to be at peace forever" <note>2 *Ibid.*, p. 27.</note>.

Undoubtedly, the crypt in every Imperial tomb is built entirely of stone blocks; at least, apart from the clause in the basic decrees <note>rescripts</note> that suggests this (see p. 1307), such is the case with the crypts of the high-ranking Imperial secondary Consorts and Heirs-Apparent, for we read in the basic constitution:
> "The crypts for Con-
> cubines of the three highest ranks and those for Heirs-Apparent
> shall be of solid stone, but those of Concubines of the lower
> ranks shall be of bricks" <note>3 妃皇太子均以石、嬪貴人以甄爲壙. *Ta Qing hui dian*, ch. 76, l. 3.</note>.

The top of the burial mound <note>tumulus</note> can be reached by two so-called *ting tao* <note>4 磴道.</note> or "rising stone paths," an eastern and a western one. We learn this from some accounts the *Da Qing hui dian shi li* gives of visits paid by Sons of Heaven to the mausoleums of their fathers or mothers during the Qingming <note>Tsʻing ming</note> season, in which it is explicitly stated that they ascended the eastern *ting tao* with the object of placing some earth upon the mound. Consequently, these four edifices are pygmies when compared to the stupendous temple of the Ch‘ang ling, which covers more than four times as much ground. The meaning of the official name they bear we need not now explain after what we have said on page 1211 about the analogous name of the temples in the Ming Cemetery. It strikes the attention that the two names so closely resemble each other, the words *lung* and *ling* presenting hardly any difference, either in sound or meaning. No doubt this similarity is not accidental. The name Lung-ngen dates from 1663, when Shing Tsu resolved that the temple of the Hiao ling, where he had just then buried his father and mother, should thereafter bear it <note>5 *T. > "This road, leading from the Great (Red) Gate in the southern wall to the tomb of Shi Tsu—a distance of over three miles—is the main artery of the mausoleum enclosure, and from it branch off the roads leading to the tombs of the later Emperors, who, as our guide remarked, were only branches of the Imperial genealogical tree; and therefore the relation of their roads to that of Shi Tsu is as branches to the main stem. It is a magnificent avenue, bordered on each side by groves of fir trees planted at regular intervals. Our guide asked me triumphantly whether the requirements of <term>Fung-shui</term> were not perfectly fulfilled by this road. I was certainly impressed by its position and surroundings. To the north, straight in front, stood the snow-covered hills under which the tomb of the founder of the dynasty is built;"

<page-num>1323</page-num>
# THE ROADS OF THE SPIRITS, AND STONE IMAGES.

The widest scope has been left in this regard to the calculations of geomancers and architects, undoubtedly in connection with the layout and dimensions of the ground allocated for every mausoleum.

In one important respect, the Eastern Cemetery differs from that of the Ming dynasty in Ch'ang-p'ing. While the latter has only one single Spirit's road—consisting of a great tablet-house, an avenue adorned with images, and a dragon-and-phoenix gate—every Imperial tomb in the Eastern Cemetery possesses such a road of its own. According to the *T. Ts. h. t. shi li*, that of the King ling has, instead of a dragon-and-phoenix gate:

> "A decorative gate of stone, 7.01 <term>chang</term> long and 2.58 <term>chang</term> high. Furthermore, there are five pairs of stone effigies of living beings, arranged on the right and left, namely: one pair of civil officers dressed in the gowns and caps worn at Imperial audiences; one pair of military officers in coats of mail and wearing helmets; and one pair each of standing horses, standing elephants, and standing lions. Besides, it contains a pair of 'viewing columns,' 2.32 <term>chang</term> high, with a stone five-span bridge in front. Southward from this bridge stands a pavilion for the tablet which commemorates the holy virtues and divine feats; this building has a double roof, is 7.25 <term>chang</term> square, and its roof is 3.16 <term>chang</term> high. It contains two tablets, 2.3 <term>chang</term> high, 0.74 wide, and 0.29 thick, raised on pedestals shaped like dragons which measure 1.6 <term>chang</term> long by 0.61 high" $^1$.

The four "sky-bearing columns," their pedestals, and their balustrades all have the same dimensions as those in the Hiao ling. An avenue of the description provided above, with buildings and monuments of the same dimensions, is prescribed for the Yü ling, but with different stone animals, namely: "a pair of standing horses, unicorns, elephants, camels, <term>suanni</term> <note>A mythological lion-like creature</note>, and—"

"...lions”$^1$. Mr. Bourne says that there are five pairs of stone images in front of the Ting ling, but that they are very small (page 30); and Mayers informs us that such figures also decorate the Hwui ling $^2$.

Although they have separate Spirit’s roads, the Eastern Mausolea clearly form one great cemetery together, as they share all the buildings that stand outside the great tablet-house of the Hiao ling; the most important of these are the red gate and the decorative gates. A similar arrangement exists for the Western Cemetery. Indeed, the T’ai ling—the first mausoleum built there, which forms its main artery and, as the preceding pages have shown, resembles the mausolea in the Eastern Cemetery in every respect—is explicitly stated by the regulations to have an avenue which, like that of the Hiao ling, ends at a great red gate. Behind this gate is a hall for preparing ceremonial costumes, and in front of it stand two stone slabs warning all visitors to dismount, as well as three decorative gates. All these structures are stated to have the same dimensions as those at the Eastern Cemetery, except for some slight differences of a few inches. However, there are two stone lions outside the red gate, and a five-span stone bridge in front of the decorative gates.

The avenues of stone figures in the Western Cemetery seem to be of very little significance. According to the regulations, the T’ai ling and the Ch’ang ling are decorated with only one pair of civil and one pair of military officers, a pair of horses, elephants, and lions—all in a standing position—and a pair of columns $^3$. Süen Tsung specifically forbade the building of statues in front of his tomb, either out of a desire to avoid lavish spending or due to superstitious ideas $^4$. We have seen above that some avenues in the Eastern Cemetery contain figures of *swan-ni* $^5$. Some works say this word refers to an animal belonging to the lion class. However, it is clearly distinguished by the Chinese from the *shi* $^6$, or lion proper, as is evident from the fact that images of this animal are also explicitly mentioned by the regulations as standing in the avenues.

# THE STONE IMAGES OF SWAN-NI AND LIONS.

The *swan-ni* is already mentioned in the *'Rh ya*. "It resembles a short-haired tiger and devours tigers and leopards,"¹ this work says; and Kwoh Poh, its commentator, adds: "Consequently, it is a lion and lives in the western regions."² The word *swan-ni* may, perhaps, be a foreign name for the lion, or its name in a local dialect of southwestern China, where we might assume this animal was, or still is, native. Perhaps the lion-like monsters in the great Cemetery of the Ming dynasty, which we depicted on page 818 in Plate XX, represent the *swan-ni*.

To those of our readers who have read our study on the Chinese eulogistic sepulchral tablets and have thus reached a proper understanding of their high significance in the Religion of the Dead, it will be obvious that the most important monuments in the various Spirit's roads of the Imperial mausoleum grounds are the tablets "commemorating the sage virtues and divine merits or feats." No one will, therefore, be surprised to hear that the biographies, carved into those stones, were entirely and piously composed by the "Sons of Heaven" [the Emperors] themselves, either in name or in reality; each of them considered it one of his sacred duties to perpetuate the glorious memory of his father with his own writing brush. Their anxiety to express their filial feelings as strongly as possible in this way soon began to drive them beyond the limits of brevity and to require the erection of two tablets in every pavilion. A single slab, even one of the enormous size they all are, became too small to contain so much praise and grandiloquence in two languages, especially if the deceased had reigned for a long time.

The first for whom two tablets were raised was Shing Tsu, the second Emperor. We read:

> "With a view to the erection at the King ling of a tablet recording the sage virtues and divine feats, a Grand Secretary, a President of the Board of Works, and a President of the Bureau of Astrology were commissioned in the third year of the Yung ching period to determine by survey and calculation a square spot suitable to build it on. They received the following instructions from the Emperor: 'The record of the life of Shi Tsu, placed on his tablet, is brief and concise. But Shing Tsu having been on the throne for more than sixty years,"

# ->SHI TSU'S BIOGRAPHY, CARVED IN STONE.<-

The measures prescribed in this edict have undoubtedly been followed in the construction of every tablet-house, as they are established as general standard regulations among the Rules and Regulations for the Board of Rites <note>In chapter 143, line 19.</note>. Our readers will be mistaken if they think that those Imperial funeral biographies—carved in solid stone and carefully protected from atmospheric influences by a strong roof and massive walls—are valuable historical documents, especially useful because no official history of the Ts'ing dynasty yet exists. Because they are exclusively laudatory—as filial piety forbids a son to criticize his father's deeds—they cannot, indeed, claim to be trustworthy sketches of the characters of the sovereigns to whose memory they are dedicated. Moreover, only bare feats and achievements are recorded within them with the utmost brevity and without any additional detail; in most cases, even the dates are omitted. We offer this judgment, however, only regarding the tablet inscriptions for the first three Emperors, as these are the only ones for which we have reprints, specifically in the *Wen hien t'ung khao* <note>Chapters 151 and 152.</note>; we have never seen a copy of the others. As our readers may wish to obtain an idea of the contents of such biographies, we paraphrase here that of Shi Tsu, the first Emperor, which is the shortest, containing only 1,435 characters. The tablet was erected in 1668.

After mentioning the parents of this monarch, the text goes on to relate that, before his birth, a miraculous light emanated from his mother's body, and that she dreamed of a mysterious individual who handed a son to her, saying he would one day rule over the whole wide world. At the birth, a red glow and fragrant scents filled the Palace. When only six years old, he could read and recite from memory, without the help of his teacher, several columns of characters at once after merely looking them over. At that tender age, he was placed on the throne of

The Board of Astronomy shall choose the auspicious dates for breaking ground and erecting the stone tablet. The Board of Works shall manage the manufacturing of the stone tablet, the construction of the tablet pavilion, and other related matters. One day before the work begins, one senior official from the Board of Works shall perform a sacrifice to the God of the Earth; one day before the tablet is erected, one senior official from the Board of Rites shall be ordered to perform a sacrifice at the Yü Mausoleum. The Sacrificial Court shall handle the ritual matters, and the Hanlin Academy shall draft the prayers. On the day the stone tablet is completed, high ministers shall be ordered to respectfully supervise the carving of the text. The Board of Rites shall submit a report regarding all high ministers who should be sent to survey the site, supervise the carving, and perform the sacrifices. — *T. Ts. h. t. shi li, ch. 348, ll. 6 seq.*

<page-num>1330</page-num>

# THE GRAVE.

China and established his court at Peking. The different parts of the empire were then reduced to submission by military force, and various measures were taken for the relief of the people, such as the abolition of taxes and tributes and the ending of oppressive forced labor at the frontiers. At the same time, the Emperor devoted his attention to the compilation of a code of laws. He behaved most dutifully toward his deceased parents and grandfather and dedicated his nights with such zeal to the study of the Manchu and Chinese languages that he became thoroughly versed in philosophy, natural science, astronomy, <term>geomancy</term>, rites and ceremonies, music, military tactics, jurisprudence, taxation, and medical science—in short, every branch of knowledge.

In dressing and eating, he observed moderation and simplicity; he spent considerable sums for the restoration of temples dedicated to Confucius and gave much of his attention to the competitive examinations for official ranks. He gave his Manchu and Chinese subjects equal rights, and he placed civil and military officers on the same level. He ordered his mandarins to be just and equitable but to execute the laws with leniency. He personally plowed the ground at the altar to the God of Agriculture, thus teaching the people by his example to devote themselves with zeal to the production of food.

Wherever inundation, drought, or any other calamity harassed his subjects, he provided relief, doing so even in Yunnan and Kwei-cheu after the people there had been reduced to submission by his armies. He established guards at the mausoleums of the Ming dynasty, issued effective prohibitions for the protection of the trees growing there, and ordained that sacrifices should be presented to the last sovereign of that extinct House; moreover, he conferred honors upon the officers who had sacrificed their lives in its cause and aided their families. It is no wonder, then, that the beneficial effect of his favors was felt even in remote regions beyond the frontiers of the empire proper, and southward even as far as the Liu-kiu islands, Siam, Holland, and the Western Ocean, so that "hundreds of overseas kingdoms, seeing that the four seas were without any waves, exclaimed unanimously: 'A holy man has appeared in the Middle Kingdom!'" <note>1. Southward to the Ryukyu Islands, Siam, Holland, the Western Ocean, and hundreds of other overseas countries, seeing the sea without waves (at peace), all said: "A Sage has emerged in the Middle Kingdom."</note>. Finally, we are informed of the exact date of the Emperor's death, his age, and the duration of his reign.

<summary>This page concludes the idealized biography of the Shunzhi Emperor, detailing his scholarly achievements, his fair treatment of both Manchu and Chinese subjects, and his efforts to honor the preceding Ming dynasty. The text emphasizes the peace and international respect his reign supposedly achieved.</summary>

# THE WALLS AND THE MILITARY STATIONS.

...as well as his admirable testamentary instructions that all useless expenditure for the embellishment of his mausoleum should be avoided, and no precious articles should be buried with him. Subsequently, the entire biography is repeated in the form of a eulogistic metrical composition of thirty-two lines of eight characters, with all the lines ending with the same rhyme, after which follow three extra lines of eight characters, constituting a hymn in praise of the mausoleum in which the remains of this great man rest.

This commemorative tablet inscription, consequently, does not essentially differ from those which the Chinese have been accustomed for many ages to display on the graves of distinguished persons (see p. 1163), nor from the <term>mo chi-ming</term>, placed in the graves of the official and non-official class for more than a thousand years. Indeed, it also consists of a biography (<term>chi</term>), followed by a poetic eulogy (<term>ming</term>). The tablet inscriptions for the second and the third Emperors are composed in exactly the same way. That of <term>Shing Tsu</term> contains more than three times as many characters as his predecessor's. This can hardly be attributed to the fact of his having reigned more than three times as long, since the tablet inscription of his successor, who wore the crown for only a dozen years, is extended to almost exactly the same length.

In either Cemetery, the oldest mausoleum stands, according to the regulations, within a vast area surrounded by a wall. This wall has a total length of 6,439.48 <term>chang</term>, or nearly 22 kilometers, in the Eastern Cemetery, with a height of 1.3 <term>chang</term>; in the Western Cemetery, it is 4,399 <term>chang</term>, or about 15 kilometers long, and 1.45 high. These enormous lengths suggest that either wall encompasses, if not the whole Cemetery to which it belongs, a very large part of it, and that the Red Gate forms its main entrance. We believe the walls were built because of geomantic considerations, as the Rules and Regulations for the Board of Works mention “<term>Fung-shui</term> walls enclosing the Eastern and the Western Mausolea” <note>Eastern and Western Mausoleum Feng-shui enclosure walls. Chapter 105, line 3.</note>. Mr. Bourne says that, in the Eastern Cemetery, “the Great Wall, forming the northern boundary, is met at <term>Ma-lan Chen</term> <note>Malan Town.</note>, a military station at the north-east corner of the enclosure, at right angles by a plain brick wall, about nine feet high, called the <term>Fung-shui</term> wall, which encloses the...

From Ma-lan Chen this wall runs nearly due south as far as <term>Ma-lan Yü</term> <note>馬蘭峪.</note>, after passing which it turns slightly towards the west and runs in a south-southwest direction until it is opposite the small town of <term>Sin-ch'ing</term> <note>新城.</note>, a distance of five miles, where it turns to the west. The eastern side of the enclosure is thus about five miles long. From the distances traversed within the wall, I should think the width of the space enclosed, from east to west, must also be about five miles. The area of the inner enclosure would be, on this supposition, about 25 square miles or 16,000 acres. But besides this, a wide tract outside the boundary wall, and the ranges of hills on the south and south-west, belong to the mausoleums and are forbidden ground. The <term>Fung-shui</term> wall only supplies a boundary when there is no natural one. It shuts off the valleys, but unlike the Great Wall, which seems to select the highest peaks and the most precipitous crags and boldly scale them, it does not ascend the hills . . . The <term>Fung-shui</term> wall is pierced at several points on the east and south by small gates, through which pass the materials used in building and repairs, and all the traffic that is allowed. The main entrance is on the southern side. It is called the great Red Gate, and is never opened except for the passage of an Emperor" <note>Pages 24 and 27.</note>.

The <term>Fung-shui</term> walls by no means form the extreme limits of the burial grounds. They are surrounded by a very broad tract of so-called ***chung ti*** <note>重地.</note>: "important ground," which term in general denotes all soil reserved for Imperial or Government use. The ***chung ti*** of the two Cemeteries are also known as "the grounds constituting the Dragon of the backside" <note>後龍地方.</note>, that is to say, the hills embodying the good celestial and terrestrial influences of the area they encircle (compare page 951). "Outside the outer wall surrounding the mausoleums," thus we read in the fundamental ordinances, "shall be placed red posts, three in a mile, within which it shall be forbidden to gather fuel or to till the soil. And outside this cordon of red posts, either at forty <term>pu</term> from there, or at twenty, a cordon of white posts shall be placed, followed ten miles beyond by a cordon of blue posts, from which boards shall be suspended, displaying a prohibition to this effect: 'Nobody belonging to the...

### *The special Mausolea of Empresses.*

After the above summary of official decrees concerning the two Imperial Cemeteries, little remains to be said about the mausolea of those Empresses who, for reasons explained on page 1286, could not be buried in the tombs of their husbands who died before them. It is a fact that the ordinances regarding the <term>Chao-si ling</term>, the <term>Hiao-tung ling</term>, and the <term>T'ai-tung ling</term>, laid down in the <term>Ta Ts’ing hwui tien shi li</term> <note>2 In chapter 711.</note>, show that these sepulchers closely resemble the Imperial mausolea in all essential features. Furthermore, the dimensions of nearly all the principal structures are identical, except for an occasional difference of a few feet or inches. However, for the burial mounds (<term>tumuli</term>) and the walls surrounding them, figures are given which show that their circumferences are barely half as large as those of the corresponding structures in the Imperial tombs. In each of the three mentioned mausolea, the square fortress is a little smaller than the average size of those in the Imperial tombs. No "moon-tips wall" is mentioned, nor is there a decorative gate in front of the grave altar. A quite different arrangement of the buildings is found in the <term>Chao-si ling</term>, as its gate with glazed ornaments stands in front of the temple, and the temple is flanked by two <term>Ling-ts'in</term> gates, each with one opening. For every mausoleum, it is prescribed that trees shall be planted along the Spirit’s road, arranged like those at the Imperial tombs. However, no mention is made of stone images, nor of any associated dragon-and-phoenix gates or tablet houses; evidently, such decorations are found exclusively at the tombs of the "Sons of Heaven" (the Emperors). One may gain an idea of the surface area of the Empresses' mausolea from the figures that the ordinances provide for the lengths of the square walls surrounding them. That of the <term>Chao-si ling</term> is stated to be 108 <term>chang</term>, and that of the <term>Hiao-tung ling</term> is 189 (or 162, according to the <term>Ta Ts’ing hwui tien tseh li</term>), while that of the <term>T'ai-tung ling</term> measures 98 <term>chang</term>.

->THE SPECIAL MAUSOLEA FOR EMPRESSES.<-

The <term>Chao-si ling</term> also has an outer wall with a total length of 136 <term>chang</term> and a height of 1.23 <term>chang</term>.
The reason why the Empresses who survived their husbands had mausolea built for them that were as grand and magnificent as those of the Emperors themselves is undoubtedly because each of these women was also the ruler of the Empire for a time during the reign of her son. For the great social law—that whatever a child possesses is the property of their living parents—allows no exception, even regarding the realm and the crown. The Imperial power that falls to an Empress Dowager in this way may be exercised by her with great determination if she possesses energy and courage. The two mothers of <term>Muh Tsung</term>, mentioned on page 1299, are well known to have bent the Empire to their will throughout his entire reign.

### *The Mausolea of Imperial Concubines.*
As was the case with the Ming dynasty (see p. 1240), the current ruling House is in the habit of giving the principal secondary wives of the Emperors a burial in the Imperial Cemeteries. In 1681, when <term>Shing Tsu</term> buried his two Consorts, <term>Hiao Ch'ing</term> and <term>Hiao Chao</term>, in the mausoleum intended for himself (see page 1290), he established nearby a tomb for his <term>fei</term> <note>1 <term>Fei</term> (妃).</note>, or Concubines of the third rank <note>2 <term>Ta Ts'ing hwui tien shi li</term>, chapter 349, line 11.</note>. About twelve of them were buried there at different times, including some who became entitled to a place in it because they were elevated to the rank of <term>fei</term> after the Emperor’s death <note>3 <term>Wen hien t'ung khao</term>, chapter 241, lines 24 and following.</note>.
Of his <term>p'in</term>, <term>kwei-jen</term>, and <term>shu-fei</term> <note>4 <term>P'in</term> (嬪), <term>kwei-jen</term> (貴人), and <term>shu-fei</term> (庶妃).</note>—Concubines of the three lower ranks, of whom he had about twenty-one in total <note>5 <term>Wen hien t'ung khao</term>, chapter 241, lines 26–29.</note>—not one is recorded as being buried in that sepulcher. It is remarkable that this same <term>Shing Tsu</term>, who was so anxious to provide a beautiful mausoleum for his own Concubines, did not show such concern for those of his father; for we read that "when the burial ceremonies for <term>Hiao Hwui</term>, the Empress Chang, were finished, auspicious times were chosen to bury the <term>fei</term> and
