### *The Administration of the Mausoleums.*

Since an all-pervading bureaucratic officialism dominates the Chinese State, it can hardly be expected that the tombs of the Imperial Family would not be under its sway. Indeed, they constitute an integral part of the machinery of the State, ranking, as they do, among the principal places for the exercise of the Imperial or official religion.

The welfare and misfortune of the Imperial House, as well as the maintenance and glory of its throne, being entirely dependent on the condition and preservation of those sepulchres, it is natural that the chief control over them is exercised by very high-ranking members of that House itself. That is to say, they are managed by certain Princes of various ranks—members of the Imperial Family entitled <term>Wang</term>, <term>Baira</term>, or <term>Kung</term>—and other High Ministers, as well as a staff of Bodyguard officers, and so on <note>1. Princes of the Blood, Baira, Kung, High Ministers, and Bodyguards, etc. Rules and Regulations for the Board of Rites, chapter 143, line 7.</note>. In either cemetery, they constitute what is called a <term>Yamen</term> for the General Management of Matters relating to the Mausoleums <note>2. Yamen for the General Management of Mausoleum Affairs.</note>, or a <term>Yamen</term> entrusted with the Management of Matters <note>3. Yamen Entrusted with the Management of Affairs.</note>, to which are attached one or two Assistant Secretaries <note>4. Assistant Secretary.</note>, and some clerks, either two or four <note>5. Work and chapter cited above, lines 9 and 11; *Wen hien t'ung khao*, chapter 84, lines 3 and 4.</note>. The buildings erected for this staff in or near the Eastern Cemetery are, according to the ordinances: a mansion for the <term>Baira</term>, consisting of 130 compartments; a mansion of 60 compartments for the <term>Kung</term>; 390 apartments for the officers and soldiers of the Bodyguard; an office building consisting of 23 apartments; and 4 apartments for each Assistant Secretary and each clerk. In the Western Cemetery, there is a mansion of 60 compartments and another of 40, respectively for the <term>Baira</term> and the <term>Kung</term>; 60 apartments for the High Ministers, 96 for the Bodyguards, and 49 constituting an office building <note>6. Supplementary *Ta Ts'ing hui tien*, chapter 48; *Ta Ts'ing hui tien shih li*, chapter 713, line 8.</note>.

These two high committees also have to point out to the Crown the most eligible locations for all the mausoleums that are to be constructed <note>7. Rules and Regulations for the Board of Rites, chapter 143, line 17.</note>.

They undoubtedly also utilize the guidance of the eighteen Chinese geomancers attached to the Imperial Bureau of Astrology with the title of **Yin-and-Yang Masters** <note>1. 陰陽生.</note>, who, besides other duties, "must perform divinations regarding the construction of buildings by observing the influences of the **Yin** and the **Yang**" <note>2. Observe the Yin and the Yang to divine regarding construction. *Ta Ts’ing hwui tien*, chapter 86, line 1.</note>.

Of the six great Boards established at Peking, none, of course, must interfere with the mausoleums as often as the Board of Works, as the execution of all technical projects planned by the State is its responsibility. We may repeat here what we have already stated on page 1310: a special subdivision of this Board, called The Administrative Bureau of Government Reservations, is charged with carrying out all the official decrees concerning mausoleums and sepulchers of every kind. This bureau is composed of four Manchu and one Chinese Senior Secretaries <note>3. 郎中.</note>, five Manchu and one Chinese Second Class Secretaries <note>4. 員外郎.</note>, and two Chinese and three Manchu Assistant Secretaries <note>5. 主事.</note>, one of whom must be a member of the Imperial Clan <note>6. *Ta Ts'ing hwui tien*, chapter 70, line 2, and the Supplementary Edition of that work, chapter 48.</note>.

In both cemeteries, this Bureau is represented by a so-called "Yamen of the Board of Works" <note>7. 工部衙門.</note>, established respectively in a place called Shih-men or Shih-men Yih <note>8. 石門 or 石門驛.</note>, located southeast of the Eastern Cemetery, and in Yih-cheu, the chief city of the department of the same name where the Western Cemetery lies (see p. 1293). These **Yamen** consist of the following members:

Senior Board Secretaries, 郎中; in the Eastern Cemetery 1, in the Western 1.
Second Class Secretaries, 員外郎; in the Eastern Cemetery 4, in the Western 3.
Assistant Secretaries, 主事; in the Eastern Cemetery —, in the Western 3.
Writers, 筆帖式; in the Eastern Cemetery 4, in the Western 2.
Hired Clerks, 書吏; in the Eastern Cemetery 2, in the Western 2.

Moreover, forty patrolling soldiers under a Pa-tsung <note>1. 把總.</note> or Sergeant are attached to each Yamen for the guarding of its stores. In the Eastern Cemetery, these men are drafted from the garrison of Ma-lan Chen, a military station situated, as we saw on page 1331, at the northeast corner of the walled grounds; in the Western Cemetery, they are drafted from the T'ai-ning Chen <note>2. 泰寧鎮.</note> garrison, a station which we cannot find on any of the maps available to us.

Each of these two Yamens uses an official seal, kept by its Senior Board Secretary. For the accommodation of their constituents, an office building and a storehouse, besides several living apartments <note>3. *Ta Ts'ing Hwui Tien Shi Li*, chapter 713, line 8; and the Supplementary Edition of the *Ta Ts'ing Hwui Tien*, chapter 48.</note>, have been built in both Shih-men and Yih-cheu. Since 1740, immediate control has been exercised over them by the Princes and Magnates entrusted with the general management of the Cemeteries. To these grandees, they must refer for verification of their estimates of the expenditures required for building and repairs, wages and food for the workmen, etc. <note>4. *Ta Ts'ing Hwui Tien Shi Li*, chapter 712, line 1; and *Ta Ts'ing Hwui Tien Tseh Li*, chapter 137, lines 15 and following.</note>. Every year, in the tenth month, each Yamen for General Management must report to the Throne regarding the repairs that are to be undertaken in the Cemetery entrusted to its supervision. A Vice-President <note>5. 侍郎.</note> of the Board of Works in Peking is then sent to the spot with a suite of subordinates to verify the report and make an estimate of the costs; thereupon, it is proposed to the Throne to allow the supreme Yamen in question to order the local Yamen of the Board of Works to undertake those repairs under its constant control. When the repairs are finished, a Vice-President of the Board of Works, commissioned for the purpose by the Throne, inspects them thoroughly, and for the proper control of all following repairs, he registers them at his Board. It is prescribed that the original cost estimate must not be exceeded for any works, nor may any supplementary funds be granted. The yearly expenditure for repairs may not exceed nine hundred taels in the Eastern Cemetery, and five hundred in the Western <note>6. *Ta Ts'ing Hwui Tien Shi Li*, chapter 713, line 14; and the Rules and Regulations for the Board of Works, chapter 105, line 2.</note>. These sums are strikingly small, but unpaid or poorly paid labor may make up the difference. In accordance with a special decree issued by Shing Tsu in 1669, the

In each cemetery, the Yamen of the Board of Works employs a permanent body of laborers at every mausoleum, placed under a <term>Ling-ts'ui</term> <note>4. 領催.</note> or "Urger," that is, a corporal. Besides the construction and the repairs of buildings, bridges, walls, etc., the Board of Works has to devote its best care to the forests with which the two cemeteries are covered in every direction, and to pay from its treasuries the expenses the planting involves. The foresters whom, as we saw above, it maintains in its service for this purpose, have to occupy themselves mainly with sowing or planting new trees in the place of those that die or are uprooted by storms. Considering how much respect and care have, since very ancient times, been shown in China for grave-trees, and how much utility for the preservation of <term>Fung-shui</term> is attributed to them, we cannot feel surprised that the present dynasty has always shown itself warmly interested in its own burial forests, issuing all sorts of edicts regulating their management. In 1694, Shing Tsu prescribed the planting of the trees at specified distances of two <term>chang</term>—that is to say (see p. 1334), the same distance that separates them in the rows flanking the several Spirit Roads. In 1748, it was decreed by Kao Tsung that the <term>Yamens</term> for the General Management of the Mausolea should hold five-year inspections in order to ascertain how many trees had in the meantime died, and report to the Throne how many new ones ought to be planted in their stead at the cost of the Board of Works, through the joint care of the Imperial Household Department and the two <term>Yamens</term> of the Board of Works.

From an edict issued in 1759, we learn that up to that year it was customary for the officials in the Eastern Cemetery to sell all the dead trees whose timber was not wanted for the construction of buildings or for repairs. That custom, the edict says, had worked very harmfully, as many good trees had prematurely fallen under the axe, a prey to official greed; therefore, wishing to put a stop to such looting, the Emperor ordered that no wood should henceforth be sold unless it was first sawn apart and broken into pieces. Reports of the proceeds, the edict further prescribed, would have to be submitted to the Treasurer of the Provincial Exchequer <note>2. 藩司 [fān sī].</note>, and the proceeds in

Some Committees do not have a Comptroller-General among their members. In such cases, the position of Seal-keeper falls to the Senior Secretary of the Board of Rites, and he shares it with an additional Senior Secretary from the Household Department. In the Committee of the *T'ai ling*, a Senior Secretary of the Board of Works sits alongside the Senior Secretary of the Board of Rites, and it includes among its members a Second-Class Secretary of the Board of Works, who replaces one of those from the Board of Rites. Not every Committee contains all the other members mentioned in the table above, but we will pass over those variations in silence.

The Committees appointed for the special mausoleums of Empresses differ little from those established for the mausoleums of the Emperors. They are not presided over by a Comptroller-General. The Committees entrusted with the care of the tombs of Concubines consist merely of Reciters of Offertories, Ceremonial Ushers, and Writers, and, in some cases, one or two Officers for the Presentation of Tea and Food, and Assistant Secretaries or Assistant Managers of the Imperial Household <note>1</note>. It is, however, probable that each of these tombs also falls under the control of the Committee for the mausoleum of the corresponding Empress. The collections of ordinances show us that every Committee was appointed as soon as the first body was deposited in the mausoleum concerned.

To accommodate these various administrative bodies, numerous buildings exist in both Cemeteries under the care of the two <term>Yamen</term> of the Board of Works. As many of these men belong to the Board of Revenue or the Board of Civil Office, and the mausolea are all garrisoned, the Supreme Boards—except for the Board of Punishments—all have their representatives at each site.

The two quotations above show us that the food, drinks, and delicacies to be offered at regular times in every mausoleum to the spirits <note>Manes</note> of its occupants are grown or produced within its grounds, and that the cattle required for the same purpose are raised on the spot. The number of cows to be kept in the King ling is fixed by the Ordinances at fifty-two, compared to only five head prescribed for the T'ai-tung ling; the numbers for the other mausolea all fall between these two. The Ordinances set the daily fodder rations for the cattle at four pints <note>shing ²</note> of peas and three bunches of hay or straw per head. The Code of Laws protects the cattle from mistreatment and thieves through a specific article, a translation of which we provided on page 909. There are also numerous horses in the two cemeteries, as the horse was inseparable from the processions of Chinese officials and especially essential to the Manchu soldiers, a unit of which is stationed at every mausoleum. Every Senior Secretary is entitled to keep five servants or followers ³ and seven horses; a Second-Class Secretary and an Assistant Secretary may have four followers and six horses; and every Reciter of Offertories and Ceremonial Usher may have two followers and three horses. These officers and their servants each receive a daily allowance of eight hoh ⁴ and three choh ⁵ (0.83 shing) of rice.

### *The Garrisons of the Mausolea.*

From our description of the principal Cemetery of the House of Ming, our readers know that—just as was probably the case with the burial places of the dynasties that have successively ruled the Chinese Empire—it was placed under the protection of a large military division with headquarters in two neighboring fortified stations, and that every mausoleum also possessed a special garrison. A similar organization exists for the cemeteries of the current reigning House.

A brigade detached from the Chinese land forces or "Green Army" ², named for the color of their standards, is garrisoned in the areas surrounding each cemetery to protect the forbidden grounds from intrusion and the Fung-shui from attacks and injury. At the Eastern Cemetery, it has its headquarters in Ma-lan Chen (see p. 1331). An office building exists there for the Tsung-ping 總兵 or "General", an officer of the second military rank; it contains eighty-two compartments. Furthermore, we find in that station a smaller office for a Yiu-kih 遊擊, an officer of the third rank; one for a Sheu-pi 守備 or "Chief of the Guards", who belongs to the fifth rank and commands the Left Battalion (左營) of the brigade; and one for a similar officer of the Right Battalion (右營). Additionally, five stations each possess an office of four compartments for a Ts'ien-tsung 千總 or "Chiliarch", a military official of the sixth rank, while ten other stations have such a building for a Pa-tsung 把總 or Sergeant, belonging to the seventh rank ³.

Regarding the privates commanded by these officers, no records are given in the ordinances. However, they are undoubtedly numerous, as the apartments assigned to them as lodgings reach the significant number of 1,368 ⁴.

The Chinese garrison of the Western Cemetery is organized on the same footing. In its headquarters at T'ai-ning Chen (see p. 1341)

They must immediately arrest every transgressor and deliver him to the Princes charged with General Management, so that they may punish him as the laws translated on pages 903, 911, and 913 require. The reader has seen that those articles prescribe well-deserved punishment to be inflicted also on the soldiers and their chiefs, should they fail to prevent such crimes as those mentioned above, or help the perpetrators in escaping. On the other hand, these men are entitled to rewards if they show extraordinary zeal in making arrests. According to a decree of the year 1807, the officers of a picket or station are to be honorably mentioned twice in the records of their superiors whenever they arrest one primary offender or three accomplices before they have done any injury to the trees, but only once for the capture of one or two accomplices. And should the soldiers act without any direct orders from their superiors, eight <term>taels</term> are to be paid to their leader and four to his associates if they catch the primary offender or three or more accomplices, but only half of these amounts if they seize one or two accomplices. No rewards are awarded for arrests made after the theft or the tree-felling was completed; but in such cases, no punishment for lack of vigilance is imposed on the arresters. Should a station or a picket, by arresting the primary offender, save any trees from damage in a tract not under its immediate control, its officers are promoted one rank, and they are mentioned once, twice, three, or even four times, according to whether one, two, three, four, or more accomplices were seized. If the capture of the primary offender was carried out by the soldiers without direct orders, their leader is rewarded with ten <term>taels</term> and one good mark for great merit, and his associates with five <term>taels</term> and one mark for ordinary merit, while for the capture of one or two accomplices the rewards are five <term>taels</term> and 2½ respectively, and for three or more accomplices, twice these sums. Foreseeing, no doubt, that all these tempting rewards might lead to the arrest and harassment of innocent people, the same decree specifically reminds them that such injustices are punishable according to the laws on illegal arrest ¹.

Reports are made about every tree blown down by storms or withered in the area placed under their special control. A report is then submitted to the Princes, who send information regarding the number and dimensions of such trees to the <term>Yamen</term> of the Board of Works, the bureau of the officers belonging to the Board of Rites, and the <term>Yamen</term> for General Management. This is done so that these departments may always know where to find good timber for the construction and repair of the buildings, and fuel for burnt sacrifices. In the event that the timber and fuel gained in this way do not meet the requirements, the deficiency must be supplied exclusively from the areas beyond the blue posts <note>1</note>, so that, clearly, no living tree on the burial grounds may be cut down for any purpose whatsoever within the sacred grounds.

Apart from the <term>Green Army</term> troops that form a garrison in either cemetery, each mausoleum is occupied by Manchu soldiers belonging to the <term>Eight Banners</term>. In an Emperor’s mausoleum, this force is organized as follows:

One <term>Tsung-kwan</term> or "Commander," an officer of the third rank.

Two <term>Yih-ling</term> or <term>Yih-ch'ang</term>, "Wing Commanders"; fourth rank.

Sixteen <term>Fang-yü</term>, "Chiefs of the Guards"; fifth degree.

Two <term>Hiao-k'i-kiao</term>, "Mounted Aides-de-Camp or Adjutants"; sixth degree.

Two <term>Pih-t'ieh-shih</term>, "Writers."

Eighty <term>Ling-ts'ui</term>, "Urgers"—namely, a kind of corporal—and <term>Ma-kiah</term> or "Horsemen," who are first-class private soldiers.

In none of the mausolea specifically built for Empresses do we find a Commander or any Wing Commanders. The mausolea for the Concubines are garrisoned on the same footing, but the Chiefs of the Guards there number either eight or four, with only one Aide-de-Camp and forty corporals and privates.

Six or seven apartments are assigned to each Commander, three or five to a Wing Commander, three or four to a Chief of the Guards, four to a Writer, and either two or three to an Aide-de-Camp, a corporal, or a soldier <note>2</note>.

By simple calculation, we find the total of those Manchu garrisons to be about 1,300 men in the Eastern Cemetery and 800 in the Western. Apparently, the Chiefs of the Guards are settled in the mausolea permanently and are succeeded by their offspring, for we read in the fundamental ordinances:

> "When any <term>Fang-yü</term> appointed for the defense and protection of the mausolea resigns—whose functions have been exercised there by more than three of his ancestors consecutively, and who is over eighty years old—one of his sons or grandsons is to be selected to succeed him. And if, though he may not have served until his eightieth year, there be among his sons and grandsons any individuals possessing an official degree and meeting the required qualifications, one of them may be selected as the chief candidate for the post" <note>1. Supplementary Edition of the T. Ts. h. t., chapter 68, line 18.</note>.

Throughout each cemetery, small "picket rooms" <note>2. 堆撥房</note> are built for the use of the Manchu garrisons. They are described as standing outside the great red gate, as well as in front of the great tablet-houses, and at the upper ends of the avenues of stone figures. Moreover, as stated above, at these locations and before every temple gate, there are two guardhouses <note>3. 班房</note> of three compartments <note>4. T. Ts. h. t. shi li, chapter 711.</note> on either side, so that all the principal passages are guarded in the same manner as the main entrance of a <term>Yamen</term> is usually flanked by police rooms.

The Manchu dynasty, currently on the throne, traces its origin to an ancestor known as <term>Aisin Gioro</term> <note>5. 愛新覺羅</note>, which means "the man bearing the surname of Gold." This suggests a descent from the Tatar <term>Kin</term> <note>6. 金</note> dynasty, or "the Golden," which conquered Northern China from the <term>Sung</term> dynasty in the twelfth century and ruled those regions...

It is stated that Aisin Gioro lived in the valley of Hotuala <note>1. 赫圖阿喇</note>, where Yenden now stands; however, his history is shrouded in mystery. He stands at the head of a lineage of ancestors, worshipped by the dynasty through established ceremonies as the protective deities of its throne and crown. He is known by the temple name of Chao Tsu <note>2. 肇祖</note>, "the Ancestor who laid the Foundation," a title conferred on him along with the honorary title of Yuen Hwang-ti <note>3. 原皇帝</note>, "the First or Original Emperor," in 1648 by the youthful Emperor Shi Tsu, five years after he ascended the Chinese throne. Since 1636, his family had worshipped him under the posthumous name of Tseh Wang <note>4. 澤王</note>, "Prince or King Tseh," which was bestowed on him in that year by Shi Tsu’s father, T'ai Tsung <note>5. 太宗</note>, a Tatar king who waged war against China at that time with remarkable boldness and energy.

Three descendants of Aisin Gioro have held a similar position in the ancestral worship of the dynasty since the beginning of its reign. They were likewise granted the title of <term>Wang</term> in 1636, and were given the following temple names and posthumous names in 1648:

Hing Tsu 興祖, Emperor Chih 直皇帝. Great-grandson of Aisin Gioro.

King Tsu 景祖, Emperor Yih 翼皇帝, fourth son of Hing Tsu. He is known in the Annals as the <term>Baira</term> of Ninguta <note>6. 寧古塔貝勒</note>, a town in Kirin.

Hien Tsu 顯祖, Emperor Süen 宣皇帝, fourth son of King Tsu.

The eldest son of Hien Tsu—known as the Wise <term>Baira</term> <note>7. 聰睿貝勒</note>, or more generally as Novurh-hochih or Nurhachu—brought several Mongol princes under his power and was proclaimed Emperor by them in 1606. In 1616, he styled himself Emperor Ying Ming <note>8. 英明皇帝</note> and adopted the reign title <term>T'ien ming</term> <note>9. 天命</note>, "Appointment by Heaven." He died ten years later at the age of sixty-eight. When his eldest son T'ai Tsung, who succeeded him, conferred the title of <term>Wang</term> on the first four ancestors as previously mentioned, Ying Ming was simultaneously granted the temple name of—

The hostilities of the Manchus against the Ming dynasty, carried on with vigor during T'ai Tsu's reign, reached their peak under his son and successor, who gave his House the name of Ta Ts'ing <note>3. 大清</note>, "The Great Pure," in 1636. In the next year, the Manchu armies captured Peking and there enthroned T'ai Tsung's ninth son, a child hardly six years old. He is the monarch who has been known since his death by the temple name of Shi Tsu, and he was the first to be buried in Chinese soil <note>6. The above particulars are gathered from the *Tung hwa luh*, chapter 1; the *Wen hien t'ung khao*, chapter 239, lines 1–13; etc.</note>.

Under the pressure, no doubt, of his Chinese councilors, the boy-Emperor—following the example of the founders of former dynasties and of the first monarch of the House just dethroned—changed the tombs of his forefathers into stately cenotaphs, expecting them to become strong foundations for the <term>Fung-shui</term> and prosperity of his family and crown. The four eldest ancestors originally rested, in the company of their respective principal consorts, at about ten Chinese miles from Hing-king <note>7. 興京</note> or Yenden, now a small village on the top of a small detached hill, with crumbling gates and walls, and containing little more than an insignificant magistrate's office <note>8. James, *The Long White Mountain*, page 231.</note>. But when T'ai Tsu in 1622 founded the city of Tung-king <note>9. 東京</note> not far from the site of the present Liao-yang <note>10. 遼陽</note>, and there established his court, he transferred there, two years later, the tombs of his father and mother, grandfather and grandmother, and that of Hiao Ts'zě <note>11. 孝慈</note>, his own spouse and his successor's mother, who had died in 1603 <note>12. *Wen hien t'ung khao*, chapter 241, line 2.</note>. # THE FUH LING AND THE CHAO LING.

» A stone tablet was raised, commemorating the relocation of King Tsu and Hien Tsu to the Yung ling <gloss>1</gloss>. The name Khi-yun was not new. Already ten years before, it had been bestowed by the same Emperor upon the hill on which the mausoleum stands; he then deemed it proper to imitate the Ming dynasty by increasing the spiritual efficacy of the heights dominating the Feng Shui <note>Fung-shui</note> of the Imperial burial grounds by giving them auspicious names. For this reason, he also bestowed an auspicious name—Tsih-khing Shan <gloss>2</gloss>, or "Felicity-accumulating Hills"—on the mounts at the graves of King Tsu and Hien Tsu, which were then still located at Tung-king <gloss>3</gloss>.

At 240 Chinese miles (about 140 kilometers) west of Yenden, and at about half that distance north of Tung-king, stands the city of Mukden, the capital of Manchuria, also officially known by the Chinese name Fengtian Fu <gloss>4</gloss>. This place, then called Shenyang <gloss>5</gloss>, was the residence of T'ai Tsung. In 1629, he buried his father there, twenty Chinese miles northeast of the city walls <gloss>6</gloss>, interring at the same time and place the remains of his mother Hiao Ts'zĕ, who was brought from Tung-king <gloss>7</gloss> for this purpose; as we have seen, her consort had buried them there five years earlier. The tomb was named Fuh ling <gloss>8</gloss> in 1636 <gloss>9</gloss>. T'ai Tsung himself passed away seven years later, and in the following year he was buried ten miles to the northwest of Mukden in a sepulcher to which, on this occasion, the name Chao ling <gloss>10</gloss> was given. His spouse Hiao Twan <gloss>11</gloss> survived him until 1651, in which year her body and soul joined him in his final resting place <gloss>12</gloss>.

In that year, the son of T'ai Tsung endowed, as we have stated, the mausoleum hills at Yenden and Tung-king with auspicious

Simultaneously, he gave the hills at the Fuh ling and at the Chao ling the respective names of T'ien-chu Shan¹, "Stanchions of Heaven or of the Imperial Dignity," and Lung-yeh Shan², "Hills ensuring Prosperity to the Imperial Rule"³. At that time, the work on these mausolea was being energetically carried out; for we read that the places from which the required materials were to be fetched, or where they were to be fabricated, were officially appointed in the year 1651, and that the large blocks of stone were to be extracted from the quarries in the hills south of Yih-cheu—a distance of over eight hundred kilometers!⁴ It certainly attests to the efficiency and power of the new dynasty that the works at the two mausolea were completed in the very same year. "The officers charged with the direction and execution of the works had titles of nobility conferred upon them and were rewarded with court dresses and saddle horses, while the subordinates employed at the works received bounties in the form of dresses and caps, saddle horses, or white metal"⁵. "It was then decided that a body of officers should be appointed for the administration of each mausoleum, as well as people to guard and protect it; and regulations were enacted for the performance of sacrificial worship there"⁶. It was not, however, until 1668 that a tablet commemorating "the sage virtues and divine feats" was erected in the Fuh ling and in the Chao ling through the care of Shing Tsu, who himself composed the biographies engraved on them⁷.

So much for the history of the so-called San ling⁸ or "Three Mausolea." It would be interesting to know something about the shape of the tombs of all those Manchu chiefs before they were rebuilt by Shi Tsu into their present form. However, we find absolutely nothing on this subject in the books. One point about which we have perfect certainty is that Shi Tsu, despite his foreign descent, modeled those graves entirely after the mausolea of the Ming dynasty. This fact, like many others, illustrates the remarkable speed and readiness with which the conquerors adopted the civilization of the Chinese and adapted themselves to their institutions. But, along with the culture of the conquered race, the victors naturally received its negative aspects—primarily the <term>Fung-shui</term> (Feng Shui) superstitions, the boasted product of China’s highest wisdom and learning. We find it explicitly stated that in 1657:

> "A proposal was approved by the Throne to the effect that such houses and dwellings occupied by officers, soldiers, and workmen in the Three Mausolea that interfered with the Fung-shui should all be removed." <note>It was resolved that the houses inhabited by officers, soldiers, and artisans at the Three Mausolea that obstruct the Feng Shui shall all be ordered to be moved. *T. Ts. h. t. tseh li*, ch. 139, l. 46.</note>

Moreover, we have seen above (p. 1356) that King Tsu and Hien Tsu were transferred from Tung-king to Yenden expressly because of the excellent geomantic qualities of the mountains there. And the *Wen hien t'ung khao* says:

> "The extensive foundation on which the existence of the Imperial Family shall rest for ten thousand generations is, in fact, rooted in those hills." <note>The grand foundation of the ancestral dynasty for ten thousand generations truly begins here. *Ch. 150, l. 3.*</note>

It was, no doubt, with the goal of encouraging them to produce—through the influence of the tombs—an ever-flowing source of prosperity for the Imperial Family, that Shi Tsu, when giving those hills grand names in 1651, also ordained that they should from then on be objects of Imperial worship. They were honored with sacrifices alongside the principal mountains, seas, and streams outside the northern wall of Peking on the great Altar of the Earth, the second highest Divinity of the State <note>*T. Ts. h. t. shi li*, ch. 346, l. 3; *T. Ts. h. t. tseh li*, ch. 80, l. 3.</note>. They have held this high position in the official Pantheon down to the present day. # RESCRIPTS CONCERNING THE YUNG LING.

Similar honors were afterward allotted also to the mountains behind the two cemeteries in Peh-chihli, as soon as burials had taken place there <note>1. *Ta Qing Huidian Shili*, chapter 346, line 6, and chapter 347, line 1. *Ta Qing Huidian Zeli*, chapter 80, lines 6 and 32.</note>.

It can be seen at a glance from the official rescripts regarding the buildings and structures that compose them that the Three Mausolea are built, as we have said, on the same lines as those of the Ming dynasty. However, they are laid out on a more modest scale; some buildings and structures found at the Ming tombs are missing. The <term>Yung ling</term>, which is the plainest, has neither a square fortress nor a Soul tower; at least, the Regulations make no mention of such structures. Its <term>Pao chʻing</term> has a circumference of 86.16 <term>chang</term>. In front of it stands the <term>Khi-yun temple</term>, a building consisting of three sections formed by the pillars; it is covered with yellow tiles, has four doors and eight windows, and is situated on a terrace with an elevation of 0.29 <term>chang</term> and a circumference of 31.9. Inside are four large "warm porches" containing Imperial couches with curtains, blankets, and pillows, and clothes racks at the service of the deified Rulers; additionally, there are four small "warm porches" for the respectful worship of the (eight) Soul tablets. In front of the porches, eight **Dragon seats** and **Phoenix seats** are placed (respectively for the Emperors and the Empresses), along with four tables, each of which holds the five sacrificial implements; furthermore, there are eight court lamps and three carpets decorated with dragons. Yellow cloth awnings (perhaps umbrellas?) are stretched over the spot to provide protection from rain and heat, three of each kind.

In front of the temple is a triple stone-paved ramp, the middle part of which is decorated with coiled dragons. To the east and west is a side temple of three sections; the western one has a tower-like building in front for the burning of sacrificial silks. Southward from the temple, directly in the middle, stands the <term>Khi-yun gate</term>. Outside this gate, the ground is enclosed by walls on the eastern, western, and southern sides; the length and width of this wall are 66.2 <term>chang</term>, and it has a **Red Gate** on both the east and west. A triple stone-paved road runs through the middle of this enclosure. To the east stands a building for the preparation of fruit, and to the west another for the preparation of sacrificial meats; in front, in the middle, stand four pavilions for the tablets commemorating the achievements and

> "The ground in front of a grave is called <term>ming t'ang</term>, and also <term>khüen t'ai</term>, 'terrace for the contract of the purchase of the ground.' The *Records of the Conversations with <term>Chu Hi</term>* say that it is not clear what a <term>ming t'ang</term> is, and therefore an explanation was later sought in the writings of the authors of the <term>Tang dynasty</term>, in which it was discovered that this dynasty ordered the name (of <term>ming t'ang</term>) to be changed to <term>khüen t'ai</term>. This term occurs in current books of <term>geomancy</term>; <term>khüen</term> means a contract (compare p. 1078), and the place where the contract for the purchase of a plot of ground is buried is called <term>khüen t'ai</term>, 'contract-terrace.' Such a purchase deed is made of either earthenware or stone, upon which is inscribed how many strings of money have been paid (for the ground). When (paper) money used on behalf of the deceased is buried on that spot, the spirits of the ground and the dragons of the earth cannot quarrel and wrangle over it; likewise, the poor and uninfluential, when having to present a sacrifice, also set out their cups and dishes there, calling them 'a repast on the soil.'" 1.

The official rescripts reviewed here show that although the <term>Yung ling</term>, even though this <term>mausoleum</term> and its adjacent grounds cover a very large area, does not greatly surpass the grandeur of the <term>mausolea</term> of high princes of imperial lineage. Nearly all the edifices and structures that constitute the cenotaphs in the Eastern and Western Cemeteries are found within their walls and are, moreover, of corresponding dimensions. For the same reason, each temple contains no more than one Dragon seat and one Phoenix seat, with one table bearing the five sacrificial implements. Moreover, it is furnished with four additional chairs, placed on the right and the left, and with four tables, six court lamps, seven carpets adorned with dragons, and fourteen yellow silk awnings to protect against rain and heat. It is worth noting that a "case containing a bow"<note>One case for containing a bow.</note> is preserved in the temple of the <term>Chao ling</term>. Might we assume this weapon to be a relic inherited from the warlike <term>T'ai Tsung</term>?

In front of the temple, in both mausolea, there is a stone ascent similar to the one in the <term>Yung ling</term>, and a similar set of buildings. However, the <term>Chao ling</term> contains two additional furnaces flanking the main one. Furthermore, in both mausolea, the temple gate, called <term>Lung-ngen men</term>, has a triple roof and a triple stone-paved ascent in the middle of the front. On its eastern side is a tea house and a refreshment house; on the west, a fruit house and a building for the cleaning of sacrificial

The inscriptions carved on these two monuments were (see page 1358) composed by Shing Tsu; from the reprints given in the *Wen hien t'ung khao* (chapter 150), we see that they possess exactly the same character as those later made for the actual Emperors of the dynasty. In each mausoleum, the tablet-house is surrounded by four columns officially named <term>hwa piao chu</term>¹, "glorifying columns." A stone road runs from this edifice to the great Red Gate. In both tombs, the road is guarded on either side by stone figures representing two lions, two tigers, two camels, and two horses; in this part of the <term>Chao ling</term>, there are, moreover, two unicorns.

The wall enclosing the <term>Fuh ling</term> on all four sides has a length of 580 <term>chang</term>, and the wall surrounding the <term>Chao ling</term> measures 496 <term>chang</term>. Both walls have a gate known as the principal Red Gate in the exact middle of the southern façade, and another gate of that name on the east and west. The first-named gate is flanked on the outside by a pair of stone lions, two stone glorifying columns, and two tower-like buildings containing stone tablets; a tablet is also erected nearby, inscribed with an order for riders to dismount. At the <term>Chao ling</term>, we find outside the gate, besides all these decorations, a pavilion for the changing of costumes³, as well as a building for the inspection of sacrificial victims, a building for the preparation of food⁴, and a stone bridge standing exactly in the line of the road, behind the columns and the lions. Finally, we find there, somewhat farther to the south, a special decoration not mentioned in the regulations regarding any other mausolea, namely "two stone life-guard horses, called the Great White One and the Little White One"⁵.

### PALISADES SURROUNDING THE MAUSOLEA.

gathering timber and fuel, agricultural pursuits, the pasturing of cattle, burials, and so on, were forbidden within the white posts, nor could any kilns for bricks or lime be built within the blue ones; boards displaying these prohibitions were to be hung from the posts ^1^.

Additionally, the three <term>Mausolea</term> are each surrounded by a boundary of palisades, called "deer horns" <margin>2. Deer horns (鹿角).</margin>. These fences consist of rows of wooden St. Andrew’s crosses that run perpendicularly through a long, heavy cross-beam, as closely together as they can be placed; the lower ends of the crosses, which are fixed in the ground, are heavy and longer; their upper ends taper to a point, and half of them point outward while the other half point inward. They are sometimes seen surrounding government offices in <term>Manchuria</term>, and being heavy and difficult to move, they make it difficult for people, and especially for cavalry, to pass. The long barriers that formerly crossed <term>Liao-tung</term> over its entire length and breadth also consisted of such fences ^3^. The fact that they stand in very great numbers around the mausolea can be inferred from an ordinance issued in 1803, which authorized an expenditure of 9,240 <term>taels</term> of silver on behalf of the three mausolea for the repair of 2,810 fences; it is also evident from an edict of the same year, which prescribed that 140 fences should be renewed every year at the <term>Yung ling</term>, one hundred at the <term>Fuh ling</term>, and sixty at the <term>Chao ling</term> ^4^. Mr. James states that the deer-horn fence of the <term>Yung ling</term> extends around the base of the hill upon which the mausoleum stands, and that it encompasses a circle of about twelve English miles ^5^.

Close to the <term>Fuh ling</term>, on its right side, stands the mausoleum of a concubine of <term>T'ai Tsu</term>, who was buried there in 1644, three months before the capture of <term>Peking</term> ^6^. She is known by the honorary name of <term>Sheu Khang</term> <margin>7. # RESCRIPTS CONCERNING RESTORATIONS.

> ...specifically in the fourteenth year of the Shun chi period, it was decided that, whenever any of the three mausolea should need repairs, the President of the Board of Works at Mukden, upon receiving written notification about the matter from the Seal Keeper of that tomb, should, in the company of the latter, verify with his own eyes whether the repairs were really necessary. The latter extends its control over the three tombs in Manchuria.

That those tombs have been objects of unremitting concern to the dynasty, as being supports for its own well-being and the nation’s prosperity, is self-evident from the long, unbroken chain of repairs, embellishments, and improvements recorded in the Ordinances <note>1. *T. Ts. h. t. shi li*, ch. 723, ll. 11 following.</note>. Shi Tsung even had the entire geomantic compound of water streams in front of the *Fuh ling* improved by extra canalization, and the direction of various brooks and rivulets modified. These works were carried out in compliance with the views of Kao Khi-choh <note>2. 高其倬.</note>, Governor of the province of Fuhkien. He was a great authority on matters of geomancy who, having come to Peking around the year 1729, was not only, as we saw on page 1293, employed by the Emperor to search for a new Cemetery, but was also dispatched to Mukden with orders to examine the system of water streams at the *Fuh ling* there. According to some rumors, this system did not correspond to the old orthodox geomantic doctrines. The learned dignitary did not, of course, fail to detect a great many faults therein. But barely five years later, when heavy rains in the summer season swelled the brooks, the results of his geomantic hydraulics were severely damaged; banks and dikes were destroyed, and new heavy charges were consequently imposed upon the treasuries.

The long series of ordinances for the preservation of the three mausolea show that they are covered with <term>Feng Shui</term> trees, and that the adjacent grounds are also wooded. This is confirmed by Mr. James, who writes that the mound of the *Fuh ling* stands on a hill, deep in a somber grove of pines, and that the *Chao ling* is likewise located in a deep grove of ancient cedars, surrounded by delightful shrubberies full of hawthorn and other sweet-flowering trees, where pheasants crow in the balmy springtime <note>3. *The Long White Mountain*, pp. 226 and 227.</note>. Some of the trees have been objects of particular Imperial attention. We read, for instance, that in 1778, "a poem by the Imperial hand, entitled 'The Spiritual Tree,' having for its theme a noble elm in front of the tumuli of the *Yung ling*, was engraved on a stone in the western accessory temple of the mausoleum, in obedience to an Imperial order" <note>4. In the 43rd year of the Qianlong reign, an imperial composition titled "The Spiritual Tree Ode," commemorating a lucky elm in front of the burial mound of the Yung ling, was engraved on stone in the western side-hall of the Yung ling by imperial decree. *T. Ts. h. t. shi li*, ch. 723, l. 16.</note>. In 1731 it was ordained by decree, that the

### VISITS PAID BY EMPERORS TO THE MAUSOLEA.

grounds surrounding the Fuh ling should be cleared of houses and cultivated fields, and compensation be paid to those sustaining loss of property as a result of this measure; and in 1778 another decree prescribed the removal of tombs from the vicinity of the three mausolea $^1$.

The best proof that these tombs have never fallen victim to neglect is found in the fact that they were often personally visited by the Sons of Heaven. Shing Tsu sacrificed at the Fuh ling and the Chao ling in 1671 $^2$, and at the three mausolea in 1682 and 1698 $^3$, and in 1722 he delegated his son to present sacrifices there in celebration of the sixtieth anniversary of his reign $^4$. Kao Tsung visited the three tombs in 1743, sacrificing at them all with a great display of pomp $^5$; in 1754 he went there again $^6$, and in 1755 ordered his son to go there and inform the ancestors and ancestresses of the conquest of Dzungar $^7$; finally, he was himself in those sacred grounds in 1778 and 1783 $^8$. The Ordinances also make mention of a visit paid by Jen Tsung to the three Mausolea in 1805 $^9$. These Sons of Heaven seem to have invariably used the high road running from Peking almost due eastward as far as Shan-hai Kwan $^{10}$, where the Great Wall terminates at the seashore, and from there, in a northeasterly direction, through the coastal districts of the Gulf of Liao-tung.

Like the mausolea in the Eastern and the Western Cemetery, those in Manchuria are each administered by a special committee. The Fuh ling and the Chao ling committees each consist of a Seal-keeper and two Assistant Seal-keepers, whose other titles and ranks are not mentioned; two officers respectively for the presentation of tea and food; one manager of the Household Department; and four writers belonging to the Mukden Board of Rites. The Committee for the Yung ling is only composed of a Seal-keeper, an Assistant Seal-keeper, and two writers $^{11}$. These three corporations were already instituted in 1651, when the first emperor of the dynasty had been on the throne for eight years $^{12}$.

# THE GRAVE.

The Manchu Banner force that occupies each mausoleum is under the general command of a Commander, who is assisted by two Wing Commanders and sixteen Chiefs of the Guards (compare p. 1352). Additionally, an officer known as the Overseer of the Workmen¹—whose rank is equivalent to the fourth degree of military rank—is assigned to each garrison². The surrounding grounds are also guarded by soldiers, as "it was ordained in 1725 to establish four watch-posts all around the reserved grounds of the Fuh ling, and to assign officers and troops to occupy them"³, and a similar order was issued twenty-five years later for the Chao ling⁴. The three garrisons likely have their headquarters at Mukden and Yenden. Mr. James mentions a village called Yung ling, which is inhabited by soldiers who guard the tomb of the same name⁵.

The Ordinances show us that during the early years of the Qing (Ts'ing) dynasty's reign, the Mukden Board of Rites was entrusted with regulating the ceremonies connected with the annual sacrifices at the three Mausolea, and that the Emperor Shi Tsu used to delegate certain Princes there on special occasions to offer sacrifices⁶. In 1660, however, he decreed that an Imperial Prince of the ninth order and a Gioro with the sixth rank of hereditary nobility should live at the Fuh ling from then on, and a Prince of the sixth or eighth order, also assisted by such a Gioro, at the Chao ling. These dignitaries were to act as his proxies for the offering of sacrifices; they were also required to travel in turn to the Yung ling to perform similar rites⁷. But this regulation was abolished in 1669 and replaced by a rule stating that the four principal annual sacrifices were to be conducted by envoys from the Governor-General of Manchuria, the Lieutenant-Governor, and the Presidents of the Mukden Boards⁸. In 1736, the old regulation was reinstated, and six Princes of the lowest ranks then volunteered to settle in Mukden to perform the duties of chief sacrificants at the tombs from that time forward⁹.

<header>ORCHARDS, GARDENS AND FIELDS.</header>
<sig>88</sig>

The Board of Rites at Mukden also oversees certain grounds within or near the mausolea that are reserved for producing the items required for the numerous sacrifices to the Imperial Dead. The Ordinances prescribe that there must be two expanses of plowed land, tilled by ninety farmers and yielding specified quantities of rice, barley and wheat, sorghum, yellow peas, green peas, small peas, hemp seed, and oil seed. Furthermore, ten orchards, under the care of 168 gardeners, must be maintained for the production of fixed quantities of pine seed, hazel nuts $^1$, grapes, Berberis seed $^2$, hawthorn fruit $^3$, dried pears, etc.; there are two orchards in the Fuh ling and one in the Chao ling, producing plums, apricots, cherries, pears, and hawthorn fruit; and finally, in each of the three mausolea, there are two gardens for the cultivation of melons and vegetables. There must be 270 honey gatherers, along with a number of pheasant hunters and fishers. During the ten days preceding each sacrifice, fifteen dairy cows must be driven from the pasturelands of the relevant mausoleum and milked regularly, as the managers of those grounds must supply 1,826 pounds of sacrificial butter every year. These men also have to provide the cattle and sheep or goats to be used as sacrificial victims; if they are unable to deliver the required number, the missing animals must be purchased at the expense of the Mukden Board of Revenues. This Board must also provide salt, eggs, and other items required for the sacrifices $^4$.

# CHAPTER XV.

## ON GRAVEYARDS AND FREE BURIAL-GROUNDS.

The inhabitants of the Chinese Empire are not bound by any institutions or laws to bury the dead in grounds specifically set apart, by official or private care, for burial purposes. Every one of them is at liberty to place them in whatever soil he has acquired the ownership of, or the right to use (compare pages 1076 and following). As a consequence, graveyards in China have quite a different character than those in most European countries. They are principally family graves, to which we have devoted a special chapter elsewhere in this volume (page 829), most of which contain a limited number of bodies; among them may also easily be ranked the mausoleums of princes of imperial lineage, and even the vast cemeteries for the "Sons of Heaven" <note>Emperors</note>.

Apart from such private graveyards, there exist cemeteries of a semi-public character in the vicinity of almost every village—namely, grounds in which, owing to their good <term>Feng Shui</term>, the villagers are laid for eternal rest in separate graves (compare page 832). We may rank them likewise among the family graveyards, as village communities are generally composed of members of one clan who consider themselves to be descended from the same common ancestor. That burial grounds of this kind existed already many centuries before the beginning of our era is, as we have shown on page 830, explicitly stated by the *<term>Cheu li</term>*. Village cemeteries often cover a vast area, as almost every family maintains its graves for years and years, as long as it is hoped they will provide blessings; and even when the owners neglect them completely, they remain untouched for a long time, as everyone stands in awe of the souls that dwell there and the strict laws protecting bodies and graves.

In mountainous regions, like <term>Fuhkien</term> and <term>Kwangtung</term>, village cemeteries seldom take much useful land away from agricultural pursuits, as they are generally located on barren, treeless mountain slopes, dried and scorched every summer by tropical heat. As they are part of the communal land owned by the villagers,

<summary>This chapter explains that Chinese burial practices are not restricted to designated public cemeteries, allowing families to bury their dead on private land or in communal village graveyards governed by clan lineage and Feng Shui. These burial grounds are often preserved for generations due to spiritual reverence and legal protections, even when located on land unsuitable for farming.</summary>

# GRAVEYARDS AT VILLAGES AND TOWNS.

They stand, like the village itself, under the control of its chiefs and elders. They generally provide enough resting-places for the dead, and it rarely happens that wealthy people—who are wiser than others in <term>Fung-shui</term> matters and highly concerned about their own fortunes and those of their descendants—prefer to place their graves elsewhere.

Grounds filled with graves because their <term>Fung-shui</term> is considered to be of excellent quality are found near towns, cities, and generally near every densely populated place. Such *t'ióng soaⁿ*^1 or "grave grounds," as they are called in Amoy and the surrounding districts, are public in the true sense of the word. Everyone is allowed to bury their dead there, regardless of their family or clan, provided they have acquired the ownership or <term>usufruct</term> of a plot from the owners of the soil. Many such grounds in the course of time become free burial-places used by the poor alone. For when a ground becomes so crowded with graves that it no longer provides room for making tombs of any significant size, it is the natural course of things that only the poor, whose graves are of the simplest sort, will continue to make use of it. Graves of the better kind, being frequently disturbed by them, will disappear in the course of time or be removed elsewhere by their careful owners. The owners of the soil, being powerless against numerous burials secretly carried out there by people who cannot afford to pay them anything, will eventually renounce their ownership, as it yields them no profit at all. And now, every poor man who has a corpse to bury merely searches out a few feet of ground between the countless burial mounds, and there thrusts the coffin into the soil, only a few inches below the surface.

Every burial-ground in the vicinity of populous places may in this way become what the Chinese at Amoy appropriately call a *bān jîn tui*^2, or an "accumulation of myriads." Being exclusively used for the burial of the poor and the childless, such free cemeteries are devoid of any monumental graves. There is no room for trees to grow, and not a handful of soil remains in the barren ground for a shrub to thrive. Even the thin patches of grass are regularly scorched away by the heat and the summer drought, or scraped for fuel by the poor. Many a *bān jîn tui* looks like a snowy field when the plastering craze of a grave-repairing society has been at work in it (compare page 865). There is no fence or enclosure of any kind around

# THE GRAVE.

Such grounds; no control is exercised over them by the magistrates or the public, but it is the dead themselves who protect the dead there. Their souls, which hover around the spot, rarely allow any desecration of the graves to go unavenged, and conversely, they reward those who respect and protect their beloved resting places.

Filial piety, combined with the belief that graves placed under the influence of good <term>Fung-shui</term> will create happiness, compels every son who has buried his parents in such a poor burial ground to move them to a more honorable place as soon as his means allow him to afford the cost. But how can he identify the grave in a plot where coffins are packed like herrings in a barrel, and where thousands of <term>tumuli</term>, uniformly plastered by charitable men, are indistinguishable from one another? The answer is that he must draw some blood from his finger and drop it onto the bones; they are certainly those of his parents if the blood sticks to them or is absorbed by the pores. The reliability of this strange testing method—based as it is on naive ideas about blood relations—is firmly believed in; it is so trusted that the Government itself officially recommends and mandates its use in legal matters and at coroner’s inquests. In the standard work on medical jurisprudence titled *Si yuen luh* (see page 137), which was written around the year 1247 by <term>Sung Ts'zĕ</term> 1 and has been used in the courts since the 15th century, we read:

> If the bones of a father or mother lie in a place belonging to others, and a son or daughter wishes to identify them, then let the child draw some blood from their body and drop it onto the bones. If they are the bones of the man or woman who gave birth to the child, the blood is absorbed; otherwise, it is not taken in.
> <note>I have heard of the following method for mixing blood. Two people draw blood into the same water, and if a relationship exists between them—such as mother and son, father and son, or husband and wife—the two drops will immediately blend together; if they do not blend, no such relationship exists.</note> — If the bones have been washed with salt water, the blood will not be absorbed, even if it actually trickled out of a father

### TESTING BONES BY MEANS OF BLOOD.

> ...and his son. This circumstance is sometimes exploited for the commission of a felony, and therefore it is necessary to be watchful against it.
> Should children have lived separated from their parents since their youth, or brothers from their brothers, and wish to confirm their relationship, then—if they find it difficult to determine whether a relationship exists in fact or only in appearance—they must be ordered to draw blood from their bodies and drop it into the same vessel. If the relationship exists in reality, the blood will coagulate into one mass; if not, there will be no clotting.
> But when fresh blood comes into contact with salt or vinegar, it coagulates under all circumstances; hence, it happens that, with the object of committing a felony or fraud, the vessel is first rubbed with salt or vinegar. Therefore, the authorities must have the vessel washed and cleaned under their own supervision before conducting an experiment with blood drops, or intentionally obtain a new vessel from a shop, by which such tricks will be entirely defeated.” <note>If the bones of a father or mother lie in another place and the children wish to identify them, let them draw blood from their bodies and drop it onto the bones. If they are the biological offspring, the blood enters the bone; if not, it does not. It is heard that there is a method for merging blood: two people each draw blood and drop it into water. If they are mother and child, father and son, or husband and wife, the blood immediately merges into one; if not, they are not related. If the bone has been washed with saltwater, the blood cannot enter even if they are truly father and son. This is a method of deception and must be guarded against. If biological children or brothers have been separated since childhood and wish to recognize each other but find it hard to distinguish truth from falsehood, let each draw blood and drop it into a vessel. If they are truly related, the blood will coagulate into one; if not, it will not coagulate. However, since fresh blood always coagulates when it meets salt or vinegar, some rub the vessel with salt or vinegar beforehand to deceive others. Whenever testing with blood drops, first wash the vessel used in person, or obtain a new vessel specifically from a shop, and then the deception will be exposed. Chapter 1, l. 57.</note>

That the Chinese place implicit trust in such testing of human bones by means of filial blood will not surprise us much if we consider that the method was known in times long past and practiced with brilliant results by a long series of virtuous generations. ### THE GRAVE.

“...make a free cemetery, and have the dead buried there” $^1$.

The majority of the free graveyards founded in past ages by the authorities probably owed their origin to their zeal to discourage cremation. Indeed, this widespread custom, looked down upon with great aversion and disgust by the Government, could hardly be fought with success unless a good opportunity were afforded to the poor for burying their dead at little expense. Some notes on this subject will be found in our dissertation on Cremation, which forms the final section of the next chapter.

The two quotations just made from Chinese books show that cemeteries laid out for free use were denoted in China many centuries ago by the term *i chʻung* 義塚, the literal sense of which is: “cemeteries owing their existence to a sense of duty toward others,” or “made by people possessed of this virtue.” The meaning of the word *chʻung* we have explained on page 442. In general, the character *i* 義 enters into the composition of terms denoting things made with a benevolent purpose and for public utility, as, for example: 義廠 *i ch'ang*, store-houses, such as are mentioned on page 922, where coffins are given freely to the poor; 義學 *i hsüeh*, free or public schools; 義井 *i ching*, wells for public use; 義倉 *i ts'ang*, granaries erected on behalf of the people to provide for their needs in times of scarcity; etc.

Even today, the term *i chʻung* is in general use in China as a name for cemeteries founded by magistrates, and so it is in Amoy, in the language of which place it has the form of *gī tióng*. On page 924, we spoke of such burial places laid out in that part of the Empire for the soldiers of the garrisons formerly occupying the island of Formosa, or for victims of epidemics and various other calamities that can no longer be traced. There is no reasonable doubt that among the events which cause such cemeteries to arise all around China, famine and floods occupy the principal place, along with rebellions entailing the death of countless loyal warriors and peaceful people. At Amoy, no special custodians are, as a rule, appointed to administer and guard such grounds. Some stand there under the patronage of notables and gentry constituting committees—

Most of these graveyards are not fenced in at all, but are accessible from every side. Only a few of those that are well cared for are enclosed by a wall of granite blocks or of packed clay and earth, just high enough to keep out cows and pigs. A broad granite ledge extends along the entire front, ending at each side at a small wall that projects from the main wall at right angles.

# ADDITIONAL CHAPTER.

## ON SOME EXCEPTIONAL WAYS OF DISPOSING OF THE DEAD.

The last chapter brought to a close our series of treatises on the Grave and the principal customs grouped around it. Sacrifices and other ceremonies performed at graves have not yet been detailed, because they concern the soul that dwells at the site rather than the physical remains; consequently, a systematic treatment of those subjects belongs in our Second Book, which is dedicated to the soul and its worship.

However, the title of this Book promises a description of the disposal of the dead in general. Therefore, we are not justified in finishing our work without providing information about other methods, besides burial, by which lifeless human bodies were formerly or are currently disposed of in the Chinese Empire—namely, abandoning them, throwing them into the water, or burning them. Given what this Book has already taught the reader regarding the unique Chinese ideas about the necessity of preserving corpses, coffins, and graves for as long as possible, we certainly do not need to repeat our remark from page 280: such methods, which cause the quick destruction of the corpse, have never reached the status of established customs in the Empire. To this day, they are seen by the Chinese as nothing more than hateful deviations from the correct path that a long succession of generations was wise and generous enough to map out clearly to maintain pure filial devotion.

### 1. On the Custom of Throwing Away the Dead.

It can hardly be doubted that in ancient China, when civilization was still in its earliest stages, it was not unusual to abandon the dead. <term>Mencius</term> refers to this custom in his vigorous style, which contrasts so sharply with that of other ancient authors of his country. "In former generations," he says, "there

It can be easily proved from historical books that many corpses were thrown away in China in every age, especially in times of high mortality. For example, we read in the biography of the virtuous official Ku Hien-chi of the fifth century—whose praiseworthy measures on behalf of the dead in Heng-yang we spoke of on page 1070: "That region had for many years been scourged by epidemics that claimed more than half of the people. As a consequence, coffins were so high in price that the dead were all merely wrapped in rush mats and cast away along the roadside. Upon arriving at his post, Hien-chi charged the district magistrates under his command to search for the relatives of those dead people and order them to bury them; and for the dead whose families had died out, he spent his own official salary, ordering measures to be taken for their protection” ². And the *Supplement to the History of the Empire of the T'ang Dynasty* ³, a collection of miscellaneous writings by Li Chao ⁴, chiefly referring to the eighth century and a part of the ninth, relates: "In the first year of the Ta-li period (766 AD), a terrible epidemic prevailed in Kwan-tung (in Henan province), and its victims became as numerous as hemp. Ching Sun, a native of Yung-yang, then placed himself at the head of some influential people, and they made one large tomb in every village for the burial of the corpses that were thrown away. He thus became known as the Elder of the Village Burials, and earned a reputation as a humane and public-spirited man” ⁵.

<header>CORPSES OF STRANGERS, BEGGARS AND INFANTS.</header>

It is unnecessary to add any more examples to the ones above, as we have previously (pages 917—921) presented the reader with a whole series of extracts recounting stories of Emperors and high officials who took active measures to bury corpses that the living lacked the means or concern to commit to the earth.

However, those instances do not at all justify the conclusion that abandoning the dead—except in the most ancient times of which Mencius speaks—has ever been practiced anywhere in China as an established system. Mainly, they teach us that it occurred only occasionally, especially during times of epidemic, famine, rebellion, and other disasters which, by decimating the population, overwhelmed the survivors with burials. Furthermore, we learn from many instances that it has always been common to abandon the bodies of strangers and childless people or, at least, to leave them unburied somewhere, which is equivalent to throwing them away. The reader has already seen on page 139 that even today, the remains of strangers are generally placed in the cheapest kind of coffins and then left on hills or in fields. Beggars and other poor people who have no descendants to care for them are often treated the same way, as are lepers, about whom we shall have a few more words to say on page 1390.

A truly systematic abandonment only exists regarding the corpses of infants. Countless are the babies who, enclosed in urns or wooden boxes, are abandoned in the open countryside and left as prey for ravens, dogs, and pigs, or left to rapid decomposition by the weather and insects. We hardly need to repeat here that this state of affairs is, to a certain extent, the result of <term>Fung-shui</term> theories, because the bones of infants are not solid enough to serve the living as durable fetishes capable of producing profit and happiness through the mediation of the graves in which they lie (compare page 1075). In many parts of the Empire, we saw numerous filled infant boxes along city walls, with the lids fastened by fragile willow withes or hempen strings. In the capital city of the department of Tsüen-cheu, some large square projections from the city walls are generally used by the people as receptacles to throw their dead children into. These curious brick structures, if seen from the outside of the walls, look like prominent crenelated bastions, but in reality, they are square chambers, completely open at the top. Having no openings whatsoever on the four sides, they are only accessible from above by using ladders. In

In those chambers, we saw the bottoms thickly covered with decaying remains and rags of clothes and matting they had been wrapped in, as well as the skeletons of some dogs that, attracted by the smell, had climbed down along the crumbling walls and, unable to get out, died of thirst.

The practice of discarding the corpses of infants probably prevails on a more extensive scale in the northern parts of the Empire than in the southern parts, where the mountainous terrain almost everywhere provides plenty of wasteland to bury them in. Consequently, special shelters built by charitable people for parents to discard their dead children in are relatively scarce in the South. Under the name of "baby-towers," such structures have often been mentioned by European authors. They are made of stone blocks or brick and measure about five meters in diameter; their shape is either round, polygonal, or square, and they consist of a single compartment with a tiled roof. Corpses are dropped in through a window-like opening, from which the winds, birds, and bats are kept out by a square wooden shutter, swinging on hinges fixed in the lintel. Anyone who wishes to throw in a corpse must first push the shutter back, which then automatically returns to its vertical position. Some baby-towers have two such openings, placed opposite each other: the one on the left, or primary side, for receiving male infants, and the other for female bodies. To prevent mistakes, the left shutter is often marked with the inscription "male infants" ^1, and the other with "female babies" ^2. Thus, any immoral interaction among the little souls within the tower is virtuously suppressed, and morality is promoted in the World of Death. Baby-towers have no doors, as they are never entered by living men, and because doors might allow greedy pigs, dogs, and rats to enter.

To inform the people that such charnel houses are intended to rid them of their dead infants, they sometimes display an inscription on a stone slab fixed to the front, reading: "Pagoda or Tower for accumulating bones" ^3, or "Place of rest for infants" ^4, etc. Not infrequently, another slab is inserted in the wall or stood nearby on a pedestal to display the names of the virtuous men who, out of compassion for the countless infant

However, the claim made by some foreign authors in their works—that such buildings owe their existence to the specific purpose of helping parents rid themselves of their living offspring—must be rejected as a myth.

### 2. Water Burial.

If the passages quoted on page 1385 from the works of Mencius and from the *Tso ch`wen* <note>The Zuo Zhuan, an ancient Chinese narrative history.</note> are to be taken in their literal sense, it would follow that it was far from unusual for the living in ancient China to rid themselves of the dead by throwing them into ditches and canals. But, certainly, it would be ridiculous to assume, based on the authority of those passages, that water burial was then practiced systematically; those ditches and canals may be mere metaphors, emphasizing the disgust and horror that throwing away the dead then raised in sensitive, filial hearts.

As far as we know, there is nothing in Chinese books to justify the theory that throwing the dead into the water has ever been considered as anything other than a crime. The reigning dynasty severely forbids it in its Code of Laws, decreeing therein—in an article which we have quoted on page 871—that anyone who is guilty of it shall be punished in the same way as those who mutilate a corpse, whether he is or is not a relative of the dead person so abused. This article was copied word for word from the Code of the Ming dynasty <note>See the *Ta Ming hwui tien* (Collected Statutes of the Ming Dynasty), chapter 130, leaf 11.</note>, as was every fundamental article in the Law of Burial. Both dynasties even prohibited the throwing of deceased relatives into the water, even in cases where the deceased themselves had ordered it to be so—

Nowadays, the Chinese people generally feel a strong aversion to water burial. This may be illustrated by the following incident, which occurred in 1888 and was witnessed by a friend of ours on board a steamer departing Swatow for the Deli tobacco districts. Two migrant workers having died of cholera, arrangements were immediately made to throw their corpses overboard; but all the passengers rose as one to prevent it. After much loud discussion, they yielded to arguments regarding the tropical heat and the dangers of infection, insisting, however, that the corpses should be floated away in a wooden water tank that stood on the deck. The whole passenger hold was then searched for paper spirit money, so useful in the World of Shades; but when nothing was found, the companions of the dead men placed real copper coins in the tank, together with a letter begging whoever might find the corpses to generously give them a proper burial on shore. In that very same year, the magistrates of Amoy—with whom the author of these lines had to communicate regarding the export of laborers to Deli—insisted with fatherly care that every passenger steamer carry a sufficient number of airtight coffins. These were intended to preserve the bodies for the harbor of destination for those who might die at sea, thus sparing them a horrid » burial in the bellies of the fish" <note>2</note>.

According to the islanders of Amoy themselves, they are in the habit of throwing the corpses of lepers into the sea, or they place them in coffins on the seashore or in the open country. This is done because it is feared that, if buried, they will pass the dreaded disease to their descendants. It is, indeed, quite logical that a people who believe that graves produce

Our readers will find some details about the custom in this peculiar form on the following pages.

### 3. Cremation.

Because the quick destruction of human corpses has, since very ancient times, been repulsive to the Chinese as endangering the happiness and safety of the living—while their preservation in the ground was always esteemed by them as the highest duty prescribed by filial piety—it must appear strange that this very same people has for many centuries frequently practiced cremation. Buddhism imported it into their country as a helpful means to transform the deceased into a better condition, or even into the highest state of bliss and perfection; consequently, cremation was first largely practiced among the Buddhist monkhood, from which it passed to the laity, reaching considerable proportions for a long time. But in a later period, during the general decline of the influence of the Church, cremation fell victim to general hatred, so that today it hardly occurs anywhere except within the bounds of Buddhist monastic life.

Being of religious origin, cremation is mostly denoted in China by clerical terms expressing the metamorphosis the funeral pyre is intended to effect, namely: 化人, "transformation of man"; 化身, "transformation of the body"; and 火化, "metamorphosis by fire." Outside the clerical sphere, it bears no such high-sounding names, being simply called 燒尸 or 焚尸, "incineration of corpses." A term of illogical composition, which is nevertheless very common in books, is 火葬, "fire burial."

There is nothing in the ancient literature of China to allow us to admit that cremation was common there in pre-Christian times. A treatise which passes for a product of the hand of a

"West of Ts'in," that work relates, "lies the State of I-khü, where people collect wood upon the death of every near relative and pile it up to burn the corpse. When the fire is blazing and the smoke rises, they say that the deceased ascends to distant regions; and they are not considered filial sons until they have done these things" <note>秦之西有儀渠之國者、其親戚死聚柴積而焚之。燻則煙上、謂之登遐、然後成為孝子。Chapter V. This passage by no means negates our premise that cremation is a foreign importation, as the province of Kansuh formed no part of the Empire proper in those early days, and its inhabitants were then classified by the Chinese among certain barbarian tribes grouped under the general name of Jung <note>戎</note>. Yet, even in the third century of our era, cremation appeared so strange and horrifying to the Chinese proper that an author of 그at time, in a book he published under the title of *Poh wuh chi* (see page 422), inserted the above passage among a series of what he called "Strange Customs" <note>異俗</note>, adding this remark: "In the Middle Kingdom, that practice has never been condemned with enough emphasis" <note>中國未足為非也</note>.

That the burning of the dead was extremely revolting to all sensibilities in ancient China is suggested by the following episode, recorded in the *Tso ch'wen* for the year 504 before our era: "After the army of Wu defeated the army of Ch'u at Yung-sheh, it was itself routed by the forces of Ts'in and retreated into Kiün. We have not been able to collect them, so they will be destroyed by the fire at the same time; we must not do it!' To this, Tszě-khi replied: 'Our kingdom is in danger of perishing; if the dead have consciousness, they will enjoy the traditional sacrifices even after being consumed by the flames;

# CREMATION DURING THE REIGN OF THE SUNG DYNASTY.

After a long series of centuries, cremation suddenly begins to stir their minds and writing brushes significantly under the Sung dynasty. The reign of that House was marked by a vigorous revival of the Confucian School, giving birth to numerous scholars who, full of contempt for all customs and manners not practiced by the ancients, turned their anger against foreign Buddhism, denouncing cremation especially and decrying it as the height of cruelty toward the dead, and the most detestable of all sins against filial devotion. Though they did not succeed in suppressing cremation, those scholars thoroughly undermined it, to the point that today it has become little more than a shadow of what it was during the Sung dynasty.

We cannot, of course, follow all those scholars in their crusades against the custom they sought to overthrow. If we were to do so, we would have to engage in much unnecessary work, as each of them simply repeats the arguments of the others. We shall only refer to such of their writings as shed some light upon the views held by their class on the matter in question, and which may show how great the development of cremation was at the time. It should be stated beforehand that cremation was far from being favored by the Imperial House of Sung, as we read that its founder

> "in the third year of the Kien lung period (A.D. 962) issued an edict, in which he decreed: 'Cremation, universally practiced during recent generations, is a great offense against the Ritual Rescripts, and ought from this moment to be forbidden'" <note>1. 建隆三年詔曰、近代以來率多火葬、甚愆典禮、自今宜禁之. *Tung-tu shi lioh* 東都事略, "Record of Matters relating to Tung-tu," the present Ho-nan-fu 河南府 in Honan province; quoted in the *Tuh li t'ung khao*, chapter 86, line 2.</note>.
