<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Sung Dynasty's efforts to ban cremation. It completes the proposal by Yung I (Rong Ni) from the previous page and introduces a later, more severe condemnation of the practice by the statesman Hwang Chin (Huang Zhen).</meta>

<page-num>1401</page-num>

### CREMATION DURING THE REIGN OF THE SUNG DYNASTY.

Despite the numerous burial grounds established throughout the Empire in obedience to such orders from the Throne, cremation continued to flourish. It reached such a high level of development that, a century later, another statesman felt compelled to speak out against it in language harsher than any used before. His name was Hwang Chin<sup>1</sup>, and he was the Chief Magistrate of the district of Wu<sup>2</sup>, which includes the surroundings of Su-cheu-fu, the current capital of Kiangsu province. In an official report, he wrote:

There is a practice known as cremation. While parents are alive, their children provide every possible comfort, fearing it might be insufficient; yet when they die, they burn their remains and discard them. Why be so generous toward the living and so stingy toward the dead? Some even burn the bodies and cast the ashes into the water. Any person of conscience is deeply moved by such a sight.

Our dynasty has decreed that those too poor to afford burial land are permitted to be buried on government-owned land. In Hedong, where land is scarce and the population is large, people burn and discard the remains even of their closest relatives. When Han Qi governed Bingzhou, he used public funds to purchase several hundred acres of land to provide for the burial of the people, an act that is still celebrated today. Thus, to spread civilization and ensure the people do not deviate from the laws of ritual is the duty of a presiding official.

At present, the tragedy of cremation is becoming increasingly rampant. As this matter concerns public morality, it should reasonably be prohibited. Officials should still be instructed to set aside unused wasteland so that the poor may bury their dead. This would somewhat aid the beauty of public morality. The Emperor followed this advice.

In the twenty-eighth year of the same period, Yung I, the Vice Minister of the Department of Revenue, stated: "Recently, because officials have petitioned for a ban on cremation and requested that the provincial districts designate unused wasteland so the poor could bury their dead—truly a benevolent policy—I have heard that the customs of Wu and Yue involve such high burial expenses that wealth must be accumulated before they can be met. Consequently, families of modest means strive for simplicity in funeral arrangements. For this reason, cremation has always been considered convenient, and the practice has become a common custom. It is difficult to change this suddenly, especially since the population has grown increasingly dense during this long period of peace in the districts. The land required must be extensive. In the areas near the city walls, the authorities find it difficult to obtain land, so there are instances where it has not yet been designated. If the ban on cremation is enforced before burial sites are provided, I fear the people will be unsettled. I request that, except for wealthy families and the gentry for whom the ban should be strictly enforced, poor people and travelers from afar who die be allowed to follow the convenient practice for now. We should wait until the districts have designated wasteland and then seek further imperial instructions." The Emperor agreed to this and again ordered the various provinces to designate land according to the previous instructions. <gloss>*History of the Sung Dynasty*, chapter 125, lines 2 and following.</gloss>

<note>2 吳縣 (Wu County).</note>

In this memorial, which is still generally considered today to be the most capable treatise ever written on the subject, he poured out his full disgust for cremation. He set forth the arguments raised against it by Chinese minds in general in such an elaborate form that no other document can be found that explains them better. It therefore calls for a full translation in these pages.

> "In the second year of the King ting period (A.D. 1261)," thus we read in the *Jih chi luh* (chapter 15), "Hwang Chin, in his capacity as Prefect of the district of Wu, requested that he should be excused from rebuilding certain pavilions used for the cremation of human bodies. The memorial which he presented for that purpose read as follows:
> 
> Due to regulations that have been in force for a long time in these parts under my administration, there is a Buddhist monastery there, frequented by the people to offer incense; it is named 'The General Succour,' and is situated one mile southwest of this city. Long ago, about ten hollow pavilions for the cremation of human bodies were built in that convent for the sake of profit. Throughout the city, the foolish people were persuaded to bring the bodies of their deceased parents there and commit them to the burning flames; they then took the remains of the bones unconsumed by the heat to throw them into a deep pool of water. Alas, what wrong had those people done that, after their death, they were subjected to the greatest degree of mutilation?¹ 
> 
> For a long time, my heart was sincerely pained by these things. On the sixth day of the fifth month, there suddenly arose a nighttime thunderstorm; it swept away nothing else than those so-called cremation pavilions, destroying them entirely. It is my conviction that their foul stench had spread so far as to cause the offended spirits of the dead to jointly lay their com—

> » When the Han dynasty reigned, Khü, Prince of Kwang-ch'wen, was a dissolute, cruel, and unjust man. It is now sufficiently proven by all the above extracts that during the Sung dynasty, cremation was especially common in the provinces of Shansi, Chehkiang, and Kiangsu, and that the ruling class waged a literary campaign against it, but without resorting to rigorous measures for its repression. Thus, no doubt, China was then moving fast in the direction of general cremation. Matters took no different turn when the Yuen dynasty, Genghis' powerful family, destroyed that of the Sung. As those Mongol conquerors could hardly discourage one of the principal religious institutions of the many Buddhist countries united under their rule, the instances of cremation mentioned in Chinese books as having occurred during their dominion are, relatively speaking, numerous. Some three instances—the mere reading of which clearly shows that cremation was then firmly rooted in the customs of the people—have been already given on pp. 737 *following*. <page-num>1411</page-num>
<header>CREMATION CHECKED BY THE MING DYNASTY.</header>

The prevalence of cremation was followed by an era of decline, as the Ming dynasty, which succeeded the Mongols on the throne, strictly forbade it. During its reign, we see no scholars or officials fighting against it with the old, worn-out arguments sought out from the ancient and medieval archives of history, for they now had effective Imperial laws at their disposal to suppress it. In fact, the first Emperor of the dynasty had ordained in the third year of his reign that public burial grounds should be laid out in the departments and districts, that water-burial and cremation should be forbidden in Chehkiang, Kiangsi, and other regions, and that heavy punishments were to be inflicted on those guilty of such acts <note>1 In the third year of Hongwu, it was ordered that counties and districts establish public cemeteries, and water-burial and cremation were forbidden in Western Chehkiang and other places; violators are to be punished for a serious crime. *Complete Collection of Illustrations and Writings from the Past and Present*, section on Rites, ch. 65.</note>. Two years after that, the same monarch gave the Board of Rites new orders to the same effect. » In ancient » times," the orders ran, » it was prescribed to bury the bony and » fleshy remains of the dead. Though the current generation » conforms to this original institution, the dead among the people » are sometimes burned and the bones thrown into the water. More » than anything, such proceedings offend the duty of » compassion toward the dead and go against good customs; they must » therefore be forbidden. Should the poor have no land at their » disposal, the local magistrates must select large vacant tracts » to convert into graveyards for free use and thus cause » such people to bury the dead" <note>2 Ancient times had orders for covering bones and burying flesh. In recent times, following Yuan customs, the dead are sometimes burned and their bones thrown into the water. Nothing harms compassion or ruins customs more than this; it must be forbidden. If the poor have no land, let the local officials select spacious, vacant land to serve as public cemeteries so that they may bury the dead. *History of the Ming Dynasty*, ch. 60, line 22.</note>.

That cremation had a difficult time under the Ming dynasty may be concluded from the fact that it was then even forbidden by the Code of Laws to burn the corpses of relatives who had themselves willed and ordered it. » Whoever, acting in obedience to the » testamentary instructions of a relative higher in the family » hierarchy, destroys the corpse of that relative by fire, or gets » rid of it by putting it in the water, shall receive one » hundred blows with the long stick; and if the corpse is that of » an inferior or junior relative of the perpetrator, the punishment » shall be two degrees lighter. <header>THE GRAVE.</header>

The permission thus granted to the people to cremate the dead if they do not have the means to send the entire body home is, no doubt, frequently used nowadays. We have often seen soldiers from the Hunan province, stationed in the Amoy harbor forts, burn their deceased comrades. Their stated purpose is simply to put the charred bones in their own traveling luggage and take them home for burial in an urn or in a coffin. Such cremations are always of the simplest kind; they are performed under the open sky on a small pyre, built against a wall or slope. As a rule, it takes hardly forty cubic feet of pine wood, moistened with some oil or petroleum, to completely burn away the flesh. Very often those soldiers resort to an even cheaper method of destroying the flesh. Placing the corpse in a poor-quality coffin through the cracks of which the air can freely move, they set it down somewhere, either in the open air, under some straw thatch, or in one of the artillery casemates built in long rows in the coastal defenses. There they leave it until natural decay has finished its work, sometimes speeding up this process by inserting chips of wood or stone between the coffin and the lid.

But, without a doubt, cremation prevails to this very hour for reasons entirely independent of those authorized by the law. It was barely fifty years ago that Hwang Jü-ch'ing (see page 1071) stated that it was then widely practiced among the inhabitants of the capital of Chehkiang province. To quote his own words:

> » In the city
> » of Hang-cheu, cremation prevails to this day. Although it is a most

> » it, nor are the gentry and prominent citizens known to have made
> » the least effort to warn against it, so that it is practiced as if it were
> » a custom inherited from antiquity. And this continues, despite
> » the fact that the citizens must report fires every day and every month—

> » or several dozen, and in the worst cases even destroy whole
> » streets, and how the magistrates and the people rush out at the
> » outbreak to provide assistance without being able to check the
> » flames. Who knows but what it may not be the accumulated wrath

<header>CREMATION ON THE PRESENT DAY.</header>

"...of the souls of the cremated, which causes such calamities?" 1.

The *Shen Pao* 2, a Chinese newspaper with a large circulation in the coastal districts and the Treaty Ports, contained a leading article on January 27, 1891, denouncing the custom of cremating young children that prevails at Yü-chang 3 in Kiangsi province. It pointed out that cremation was introduced to China by Buddhists and should, therefore, be restricted to Buddhist priests 4. In many works belonging to the extensive category of "Memoirs" concerning provinces, departments, and districts (see page 746), formal arguments against cremation can be found. Since these appear in every new edition, they prevent us from believing that the custom they fight against belongs entirely to the past. However, considering that cremation is hardly ever mentioned by foreigners as having been witnessed in the coastal regions and the Treaty Ports; considering, moreover, that no rumors about cremation actually being performed ever reached our ears in the many provinces through which we traveled, and that we saw cases of it only in military garrisons and Buddhist monasteries; and considering, finally, that the spirit of the nation strictly condemns it, and that the authorities—fully empowered by law to forcibly eradicate it—can be expected to rarely leave this right unused, the conclusion is, we believe, justified that cremation is now limited to very narrow circles. It is fast dying out, much like the foreign Church itself that planted it in Chinese soil.

The dual facts that deep-rooted customs are nowhere easily eliminated and that no laws in China are strictly obeyed fully explain why a sort of middle ground is currently observed by the people in Zhejiang and Jiangsu, where generations have been in the habit of burning the dead. This compromise exists between their preference for cremation and the requirements of the law. "In the part of the country lying north of Hang-cheu

<meta>This page continues the translated diary entry of Van Braem Houckgeest, describing the burial and cremation customs observed during his journey through the Zhejiang and Jiangsu provinces in 1795.</meta>

<page-num>1417</page-num>
<header>CREMATION.</header>

> » corpse they contain; they collect the ashes, which they put
> » into covered urns and then bury halfway in
> » the ground. Along my route, I have seen urns arranged in this way.
> » Today is the first time I have learned that
> » the practice of burning the dead and of collecting their ashes
> » took place in China, just as it did among the Greeks and the Romans.
> » I do not recall, at least in what I have previously read
> » about China, any mention of such a thing, and
> » I had heard nothing of it in the thirty-six years that I have per-
> » sonally known this country—a period during which I have very often
> » inquired of learned and scholarly men about everything
> » that might relate to the history, customs, and other particu-
> » larities of their country" ¹.

This interesting extract precisely depicts the state of affairs at the present day in that part of China. Foreigners living in Shanghai are quite familiar with the sight of unburied coffins along the roads and in the fields of the surrounding lowlands, each under a thin layer of turf that merely covers the lid, leaving the case entirely bare. It is hard to believe that the possibility of buried coffins lying in water is the primary motive for leaving them so poorly covered; instead, it is probable that an aversion to burial—naturally caused by a long familiarity with the much less repulsive process of cremation—prevails here over all other considerations.

Upon sending this final sheet to the press, the author wishes to gratefully acknowledge the kindness of several friends and scholars who assisted him in various ways during the compilation of the First Book. Above all, he is indebted to the late Dr. Rost, Principal Librarian of the India Office, who placed at his disposal various important books from the library entrusted to his care, even allowing him to take them to Holland for consultation in his own study. Likewise, the author is indebted for the use of Chinese and other books to the current management of that library, and to Professor Douglas, Keeper of Oriental Books and Manuscripts at the British Museum, as well as to F. G. Kramp, Esq., in Amsterdam, to whose scholarship he also owes several valuable suggestions. The author also offers special thanks to Professor Dr. W. Grube, through whose polite intervention the General Directorate of the Royal Library in Berlin kindly lent him, for a considerable length of time, some important Chinese books that were indispensable for the completion of this volume. The assistance provided by that scholar was all the more precious because the loan of those works had been flatly refused to the author by the then-Director of the Chinese library at Cambridge University, and they were not obtainable anywhere else. Finally, the author is pleased to take this opportunity to express his thanks to W. J. Oudendijk, Esq., formerly his pupil and now Secretary to the Netherlands Legation in Peking, who from there has enriched the University Library of Leyden, as well as the author’s own collection, with several valuable Chinese works; and to G. Unidale Price, Esq., who sent him from Amoy some fine photographs he took himself to illustrate this work.

» 699 lines 15, 16, 17. An » erect cucumber ” 立 瓜 was a gilded wooden ball on the top of a bamboo staff, with a dragon’s head placed on top. A *kwuh-t°o* was also a type of ornamental weapon on the top of a long bamboo staff. A *hiang-tsieh* was a bamboo pole with an iron wire on which twelve copper coins were strung; these coins bore the inscription 天 下 太 平, » universal peace throughout the Empire ”, and were wrapped in a piece of yellow silk. A *tan-ma* or » honorary horse ” was a horse of state, decorated with red reins, a yellow bridle, and an embroidered saddle-cloth. See the list of objects carried by the attendants of high officials, which is given in chapter 148 of the *Ta Ming hwui tien*.
